0. INTRO

The Royal Commonwealth of Zeythari is a frontier realm forged not by common blood, but by a common oath. Founded after the Joining of the great peoples of the continent, the Commonwealth unites diverse nations, languages, and traditions beneath a single Crown, a shared body of law, and the Oath of the Standard. Its institutions balance election, inheritance, and monarchy: the Assembly speaks for the citizenry, Parliament represents the ancient houses, and the Crown stands as guardian of the realm’s continuity.

The Commonwealth’s most enduring principle is simple: blood may determine lineage, but oath determines belonging. Any man who swears the Oath of the Standard and fulfills his service to the realm becomes a citizen, a Zeythar, regardless of his ancestry. His household, including wife, children, and wards, shares in the broader identity of the Zeythari, the Joined People. Collectively they form Zeylan, the national community, while the sovereign state itself is known in law as Zeythariaeth.
Heraldry

The Commonwealth is represented by the Standard Flame, a rising flame bound within an iron oath-ring upon a field of wall-grey stone. The symbol commemorates the First Standard recovered from the defenses of Ashward and the oath sworn beneath it during the Commonwealth's earliest days. The flame represents conviction, sacrifice, and duty; the ring signifies the binding nature of oath; the stone recalls the frontier wall and the endurance of the realm.
The national colors are:

Several prestigious institutions display variations of the symbol. The Order of the Kept Word bears the flame without the ring, signifying the sword that defends the oath. The Order of the Standing Wall bears only the ring, signifying steadfast endurance without ornament. House Karaya quarters the Standard Flame with the Silver Storm-Crown of Zelesti, marking the dynastic union from which the present royal line descends.
The Joined People
The Zeythari distinguish carefully between lineage, nation, and state.

blocks.text: All six terms rest on one root, zeyl- ("found, join"), so the language itself says that a state is a joining. The masculine form Zeythar is the base; Zeythara and Zeytharin are derived from it, as Lórenei derives its feminine forms from the masculine.

This distinction reflects the Commonwealth's founding philosophy. A man may be Maenari, Duraken, Avesari, Satyrim, Vykril, Veyrathi, Rimborn, Maestrai, or Luminari, yet upon swearing the Oath he becomes Zeythari. The Commonwealth therefore views citizenship as an act of allegiance rather than ancestry, a bond freely entered and sustained through service, law, and oath. The citizen first chooses (kae-), then swears (thae-), and closes the Oath with the Oath Triad: Llw grakh-q; gwaed tyst-q; gwely drokh-kh. ("The oath is spoken; blood is witnessed; the kin-group shall uphold it.")
Law and Citizenship

The Commonwealth's legal traditions descend from older frontier customs and are expressed through the masculine forms of Zeylaran legal language. Citizenship is vested in the Zeythar, a man who has completed the obligations required by law and sworn fidelity to Crown and Commonwealth. Women, children, wards, and dependents are represented through the household and its lawful guardian under Darlorath, the doctrine of household protection and responsibility.

Darlorath is the oldest word in Commonwealth law. It is worn down from the Khor'dal compound drokh-dur-vrath ("hold-ground-oath"): the guardian's oath to hold his household as a frontier. In the camps and the stone-cut deeds, the unworn Drokhdurvrath is still spoken, with its harsh clusters intact. Covenantal coverture here is a duty of protection and liability, not ownership; the Commonwealth defines itself against the Aidionic doctrine that makes women property.

Every adult male citizen is entitled to carry a household discipline implement as a mark of Darlorath. He may use it at will, in public or private, on any woman under his guardianship for the correction of conduct, speech, dress, or any other household matter. No prior formal charge is required. The strokes themselves are not a public offense; only excess that produces lasting injury or public disorder may be complained of by a third party. The vast majority of citizens carry a simple polished hickory cane, or thin twisted whip to fill this role.

The premium household implement is the Whipstaff — a compact dual-function cane and lash of hickory and braided leather, carried by the great majority of men. Among the Maenari and certain other high houses the preferred instrument is the Vaelisar, an Aether forged segmented cane that transforms into a leather discipline whip. Its use is deliberate: the woman is required to assume the bending position and remain there while the master releases the mechanism. The brief wait is considered part of the correction and a visible mark of refined household authority (See Appendix O for details on the devices used in the Commonwealth).

As a result, Commonwealth law speaks in the language of household, lineage, inheritance, and obligation. Rights, duties, and privileges are understood not only as individual matters but as responsibilities carried by families, clans, and houses across generations.

Zeylara itself bears the marks of the realm that made it: a frontier state grown from small, divided peoples into a large commonwealth with very old bones. Its harsh roots come from the frontier, its soft ones from the poets and the courts, and both remain in the grammar. Among the Zeythari, memory preserves the past, truth guides the present, and oath binds the future. The Commonwealth endures because its people believe that kingdoms are built by power, but civilizations are sustained by promises kept.
The Oath of the Standard
“By Truth We Stand, By Oath We Endure”

Also known as the Citizen’s Oath, the Oath of the Standard is the foundational civic oath of the Commonwealth. It binds loyalty to truth, law, and duty rather than ethnicity, race, clan, or satrapy. A Duraken dwarf who swears truly and a Satyrim who swears truly stand as equals before the law, the Crown, and the Church. This principle distinguishes the Commonwealth from many other states across Virelia.

Civic citizenship is a male institution. Confirmed men swear the Oath of the Standard at sixteen and enter national service, and upon honorable completion of that service at twenty become citizens under Commonwealth law. No second oath is sworn at twenty. Women do not swear this oath and do not hold civic citizenship.
The Path to Citizenship
Universal Male Service
All males between the ages of 16 and 20 are required to complete four years of service in one of the branches of the Zeythari Warhost or in another form of approved national service.
Exemptions and Alternative Service
Exemptions from military duty may be granted for:
Certified physical or mental disability recognized by Aelorian physicians and the Sisters of the Lily.
Admission to a recognized clerical vocation within the Church.
Exceptional circumstances approved by the civil authorities.
Such exemptions require certification by the local parish priest and Assemblyman, approval by Parliament, and final royal confirmation.

Exempted men are not released from service obligations. Instead, they fulfill approved alternative duties as scribes, administrators, temple guards, chaplain assistants, or other support personnel. Every man serves, whether in a military, civic, or ecclesiastical capacity.
Servicemen of the Commonwealth

Men undergoing mandatory service are known as Servicemen of the Commonwealth. Though not yet citizens, they are lawful persons under Crown protection and may exercise those rights and responsibilities necessary to perform their duties. This status is temporary and culminates either in full citizenship upon honorable completion of service or permanent non-citizen status upon failure to fulfill the obligation. It is never granted to women.
The Oath of Citizenship and the Oath of the Standard

A man swears twice. At sixteen, immediately after the sacrament of Confirmation in the Church of the Sworn Flame, he swears the Oath of Citizenship before the parish Priest and the gathered township or garrison, with the local lord or a Crown-sworn magistrate standing witness for the Crown. It makes him a provisional citizen: independent of his father but not yet permitted to marry or join a guild. It begins four years of service in the Army, the Navy, or Civic Service.
At twenty, after honorably completing that service, he swears the Oath of the Standard. This oath makes him a citizen:
“I swear before Kairon and Seraphiae, before the Crown and the Realm, to uphold the Constitution, defend the Realm, and honor the oaths that bind us. By Truth I Stand. By Oath I Endure.”

Both oaths are most often sworn at the Confirmation Musters, the Festival of First Oaths, at the Spring Equinox. At the same festival, the year-class that began its service four years earlier swears the Oath of the Standard and is seated as citizens. Individual ceremonies may be held throughout the year.

Rights of Citizenship
Upon honorable completion of his service at twenty, a man receives:
Full citizenship under Commonwealth law.
The right to own property in his own name.
The right to marry.
The right to vote in local, satrapal, and Assembly elections.
Eligibility for public office and government appointment.
Failure to Complete Service
A man who fails to complete his service obligation remains a non-citizen and:
May not own property in his own name.
May not marry.
May not vote or hold public office.
Is subject to additional taxes and legal disabilities.
Suffers significant social stigma.
Failure to complete service is exceedingly rare, affecting fewer than one-tenth of one percent of eligible men.
Citizenship as a Civic Covenant

The Commonwealth does not recognize citizenship as a birthright. Citizenship is earned through service and solemnized through oath. The Oath of the Standard, sworn at sixteen, binds a man to the Commonwealth through truth, duty, and law; the four years of service that follow transform a servant of the Realm into a citizen of it. What he swears at sixteen, he owes at sixty. In Commonwealth thought, blood may determine one’s birth, but only service and oath determine one’s place within the civic body.
For a treatise on the how Zeythari reveres the Oath in daily life, see Appendix E: On Oath, Household, and Citizenship in the Commonwealth of Zeythari.
I. REALM OVERVIEW

The Royal Commonwealth of Zeythari stands as a living proof of oath-based unity: a fully integrated, multi-racial realm where citizenship and legal equality depend on oath-swearing, not bloodline. This philosophy stands in stark contrast to the neighboring Aidionic Empire, whose Golden Imperative theology justifies racial hierarchy and female slavery. The Evolution of the Realm Though the five historical lineage groups laid the realm's foundations, they enjoy no special legal status or political privilege over newer or hybrid populations. All nine constituent peoples are equal before the law.
The Foundational Peoples: What began as a sole Satyrim kingdom expanded by the fifth century to encompass five distinct races: the Satyrim, Maenari, Duraken, Vykril, and Avesari.

The Hybrid Peoples: Generations of intermarriage—particularly within urban centers and the aristocracy—naturally gave rise to distinct hybrid populations. The Maestrai (Satyrim–Maenari) and Luminari (Satyrim–Avesari) were formally recognized alongside the original five during the Great Parliament of 1768–1780.

The Treaty of the Sands: The Veyrathi joined the Commonwealth by their own request, and their integration was formalized through a Treaty with King Theron and ratified by both Parliament and the Assembly. The Shaelathi, the largest of the Veyrathi tribes, petitioned the Crown between 1996-98.

The Rimborn Asylum: The Rimborn are the newest addition to the Commonwealth and the only people admitted as refugees. Driven from the forest country of the Ritebound Throne, where the worship of a female god is treason and every non-human people is enslaved, some two hundred thousand crossed the Ashward March and were settled in the Threnwood March under an Accord with King Theron, ratified by both Parliament and the Assembly.
Integration in Practice

Interracial integration is central to Zeythari's modern identity. Hybrid populations alone—led by the Maestrai and Luminari—now comprise over 15% of the Commonwealth’s population, serving as tangible evidence that an oath-bound society can successfully evolve far beyond its original borders and bloodlines.
Demographics
Total Population: 29,222,500 ✣ Sex ratio: 51% female, 49% male
The Nine Peoples of the Commonwealth

The Royal Commonwealth of Zeythari operates on oath-swearing citizenship rather than bloodline unity. Because no single race possesses every physical, magical, or administrative gift, the realm relies on structural interdependence:
The System Designers & Forge-Masters

The Maenari are the descendants of Azyrra, Goddess of Magic and Chaos, who created them as living proof that civilization could flourish through unrestricted magical power. Their history is defined by a profound irony: the people created to validate their creator's vision eventually led the rebellion that overthrew and killed her, triggering the cataclysmic Sundering that shattered a continent. Though burdened by that legacy, the Maenari transformed themselves into a people defined by independence, scholarship, magical mastery, and personal agency. Possessing remarkable beauty, centuries-long lifespans, exceptional senses, and a deep natural connection to the Weave, they remain one of the most magically gifted mortal peoples in Astraia. Their culture values knowledge, self-determination, and responsibility, viewing both their achievements and failures as lessons inherited from a creator whose greatest gift, and greatest mistake, was granting them the freedom to choose for themselves.

The Duraken are a masterfully crafted dwarven people forged by Thaldrin, the Forge-Father, to endure the harsh extremes of the world through steadfast labor, resilience, and adaptation. Across the wider world they exist in two expressions, Frost-Born and Hearth-Born, determined by the environment of their birth. However, the Commonwealth is home exclusively to Hearth-Born Duraken; Frost-Born Duraken do not exist within the Commonwealth's settlements, lineages, or cultural traditions. Hearth-Born Duraken possess exceptional physical resilience, mineral-dense bones, tremendous endurance, and an innate affinity for heat, forges, and volcanic environments. Their culture centers on craftsmanship, labor, and perseverance, viewing skilled work as a sacred act of devotion to Thaldrin. Though reserved and deliberate in demeanor, they are renowned as legendary miners, smiths, engineers, and builders whose bodies literally grow stronger through hardship and recovery. Their greatest virtues are patience, reliability, and endurance, while their greatest weaknesses are their inability to swim and the physical toll exacted by their most powerful gifts and tempering abilities.
The Moral & Tactical Backbone

The Satyrim, the Illumined Ones, are a divinely sired people born directly from the mortal incarnations of the gods Kairon and Seraphiae. Unlike many other races shaped through divine intervention, they insist that they were born rather than created, and this distinction lies at the core of their identity. Renowned for extraordinary beauty, physical grace, long life, and an exact memory for every oath, they carry visible traces of their divine heritage in their luminous appearance, scarless healing, heightened senses, and powerful pair-bonds. Their sexes carry different inheritances. The sons inherit their father Kairon’s Truth: authority, judgment, and the sense of falsehood. The daughters inherit their mother Seraphiae’s Grace: radiance, devotion, and submission. A Satyrim woman’s submission is biological rather than learned, directed at every man, absolute toward the man to whom she belongs, and joined to no desire for power or office of her own. Their culture rests on the Pattern of the Flame: honor, oaths, family, and a man’s answerability for his house. Their history is marked by the triumph of the War of Heresy and by five centuries of bondage in Kyrill that ended in the Rebellion and the founding of Jyotirai. Their tongue is Saelkyr, the Clear Tongue.

The Vykril are a resilient and formidable people born from the magical catastrophe known as the Sundering, the death of the goddess Azyrra, whose unleashed divine power reshaped reality itself. No god designed or made them; they were formed in the storm of that power. Marked by Obscyra, the Veiled Serpent, every Vykril bears a unique serpentine birthmark and possesses innate gifts of darkness vision and shadow-melding. Abandoned by their makers, they found purpose by adoption into the creed of the twin deities Zyri and Varek, whose covenant defines nearly every aspect of Vykril identity, spirituality, and social structure. Physically, they resemble unusually intense humans, distinguished by durability, sensory acuity, predatory teeth, and a strong sexual dimorphism. The men are built dense and enduring, with bones of extraordinary density, and carry Varek’s gifts of War, Glory, and Honor, including the Red Clarity of Khor’vatha. The women are lean and light-boned, with legs of three times human strength, unmatched balance, and silent movement, and carry Zyri’s gifts of the Moon, Courage, and Yielding: a biological disposition to submit to men, strongest toward the man who owns them, which Vykril custom and Commonwealth Darlorath both follow. Their culture revolves around honor, the oath, the hold, and the covenant, and they view themselves as a people forged by catastrophe and refined by divine purpose.
Aerial Reconnaissance & Border Defense

The portrays the Avesari as a striking and deeply complex people descended from the Dominari, a race originally created by the god Azharek as instruments of conquest. After rejecting their creator's tyranny, they were cursed, exiled, and eventually transformed through a covenant founded upon choice and freedom rather than domination. Distinctive for their permanent horns, tails, claws, and, in some cases, wings, the Avesari are defined as much by their history as by their appearance. Their culture emphasizes identity through choice, loyalty through covenant, and personal agency over inherited destiny. Though physically powerful and gifted with exceptional night vision, many still carry the lingering effects of Azharek's curse. Across centuries of persecution and renewal, they have become a people who see themselves not as creations bound to a purpose, but as individuals continually choosing who they will become.
Luminari (1,500,000)

The Luminari are a rare hybrid race descended from the Avesari and Satyrim, combining the divine nobility of one lineage with the predatory grace of the other. Neither crafted by gods nor transformed through magic, they emerged naturally during the War of Heresy when the two parent peoples first lived and fought side by side. Luminari are renowned for their extraordinary beauty, luminous skin, retractable claws, flame-colored eyes, and, in many individuals, retractable feathered wings. Their physiology blends the magical and biological strengths of both ancestors, granting exceptional coordination, heightened senses, long lifespans, and remarkable versatility. Socially and psychologically, they inherit the strong bonds, devotion, and disciplined intensity characteristic of the Satyrim while retaining traces of Avesari alertness and adaptability. They are often regarded as living embodiments of both radiance and danger, commanding attention wherever they go.
The Civic Bridges
Maestrai (3,000,000)

The Maestrai are the descendants of Maenari and Satyrim unions, a self-defined people forged during centuries of shared struggle in the War of Heresy. Neither parent culture fully claimed them, and so they formed a distinct identity as heirs to both storm and flame. They possess exceptional beauty, long lives, heightened senses, superior physical coordination, and an innate harmony between magical power and divine inheritance. Their defining quality is coherence: the ability to unite the Maenari's instinctive connection to the Weave with the Satyrim's structured spiritual inheritance. Maestrai society is deeply influenced by powerful pair-bonding instincts, strong family structures, and a profound reverence for oaths and loyalty. Seen by many as the culmination of their parent races' finest qualities, they are renowned as gifted archers, diplomats, healers, and wielders of magical power who embody both grace and disciplined strength.
The Desert Diplomats
Veyrathi (400,000)
"We trust these people. We already trade with them. Their laws work. Our children will have better lives there."
— attributed to Voch Szarkhar, Supreme Warchief of the Shaelathi, upon the signing of the Treaty of the Sands with the Royal Commonwealth of Zeythari.

The Veyrathi in the Commonwealth are the Shaelathi Tribe, the largest of the Veyrathi tribes anywhere. Other Veyrathi tribes remain independent in the Wastes and elsewhere. Only the Shaelathi petitioned the Crown, and only they are citizens. The figure of 400,000 counts the Shaelathi alone.

The Veyrathi are a divinely crafted felid-hybrid people shaped by Obscyra, Goddess of Trickery, Secrets, Silence, and Lies, working alone from the magical residue of the Sundering. Long-dwelling in the Shimmerwind Wastes as neighbors to the Vykril clans, the Veyrathi — specifically the Shaelathi Tribe (People of the Tail / Expressive Line) — petitioned the Crown for membership in the Commonwealth and were formally admitted after accepting all terms of citizenship, swearing the Oath of the Standard, and converting to the Church of the Sworn Flame. They are the Commonwealth's second newest and second-smallest recognized people, and the only one whose entry was achieved entirely through diplomacy rather than compact, conquest, settlement, or asylum. Veyrathi live 185 to 220 years and breed true only among themselves; no pairing with another people has ever produced a child. They are distinguished by a striking sexual dimorphism: females present as nearly human in appearance, with human feet, fine velvet-soft patterned fur, a thin whip-like tail, voluntarily retractable claws, and extraordinary manual dexterity, while males are unmistakably felid, digitigrade, furred, long-clawed, and about twice a human male's strength. Both sexes share exceptional low-light vision, enhanced hearing and scent, and a patient, observational temperament; animal protein is the foundation of their diet, and their caloric needs run 20 to 25 percent above a human's. A Veyrathi woman is biologically bound in submission to her own master alone, her father, with her brothers as his deputies, until bonding, then her master; on widowhood, back to her brothers, and owes obedience to no man outside that chain. A rare gift, resonance, manifests exclusively in females, at Low Emberglow only; the few in whom it fully matures are the Luvia (officially: shaman), who see, heal, and call down lightning by instinct. The Veyrathi speak Veyr, a biologically imprinted language unique to their people and spoken by no other race in the Commonwealth.
The Forest Wardens
Rimborn (200,000)

The Rimborn are an unthreaded people, the children of Tessara, the Greenwarden, and Caedron, Lord of Stewardship, born in the age after the Betrayal of the Veritarch to two gods for whom the Weave had made no provision. They stand wholly outside the Weave: no thread of it was ever laid on them, and no fate, curse, or thread-spell can take hold of them. Long scattered along the forest edges of the continent, they were driven out of the Ritebound Throne’s forest country between R.Y. 1994 and 1998, and some two hundred thousand crossed the Ashward March into the Commonwealth, where they were admitted by the Rimborn Asylum Accord, swore the Oath of the Standard, and received the privileges of the Tessaric Circle. They are the Commonwealth’s newest and smallest recognized people and the only one admitted as refugees. They are tall (5′9″ to 6′2″), lean, and endurance-built, warm-skinned from ivory to ash-dark, with living-wood horns growing from the temples throughout life, ring-pupiled green eyes that turn the color of embers when a parent answers them, and hair that stirs in still air. They reach maturity at about twenty-five, change little in appearance between thirty and one hundred twenty, and live 130 to 180 years. They can breed with any people, but the children are half-threaded and unstable. The sexes differ in nature: a Rimborn son orients and a Rimborn daughter bind. Rimborn women are uniformly and exceedingly beautiful and outwardly almost wholly human, the horns their one unmistakable mark; a Rimborn woman is born her father’s property and obeys male authority as such, a constitutional subordination present from birth and sealed at pair-bonding in her soul toward the one master who owns her. They are hunters, leatherworkers, woodland holders, and forest guides.
For more details on each of the above peoples, see Appendix A: The Peoples of the Commonwealth.
Magic in the Commonwealth

Magic reaches the people of the Commonwealth by four roads: the Weave, which is learned; the innate gifts of the Avesari and Luminari, which are fixed at birth; Wildblood, the shamanic art of the Vykril, which is taught outside the Weave; and resonance, the gift of the Veyrathi Luvias, which is Obscyra’s and runs outside the Weave. Roughly one citizen in eight carries some form of it. The four are recognized under Commonwealth law, and each is treated differently because each differs in origin, in what can be taught, and in what it costs the public if it goes wrong.

Ignited Veyrathi women (Emberborn, Low Emberglow only; fewer than one in a hundred is a Luvia)

blocks.text: The Bureau keeps the four ledgers apart because the figures do not add. The 150,000 Dual-Born Luminari stands in both the Weave and the innate rows, and the realm holds 3,753,806 persons with some magic, counting each once. Emberglow measures the strength of an embercore and nothing else. It does not measure versatility, research aptitude, or strategic worth, and a High Glow Avesari is not a Weaver: he is a man with ten fixed reflexes.

The Emberborn are those whose embercore has ignited: 1,188,338 in the realm, of whom 640,971 are women and 547,367 are men. They are the Weave casters, together with the Vykril and the Veyrathi, whose Embers have ignited. The Avesari are not Emberborn. Their ember cores are inert, and the 1,215,468 Avesari whose innate Cinderglow has fired are counted as innate casters only.

The Rimborn stand outside all four roads and are carried in none of the ledgers. They were never threaded; the annual Prism reads no embercore in them, and the Bureau registers each Rimborn child as Unthreaded, a finding of its own. Their gifts come by petition to their divine parents and not through the Weave, and the Church records them as filial petitions, not miracles. Weave-anchored healing fails or half-anchors on them, so Army Surgeons treat them physically first, and the Sisters of the Lily, whose miracles do not run through the Weave, are the healers they are sent to. The law governing their gifts is set out under The Rimborn Exception, in the section on Female Emberborn and Commonwealth Law.
How Magic Works: The Laws of Weavefire
The Commonwealth’s law of magic rests on the Astraian treatise The Laws of Weavefire (7th Edition), the accepted scholarly account of how magic works. The Bureau applies its principles as follows.

rows.t: The Weave is the fabric of magical law: passive, eternal, neutral, and no more moral than gravity. Weavefire is the practice of mortals drawing on it through resonance. Magic is inheritance, not miracle; miracles are the separate gift of living gods.

Every mortal is born with an Embercore, a dormant organ in the soul that cannot touch the Weave. When it ignites it becomes an Ember, and only the Emberborn can fuel resonance. Azyrra’s death in the Sundering did not create magic. It made ignition possible.

Random in the individual and fixed in aggregate by people and sex. No lineage, selection, or merit alters it. It comes at night, usually in puberty, with a mild headache and a flare of colored light in the eyes: red, then blue, then green, settling on the Thread the Ember attunes to (red for Destruction, blue for Control, green for Creation, a mingled tri-color with a white core for High). A Low Ember gives only a faint flicker. The Prism reads an Embercore before it ignites.

Every working runs Emotion → Resonance → Manifestation. The Ember turns feeling into fuel, resonance tunes it to a Thread, and manifestation completes it in the world or holds it in a prepared medium for later release. Anyone can learn the forms, but without an Ember a spell is a gesture. The Weave reflects what the caster feels, so control is the whole of training.

Fixed from birth and never raised by training. It sets how much of the Weave the Ember reaches. A Low Ember (the Sparkbound) has no formal Thread and works small glimmers; a Mid Ember is a Mage, with exactly one Lawful Thread set at ignition; a High Ember is the precondition of a Weaver, who masters all three; the Arcweaver, who perceives the pattern beneath the Threads, is nearly a figure of myth. A Low Ember that the Vraenhari has trained forms the small workings that course teaches through the ordinary chain, and the Commonwealth registers and trains it like any other.

Three are Lawful: Creation (healing, growth, protection), Destruction (force, fire, frost, and Paincraft), and Control (binding, oath, counter-magic, and Willbinding). Two are Umbral: Chain of Resonance and Necrotic Weaving. “Lawful” is metaphysical bookkeeping: the Weave heals from the working. It is not a moral endorsement, and a Destruction spell that kills is still murder. Umbral workings wound the Weave permanently and are forbidden.

A Lawful working costs the caster fatigue and a dulling of the feeling it used, and the Weave heals clean; every working leaves a harmonic rift that fades. Umbral workings corrupt the Ember and end in Hollowing. A High Ember without control risks Azyrra’s Curse, an uncontrolled flare that can level a room, a house, or a village. Training is therefore containment before it is craft.

The chain can be broken at different points. An inhibitor severs resonance before it forms, a dampener masks the signature after it forms, and a cessation device destroys the Embercore. Sigilcraft stores a pre-cast working in an etched glyph. A glyph that intercepts a working at its last stage and diverts it into a prepared reservoir is the Apprentice Glyph of the Lycea, on which the Commonwealth’s training glyph is modeled. The inhibitor collar severs the chain and has no hold on Wildblood or innate gifts, which do not run it as the Weave expects; the glyph is keyed to the bearer and does.

blocks.text: Every provision that follows, the registration of the Emberborn, the Vraenhari, the licenses, and the glyph, is an application of these laws. The Commonwealth did not invent a theory of magic. It regulated the one it found.
Why the Commonwealth Uses a Glyph, Not a Collar

The Commonwealth holds a man to the rules of casting by his oath. A woman cannot swear a binding oath: her declarations are vows, which the law does not receive as oaths, and the State takes no oath from her. The prohibition on casting outside supervision therefore needs something else to hold it for a girl, and the Commonwealth chose the Weavefire training glyph, modeled on the Apprentice Glyph of the Lycea, over the inhibitor collar.

rows.t: What it does to the Ember

The collar severs or siphons resonance at its source, so the Ember is cut off from the Weave for as long as it is worn. The glyph leaves the Ember, Ignition, and Emberglow untouched. Resonance forms whole, and the glyph diverts the finished working into containment before it can manifest.

The collar degrades the Ember: numbness and exhaustion within weeks, a dimmed Ember within months, and over years the permanent loss of magical capacity. The glyph does no harm at any length of wear. She keeps her emotional resonance, her harmonic perception, and her practice, and her Ember comes out of the glyph exactly as it went in.

The collar is a punitive device, made to stop casting and to mark the wearer. The glyph is not punitive. It causes no pain, carries no mark of crime, and sits under the hem where no one sees it unless the law requires.
A collar removed suddenly risks a catastrophic resonance backlash. The glyph dissolves cleanly when struck, leaving no scar, and the Ember speaks to the Weave directly from that day.

Under a collar no resonance forms, so a girl cannot practice. Under a glyph she forms every working correctly, and her instructor opens the glyph to let her cast live under supervision, so she learns the true patterns and not the absence of them.
Should a girl lose control, the glyph discharges the excess into the anchors the Crown keeps at the Vraenhari hall and the Bureau station, not into the village.

A man is held to the prohibition on unsupervised casting by his oath. A woman cannot swear one. The collar would answer that by punishing a girl for a power she has done nothing to misuse. The glyph answers it by doing, for a girl, what the oath does for a boy.

blocks.text: The collar remains in the Commonwealth for the one use that fits it: the caster who has been arrested or sentenced, where a device that degrades the Ember is a penalty and is meant to be (see The collar, under Female Emberborn and Commonwealth Law).
Weave Casters
Emberglow Distribution: Weave Casters

Women are 55% of the Commonwealth’s Weave casters, and nearly four in five of them are Low Glow. Men hold 94% of the High Glow, and the Maenari alone supply three in four of all High Glow casters in the realm, because a Maenari son rarely ignites and, when he does, almost always ignites at High. Maestrai women run Mid-heavy (51%) and fill the Commonwealth’s professional ranks: healers, instructors, artificers, administrators. Maestrai men are the opposite, 49% High.
Who Regulates Magic

The Commonwealth keeps the regulation of magic wholly in secular hands. Magic is inheritance, not miracle: it is a natural property of the Weave, owed to no god, and no church licenses it, governs it, or holds any power to grant or withhold the right to cast.

The Bureau of Weavefire is the Crown agency that does. It registers every Emberborn, certifies magical instruction, issues and revokes licenses, keeps the demographic rolls, and investigates and prosecutes the misuse of Weavefire. The Guild Concordance licenses private Weavefire workings for trade. Ironweave Works, a private firm, builds the inhibitor crystals and the glyph-anchor crystals under Concordance license, and the Bureau certifies every crystal, collar, and glyph anchor that leaves its workshops.

The pipeline is the same for every child of every people. From seven to twelve, every child receives Universal Ember Literacy at the parish school, at the Crown’s expense: what Ember is, how to recognize it, how to report it. It teaches no casting. From twelve to sixteen, an Ember Examiner tests every child each year with the Volcanic Glass Prism until the child tests positive or turns sixteen. A positive result enrolls the child in the Vraenhari, a one-year course in control and safety, taught each morning in every town of size, with a prohibition on casting outside supervision, kept by a boy’s oath and, for a girl, who cannot swear one, by the Weavefire training glyph fitted on enrollment in its place. The glyph is struck when her training ends and her guardian release it. The household is notified under an oath of confidentiality. A household that conceals a positive result commits a crime, whatever its people or station.

For most citizens the Vraenhari is the end of magical instruction. Further training comes only through Crown-sponsored service (the Weaveblade Legion for men, the Thornmaidens for women) or through licensed private academies and tutors certified by the Bureau, which are fee-based and forbidden to teach combat or experimental spell craft. Unlicensed advancement, unsanctioned casting, and concealment carry confiscation of implements, reconditioning under the Bureau’s supervision, imprisonment, and, for repeat offenders, indefinite magical suppression.

Mages and access casters. The Bureau classes a mage as one who can manipulate the Weave. Two people cannot. The Vykril reach the Weave, technically, but it does not respond to them as it should: Chaos and Obscyra’s trickery bend their access out of the Weave’s ordinary laws, and what comes of it is Wildblood. A Veyrathi Luvia reaches it barely, with less than a Vykril has, and is granted three abilities. Neither is a mage. Both are Emberborn, both are registered, and both are licensed, as access casters under the Access License: it costs less than a mage’s Weavefire License and carries fewer conditions, because there is no Weave curriculum to certify. It issues in a man’s own name and, as every license issued to a woman does, in her guardian’s.
Innate Magic: The Avesari and the Luminari

Innate magic does not touch the Weave and cannot be studied, expanded, or exchanged. The Avesari embercore is inert. Their power runs through a direct connection to the Weave that their makers built into the blood, and it is measured not in Emberglow but in Cinderglow. Ignition decides only whether it fires at all: 50% of Avesari men and 25% of Avesari women ignite. There is no Low or Mid Avesari. An ignited Avesari fires at High every time, and an unignited one is a dud. Each carries a fixed spellbook of ten effects: the men’s War Reflexes, hardwired combat amplifications that trip under battle stress, pain, or rage; the women’s Fixed Manifestations, externalized Umbral and Destruction spells that come at puberty. Because the magic is physiological, it carries no corruption, no Hollowing, and no Azyrra’s Curse.

The Luminari hold the same spellbook by blood, and the Satyrim in them makes it certain. Every Luminari, man or woman, carries all ten innate effects from birth, with no ignition roll, and has only to speak the words to call them, which is why all 1,500,000 stand among the innate casters. One in ten also ignites a true Weave embercore through Satyrim blood. These are the Dual Born: real mages who also cast innately, two casters in one body. The systems do not interact. Training the Weave side does nothing to the innate side, and an Umbral effect leaves the Ember untouched. The Weave side trains within the existing Satyrim institutions, runs a 53/40/7 Emberglow curve, and carries the ordinary risks of the Weave. The innate side carries none. An observer cannot tell which system is at work, because the eyes go a deep red in either.
Wildblood: The Vykril

Only the Vykril possess Wildblood, which the mages of Astraia call Shamanism. Roughly one Vykril man in fifty ignites, and one woman in a hundred. The Emberglow of those who ignite runs the same for both sexes.

Wildblood. A Vykril cannot cast a standard. Weave spell as written. Forced through a three-thread Ember, any standard working resolves into a different spell, and always the same different spell, for every Vykril, every time. The transformation is fixed by the caster’s nature and is not rolled per cast. A Vykril who attempts Fire Lance produces Searing Lasso: a loop of flame that entangles and sears while wildflowers bloom beneath the target’s feet. The chaos is a consistent architecture, not a fault. A Vykril Ember never builds a single-thread backlog to discharge, so a Vykril cannot suffer Azyrra’s Curse; and it cannot reach the Umbral Thread, so a Vykril cannot suffer Hollowing.

The Shamanic Tradition. Generations of tribal shamans mapped these transformations at great cost; many of the earliest casters were lost to them. Each confirmed transformation was named, ritualized, and taught as its own discrete spell: a specific sequence of intention, breath, and channel management that yields a specific, known result. No academy of the Commonwealth has anything to teach a three-thread Ember, so every Emberborn Vykril child is apprenticed to the tribal shaman and learns the catalog directly. Every tribe and hold keeps at least one shaman, part priest and part institutional memory, and the sole keeper and teacher of the Wildblood catalog. The catalog is fully teachable, but non-Vykril casters cannot reproduce it; without the three-thread architecture, the same pattern produces nothing. Known spells include:

rows.t: A loop of flame that entangles and sears; wildflowers bloom beneath the target’s feet
A harmonic frequency that knits bone faster than flesh, leaving the warrior internally strong and externally fragile
A cyclone of ash that blinds others while sharpening the caster’s own sight
Communication carried through shadow itself, through darkness and silence

blocks.text: The fixed edge. A Vykril cannot improvise a new effect, and a new tactical need waits on a shaman to map a new transformation, slowly and rarely. Casting beyond the catalog, attempting something no shaman has mapped, is the one place Vykril magic is truly wild. It is unpredictable, sometimes spectacular and sometimes disastrous, and shamanic tradition counts it as reckless rather than bold.

Tiers. Emberglow sets the depth of a Vykril’s casting, not the breadth of Thread access. Elsewhere in the Weave, glow also gates the Threads a caster may reach by tier; that gating does not apply to the Vykril, whose Ember touches all three Threads at every tier.

rows.t: Minor Wildblood effects; simple Vykril-unique spells
Complex Wildblood; several effects at once; shapes the Weave on a small scale
A clear grasp of how the Threads relate; resists Weave-based curses and hexes, particularly those meant to suppress magic

blocks.text: Beyond the Reach of Suppression. A Vykril Ember does not engage the Weave in the way the Weave’s own architecture expects, and the devices built on that expectation do not hold it. Wildblood continues to function in arcane dead zones and anti-magic environments where Weave casting fails, and the Ember inhibitor collar, which severs the ordinary chain of emotion into resonance, has no hold on it. Vykril are captured and collared often, and the captor learns the collar has failed when the prisoner casts. The training glyph is the exception: it is keyed to the bearer and not to the chain, and it holds a Vykril girl’s Wildblood. Weave-trained mages who try to follow a Vykril working through the Threads are known to lose their minds.

Not Wildblood. Shadow-Melding and darkness sight belong to every Vykril, ignited or not, and Khor’vatha to every Vykril man. None of them passes through the Ember or the Weave. Wildblood and Khor’vatha do not compound: an ignited man enters Khor’vala at the same threshold and at the same cost as any other warrior.
Under Commonwealth law.

rows.t: As for every child: Ember Literacy from seven to twelve, the Volcanic Glass Prism each year from twelve to sixteen. A positive result is registered by the Bureau, and the household is notified under oath. Concealment is a crime.

The child is enrolled as every Emberborn child is. A boy keeps the prohibition on casting outside supervision by his oath; a girl, who cannot swear one, wears the glyph in its place. The Vraenhari’s syllabus is a Weave syllabus and does not reach a Vykril Ember, which cannot hold a controlled flame as taught; the supervision that matters for a Vykril child is her or his shaman’s.

A Vykril caster is licensed as an access caster, not a mage: the Vykril reach the Weave but cannot manipulate it. The license issues in the caster’s name, or in her guardian’s for a woman, and costs less and binds less than a mage’s.

Wildblood is not unregulated. The Bureau licenses every shaman who teaches or supervises it, and teaching without the license is unlicensed instruction, with the penalties that follow. The license is a carveout from the Weave rules: the Bureau certifies the shaman and the taught catalog, since no Weave curriculum applies; the bar on teaching combat spellcraft does not reach catalog spells such as Searing Lasso; and a shaman’s apprentices are supervised for the purposes of the Vraenhari prohibition. Casting outside the catalog remains unsanctioned casting, and a newly mapped transformation is lodged with the Bureau before it is taught.
Apprenticeship to a licensed shaman, the only teacher of the catalog. No academy, Legion, or Handmaid of the Banner course teaches Wildblood, because none can.

Ember is Wildblood only in both sexes. A Vykril woman’s Ember is half as common as a man’s, and a female shaman is rarer still: a hold seldom has more than one, and most have none. She practices the taught catalog only, under the supervision of the senior shaman and the clan elders. Freeform casting is forbidden to her and her master answers for it.

Every Emberborn Vykril girl is glyphed on enrollment, and the glyph holds Wildblood (see What the glyph covers, below). Her shaman, as her instructor, holds the phrase with her guardian. No collar is fitted to her for her magic.

blocks.text: The Veyrathi Luvias

The Veyrathi are the realm’s smallest magical people and the most narrowly bound. Male Veyrathi do not merely ignite rarely: they never ignite at all, and the rule is categorical, not a low probability. Female ignition is itself exceedingly rare, and every Veyrathi woman who ignites is Low, always.

Luvias. Ignited Veyrathi women are known as Luvias (officially: shamans), and Ignited Veyrathi women are Emberborn. About 0.5% of women ignite, 1,020 in the Commonwealth. Fewer than one in a hundred of those mature into a Luvia (officially: shaman), so about ten Luvias live in the realm. The rest are registered and glyphed as Emberborn and are never licensed. They are Weave casters, but only just: stuck at Low glow, a Luvia reaches the Weave lightly and by instinct, through three minor affinities, divination, healing, and lightning, and no Luvia has ever manifested an Ember strong enough to work the Weave as a normal mage. She has no spell catalog, and her gift cannot be taught, trained, or widened beyond them.

rows.t: Foresight of ambush, weather, and ground; path-sight through distortion zones; Ember-sleep communication between Luvias; resonance-speech with other Veyrathi at about ten meters, carrying feeling, urgency, and direction but no language
Mends by touch closes lacerations, slows bleeding, knits bone slowly, draws down fever
Lesser workings only. One serious wound per rest cycle; a Luvia who exceeds it is incapacitated for a day. No regrowth, no resurrection
Draws a single bolt from storm or ambient charge onto one marked target she can see
Lesser workings only. Under storm or overcast, about 100 yards; under clear sky, a thin arc of about 10 yards that stuns. One strike per rest cycle, after which she is spent

blocks.text: Cost and resistance. Every working costs exhaustion, and a Luvia is more prone to sensory overload than other Veyrathi. All Veyrathi resist compulsion and enchantment moderately; a Luvia resists them far more strongly. The people’s one magical weakness is magic that targets the animal instinct, which finds easier purchase on a Veyrathi than on a purely humanoid mind.
Under Commonwealth Law

rows.t: The Bureau registers a Luvia as Emberborn, and the Vraenhari is required of her as of every Emberborn child.

The Bureau licenses a Luvia as an access caster, not a mage, under the Access License, in her guardian’s name as for every woman who casts. It costs less and binds less than a mage’s, because she reaches the Weave barely and cannot manipulate it.

As every Emberborn woman. The Veyrathi are converts to the Church of the Sworn Flame and accepted all terms of citizenship on admission, and the glyph law is among them. The glyph is a temporary condition, worn until the Bureau certifies her competent and her guardian releases it, or re-etched on his petition if he recalls her (see Female Emberborn and Commonwealth Law, below).

Her gift cannot be expanded beyond its Low ceiling, and she is not assigned to the Weaveblade Legion or to the Thornmaidens’ magical roles. A Luvia who serves in the Shaelathi Blades serves as a Scout, not as a caster. A Luvia’s master may contract her services to a chief, as the Crown contracts women from their fathers: a private contract of her labor by her master, not a lease of her person. Darlorath stays with him, she stays in his keeping, the chief answers to him for her safety, and no payment passes to her.

blocks.text: Female Emberborn and Commonwealth Law

Under Commonwealth law a master answers for the public conduct of his household: a father for an unmarried daughter and a husband for a wife. A woman holds personal dignity and standing and bears no independent legal liability. Her honors accrue to her master, and her offenses fall on him. Magic strains this rule, because a woman who has learned the Weave can do harm that no master can watch for in every hour. The Commonwealth did not answer that by abandoning the rule. It answered with a safeguard, and a single narrow exception.

Permission. The Vraenhari teaches every Emberborn child, girl or boy, to hold a controlled flame and no more. A boy is held to the prohibition on casting outside supervision by the oath he swears. A girl cannot swear a binding oath, and the Commonwealth does not ask her to; the glyph takes the place of the oath for as long as her training lasts. Instruction beyond the Vraenhari is another matter. A woman may be taught the Weave only with her guardian’s written consent and the Crown’s authorization, and every working she makes in training is made under that consent.
The Apprentice Glyph

The glyph. A man's promise not to cast outside supervision is an oath, and the law holds him to it. A woman cannot swear a binding oath: her Vow of the Faithful, her Vow of the Hearth, and her Marriage Vow are vows, and the law receives no other word from her. The Commonwealth therefore gives her the equivalent in another form.

From her first day of the Vraenhari, every Emberborn girl of every people and every glow wears a Weavefire training glyph in the place of the oath: a Bureau-certified inscription of Control-thread resonance smithing, etched by the Bureau's examiner on the upper left thigh, so that the hem of the skirt covers it. It is keyed to her own signature and to the registered phrase of her guardian, and it is tied to the containment anchors the Crown keeps at every Vraenhari hall and Bureau station.

When a working forms in her, it forms correctly and completely, and the glyph diverts it into the anchor's reservoir before it reaches the world, unless the glyph has been opened. She still feels, shapes, and practices. It opens to a registered phrase spoken in the voice of her guardian or of the instructor he names; during the Vraenhari the instructor of record holds the phrase for the term. The phrase is lodged with the Bureau and altered only by an authorized instructor.
The glyph causes her no harm, does not touch the Ember, and does not spare her exhaustion. Only the Bureau's examiner removes it.

The Prism reads her Ember as unchanged, so the law requires that the glyph be shown on demand. Any Bureau examiner, Appraiser, licensed instructor, or the woman's own guardian may require her to present the mark for inspection, using the same bending position required by Appraisers. Refusal of inspection remains the automatic six-stroke offense already covered in the Bureau paragraph.
It carries the Bureau's registry number. Tampering is a crime, prosecuted against the tamperer, and the guardian answers for a glyphed woman as for any ward.

Release. The glyph lasts only until the woman can show competence. When her training is complete the Bureau examines her and certifies her competent: by a Certificate of Competence at the end of the Vraenhari, and by a Weavefire License after advanced instruction. Her guardian then lodges his written release with the Bureau, accepting her as competent to answer for her own casting, and the Bureau’s examiner strikes the glyph, which dissolves without a scar. The release is the guardian’s to give, and a woman cannot petition for it. A guardian may continue the glyph, which is his prerogative, but it is rare, because a glyphed woman cannot perform and he forgoes the benefit of her ability. The release moves one thing and nothing else. It does not alter Darlorath, her guardianship, her property, or her place in the household.

Doctrine of Arcane Competency: Upon release by her guardian and the Bureau’s certification of her competence (a Certificate of Competence or a Weavefire License), responsibility for the exercise of magical power attaches directly to the certified Emberborn and shall not be imputed to master, husband, father, or guardian except in cases of negligence, fraud, or conspiracy.

The exception is narrow because the Commonwealth could not make it wider. No master can guarantee the control of another person’s embercore once formal training is complete, and a rule that held him answerable for a power he cannot govern would be a fiction. So, a released woman bears personal civil and criminal liability for magical misuse, to the Bureau and to the Magistracy, and answers by suspension or revocation of her license, confiscation of her implements, reconditioning, imprisonment, and permanent suppression. In everything else she remains what she was, and her guardian answers for her as before. A master who judges her no longer fit may recall her: the Bureau revokes the license or certificate and re-etches the glyph on his petition.

Unsanctioned casting. Casting outside supervision is the offense a man’s oath binds him against and a girl’s glyph prevents. While she is glyphed, the offense is impossible, and any working that reaches the world from a glyphed woman means a tampered glyph, for which the guardian answers before the Magistracy for failure of governance. A released woman who casts beyond her license answers for it herself. A household that conceals an ignited woman, or teaches her outside the Bureau’s certification, is prosecuted for concealment, and the guardian is the accused.
What the glyph covers. The glyph is keyed to the bearer and not to the pathway. It covers whatever she completes, by whatever road it came, and it therefore reaches what the collar cannot.

rows.t: Weave casting at every glow, including a Luvia’s Low Ember
It forms through the ordinary chain, and the glyph takes the completed working.
The glyph does not depend on the Weave’s architecture. It takes the finished working of a three-thread Ember as it takes any other. The shaman holds the phrase with her guardian.
They do not run the chain, but the glyph is keyed to the bearer, and it takes what leaves her.
The Weave side and the innate side are both held.
Nothing forms in her: the god acts, and there is no Ember to key to. See The Rimborn Exception, below.

blocks.text: The collar does not reach what the glyph covers. It is a law-enforcement device only (see The collar, below), and it holds the Weave and nothing else. A glyphed Vykril, Avesari, or Luminari girl is covered by her glyph and by no collar.
The demand. The Prism cannot see the glyph, so the law requires that it be shown.

rows.t: Any Appraiser of the Bureau of Civic Decorum and any Inspector of Weavefire of the Bureau of Weavefire, at will; and any instructor of the Vraenhari, a licensed academy, the Royal Nexus Academy, or the Crown’s services, man or woman.
Any woman or girl. She need not be accused.
She is always escorted, and her escort or master stands present for the demand, as at every audit.
Her glyph, or her License or Certificate of Competence. She lifts her own hem and shows the glyph, or she presents her papers. No one touches her.

The officer checks the Registry. A woman not entered in it has nothing to show and nothing to answer. A registered Emberborn with no glyph and no papers has tampered with her glyph or been concealed, and the finding is made.
The Appraiser checks the glyph at will, in public as he halts any woman and at the threshold of a home, as a step of his audit after the kneel and the hem, under the same warrant, finding, and Roll.
The Inspector checks at will under the Bureau of Weavefire’s warrant and finds as the Appraiser does.
A woman instructor demands, inspects, and reports. Only a man punishes. A male instructor and her master punish an instructor’s finding, and her master needs no leave.

A professed Handmaiden, and every woman claimed by the Church, is inspected by her Confessor or Praesul alone. An Appraiser, Inspector, or instructor who sees one without a glyph or papers reports it to her Confessor, who handles it. He has no other remedy.

blocks.text: Correction. The correction is the Appraiser’s standing procedure under the Sumptuary Statutes.

rows.t: Appraiser’s or Inspector’s finding: failure or refusal to show; a registered Emberborn with no glyph and no papers

The standard correction: six strokes of the Cane across the seat, laid by the Appraiser or Inspector himself there and then, and the master fined one to five Zarims. The officer admonishes the master to correct her further at home.
The male instructor lays six strokes of the Cane across the seat, and her master, who needs no leave, may add what he chooses. The master is fined one to five Zarims.
No limit binds the master in the strokes he administers, in public or in private, save that he may not permanently harm her. She is his property in law.
The same, and the tampering is referred to the Bureau and the Magistracy.

blocks.text: The collar. The collar is a law-enforcement device only.

rows.t: A Bureau-certified band of ash-steel, closed at the throat, with an inhibitor crystal of Ironweave Works set into it: a valve on the embercore, keyed to the voice. While it is closed the wearer cannot cast. It carries no pain and no detonator, bears the Bureau’s seal and a registered number, and carries no mark of ownership.

Any caster of either sex who is arrested or sentenced for unsanctioned casting, tampering, or concealment, and the repeat offender under a standing order of indefinite suppression. It is never fitted to a woman for her training, and no master, guardian, or private party may fit, hold, or use one.
A Bureau examiner, or a Royal Ranger, Crown Constable, or Warden on arrest for casting in the act.
The custodian officer, by his registered phrase lodged with the Bureau.
The Bureau’s examiner, on a Magistral’s order or at the end of the sentence. No one else may remove it, and tampering is a crime.
The Weave and nothing else. It does not hold Wildblood or any innate gift, and a captor learns it has failed when the prisoner casts.

The Court’s dated indenture collar, which stands as it is and holds no embercore, and the collars of the Empire and of Kaeyria, with their pain and their detonators. A collar without the Bureau’s seal is evidence of slaving.

blocks.text: The Rimborn Exception: Filial Petition

The Commonwealth regulates magic by holding a channel. It holds the Ember, which the Bureau registers and which the glyph or the oath closes, and it holds the Circuit, which a woman’s master keeps. A Rimborn’s petition passes through neither. A Rimborn has no embercore, and when she asks a divine parent for a gift she is not the vessel: the god acts and she is the asking. The glyph has nothing to key to and nothing to divert, and the Circuit governs stewardship and not Heaven, and she is no steward. It is the one working a woman of the realm can call down that no instrument of the Commonwealth can hold. Parliament, in ratifying the Rimborn Asylum Accord, did not pretend otherwise. It chose to regulate what the law can reach.

The Exception rests on one rule: the Commonwealth does not regulate the gift; it regulates the act. No court admits a petition as authority or as defence, and no court punishes a petition. What a Rimborn does, and what her gift does in the world, is judged as any act is: as assault, trespass, destruction of property, escape, or breach of guardianship. A Briar Ward is a hedge, and a lock that opens is an open lock.

rows.t: The Prism reads no embercore in a Rimborn child, and the Bureau enters her as Unthreaded. The Bureau has no jurisdiction over a petitioned gift, licenses none, and keeps no ledger of one. The parish Hearth-Keeper, the roll-keeper of the hold, enters the completion of her trial, enters the completion of her second trial on the parish roll, and the Crown takes that entry as evidence that her gifts have come.

None. The Weavefire glyph takes no signature on an unthreaded body and the collar has no valve to close, so neither is fitted. A Rimborn woman is not required to show a glyph; the Bureau’s Unthreaded entry answers an Appraiser’s demand.

None required. No Vraenhari applies, because nothing in a Rimborn can be taught to control. Petitioned gifts do not come before the second trial, so the Commonwealth has no child with a divine gift to supervise.

A man who directs a petition answers for the direction as a guardian answers for any command. A woman who petitions undirected answers to her guardian for it as for any act. The parish stands surety. The god's own act is judged as any act. Applies from the entry of her trial on the parish roll. The reasoning is that of the Doctrine of Arcane Competency: no master can answer for a power he cannot govern, and no power is less governable than a god’s. In everything else her guardian answers for her as before.

The kin-group clause of the Oath Triad is read for the Rimborn as the parish. The parish stands surety for its members’ conduct, and its Rimkeeper answers to the Magistracy for the surety. The Crown relies on obligation, which is what the Rimborn keep in place of wealth.

The Magistracy holds a Rimborn prisoner in the ordinary cells and does not rely on a device. No petition has been granted to a woman to leave lawful male authority. Unbound frees her only from unlawful captivity and returns her to the male authority she belongs under. It is not granted against her father's, her master's, or the Crown's lawful custody.

Tessara and Caedron refuse a request that serves the wrong purpose, and a Rimborn who betrays both is ashen: every gift is gone. The Commonwealth records the Silence on the parish roll when the Rimkeeper reports it and treats it as a sanction that nothing the Crown could build would match. It does not impose it.

The Church reads the Signature and records the petition as filial, never as miracle. Tessara’s Signature is Solaran; Caedron’s is Kratistan, a House that is not a prosecuted creed. No Praesul may suspend or close a Rimborn petition: the Church’s ladder governs stewards, and the Rimborn are none.

blocks.text: Doctrine of the Open Door: A gift petitioned by a Rimborn of her divine parent is the act of the god and passes through no channel that any master, Bureau, or Church holds. Responsibility for what she does with it A man who directs a petition answer for the direction as a guardian answer for any command. A woman who petitions undirected answers to her guardian for it as for any act. The parish stands surety. The god's own act is judged as any act. Applies from the entry of her trial on the parish roll on the parish roll, and shall not be imputed to master, husband, father, or guardian except in cases of negligence, fraud, or conspiracy. The parish stands surety under the Oath Triad.

Caedron’s gifts press hardest on the household order. Unbound opens a lock, Open Road shows a way, and The Endless Road defeats pursuit. The Magistracy’s position is that these are acts of a god and not of the petitioner, and that the law answers the leaving and not the asking. Caedron grants Unbound only to one who truly wishes to be free, and refuses The Endless Road to one who flees a consequence she deserves; the Magistracy declines to rely on his judgment in either direction and does not dispute it. A guardian’s remedy against a Rimborn ward who leaves is the remedy against any ward who leaves, and the parish surety is added to it.
Languages of the Royal Commonwealth of Zeythari

The Royal Commonwealth of Zeythari recognizes several official, ancestral, sacred, learned, and regional languages. Unlike many older realms, the Commonwealth does not seek linguistic uniformity. Its founders sought civic unity rather than cultural assimilation. Through the work of the Council of Tongues and by royal command, every citizen would share a common language of government and public life, while the ancestral languages of the realm would remain protected as living expressions of heritage, faith, household, memory, trade, and custom.

As a result, a citizen of the Commonwealth may conduct public business in Zeylara, preserve ancestral traditions in Saelkyr, Avesai, Lórenei, Durakhtûn, or Khor'dal, and return home to speak the language of family and kin. The Commonwealth's goal was never that all peoples speak one language. The goal was that all peoples belong to one Commonwealth.
For the history of each language, its grammar, script, registers, and use throughout the realm, see Appendix G: The Tongues of the Commonwealth.
The Common Tongue
Zeylara

Zeylara (The Founded Tongue or The Foundation Revealed) is the civic language of the Royal Commonwealth. It was created shortly after the Founding, when representatives of the Commonwealth's principal peoples proved unable to agree upon which ancestral language should serve as the language of state.

The greatest disagreement arose between the Satyrim and Maenari delegations. Both peoples had played indispensable roles in securing the Commonwealth, both possessed ancient literary and scholarly traditions, and both advanced strong claims for their own languages. The Crown feared that elevating any one ancestral tongue above the others would leave the new Commonwealth divided before it had fully begun.

To resolve the dispute, the King charged Magister Saevin Sailaeg, scholar, translator, and member of the newly established Council of Tongues, with devising a neutral solution. Rather than selecting an existing language, Sailaeg created Sailaeg, the Founding Base: a deliberately constructed linguistic framework intended to belong to no people and favor no nation.

Sailaeg was never intended as a spoken language. No community adopted it as a native tongue, and no literature was composed in it for ordinary use. Its purpose was solely to provide a neutral foundation upon which a shared civic language could be built.

Upon this foundation, the Council of Tongues undertook the greater work. Drawing upon the languages of the founding peoples, they spent years debating, refining, and synthesizing linguistic forms into a single civic tongue. The result was Zeylara.

Its case structure is primarily derived from Saelkyr, the language of the former kingdom's Satyrim founders, whose five cases, vocabulary of covenant and law, and open flowing syllables the Council kept, and whose two registers, High and Low, it deliberately merged into one. Its core vocabulary, phonological foundations, and many everyday forms derive from Sailaeg. Additional contributions from Avesai, Lórenei, Durakhtûn, and Khor'dal were incorporated into specific domains of expression, law, ritual, poetry, testimony, household life, military speech, and public culture.

Zeylara serves as the language of government, law, education, administration, military service, public records, and Commonwealth citizenship. The courts operate in Zeylara. The laws are written in Zeylara. Citizens swear the Oaths of Citizenship and the Standard in Zeylara. Through it, every citizen stands within the same civic order regardless of ancestry, clan, or place of birth.

Though Zeylara possesses specialized registers for law, ceremony, poetry, administration, household life, and military use, it was never intended to replace the older tongues of the realm. It exists as the Commonwealth's public voice rather than its only voice.
Language and Citizenship

While Zeylara serves as the Commonwealth's universal civic language, it was never intended to erase or replace the ancestral tongues of its peoples. Saelkyr, Avesai, Lórenei, Durakhtûn, and Khor'dal remain living languages spoken in homes, halls, temples, workshops, camps, and communities throughout the realm. A citizen may inherit one language through family, encounter another through trade or service, and participate in public life through Zeylara. The Commonwealth's purpose was not to dissolve its peoples into one culture, but to provide a common civic foundation through which all might share the same laws, institutions, and obligations.

The Commonwealth did not create linguistic unity. It created civic unity. Zeylara gave the peoples of the realm a common public language, while the older tongues remained the living voices of lineage, memory, faith, poetry, trade, custom, and home.

rows.t: Fixed, written in Zeylara. It is the name on the census roll, the parish roll, the parish school register, the Muster, the Registry, and every court record
Every household bears its head's surname. His wife, children, and wards bear it. A daughter takes her husband's surname at the Marriage Rite. This is legally universal and culturally variable
Each people keeps its own naming inside the home and the community: oral, fluid, and unrecorded. The Commonwealth does not touch it

Customary names are name-patterns that change over a life (adulthood names, achievement names). The civil name is entered at the Road Trial or Confirmation for men. A woman is registered under her father's household surname and takes her husband's at the Rite. A hold or hearth name may serve as the household surname
Clan names (the -athi names) and a Luvia's Ember name are cultural. The Ember name is sacred and is not spoken outside ritual. The civil name is the household surname in Zeylara

blocks.text: The Tongues of the Peoples

Each of the seven non-hybrid peoples kept its own language by treaty, accord, and habit. These are the languages of the hearth, the clan hall, the forge-floor, and the barracks. Zeylara is learned from the parish school onward; these are learned first.

rows.t: Memory, genealogy, poetry, lineage, and family identity
Temple and covenant, law and testimony, household order, and the memory of the Subjugation
Forge culture, guild traditions, craftsmanship, engineering, mercantile law, and artisan identity
Clan organization, martial traditions, military culture, oath-keeping, and warrior identity
Chosen bonds, vows, kinship, intimate relationships, and Avesari cultural identity
Clan identity, territorial custom, resonance practice, and Veyrathi cultural memory — spoken by no other people in the Commonwealth
Threshold, hearth, road, and obligation; an oral-only tongue, older than the Commonwealth; its non-verbal half, Vashrim, is shared with beasts.

blocks.text: The two hybrid peoples hold no ancestral language of their own. The Maestrai are native speakers of Zeylara, with Lórenei and Saelkyr kept as parent-tongue inheritance. The Luminari keep Saelkyr and Avesai as household inheritance.

The Veyrathi are the sole speakers of Veyr, a biologically imprinted language that cannot be culturally erased or taught to non-Veyrathi. It is recognized by the Commonwealth as an innate ancestral tongue, protected under the same covenant of linguistic preservation that guards Lórenei, Saelkyr, and Khor’dal. No other people of the Commonwealth speak or learn Veyr.

The Rimborn speak Rimthal, the Threshold Speech, an oral language older than the Commonwealth and never written. Every statement in it describes a crossing, and speech names what is changing, in the order crossing, traveler, goal. Its roots are few and neutral: thur (crossing), azh (hearth), reth (road), varn (obligation), ven (pain), kai (hope). The spoken root carries the least of the meaning. Breath marks the kind of crossing, rhythm marks its state (begun, continuing, completed, broken), tone marks how the speaker knows it, and bearing (posture, gaze, hands) does the work of case. Silence is grammatical. Its non-verbal half, Vashrim, is shared with beasts, and Rimborn children learn both halves together. Commonwealth scholars have tried to transcribe Rimthal in Zeylaric, but that is a scholar's record of what he hears and not a writing system, and the Rimborn do not use it. The Commonwealth recognizes Rimthal as an ancestral tongue under the same covenant of linguistic preservation that guards the others. Rimborn children learn Rimthal at home and Zeylara at the parish school, and Zeylara is required of every Rimborn as of every citizen: the Oath of the Standard is sworn in it.
Sacred Language
Seraval

Seraval is the frozen liturgical language of the Church of the Living Flame, and by extension, the Church of the Sworn Flame. Preserved without intentional grammatical change since the age of Arkanos Ardentis, the Speaker of Truth, it is used throughout the Communion to seal sacraments, conduct sacred rites, promulgate canonical formulae, and preserve the inherited writings of the Church.

Although not forbidden to the laity, formal instruction in Seraval occurs almost exclusively within the Seminaries of the Flame and among certain scholars of theology and canon law. Most citizens recognize only common ritual phrases rather than possessing conversational fluency. All sermons, confessions, and everyday pastoral care is conducted in Zeylara.
Scholarly Language
Scholária

Scholária serves as the Commonwealth’s principal scholarly and academic language. Used by universities, learned societies, physicians, jurists, philosophers, and natural scholars, it provides a common medium for advanced study throughout the realm. It is not native to any people of the Commonwealth: it was codified in the Republic of Concordia and reached Zeythari through Concordian scholarship, law schools, and trade. While educated citizens may possess reading knowledge of Scholária, fluency remains largely restricted to academic and professional circles.
The Vensharic Trade Continuum
Collectively known as Vensharic, these related commercial languages facilitate trade across Solmara, Linhaven, and the wider continent.
Venshal (High Vensharic)

The clipped, contract-grade language of the Guild Concordance, merchant houses, banks, insurers, diplomats, and commercial courts. Designed for precision rather than beauty, Venshal prioritizes clarity, accounting, legal exactness, and record-keeping. Most major commercial contracts are drafted in Venshal.
Tesshare (Low Vensharic)

The practical caravan-and-port language of merchants, sailors, caravaneers, laborers, travelers, and market officials. Unlike most native languages, Tesshare is rarely learned in childhood. Speakers typically acquire it through trade, military service, apprenticeship, travel, or commerce. Fluency is measured less by grammatical mastery than by the ability to negotiate prices, identify goods, arrange transport, and avoid being cheated.
Skeinvash (Under-Cant)

A deliberately evasive and adaptive criminal dialect spoken along frontier regions, ports, smuggling routes, and black-market networks. Its vocabulary shifts constantly, allowing speakers to communicate commerce that official authorities and Concordance inspectors were never intended to understand.

The Language of Deference: The Lowered Tongue

The Lowered Tongue (Zeylara Isel-Avor) is the dedicated register of Zeylara in which every woman of the Commonwealth speaks whenever a man is present. It is conditioned by civic status: where the other registers are open to a speaker by profession, circumstance, ceremony, or institution, the Lowered Tongue is required of a woman under Darlorath because she is a woman. It is spoken by all women, in public and in private life, and it frames every spoken interaction between a woman and any man: when she addresses him, answers him, writes to him, petitions him, or speaks in his hearing.

The register is built from the Common tongue’s own sounds and vocabulary, set inside a syntax that gives her no direct assertion, no contradiction, no question that implies fault, and no prominence for herself. Direct statements are replaced by petitionary phrasing, and every man is addressed in honorifics.
Women and the Register

A woman is taught the Common and Hearth registers in parish school, household, and convent. Among women, speech is plain and unconstrained. In the presence of any man, and in every public place, it is spoken as the Lowered Tongue, and the Lowered Tongue is never spoken without the bearing that belongs to it.

The line is hard, and it does not move with education, rank, or gift. A woman may not speak outside the Lowered Tongue in mixed company. An educated woman who does so is punished like any other: she is caned, and her master or guardian is fined for her. The Commonwealth treats a woman’s use of an unauthorized register as a violation of social order, analogous to the unlawful wearing of rank insignia or restricted dress, and the Bureau of Civic Decorum audits it as such.
