blocks.text: The Royal Nexus Academy is the one institution where educated women live and study together, and Common is its working speech for a single reason: its halls and classrooms hold women only. Nothing in the Academy’s teaching widens a student’s register. The moment the Rector, the Confessor, a Crown warden, an Appraiser, or any other man enters, the company is no longer wholly female, and every student, Sister, and woman of the staff speaks the Lowered Tongue until he has gone.
The Body of the Register: Deference Postures

The Lowered Tongue is spoken with the body as much as with the mouth. A woman’s submission must be seen as well as heard, and a sentence in the right register without the bearing that belongs to it is a breach as surely as the bearing without the sentence. The postures are those of Article IX.

rows.t: When a man enters a room of her household, passes her, or addresses her, she stands and curtsies before she speaks, and holds her place until he has passed or given her leave.
Lowered before any man. She meets his eyes only when ordered to look up.
One to two paces behind her master, husband, or guardian. She yields every door, stair, and path, and stands aside to let a man pass.
Where no seat is given and leave is not granted, she may kneel, hands in her lap, and speaks from the kneel.
She speaks only when spoken to or when her master bids; briefly; and not at all in a gathering where men speak, without her master’s express permission.
Low and soft. The sounds of command are not given to her, and she does not raise her voice to a man.
Every man is addressed in honorifics (see Core Rules below). Omitting them is a breach of the register.

blocks.text: Speech without posture, and posture without speech, are each read as a failure of the register and corrected as one.
Core Rules of the Register

Honorific Address: Every man must be addressed using formal markers of deference, such as sir, master, my lord, by your leave, or as you will. She addresses her master as Naevor, a man of rank as Arglwydd, and any other man by his title.
Prohibition of Direct Negation: Direct refusals or contradictions are grammatically and socially prohibited, replaced instead by conditional framing and requests for leave to clarify.
Minimization of Self: A speaker using the Lowered Tongue refers to herself as infrequently as possible, avoiding declarative statements about her own thoughts, wants, or judgments.
Obligatory Deference Transformations:

rows.t: “As you will, Sir, though may I beg your leave to say what troubles me?”
“Forgive me, Master, if I have misunderstood.”
“If it please you, my lord, I would ask.”
“It may be, by your leave, sir.”

blocks.text: Sociolinguistic Function and Enforcement

While rooted in the Darlorath doctrine and religious sumptuary standards, the Lowered Tongue operates as a daily linguistic habitus throughout Zeythariaeth. The preservation of this register is actively enforced across two main avenues:

The Bureau of Civic Decorum: As the official Crown administrative body charged with upholding sumptuary laws, public markers of rank, and behavioral standards, Appraisers routinely monitor marketplaces, public squares, and transit hubs.

Enforcement by Any Male Citizen: Compliance is not restricted to state officials; any male citizen of the Commonwealth who is spoken to without the required deference is entitled by law and custom to demand correction.

A failure to employ the Lowered Tongue, or an omission of the required bearing in mixed company, marks a breach of Civic Decorum. The woman is corrected with the Cane—up to six strokes across the seat where an Appraiser finds the breach, and her master may add what he chooses; she is further subject to official censure. Her master or guardian is fined one to five Zarims for a lapse in her instruction.
Geography

The Commonwealth covers 1.7 million km² of western Virelia, a broad realm some 1,350 km from west to east and 1,250 km from south to north. Land closes it on four sides. The Ritebound Throne holds the whole northern frontier, beyond the Thaldrin borderlands. The Kingdom of Kaeyria holds the mountain passes of the northwest. The Forest Realm of Zelesti and the Great Zelesti Dark close the west. The Aidionic Empire presses on the southwest and the south, across the Sundral Highlands and the Shimmerwind Wastes. Only the east is open: 1,100 km of seaboard on the Western Sea. Beyond that coast lie the Ember Isles, a Crown-held island chain some 150 km off the Solmara Coast. They hold no towns: one islet carries a naval station, and the others carry five small fishing and farming settlements.
Capital: Suraela — seat of the Crown, Parliament, and Assembly; home of Kaervast Cathedral

Primary Terrain: Radically varied — fertile volcanic valleys, mineral-rich mountain ranges, deep old-growth forest, and a true desert wasteland, bound together by two navigable rivers and a long, harborous coastline
The Shape of the Realm

Seven major geographic regions define the Commonwealth. The Thaldrin Ranges form the northern spine of the realm, named in the Duraken tongue for the god of the forge and serving as the source of the Commonwealth's iron, silver, and rare deep-vein resonance ore. Together with the Sundral Highlands of the southwest, they constitute the principal mountain regions of the kingdom, providing both natural defenses and the mineral wealth upon which much of the Commonwealth's industry depends.

South of the Thaldrin lie the level Suraelan Plain, the central lowlands surrounding Suraela and crossed by the Venshal contract-roads linking the capital to both major ports and the Kaeyrian border crossing, and the volcanic Kaelvash Valleys, a chain of fertile valleys whose ash-fed soils support vineyards, grain fields, orchards, and terraced farms. Renewed rather than ruined by their dormant vents, the Kaelvash Valleys serve as the Commonwealth's breadbasket. Their rich black soils, warmed in places by geothermal activity, make them the most productive agricultural region in the realm and the center of its famed orchard and wine-growing traditions.

The old-growth Threnwood fills the western marches, bordering the Maenari Forest Realm of Zelesti and the Great Zelesti Dark beyond it, Zelesti's vast interior forest. Rich in magic and poor in steel, the Great Zelesti Dark is home to rangers, archers, and mages without peer on the continent. The Threnwood itself provides timber and game and shelters the ritual groves of Maenari communities who continue to keep the older ways.

The Sundral Highlands and the Shimmerwind Wastes form the southwestern and southern reaches of the realm and comprise the Commonwealth's principal frontier region. The Sundral Highlands provide a natural mountain shield along the Aidionic frontier and are held by the Satyrim clans descended from House Marren. Beyond them, the Shimmerwind Wastes form the Commonwealth's only true desert, the adopted homeland of the Vykril clans who were displaced there generations before the Commonwealth's founding. The Wastes constitute the frontier facing the Aidionic Empire and are crossed by a caravan route that is garrisoned and taxed rather than closed, reflecting the Commonwealth's conviction that even a rival's desert is a road if it is bold enough to hold it.

"Though the maps of Suraela had long painted the Shimmerwind Wastes in Commonwealth red, authority there rested more upon treaty than decree. For generations the Veyrathi tribes and independent Vykril clans kept the desert roads, resisted Imperial encroachment, and guarded the frontier. The accession of the Great Tribe of Shaelathi was no conquest of the Wastes. It was simply the day the greatest power already dwelling within them chose Commonwealth citizenship over independence." ― Cartographer Varric Haldenport

The Ashward March occupies the northern borderlands facing the Ritebound Throne directly. Site of the Commonwealth's founding legend, it remains the most heavily garrisoned frontier in the realm. Its chain of stone wall-forts descends from the original fortified palisade line established to guard the border. To the northwest lies the open frontier shared with the Kingdom of Kaeyria, a fortress realm that controls the mountain passes north of the Great Zelesti Dark and provides a connection through to the Aidionic Empire on its far side. Unlike the Ashward March, this frontier is watched rather than walled, sustained by a trade alliance that has endured, uneasily, for generations.

The Seaboard runs the full length of the Commonwealth's eastern coastline and serves as the outlet for most maritime trade. Divided broadly between the northern coast of Linhaven and the southern coast of Solmara, it is dotted with fishing villages, merchant ports, naval facilities, and coastal market towns. Offshore lie the Ember Isles, whose volcanic soils support small farming and orchard communities alongside their fishing fleets. Together, the coastline and its islands provide the Commonwealth with access to overseas commerce, fisheries, and maritime defense.

Two navigable rivers cross the realm. The River Ashvael enters the realm at the Kaeyrian Gate, crosses the Suraelan Plain through the capital, takes the Thaldrin waters at Duskhearth, and runs east to the northern port of Linhaven, carrying the plain's freight, together with the ore, timber, and Duraken craft-goods of the Thaldrin, to open water. Above Linhaven it is navigable only by shallow-draft river craft. The River Solmir flows from the Kaelvash Valleys to the port of Solmara and serves as the Commonwealth's principal grain-, orchard-, and wine-artery. No other waterways within the Commonwealth carry significant cargo.

Trade beyond the rivers moves primarily along the Venshal contract-roads linking Suraela to the ports and frontier crossings, together with the caravan routes that cross the Shimmerwind Wastes. Major defensive positions include the fortifications of the Ashward March, the natural barrier of the Sundral Highlands, and the Zelesti citadel-city Caer Mithren¹, ceded to the Commonwealth as part of the marriage compact between King Alexi and Princess Ilyara Thessandrion of Zelesti. The citadel commands the forest road and the principal Aidionic approach beyond the Great Dark of Zelesti. Garrisoned by a permanent Commonwealth cohort of infantry, crossbowmen, and engineers, it serves as both the foremost bulwark of the alliance and one of the realm's most important overland trade gates.

¹Caer Mithren is a Lórenei-Zeylara hybrid meaning "Fortress of the Oath-Lineage." The Zeylaran caer means fortress or citadel, while the Lórenei compound mithren combines mith (oath) and vathren (lineage, succession, inheritance). The name commemorates the dynastic compact that bound the Crown of Zeythari and the Forest Realm of Zelesti through marriage, transforming a frontier fortress into a permanent symbol of shared defense, common interest, and joined bloodlines. The Zelesti knew the citadel-city as Faelcaer Mitrora; the Commonwealth renamed it on the cession.

blocks.text: Seasons

The Commonwealth has four seasons, but ground this varied does not keep them evenly. The heartland valleys are hot and humid for most of the year; the north is snowbound for months; the desert swings from furnace days to freezing nights. The civic calendar fixes the turns of the year: spring begins at the equinox, with the Confirmation Musters.

Spring (the Greening). Rain comes up from the sea and snow-melt comes down from the Thaldrin, and the Solmir and the Ashvael run high. The valleys green quickly, fields are sown and Ember crop augmentation is at its busiest, and the roads soften to mud. The Ashward passes thaw, and the March goes to its highest alert as the Ritebound line becomes passable. The Confirmation Musters fall at the equinox and the Council of Tongues Day in late spring.

Summer (the High Heat). Kaelvash and the plain are hot and humid, with violent afternoon storms. The coast keeps a steady sea breeze, the Sundral Highlands stay cool, and the Shimmerwind becomes unfit for large columns, so the frontier wars sink to their lowest ebb. Drill is moved to dawn and dusk across the Warhost, and caravans cross the Wastes by night. The Festival of the Flame is held in summer.

Autumn (the Gathering). The harvest comes in, and the valleys press the vintage. Barges crowd the Solmir, the Royal Granaries are restocked, and the Vintage of Kaelvash and Hammer-Day are held. Gales begin to rise at sea in late autumn, and the Weather Clerks of the Auxiliaries hoist storm signals along the whole seaboard.

Winter (the Cold). Winter is mild in the valleys and on the coast, with only light frost on the higher terraces, and the geothermal greenhouses keep producing. It is hard in the north: the Thaldrin and the Ashward March lie under snow, the passes close, and the roads are shut for weeks. The Wall Line is kept open by the Track Companies. Rain and fog settle on the Threnwood, and the desert nights turn cold. The Vigil of the Standard is kept at midwinter and the Jyotirain Remembrance in the cold months. A short harvest turns a winter dangerous in the Commonwealth; the Grain-Short Winter is remembered as the worst, and the Royal Granaries exist to prevent another.

blocks.text: Satrapies and Marches

The realm is divided into eight provinces of two kinds. The five Satrapies are the interior civil provinces, each under an elected, Crown-confirmed Satrap, a man who commands no soldiers and carries the Crown’s will into his satrapy and the satrapy’s needs back to the Crown. The three Marches are the frontier provinces, each under a Crown-appointed Marshal who holds military and civil authority together. Before the Constitution of 1780 the Satraps held commands; the Settlement stripped them of them and gave the frontier to Crown Marshals. The Satrapies are numbered in the order of their enrolment under the Constitution, which ratified the numbering already in use (Duskhearth had been the Fifth since the reign of Aldas Marren XI), and the numeral is the one a citizen gives on the oath-roll: a Zeythar of the Fourth Satrapy is a man of the Linhaven Coast. The Marches are known by name only.
The Church’s dioceses follow the same map. Kaervast is the Archsworn’s own diocese, governed from Kaervast Cathedral. Each of the other seven provinces is a Praesul’s see.
The Satrapies
The First Satrapy: Kaervast
Seat: Suraela. Satrap: Merovane Soleth, Maestrai, who came up through the Suraela city council.

The capital satrapy lies on the Suraelan Plain, the broadest level ground in the realm, farmed to its edges and crossed by every trunk road and rail line the Commonwealth owns. Suraela stands at its centre on the River Ashvael, with the Crown, Parliament, Assembly, Kaervast Cathedral, the Royal Archive, the Arcana Scholium, the Archivist Lyceum, and the Revenue Office. Hearthwall, the citadel-city of the Warden of the Oath, closes the plain’s western gate 140 km from the capital. Kaervast gave a western strip of its land to make the Threnwood March. It is the Archsworn’s own diocese and has no Praesul.
The Second Satrapy: Kaelvash
Seat: Kaelvash. Satrap: Ervane Tulleth, Maenari, a vintner and orchard-holder of the valley terraces.

A chain of volcanic-soil valleys runs south and east of the plain toward the coast. The satrapy is hot, humid, and the most densely settled in the realm. Vineyards, grain, and orchard terraces climb ash-fed slopes watered from dormant vents, and geothermal greenhouses keep the valleys producing through winter. The Solmir rises here and becomes navigable at Maelvine, the satrapy’s river-port, which loads the grain and wine of the valleys onto barges for Solmara. The Royal Granaries are thickest in Kaelvash, and the Vintage, the Commonwealth’s largest civic celebration, is held here each autumn. A western strip of the satrapy went to the Threnwood March.
The Third Satrapy: Solmara Coast
Seat: Solmara. Satrap: Rhazik Vel’Torren, Vykril, once a caravan master and a factor of the Guild Concordance.

The southern half of the seaboard, about 500 km of coast, from Brine Cape south to the edge of the Wastes. The Solmir’s delta plain is green and irrigated; south of it the coast turns to salt flats and the grey basalt headlands of the Grey Coast, where almost nothing grows. Solmara, a civilian deepwater port, holds the Guild Concordance, the Venshal contract courts, and the Royal Bank of Zeythari. Greywake, a closed naval city, lies 110 km down the Grey Coast. Offshore lie the Ember Isles, a civilian district of the satrapy whose five fishing and farming settlements are governed through a Crown Magistrate answerable to the Satrap; the naval station on Vaelance Isle does not answer to him.
The Fourth Satrapy: Linhaven Coast
Seat: Linhaven. Satrap: Eshren Vaelun, Avesari, twenty years a man of the Skyguard before his election.

The northern half of the seaboard, about 500 km of coast, from Brine Cape north to the foot of the Ashward March. Cliffs and timbered headlands alternate with the lower Ashvael valley, which carries the freight of the Suraelan Plain and the ore, timber, and Duraken craft-goods of the Thaldrin to open water. Linhaven, a civilian deepwater port, holds the ore and timber exchange. Keelhold, a closed naval city and home of the Royal Shipyards, lies 90 km up the coast.
The Fifth Satrapy: Duskhearth
Seat: Duskhearth. Satrap: Brundar Kelmhold, Duraken, a master of the Forge-Hall.

The southern foothills of the Thaldrin Ranges and the Commonwealth’s mining district: iron, silver, and the rare deep-vein resonance ore. Duraken guild-halls dominate its towns. Duskhearth holds the Magitek Arcaneum, Etherforge University, and the Ironweave Works with its proving ground and rolling-stock shops. The Thaldrin waters that feed the Ashvael rise in these hills and join it at Duskhearth, and the first leg of its cargo-way begins in the guild-hold.
The Marches
Ashward March
Seat: Ashward. Marshal: Osric Dunmere, Maestrai, a general of the Crown Regulars who rose by examination and field service.

The northern frontier: the Thaldrin’s northern slope and the borderlands beyond, to the Ritebound line. Its chain of stone wall-forts, descended from the original palisade, runs some 850 km east to west and holds eight citadels, the most of any March. Ashward itself holds the First Standard Shrine, guarded by the Flameward, and the Royal Military Academy. It is the most heavily garrisoned frontier in the Commonwealth. Snow closes its passes for months of every year.
Sundral March
Seat: Sundralkeep. Marshal: Grakhal Vrakhur-zan, Vykril, a general of the Crown Regulars and of House Vrakhur, whose line runs back to the founding of the Commonwealth.

The southern frontier holds two kinds of ground under one Marshal. The Sundral Highlands in the southwest are a natural mountain shield on the Aidionic frontier, held by the Marren-descended clans, whose seat is Sundralkeep, and kept with seven citadels and the old highland chapels. The Marshal’s office occupies the Crown wing of the keep. The Shimmerwind Wastes in the south are the true desert, ancestral ground of the Vykril clans and the scene of the low, unending frontier wars. The caravan track runs south through them from Kharvesh to the Aidionic border, held by two forts and taxed rather than closed.

The Shimmerwind Homesteading Grant. After the Treaty of Kharvesh closed the Second Aidionic Wars in R.Y. 1178, Parliament issued a Homesteading Grant to discharged veterans of the Warhost: a wellstead and its water-rights on Crown-held ground along the Caravan Track, in return for service as frontier militia. Its purpose was to people the desert march and to draw landless and discharged men, the idle hands that fed the smugglers’ trade, out of the lowland towns and onto the frontier. The grants lie only on the Crown’s side of the Track. The Vykril keep the clan ground and the wells of the Compact, and the first homesteaders held their water by well-rights granted by the clans in return for a settled line against the Empire. Parliament has renewed the Grant under every Parliament since. Eight centuries of wellsteads, deep-bored by the Crown Engineers and Duraken guildsmen, now hold some 400,000 people in the Wastes, most of them in three towns: Sunderwell (150,000), the muster-town and seat of the Grant; Dunemark (90,000), a salt and caravan town at the Track’s midpoint; and Southgate (60,000), grown around the southern of the two forts. About 100,000 more live in the wellstead villages between.

The Marshalcy. The Marshalcy of Sundral is held by a Vykril of House Vrakhur, appointed by the Crown from the senior officer corps in recognition of the Vykril clans’ place among the founding peoples and of their management of the Wastes, which are the March’s real frontier and their ancestral ground. His House stood with the Crown in bringing the Shaelathi Tribe, the largest and most powerful of the Veyrathi tribes, into the Commonwealth. The Marshal administers the Homesteading Grant for the Crown in concert with the clans, and the Highland clans and the Order of the Standing Wall keep the seven citadels of the Highlands under him.
Threnwood March
Seat: Aerendal. Marshal: Caelor Vaeryn, Maenari, a general of the Crown Regulars raised in the grove-parishes.

The western frontier, cut from the western strips of Kaervast and Kaelvash: deep old-growth forest, the ritual groves of the older Maenari, and the timber that feeds the realm. It bounds Zelesti and the Great Zelesti Dark in the west and includes the Northwest Borderland, the open frontier shared with Kaeyria, held with five citadels, two of them on the Kaeyrian border. The Zelesti citadel-city (Caer Mithren, formerly Faelcaer Mitrora), ceded at King Alexi’s marriage, lies just beyond the March’s western edge, and the forest road to it is the March’s most guarded road.

Since R.Y. 1998 the March has also held the Rimborn parishes: some two hundred thousand refugees from the Ritebound Throne, settled along the forest edge between the old groves and the farmland. Their hunters, leatherworkers, woodland holders, and guide-companies work the March’s edge and keep the forest road to Caer Mithren.
Major Settlements

Civilian deepwater port (south coast); Guild Concordance seat, Venshal contract-law courts, Royal Bank

Closed naval city; fleet base and repair yards; home of the Solmara Fleet

Vykril caravan city at the edge of the Wastes; terminus of the Shimmerwind track; customs and garrison
Homesteading Grant seat; veterans’ muster-town on the Shimmerwind track; deep-bore and cistern works

blocks.text: Hearthwall stands on the Hearth Gap, where the roads from Sundral and Threnwood meet before the capital plain. A field army can winter inside its walls. The Crown Timetable of every military and Crown train in the realm is set in its Timetable Hall.
Maelvine is the Commonwealth’s third-largest producer of grain handling after the two ports. Its barge yards build the flat river craft that carry the Kaelvash harvest down the Solmir.

Aerendal is a Maenari city, the largest in the Threnwood, built among the groves the Church tolerates. Its sawmills and cooperages work the March’s timber, and the forest road, jointly kept with Zelesti under the Treaty of the Threnwood (Realm Year 1287), runs west from it to Zelesti.

Kharvesh is the southern end of the Oath Line and the desert’s trading door. Tesshare-speaking caravan masters assemble here for the crossing south, and Skeinvash is heard in its back streets. The Crown garrisons it, taxes the track, and watches the smugglers it cannot stop.
The Closed Naval Cities
The Royal Navy has no berth in either civilian port. It sails from two closed cities built for it alone, and holds one forward station offshore.

rows.t: 90 km up the coast from Linhaven
110 km down the coast from Solmara
The head of a long drowned valley, with one narrow mouth closed by a sea-gate
A horseshoe bay under grey basalt headlands
Linhaven Fleet, ~160 hulls: line ships, cruising squadrons, anti-piracy flotillas
Solmara Fleet, ~140 hulls: coastal frigates, patrol cutters, harbor guard
The Royal Shipyards, the only yards in the realm where line ships and heavy frigates are laid down
Repair, refit, and drydock yards; cutters, sloops, brigs, and tenders are built here
The Admiral of the Navy, who also commands the Linhaven Fleet

blocks.text: The fleets keep the names of the ports that once held them, though neither sails from them.
Access. Both cities are closed districts. Only the following may enter:
Serving men of the Royal Navy and the Crown yards;
Guild shipwrights, riggers, smiths, and ropewrights holding a sealed Yard Pass;
The households of these men, who live within the walls;
Crown Wardens, Constables, and Magistrals on lawful warrant;
The Church’s Field Priests;
Camp Servitors posted to the victualling yards, barracks, and galleys.

Merchants, foreigners, pilgrims, visitors, and idle citizens do not enter. There is no exchange, no foreign quarter, and no market beyond the victuallers who provision the resident households. The cities exist for the fleet and the yards and for nothing else.

The walls and the waters. Each city is ringed by a wall and a cleared belt of ground. The Closed Waters extend 40 km to sea and 15 km up and down the coast on each side, and no vessel enters them without a Crown pilot. Fishing boats are barred. The Seaboard Road turns inland around each district and rejoins the coast 20 km beyond it. No road crosses the walls from the civilian side.

The Ember Isles Station. The Royal Navy keeps one station beyond the two closed cities: Vaelance Isle Station, on the primary islet of the Ember Isles, some 150 km off the Solmara Coast. It is a forward anchorage, repair slip, and watch-station of the Solmara Fleet, and it holds the seaward lookout over the eastern approaches. It has no town, no civilian quarter within its perimeter, and no rail spur; its stores and relief crews come by sea from Greywake. Like the two cities, it is closed: no civilian may enter the station without naval permission, and the channels to the neighbouring islets are under naval patrol. The station answers to the Admiralty and the Solmara Fleet, and to no satrap. The civilian district beside it, including the civilian quay in Vaelance Harbor, is described under The Ember Isles, below.

The Naval Spurs. Each city is joined to the realm by a sealed rail spur with no civilian station. The Keelhold Spur leaves the Ashvael Cargo-way 190 km inland, so that Thaldrin iron and Threnwood timber reach the Royal Shipyards without passing through Linhaven’s merchant yards. The Greywake Spur leaves the Solmir Line at Maelvine and runs 300 km without touching Solmara. The junctions are manned by the Rail & Cargo-way Corps, and a train for either city does not stop at any town on the way.

Authority. The Satrap’s writ stops at the district wall. Inside it the Admiral (at Keelhold) or the Commodore (at Greywake) holds the gate, the yards, and the fleet, but not the law. The Crown Wardens keep order, the Magistracy hears the cases, and neither answers to the Admiral.
The fleets abroad. Keelhold and Greywake are a day’s sail from Linhaven and Solmara, and the fleets cover both ports from their own bases.
The Civilian Ports
Solmara and Linhaven are civilian deepwater ports, and nothing else.
No warship of any flag, no naval establishment, and no naval officer on duty may enter either harbor.

The Crown Naval Basins are gone, and the harbors are open to merchant hulls of every nation, foreign included. The Customs Ward and the Pilot Guild, once the work of the Suraela Entrepôt, sit at both ports.
The harbors are governed by their own city magistracies and Harbor-Masters, under the Satrap’s oversight and the Crown Wardens’ law.
Solmara carries the grain and wine of the Solmir, the business of the Concordance, and the commerce of the Drazhmir lanes. Linhaven carries the ore, timber, and Duraken craft-goods of the Ashvael.
Coastal Settlements
Fishing Villages — Local Maritime Communities
The Commonwealth’s 1,100 km coastline supports numerous small fishing villages.
Inshore Boats — small craft operating close to shore.
Village Watch Crews — local militia reporting suspicious activity to Solmara or Linhaven.
Saltworks & Smokehouses — food production supporting both civilian and naval supply chains.
Role: Provide food, local knowledge, and auxiliary support without interfering in Crown naval operations. Notes: These villages cannot host foreign ships or large merchant vessels.
The Ember Isles
Crown Territory, 150 km offshore of the Solmara Coast

The Ember Isles are a small Crown-held archipelago about 150 km off the southern seaboard, administered under direct Royal Navy authority. They contain no towns, but they hold a strategic naval installation and five permanent civilian settlements spread across several islets.

rows.t: Forward anchorage, repair facility, communications center, and lookout post
Boats work the offshore banks within sight of the naval beacon
Western waters, sister settlement to Brinemoor
Deep-water net fishing; maintains navigational beacons
Largest farming settlement; volcanic-soil barley and orchard plots
Shares an easterly islet with Maelvinelet
Shares an easterly islet with Stonebank
Terraced fields; grain, produce, and livestock

blocks.text: The archipelago supports no foreign trade or shipping and answers directly to the Crown in all external affairs. Most supplies arrive from Solmara or by naval tender from Greywake.
Vaelance Isle Station

"Vaelance is the fleet's eyes on the horizon and the trade lanes' shield. Its purpose is not to withstand a months-long siege, but to ensure no threat reaches the Solmara Coast unseen, and to buy the Royal Navy time to strike."

Vaelance Isle Station is the Royal Navy's forward base in the archipelago. It hosts the Solmara Fleet's forward anchorage, repair slips, communications center, and principal lookout over the maritime approaches to the Solmara Coast.

The station's military docks, defenses, magazines, and operational facilities are under exclusive Admiralty jurisdiction. Civilian access to the station is strictly prohibited and requires explicit naval permission. The civilian settlements are separated from the station by patrolled waters, and no civilian resident may enter the station without authorization.
Strategic Doctrine

rows.t: Trade lane security and quick-response interdiction

blocks.text: Trade safeguard. The station's cutters and sloops continuously patrol the merchant routes about 150 km offshore, deterring commerce raiders, protecting shipping, and keeping the regional trade lanes safe.

The tripwire role. In the event of foreign naval intrusion or open warfare, Vaelance Station acts as a forward picket. Its vessels and marine outposts give the Solmara Fleet immediate warning and delay hostile forces long enough for the mainland defenses and fleet elements to mobilize.
Garrison and Flotilla

rows.t: Senior Captain (Grade 3), Crown-commissioned; commands the station and its flotilla; may dispatch warning directly to the Commodore of Solmara and the Admiralty
Seven Hearths of Marines (~900 men), under a Colonel
~900 shore staff: shipwrights, armorers, and command personnel

blocks.text: The Commandant of Vaelance, a Senior Captain commissioned by the Crown, commands the station. The Marine regiment is led by a Colonel, his peer in grade. The Commandant answers to the Commodore of Solmara at Greywake, and through him to the Admiral of the Navy. In a tripwire event he may send warning directly to the Commodore and the Admiralty without waiting on any other authority.
The Settlements

Brinemoor is a fishing village on the islet north of Vaelance Station. Its vessels work the offshore banks within sight of the naval beacon. Civilly it answers to the Solmara Coast Satrapy, but its watch crews report directly to Vaelance Station.
Tidewatch is a smaller sister settlement to Brinemoor. It specializes in deep-water net fishing and the maintenance of navigational beacons.
Embercroft is the largest agricultural settlement, on its own islet, known for volcanic-soil barley production and orchard plots.
Stonebank and Maelvinelet are smaller hamlets built among terraced fields and rocky ridges. They share a neighboring agricultural islet and raise grain, produce, and livestock.

rows.t: Western group (Vaelance Isle and the islet to its north)
Vaelance Isle Station; Brinemoor and Tidewatch
Naval operations; seafood production, coastal labor, beacon maintenance
Barley, orchards, terraced agriculture, livestock, and produce

blocks.text: Vaelance Harbor

Vaelance Harbor is the only true deep-water port in the Ember Isles. It serves military and civilian purposes through two separate administrations sharing one natural anchorage. By long precedent the harbor keeps a civilian quay, set apart from the station's docks, so that civilian traffic can use the only deep-water port in the archipelago without touching the naval installation. The quay carries island supply and fishing traffic only; the Ember Isles conduct no foreign trade.

rows.t: All military docks, repair slips, anchorages, magazines, and restricted waters; naval movements and security
Appointed through the Ember Isles Magistrate
The civilian waterfront outside the station perimeter: civil quay, warehouse district, fishing moorings, cargo records, and distribution of island supplies

blocks.text: Most vessels arriving at Vaelance are Commonwealth supply ships, fishing craft, mail packets, or government transports. On arrival, the Civil Harbor Master reviews each civilian cargo manifest to verify destinations and compliance with island regulations. Goods are unloaded into the civilian warehouses, and licensed contractors and local carriers move them by small coastal craft to Brinemoor, Tidewatch, Embercroft, Stonebank, and Maelvinelet.

The Ember Isles are not an international port of trade and keep no permanent customs service. Foreign commercial shipping is directed to Solmara, the Commonwealth's designated seaborne entrepôt and customs authority. Foreign vessels enter Vaelance Harbor only under special circumstances, such as diplomatic missions, naval visits, or emergencies at sea, and are handled under Admiralty and Commonwealth regulations.
This arrangement lets the civilian settlements receive regular supplies and trade among themselves without opening the naval station to the public.
Administration of the Ember Isles

The Ember Isles are attached to the Solmara Coast Satrapy and form a recognized civilian district of the Royal Commonwealth. Their residents hold the same rights, protections, and obligations as all Commonwealth citizens.

A Crown Magistrate, permanently stationed on Vaelance Isle, conducts civil administration. Appointed by the Crown and answerable to the Satrap of Solmara Coast, the Magistrate is the senior civilian authority for the archipelago and oversees:
Taxation
Public records
Accommodation and records for the Ember Isles Municipal Court
Harbor regulation
Public works
Relations among the settlements

The mayors and village councils of Brinemoor, Tidewatch, Embercroft, Stonebank, and Maelvinelet report to the Magistrate on matters of civil governance. Matters beyond the Magistrate's authority go to the Satrap of Solmara Coast, who carries them to the Crown.

Justice on the islands belongs to the Magistracy, not to the Magistrate. The Ember Isles Municipal Court sits on Vaelance Isle with a single Magistral and a leased Harmonist, hearing minor civil and criminal matters and guardianship and indenture review. Its appeals run to the Solmara Coast Regional Court and from there to the Grand Bench of Suraela.

The Royal Navy holds exclusive jurisdiction over Vaelance Isle Station and all military facilities. Naval officers exercise no ordinary civil authority over the island settlements, except as Commonwealth law provides during emergencies, wartime mobilization, or declared disasters.

The arrangement follows the Commonwealth principle that military forces serve the Crown and its citizens and are not instruments of civil government. Whatever the size of the naval presence, the Ember Isles remain a civilian district governed through Commonwealth institutions under the Solmara Coast Satrapy.

"The presence of Vaelance Isle Station does not alter the civil status of the Ember Isles, whose inhabitants are represented and governed as citizens of the Royal Commonwealth under the authority of the Solmara Coast Satrapy."
Civil and Military Hierarchies
Judicial: Ember Isles Municipal Court → Solmara Coast Regional Court → Grand Bench of Suraela
Civil administration: Village Council / Mayor → Ember Isles Magistrate → Satrap of Solmara Coast → Crown
Military: Commandant of Vaelance → Commodore of Solmara (Solmara Fleet Command) → Admiralty
Civil–Military Interaction

Population
Suraela Entrepôt: The Land Trade

Suraela is the Commonwealth’s sole port of call for foreign overland commerce. It has no foreign quay: the only water at Suraela is the Ashvael, and the capital’s River Quay is closed to every foreign hull. The old Merchant Docks, the Pilot Guild, and the Merchant Harbors are gone. In their place the Entrepôt works as a land trade-city beside the capital’s rail-head.
Merchant Yards. Bonded wagon-parks and warehouses where caravans from the Calvesset Consortium, the Kaeyrian crossing, and the Shimmerwind track unload and reload under seal.
Customs Ward. Crown inspectors who assess tariffs on every load that enters or leaves the Entrepôt.
Carriers’ Guild. The licensed caravan masters, wagoners, and guides who move foreign goods along the authorised routes; it takes the place of the Pilot Guild.
Foreign Quarter. The licensed lodging, counting-houses, and chapels of resident foreign factors.

The River Quay. The Suraela River Quay and dockyard serve the Ashvael and carry the capital’s river trade. The river above Linhaven passes only shallow-draft craft, so no sea-going hull, foreign or Commonwealth, can reach the capital. Foreign cargo landed at Linhaven passes the Customs Ward there and goes upriver under seal in Commonwealth-flag barges of the River Guild. Foreign craft coming down from the Kaeyrian Gate stop at the Gate’s customs yard, where their loads are re-loaded to Commonwealth barges, as at every other frontier crossing. Foreign crews go no farther than Linhaven or the Gate.

Goods that arrive by sea at Solmara or Linhaven and are bound for the interior pass the Customs Ward at the port, and may go on by rail, road, or sealed barge; the Entrepôt itself handles only what comes by land and by rail.
Infrastructure
“The Crown pipes the square. The house pipes itself.” — Zeythari saying

A foreign lord who rides in on the Oath Line sees clear water in every town and takes it for plenty. It is not plenty. The Commonwealth has not put clean water in its houses; it has put it in its squares. Every town has a stone well-house fed by a warded main, and its households come to it with jars and carts as their grandfathers came to the old well. A tap in a private kitchen costs a laborer a year of wages or more, and hot water in a private house costs many times that. For nearly every household, hot water means the public bathhouse, which is two halls under one roof, one for men and one for women. What the Crown builds for every household is the well-house, the cesspit and the drain, the bathhouse, and the streetlamp. These are the necessities, they are very costly, and the Crown pays for them. Everything beyond them, the lamp in the private hall included, is a luxury, and a household that wants it buys it.

The realm builds far ahead of the way it lives. This section sets out what the Crown, the guilds, and the Ember trades have built, what each system is for, and who may use it. For more details on the Infrastructure of the Commonwealth, see Appendix P: Works and Industry of the Commonwealth.
I. Foundational Principle
The infrastructure of Zeythari is not ornamental, nor indulgent. It exists to serve three inseparable purposes:
Preservation of Life
Sustainment of Industry and Defense
Endurance of the Realm under Siege or Isolation

Unlike neighboring powers, Zeythari treats Weavefire not as spectacle or privilege, but as regulated applied engineering. Every system described here is designed for reliability, redundancy, and survivability in war.

The Crown builds for the town and the realm and does not build for the house. Every mile of main, every ward, every crystal, and every licensed Ember worker is paid for out of a treasury that also pays the Warhost, so the Crown spends first on what keeps a town alive and a siege survivable and puts it where every household can reach it. What remains, a household buys.

rows.t: Necessity: Crown-built, open to every household
The well-house: piped, purified water drawn at the spout, free of charge
The town cesspit or city drain, cleared and broken down by the town
A water-closet on the city sewer trunk
The public bathhouse, three Thal at the door
Hot water laid on in the house
Ever-lamps on the streets and in civic buildings

blocks.text: II. The Road System

The Commonwealth is a realm of the older age on its roads. No engine runs on them. Coaches, wagon-trains, mounted couriers, and foot travelers move over stone and gravel laid and kept by the Crown and the guilds. An express coach covers about 120 km a day with changes of horses, a freight wagon about 28 km, and a man on foot about 30.

Contract-Roads. Three trunk roads link Suraela to the realm’s outer doors. They are built, graded, and kept under Venshal contract by the road-factors of the Guild Concordance, paid by tolls at a Crown-fixed rate, and certified by the Crown Engineers.

rows.t: Suraela, Hearthwall, Aerendal, the Kaeyrian Gate

blocks.text: Crown Roads. Roads of the Warhost, kept by the Crown Engineers and held open in war by the Auxiliaries. They are the Oath Road from Ashward through Duskhearth, Suraela, and Kaelvash to Kharvesh; the Sundral Road from Hearthwall to Sundralkeep; and the Wall Road, which runs behind the Ashward wall-forts from citadel to citadel. They have strategic priority over civilian traffic.
Satrapy Roads. The lesser roads of each satrapy, built from public-works grants the Satraps petition the Assembly for and kept by the town councils.
The Seaboard Road. About 950 km of coast road linking the fishing villages and saltworks. It runs inland of the two closed naval districts.

The Caravan Track. From Kharvesh south through the Shimmerwind to the Aidionic border: a marked track with wells about every 35 km, held by two forts, garrisoned and taxed. Wellstead towns and villages of the Homesteading Grant line it, among them Sunderwell, Dunemark, and Southgate.
The Pilgrim Ways. Church-secured routes to the First Standard Shrine at Ashward, the Sundral High Chapels, and the Threnwood Groves, held in time of war by the Emberward Host.
Every trunk road carries a posting-house about every 35 km, with stables, an ever-lamp, a Constable, and a bed for travelers, and a line of semaphore towers every 15 km runs beside it.

The rivers. The Solmir River carries barges from Maelvine to Solmara. The Ashvael River carries them from the Kaeyrian Gate through Suraela to Linhaven and is the only river that runs through the capital. Both carry the bulk goods that rail cannot afford, in shallow-draft river craft; no sea-going hull ascends either.
III. The Rail System

The Commonwealth’s railways are its most visible wonder and its costliest. Every mile belongs to the Crown. No private line exists, and no foreign rolling stock runs on Commonwealth track. The locomotives burn no coal. Each is driven by destruction-threaded arcana, sustained by a licensed Weaver aboard or by a bank of blood-quartz crystals, and re-charged at Quartz Houses placed every 250 km along the main lines. The Ironweave Works at Duskhearth builds them. Civil trains are run by the Crown Rail Service of Infrastructure & Works. Military trains are run by the Rail & Cargo-way Service under the Warden of the Oath’s timetable, and they take precedence over everything else on the line.

Express trains average about 60 km/h, freight about 35, and loaded military trains about 50. The network exists first for the Warhost, Crown administration, and guild commerce. Civilian passage is permitted only when military movements, Crown traffic, and contracted freight do not require the available capacity. Passenger coaches are attached to scheduled mixed trains or to dedicated passenger services run when the line is free. Passage costs 1 Zarim per 100 km travelled. Civilian trains may be delayed, canceled, or rescheduled without notice when military necessity or guild freight receives priority. A cargo-way is a freight-only line.

Double-tracked trunk to the northern port
Joins the Oath Line at Kaelvash; double-tracked trunk to the southern port
Suraela, Hearthwall, Aerendal, the Kaeyrian Gate
Single track, with branches to the Sundral wall-forts
Behind the Ashward wall-forts, citadel to citadel
Lateral line joining the Oath Line at Ashward

The only rail in the Wastes

blocks.text: In all, some 5,800 km of line serve the realm. They reach every major city and twenty-one of the twenty-four citadels. The three that stand off the rail are the outer Shimmerwind fort and two high-pass forts of the Sundral March, which are served by Crown Road and mule-train. No line crosses a frontier. The Threnwood Line ends at the Kaeyrian Gate’s customs yard, and the Zelesti Spur ends at the citadel wall, and goods bound across the border are re-loaded to wagons.

The Crown Rail network is the largest of the realm’s magical works. Its locomotives use the same smokeless arcano-steam principles as the naval engines, and its lines are engineered with redundant bridges, hardened tunnels, and rapid-repair engineer detachments.
Strategic Effect: The Commonwealth can redeploy troops, supplies, and relief forces faster internally than any neighboring power can march externally.
A. How the Realm Is Connected

Suraela is the hub of both systems, and Hearthwall is the hub of the Warhost. Every trunk line and every Contract-Road run to the capital, so that goods, officials, and armies converge on the plain. Hearthwall sits on the western approach, where the Threnwood and Sundral lines meet, and from there the Warden of the Oath can send a field army to any frontier. The two ports and the two naval cities are each reached by their own line, and the Oath Line joins the northern and southern frontiers to the capital and to each other.
IV. Water: The Well-House Network

Water is drawn by deep-well arcano-steam pumps, stabilized by Control-Thread lattices, and carried by aqueduct and pipe to the well-house of every town. Creation-Thread purification wards operate continuously within the cisterns and main lines, so that the water at the spout is clean whatever the river upstream. In a city the well-house stands at the head of each quarter. In a town it stands on the square.

The well-house is the Commonwealth’s unit of provision. The well-house is the Commonwealth's unit of provision. It is a walled and roofed stone house with spouts at which registered households may draw purified water. Each household is entitled to draw two large buckets per day for a fee of one Thal per bucket. The fee pays for upkeep of the mains, cisterns, wards, and the circuit-riders who inspect and renew the blood-quartz purification crystals. Households remain free to draw water from private wells, springs, and cisterns where these exist, but such sources lack Crown purification and protection. The Crown builds the main and the well-house through Infrastructure & Works. The town council keeps them, as it keeps the satrapy roads, and a licensed Ember worker of the Crown walks a circuit to read the wards. Etherforge engineers lay the baseline works of aqueduct and gravity main that need no Ember; the Magitek Arcaneum supplies the pumps and the wards. Additional water may be purchased during periods of surplus at the discretion of the town council.
Villages below the rank of town are not on the main. They keep their parish wells and springs.
Result: The water-fevers that empty a medieval town every few summers do not take hold where the whole town draws from one warded main.
V. Sanitation and Waste
Waste leaves the town by one of two ways, and every household has the use of one or the other.
In the cities, the household privy empties by drain into the street trunk, a sealed, resonance-reinforced channel, and is flushed by hand with a bucket from the household’s water-jar.
In the towns, the household keeps a privy over a cesspit, sealed and ward-lined, that the town’s sanitation wardens clear by cart on a fixed round.

Both ways end at a municipal node, where controlled Destruction-Thread arrays break the refuse down. No open sewage runs in a Commonwealth street. A cesspit may be dug only sealed, ward-lined, and entered in the town’s register, and the town council fines the household that lets one overflow.
Strategic Effect: Cities remain habitable during prolonged sieges without internal collapse from disease or contamination.
VI. Hot Water: The Public Bathhouse

Hot water is a public service. Every town keeps a bathhouse of the Crown: two halls under one roof, a men’s hall and a women’s hall, with separate doors, separate attendants, and a boiler-house between them. Where a geothermal exchanger is at hand the boiler-house draws on it. Elsewhere it runs on a Destruction-Thread furnace or an Ember-crystal core. Entry is three Thal. The fee helps fund attendants, crystal maintenance, and the circulation and purification systems that keep the baths clean. Though subsidized by the Crown, the bathhouse remains a service rather than a necessity, and most households attend weekly rather than daily.

The women’s hall. A woman enters the women’s hall on the leave of her master or guardian; written in a note he gives her. She presents the note and her Thals at the door, and the attendant admits her. Her escort waits outside. He may call her out at will by motioning to an attendant, who carries the summons in, and she comes. A man who enters the women’s hall commits a criminal offense, whoever he is and whatever his errand. If a girl will not leave the hall when called, the matter is a major event. The attendants send for the Crown Constable. When he arrives, every woman in the hall leaves, and only then may the guardian or his escort enter to retrieve her.

A household bathes at the bathhouse as it draws its water at the well-house. Hot water in quantity, enough to fill a bath, is found nowhere else outside the houses of the very rich. A laborer’s house heats a kettle at the hearth.
VII. Private Fixtures

A house standing on or near a main may take a private connection. A licensed pipefitter of the guilds lays it, an inspector of Infrastructure & Works passes it, and the household pays the main rent each year thereafter. Few houses do. The Crown-funded project of the Magitek Arcaneum to extend piped, purified water to private homes is under way in the cities, and it is slow, because each connection is paid for by the household that takes it. A private ever-lamp is a lamp-wright’s fitting around a resonance crystal, and the crystal is checked against the gauge each year with the streetlamps, on the Night of Kept Lamps. Light in a private house is a major luxury.

blocks.text: VIII. Public Lighting & Urban Stability
Streets and civic buildings are illuminated by ever-lamps powered by resonance crystals. Ever-lamps in a private house are a luxury (see Private Fixtures).
Illumination is smokeless, flame-free, and continuous.
Nighttime crime rates are statistically negligible in lit districts.
Doctrine Note: Lighting is classified as a public safety system, not a luxury.
IX. Smokeless Arcano-Steam Power Systems
A. Core Engine Architecture
Zeythari steam systems are heated not by combustion, but by Destruction-Thread furnaces or Ember-crystal cores, stabilized by Control-Thread matrices.
No coal
No soot
No visible exhaust
No fuel logistics dependency beyond water and trained personnel
This renders Zeythari engines exceptionally difficult to sabotage or interdict.
B. Applications

1. Steamships. Arcano-steam engines supplement sail power. Operational range is limited only by food and water. Engines are buried within armored hull sections, with no exposed boiler stacks. Naval Advantage: Enemy vessels relying on coal combustion present visible, vulnerable targets; Zeythari ships do not.

2. Factories & Power Generation. Centralized arcano-steam plants drive mills, forges, and manufactories. Power output is stable and continuous, independent of weather or fuel convoys. Industrial zones are deliberately separated from residential districts for resilience.
X. Geothermal Power & Heat Networks
Zeythari cities situated near volcanic or tectonic zones tap geothermal Weavefire exchangers. These systems provide:
District heating, including the boiler-houses of the public bathhouses
Industrial steam input
Redundant power during wartime disruption
Strategic Classification: Geothermal nodes are designated critical infrastructure and receive fortress-grade protection.
XI. Fortress-Based Anti-Air Systems (The Ember Veil)

Every citadel of the Ashward March carries a permanent anti-air defense lattice, collectively known as The Ember Veil. King Alexi authorized it in 1580 A.K. and King Theron saw it completed in 1598 A.K. It exists because of the Umbral drake raids of 1571–1574 A.K. and the wyverns that followed. Ritebound Warlocks hundreds of miles away set a target into each drake and release it, and a drake does not turn back. Walls built against ground assault left the interiors open from above.
“The mobile arm cannot be over every citadel; each citadel must kill what is sent to it.”
System components
Long-range bolt artillery
Area-denial shard and fire systems
Weather-manipulation pylons
Hardened-air barriers over the highest-value sections
A watch network of Maenari spotters, Weave-Sense watchers, and lamp-and-tube signals tying the layers together
The layers work independently or together. They are built to kill what is sent, not to turn it back.
Design estimate: 70–95% enemy attrition before the interior is reached under standard conditions.
Friend or foe: Skyguard, Farwings, and Lifewings wear a ward-token that the citadel’s Ember Veil reads as friendly.

Strategic consequence: The Ember Veil lets the Ashward citadels hold without a constant field army. The Skyguard strike enemies the Veil has already weakened, and no single aerial power can coerce Zeythari through terror raids. For more details on the Ember Veil system, see Appendix Q: The Ember Veil: Fortress-Based Anti-Air Defense

The Crown holds twenty-four months of national consumption in reserve, so that the well-houses and the lamps keep running if supply is cut (see Financial Reserves). The roads, bridges, harbors, and canals built by the Warhost in peacetime are described in Section IV, Infrastructure and Public Works. Healing and education, the realm’s other standing public works, are set out in Appendix B: Healing, Education, and Strategic Capacity of the Royal Commonwealth of Zeythari, and Appendix D: the Aelorian Healing Complex.
II. GOVERNMENT STRUCTURE
Government Type: Constitutional dynastic Commonwealth, tricameral in practice, consisting of the Crown, Parliament, and Assembly, each exercising a distinct sphere of authority.

Ruling House: House Karaya, Maenari in origin, was elected to the throne when the male line of the old Satyrim royal house, House Marren, failed. House Marren is extinct: its surviving lines and lands were subsumed, over the centuries, into House Karaya and the other Houses of the peerage and the Satyrim clans. Through some four centuries of repeated intermarriage with those Marren lines, the dynasty has become Satyrim by blood in all but name. The reigning branch, the line of the present King, is House Karaya.

Succession: Strict agnatic (male-line) primogeniture. No woman of any House, among any of the Nine Peoples, may inherit the Crown, hold a hereditary seat in Parliament, or claim any hereditary office under any circumstances.
Rule of Law
Vorai a’n harwain. Mith a’n cynhalia. – Truth guides us. The Oath sustains us.
The Constitution of the Royal Commonwealth of Zeythari
For the complete text of the Constitution of the Royal Commonwealth of Zeythari see Appendix F: The Constitution of Zeythariaeth.

The Constitution of the Royal Commonwealth of Zeythari (established by the Settlement of Suraela) serves as the supreme law of the realm, dissolving the former absolute monarchy and replacing it with a constitutional dynastic Commonwealth. It establishes a government of limited powers operating under strict legal supremacy where no office or institution stands above the law. Key elements of the Constitution include:

Foundational Citizenship & Service: Citizenship is earned through mandatory military or civic service and solemnized by the Oath of the Standard. Full citizen rights (voting, property ownership, legal standing) are held exclusively by enrolled male citizens (Zeythar).

Entrenched Household Structure (Darlorath): Article III strictly codifies the domestic order, placing women under male wardship (Darlorath) while maintaining that they are moral/spiritual persons under divine law rather than chattel property.

Separation of Governance & Law: It divides authority among distinct bodies, establishes an independent Magistracy to interpret law and review constitutional challenges, and ensures the Church maintains its own distinct domain over doctrine and sacraments while surrendering direct temporal rule.

Rigid Constitutional Safeguards: It outlines strict legislative procedures, provincial and frontier protections, emergency limits, and highly entrenched amendment requirements to prevent any single institution from seizing total power.
The Four Pillars

Constitutional scholars traditionally describe the Commonwealth as resting upon four distinct pillars built UPON the foundation of the Constitution (distinct from the Church’s Four Pillars of Sacred Femininity — Obedience, Grace, the Cultivation of Beauty, and Feminine Dress — set out in the Holy Book of Truth and Grace, Part Nine):
The Crown, which governs;
Parliament, which restrains;
The Assembly, which funds;
And the Church, which binds.

No pillar is sufficient alone, as all four derive their authority from, and are bound by, the supreme text of the Constitution. A King without revenue depends upon the Assembly. An Assembly without Parliament’s assent cannot legislate. Parliament cannot govern without the Crown. Even Crown and Parliament together must account for a Church whose schools, courts, charities, convents, and military orders command loyalties extending into every satrapy of the realm. Yet above all four stands the Constitution as the foundational bed-rock, ensuring no single pillar can alter its own limits or govern the Commonwealth alone.
Governance in Practice

Power within Zeythari is deliberately distributed rather than concentrated. Each institution operates within clearly defined limits, and no authority exists without oversight. Emergency powers may be exercised when necessary, but they remain subject to review and accountability. Oaths carry legal force rather than merely symbolic value, and institutions are designed to favor procedure over personal dominance.
As a result, Zeythari governance derives its resilience not from the absence of conflict, but from its capacity to absorb and contain conflict without jeopardizing the stability of the state.
Constitutional Foundations

rows.t: The Constitution is written and entrenched. It is the product of the Constitutional Settlement (see Section X), which in Realm Year 1780 (1380 A.K.) dissolved the old Kingdom of Zeythar and replaced it with the Commonwealth. Crown, Parliament, Assembly, Church, and Magistracy each hold their sphere under it, and no office stands above it.
The Magistracy alone. The full Grand Bench of fifteen sits on constitutional questions and may rule any law or decree unconstitutional.

Passed by two-thirds of the Delegates of the Assembly and by two-thirds of Parliament, then given Royal Assent. An amendment touching oaths of office, the sacraments, or the order of the household also requires the concurrence of the Holy Synod. The marcher protections are entrenched and may be amended only by the same two-thirds vote in both chambers.

A man is Confirmed at sixteen and swears the Oath of the Standard; serves four years; is discharged at twenty at the Confirmation Musters; and is enrolled on the oath-roll kept by the Royal Census and Demography Office. Enrolment makes him a Zeythar, with the vote, the right to sue, and the right to speak before the Crown. A citizen convicted by the Magistracy of oath-violation or treason is struck from the roll and loses vote, dagger, and standing among men.
No woman is a citizen, a party, or an officer. She stands in law by her relation to her master or guardian, and every act touching her is his, brought and answered in his name.
Each March returns a fixed bloc of Assembly seats that no redistricting may reduce, and the Office of Marcher Affairs hears frontier petitions as of right.
Suraela: the Royal Palace and Great Hall of Audience, the House of Peers, the Assembly Hall, the Grand Bench of the Magistracy, and Kaervast Cathedral.

blocks.text: Impeachment
The Assembly alone may initiate it. Parliament sits as the high court for the trial and, on a finding, removes the officer. Any criminal sentence thereafter lies with the Magistracy alone.
Relationship with the Church
Zeythari follows a dual-pillar model of governance, in which spiritual and temporal authority remain distinct yet complementary.
The Church governs doctrine, sacraments, oaths, and trials of heresy.
The Crown governs civil law, military command, the economy, and public infrastructure.
Matters concerning oaths of office, moral legislation, and other areas of shared jurisdiction require cooperation between both institutions.

The Church of the Sworn Flame is institutionally independent and retains the authority to withdraw sacramental or military support if it judges doctrine to be endangered. It neither commands the armies of the Crown nor submits its theology to royal direction.
Household Authority and Canon Law

In Zeythari doctrine, the household is the smallest and most sacred unit of order, from which all higher authority flows. As the Crown governs the realm and the Church guards the soul, so too does the father or master govern the hearth entrusted to him. This authority is not merely customary, but sacramental in nature: the father stands as first guardian of his children, and master of his wife. The master assumes that charge by covenantal vow upon marriage. Within the bounds of Crown law and Church doctrine, his word in the household is binding. The Church does not presume to sever a woman from her lawful master, nor to claim her service without his consent, for to do so would be to profane the very order it is sworn to uphold.

This authority is understood not as license, but as sacred trust. Canon law teaches that a guardian’s power exists for protection, provision, and moral guidance, and that cruelty or neglect constitutes oath-violation rather than rightful rule. Accordingly, the Church honors the decisions of fathers and husbands in matters of marriage, service, and recall, while reserving judgment against those who abuse their charge. A woman who enters permanent sacred service does so only when lawfully offered, and once received, she passes fully into the guardianship of the Church. In this way, Zeythari preserves a clear and visible chain of responsibility—from hearth to altar to Crown—ensuring that authority is never unclaimed, and obedience is never without account.
Leadership Hierarchy

rows.t: Executive head of state and supreme commander of the armed forces. Sets foreign policy, ratifies treaties (with Parliament’s concurrence), appoints Marshals and confirms elected Satraps, and convenes or dissolves the Assembly. Holds no ordinary vote in either chamber but must give Royal Assent before any bill of Parliament or Assembly becomes law. Exercises direct command authority over military rank and precedence, as the King’s Reckoning (see Section IV) currently demonstrates. The Crown cannot levy taxes or authorize spending without the Assembly’s consent, cannot alter property rights unilaterally, and is bound by the Constitution like any other office — a monarch can be tried by the Magistracy for criminal acts committed as a private man, though never for acts of state. The Crown sits as the final court of appeal in capital cases. The Crown may respond to raids, piracy, demonic incursions, and border emergencies under its ordinary military authority. Formal declarations of war against a foreign sovereign power require certification by Parliament.

The upper, hereditary chamber. Seats are held by the great Houses of the Maenari, the clan-lords of the Satyrim (the Marren-descended clans foremost among them), the Grand officers of the three military orders by courtesy seat, and the Maestrai Houses (born of unions between the other two peoples). Holds the final word in legislation, with an absolute veto over any Assembly bill; alone competent to certify a formal declaration of war; sits as the high court for trials of treason. Though formally united by chamber, Parliament is rarely a single bloc. Maenari lineage-lords, Satyrim clan houses, military-order representatives, and Maestrai cadet branches maintain distinct interests and alliances. The chamber’s reputation is one of stubborn caution; peers often describe their role less as making policy than preventing reckless policy from being made.

The lower, elected chamber. Elected by universal male suffrage among male citizens of all nine peoples — Confirmed at sixteen, but seated on the franchise only upon completing the mandatory four years’ active service at twenty. Controls ordinary legislation, all taxation, and the Commonwealth Treasury (the Royal Chancellery collects and pays under its authority), and alone holds the power to initiate impeachment.

Provincial administration, divided by the character of the ground governed. Marshals hold combined military-civil authority over the frontier marches (Ashward, Sundral, Threnwood), where war readiness and civil law cannot be cleanly separated. Satraps — the term itself a holdover from the pre-Commonwealth Satyrim kingdom, when the realm still governed in the Saelkyr idiom — hold purely civil authority over the five interior provinces (Kaervast, Kaelvash, Solmara Coast, Linhaven Coast, Duskhearth). A Satrap commands no soldiers, issues no binding legal judgment, and legislates nothing; he carries the Crown’s will into his satrapy and carries his satrapy’s needs back to the Crown, overseeing tax collection, logistics, and petitioning the Assembly for public works, law enforcement, and emergency relief funding on his satrapy’s behalf.

blocks.text: The Elder Minister. The Peer of longest tenure in Parliament, not the eldest, holds the title of Elder Minister. He sits on the Privy Council with voice and no veto, and his only influence is that he sets the schedule and agenda of Parliament. The Commonwealth is some 150 years away from a true Prime Minister, and the Elder Minister holds no executive power.
The Peerage

The peerage is the hereditary nobility of three peoples: the Maenari, the Satyrim, and the Maestrai (whose Houses descend from unions between the other two). Succession is strict agnatic primogeniture. A peer’s wife, daughters, and widow hold no title of their own: their style comes from the man who holds them.

blocks.text: Exemption and Discipline of Royal Women

While the women of the Royal House (including the Queen, Queen Mother, the Heir’s wife, and the Princesses) remain exempt from public Appraiser audits and hands, they are not exempt from physical correction. They may be caned or disciplined using the Vaelisar when required, but any such correction administered by the Oathguard must be formally justified afterward to the Captain of the Oathguard.

The Twelve – Daily and Infraction Discipline: The twelve women serving the Oathguard as arbalest archers, healers, and creation mages are subject to strict military-household discipline. In addition to potential caning throughout the day for minor infractions, all female members of the Oathguard are whipped daily by the Oathguard sergeant prior to the start of their daily duty watch to maintain posture, compliance, and operational readiness.
Legislative Process, Sessions, and Decrees

Composition. The Assembly seats 360 Delegates, five-year terms, apportioned among the eight provinces by the citizen-roll of the Census Office, with a floor of twenty seats for each March. A general election is held at the Confirmation Musters, when the year-class that swore four years earlier is discharged and enrolled. Parliament seats the hereditary heads of the Great Houses (roughly seventy seats of Maenari lineage-lords, Satyrim clan-lords, and Maestrai Great Houses) and three courtesy seats for the Grand officers of the military orders. The Elder Minister sets its agenda.
See Appendix M: The Great Houses of Parliament for the Roll of Great Houses and the courtesy seats.

rows.t: Any bill may originate in either chamber. Every bill of taxation or appropriation originates in the Assembly alone. The Crown does not introduce bills; it sends Messages to either chamber.
Debate and passage by a majority of Delegates.
Passage, amendment, or absolute veto. An amended bill returns to the Assembly. Both chambers must agree on one text.
The Crown assents or withholds. A bill withheld may be presented again after one session.
The Royal Clerks enter the statute. The proceedings and the text are recorded in the Lore by a leased Harmonist, and a fair copy passes to the Royal Archive.
The Magistracy hears any challenge to the statute’s constitutionality, and its ruling binds Crown, Parliament, and Assembly alike.

blocks.text: Sessions. Both chambers sit in two sessions each year: one opening after the Confirmation Musters in spring and one after the Vintage in autumn. The Crown convenes both, and dissolves the Assembly only by a writ that orders a general election within ninety days. The Assembly meets in the Assembly Hall and Parliament in the Hall of Memory and Stewardship. The Joint Treasury Commission sits permanently.

Royal Decrees. Within its own sphere (command of the armed forces, military precedence, foreign policy, appointments, and the ordering of the Royal Household) the Crown acts by decree. A decree binds the Crown’s own servants. It is not statute, a statute supersedes it, and the Magistracy reviews it. The King’s Reckoning stands as a decree of this kind (see Section IV).
Emergency Powers

rows.t: Raids, piracy, demonic incursions, and frontier alarms are met under the Crown’s ordinary military authority, with no declaration.
Declared by the Crown with the Privy Council for invasion, rebellion, famine, or a disaster of the realm.
Thirty days. Renewal requires a resolution of both chambers.

The Provincial Administration’s emergency authority takes effect; Marshals may extend authority across a provincial border on the Crown’s order; the Crown Roads and the rail network pass to the Crown Timetable; reserves are drawn only on release by the Joint Treasury Commission with Royal Assent.
The Crown may not suspend the Magistracy, alter the succession, levy a tax, or alter property rights. Every act is reviewable by the Magistracy afterward, and the Lore keeps the record.
A formal declaration against a foreign sovereign power is a separate act and requires certification by Parliament.

blocks.text: Succession and Regency

rows.t: Strict agnatic primogeniture in House Karaya. No woman inherits the Crown or transmits a claim.

A Council of Regency of three, confirmed by Parliament: the nearest adult male of House Karaya as Regent, the Elder Minister, and the Archsworn. The Queen Mother holds the child King’s person and household only, and sits on no council.
The Privy Council certifies it, Parliament affirms it, and the Council of Regency governs until the King recovers or dies.
As in Realm Year 1752, Parliament elects a lord of one of the Great Houses, the Assembly is informed, and the Archsworn crowns him.

blocks.text: Administrative System
Civil governance

The realm is divided into eight provinces of two kinds. The five interior Satrapies are administered by elected Satraps, confirmed by the Crown. The three frontier Marches are each under a Crown-appointed Marshal whose jurisdiction blends military readiness with civil law. The provinces, their seats, rulers, areas, and populations are set out in Section I (Satrapies and Marches). The Threnwood March was carved from the western strips of Kaervast and Kaelvash to strengthen frontier defense; Kaervast is the capital satrapy; Duskhearth is the Thaldrin mining district.
Regional divisions

For civil matters, each march or satrapy answers to its Marshal or Satrap. For church law, they answer to a Praesul or diocesan Priest Confessor. These civil and ecclesiastical hierarchies operate in parallel; neither commands the other, and each maintains its own courts, records, and procedures.
Provincial Government in Practice

Crown Wardens and Constables, answerable to the Magistracy and not to the Satrap
Wardens and Constables answer to the Magistracy, but the Marshal holds the civil power in the March
A Praesul’s see (Kaervast is the Archsworn’s own diocese)
The Office of Marcher Affairs, and the Marcher seats of the Assembly

blocks.text: Municipal Authority

Towns, cities, and villages govern themselves through elected town councils, city magistracies, and village reeves, typically headed by an elected Mayor. Only citizen‑men of full standing (age 20+, service completed, Oath sworn) may vote. These bodies oversee markets, roads and waterways, sanitation, guild licensing, town watches, and other civic concerns. Their authority is strictly local and subordinate to provincial law. Unlike Marshals or Satraps, they hold no military jurisdiction and may levy no independent taxation beyond what Crown and Assembly statutes permit.

In practice, a Zeythari citizen is more likely to encounter his elected town council than a provincial Satrap. The Commonwealth’s local institutions are therefore widely regarded as schools of civic participation rather than rivals to royal authority.
Bureaucratic Institutions
The Commonwealth’s administrative apparatus is broad, specialized, and deliberately divided to prevent the concentration of authority. Its major institutions include:

Guild Concordance — Venshal‑speaking trade inspectors and contract courts headquartered in Solmara, responsible for regulating commerce, adjudicating guild disputes, and enforcing the Commonwealth’s trade codes. It also licenses private Weavefire workings for trade.
Canon Almoners — Church‑appointed auditors charged with reviewing every convent and diocesan ledger. They ensure ecclesiastical finances remain transparent, lawful, and doctrinally compliant.

Magistracy — The Commonwealth’s independent judiciary, overseeing civil and criminal law, maintaining courts across all marches and provinces, and serving as the sole authority competent to declare a man criminal.
Circle of Memory — The Church’s Order of Harmony, keeper of the Commonwealth’s official record. Maintains archives, lineage rolls, treaties, charters, and the sworn oaths of public office.

Royal Chancellery of the Treasury — Collects revenue, maintains the Commonwealth’s accounts, oversees the Mint, and manages bullion reserves. Executes the Assembly’s appropriations under constitutional constraint.
Treasury Office — The Assembly’s fiscal arm. Sets tax rates, drafts appropriations, and prepares the annual budget submitted for reconciliation with Parliament.

Office of Weights & Measures: Responsible for maintaining standardized units of length, mass, volume, and currency weight across the Commonwealth. Certifies scales, balances, and commercial instruments; inspects markets and guild workshops; prosecutes fraud involving adulterated goods or false measures. Ensures uniformity between the Mint’s coinage standards and commercial trade practices.
Royal Mint Authority — A major sub‑office of the Chancellery. Oversees coinage, anti‑counterfeiting measures, and the Commonwealth’s bullion reserves.
Royal Bank of Zeythari — The chartered national bank, independent of the Crown and Assembly. Manages public credit, stabilizes currency, and oversees large‑scale financial instruments.

Joint Treasury Commission — Ten members drawn from each chamber, standing permanently to reconcile the budget, audit Crown accounts, and authorize any expenditure above 500 Sol (50,000 Zarims). Prevents either chamber from starving or inflating the Treasury unilaterally.

Bureau of Weavefire — The civil authority responsible for licensing, registering, and educating all emberborn. Maintains demographic records, certifies magical instruction, investigates misuse of Weavefire, and coordinates with both Marshals (for frontier defense) and Praesuls (for sacramental compliance).
Office of Provincial Works — Oversees roads, bridges, canals, public buildings, and emergency infrastructure repairs. Works closely with Satraps and municipal councils to maintain civil cohesion.
Royal Census and Demography Office — Maintains population rolls, land registries, tax assessments, and migration records. Essential for administering universal male suffrage tied to service.
Office of Frontier Logistics — Supports Marshals with supply chains, fortification maintenance, and emergency provisioning during raids, incursions, or demonic threats.
Commonwealth Education Concord — Standardizes curricula, certifies instructors, and oversees civic education, including the oath instruction required before full citizenship.

Office of Heraldry and Lineage — Maintains noble genealogies, coats of arms, succession records, and peerage legitimacy. Works closely with Parliament and the Circle of Memory to prevent disputes of rank or inheritance.
Office of Maritime Safety — Regulates ports, shipping lanes, lighthouse maintenance, and piracy reporting. Critical for the Solmara and Linhaven coasts.
Office of Guild Oversight — Works alongside the Guild Concordance to review guild charters, mediate labor disputes, and enforce professional standards across all trades.

Office of Public Oaths — A joint Church–Crown bureau that records sworn contracts, marriage covenants, apprenticeship oaths, and service pledges. Ensures that all binding promises carry legal and sacramental force.
Office of Satrapal Review — Audits Satraps, investigates corruption, and ensures provincial compliance with Commonwealth law. Acts as a safeguard against local overreach or neglect.

Office of Marcher Affairs — Established after the Marcher Siege. Ensures frontier petitions are heard, coordinates with Marshals, and prevents the neglect that once threatened the stability of the realm.

Bureau of Civic Decorum — Enforces Commonwealth sumptuary laws governing dress, luxury goods, heraldic display, and public markers of rank.
