Works jointly with the Office of Heraldry and Lineage to prevent unlawful appropriation of noble styles, and with municipal councils to regulate markets selling restricted items. Investigates violations, issues fines, and maintains the Commonwealth’s register of permitted garments and insignia by rank, profession, and oath‑standing.

Office of Foreign Affairs (the Chancery of Envoys) — Staffs the Crown’s envoys, receives foreign ambassadors, and drafts treaties in the name of Zeythariaeth for the Chancellor’s seal and Parliament’s concurrence. Works with the Customs Ward and the Foreign Quarter of the Suraela Entrepôt.
The Bureau of Civic Decorum
The Register keeps the truth of the realm’s dress. The Appraiser sees that it is worn.

The Bureau of Civic Decorum is the Crown’s standing office for the visible truth of the Commonwealth. The Church sets the marks of estate, the master or guardian sets the dress, and the Bureau sees that every mark is worn, worn truly, and never falsified, so that no man need guess at a woman’s standing, a man’s oath, or a peer’s rank (see Section VII, Dress, Status, and the Visible Oath). Its writ is the Commonwealth’s sumptuary law, the statutes on dress, luxury goods, heraldic display, and public markers of rank, together with the law against falsification of status.

Appraisers of the Bureau of Civic Decorum are authorized, during any audit of public decorum, to require an unmarried girl or woman under guardianship to bend and touch her toes so that the sigil on the upper thigh may be inspected and, where a breach is found, to administer up to six strokes of the cane. The same six-stroke tariff applies automatically to any refusal of inspection. Every adult male citizen carries a household cane or light whip as an ordinary instrument of Darlorath and may apply it at will to any woman under his guardianship; the strokes are private household correction and do not themselves constitute a public offense.
The Standard Position

Bend forward, feet slightly apart, and touch the toes (or the ground if she cannot reach). This single posture serves both glyph inspection and caning. It is practical for public audits, presents the target cleanly, allows free swing of the cane, and leaves the girl able to stand and move immediately afterward. Kneeling remains reserved exclusively for hem-length measurement by appraisers.

During any public audit, an appraiser of the Bureau of Civic Decorum may require an unmarried girl or woman under guardianship to assume the bending position so that the Apprentice Sigil may be inspected and, where a breach of decorum, dress, speech, or the Lowered Tongue is found, may administer up to six strokes of the cane. Refusal of inspection is itself a summary offense and draws an automatic additional six strokes, administered at once. The strokes are recorded against the guardian’s household.

rows.t: A Crown bureau within the Crown Administrative Service. Not a court, not a police service, and not a department of the Church. It registers, inspects, cites, fines, and seizes, and it does not sentence.
The Hall of the Register at Suraela, with a Commissioner of Decorum in each of the eight provincial seats.
The Registrar of Civic Decorum, installed through the Crown Administrative Service by examination and oath.
Citizens, installed by examination and oath. Hereditary appointment is banned.

The Office of Heraldry and Lineage (noble styles); municipal councils (markets); the Office of Weights & Measures (stamps the Appraiser’s Rule and Cane); Crown Wardens and Constables (summons and collection of fines).
The Magistracy (legality); the Joint Treasury Commission (audit); annual Returns laid before both chambers.

blocks.text: Divisions

rows.t: Keeps the Commonwealth’s register of permitted garments and insignia by rank, profession, and oath-standing. Nothing is reserved, licensed, or forbidden unless it is entered here.

With the Office of Heraldry and Lineage, prevents unlawful appropriation of noble styles: reserved metals, gemstone arrangements, and the arrangements of the peerage in the caerwevra. A merchant’s wife may wear more gold than a baroness owns, but she may not wear it cut, set, or marked in a reserved pattern. That is impersonation, and the Magistracy treats it as such. It also screens the reserved arrangements in household braids and sandal straps.
With municipal councils, regulates markets selling restricted goods and inspects stalls and goldsmiths for reserved cloth, metals, and stones.

Inspect the markings of men and the forgeries of both sexes: the Oath Dagger and its Flame sigil and First Oath glyph, the hair-bound hilt, mandatory trousers, the parish pair-mark on a Band and its marriage dagger, and counterfeit Oath-Bands and caerwevrai. A man claiming protection, authority, or marital standing without the proper dagger markings is cited for fraud.
Audit the dress of women throughout the Commonwealth. See below.

blocks.text: Ranks. The Registrar; the Commissioners of Decorum (eight); the Inspectors of Insignia and Market Inspectors; and some seven hundred Appraisers, working in circuits of a district each, about one to every forty thousand souls. The Clerks of the Register serve all of them.
The Appraiser

An Appraiser of Civic Decorum is a Crown officer of the Bureau charged with the random audit of women’s dress. He audits without notice, without complaint, and without cause, and he answers for his audits to the Commissioner of his satrapy.

rows.t: A male citizen of thirty or over, married and master of a household of his own, of clean record. Examined in the sumptuary statutes, the Register, and the use of the Rule; two years’ probation under a senior Appraiser; sworn before the Office of Public Oaths.
A grey coat and a gorget bearing the Bureau’s seal; his Oath Dagger; the Rule; the Cane; and his warrant tablet and Audit Roll.

A brass-bound rod, stamped each year by the Office of Weights & Measures, notched at the knee-line (girls twelve to fifteen), the mid-thigh line (women sixteen and over), and the band-measure (the fit of an Oath-Band upon the upper arm).
A rattan cane of the Bureau’s issue, of a length and thickness fixed by the Register and stamped by the Office of Weights & Measures. He carries no other instrument and uses no other.
One district. His warrant covers every street, market, quay, field, yard, and household in it. He does not audit within a consecrated house of worship or the Church’s cloisters.
His own. No woman need be accused, and no complaint need be filed.
He may halt any woman in the street, market, field, or road and audit her where she stands.

He stands at the threshold and calls for the master. He does not cross it without the master’s leave, and he needs no leave to summon: the master brings or sends out every woman of the household (wife, daughters, wards, widowed mother, indentured daughter) to the door or the yard. The household stands in public for the audit, and each woman presents herself in the dress her estate requires abroad. A master who refuses to produce his women is cited before the Municipal Court for obstruction of a Crown officer, and the Appraiser enters the refusal in his Roll. If the master is away, the audit proceeds at the threshold on his household, and the correction and the fine stand against him.
None exempts a household. A peer’s women are audited as a laborer’s are, and a duke is fined as a freeholder is.

blocks.text: The Audit

rows.t: The woman is halted in public, or the women of the household are called to the threshold. Each is audited alone and in order of age, eldest first.

A girl under twelve: none required. An unmarried girl of twelve and over: the face veil (Umbrmiren); a daughter under Court-ordered indenture wears the dated collar in its place. A wife: the caerwevra of her household’s station upon her hair, the face bare. A widow of working age: the caerwevra in black. A widow past the marriage market: the black caerwevra beneath the black veil. A woman wearing a covering that is not her estate’s (a caerwevra on an unmarried girl, a maiden’s veil on a wife) has falsified her status.

He orders her to kneel. She kneels upright, and he lays the Rule along the outer thigh. Girls of twelve to fifteen: a single-piece dress, the hem at the knee-line or just above it; a two-piece garment or any adult silhouette fails. Women of sixteen and over: the hem at or above the mid-thigh line; a hem below it fails. The long black dress of a widow past the marriage market is the sole exception on the road. The royal gown is read against the Register and audited at the Palace threshold (see The Royal Gown). Where a household braid is worn, the Rule is laid to its lower edge. Where she wears a cloak, he lifts it at the hip and lays the Rule on the dress hem beneath. He may then order her to lift the hem and show her glyph, or present her License or Certificate of Competence; a girl with neither is found against (see Female Emberborn and Commonwealth Law).

On a wife or a widow, he orders the arm bared where it is sleeved and checks the Band against the band-measure. It must sit on the upper arm, visible, never removed, in the metal of her station (iron, ash-steel, silver, or gold), engraved with the First Oath glyph and the sworn guardianship mark. The Band-measure is taken over the band-bed. Where she wears a cloak, he reads the Band at the window or orders the cloak opened; a cloak that cannot be opened over the arm is a concealment of the Band. A band worn by a woman unmarried is marital fraud and is reported to the nearest Constable.
His alone. He sees what he sees. No witness, no Harmonist, and no second opinion is required, and the finding is not before any court.

Every woman found non-compliant receives six strokes of the Cane across the seat, laid by the Appraiser himself there and then, at the nearest rail, post, or cart. Her master is fined five Zarims for each woman so found. The Appraiser then admonishes the master to discipline them further.

Each woman kneels and thanks the Appraiser for the correction and her master for his. The Appraiser stamps the household’s audit-slip, which protects it from a second audit that day, and enters the audit in his Roll.

blocks.text: The unescorted woman. A woman halted by an Appraiser in public with no visible male of her household (or male expressly authorized by her master) present is also subject to the Constable’s detention (see Section III, Unescorted Woman in Public). The Appraiser audits her first. If she is non-compliant, she receives her six strokes there and then, and is afterward sent to the nearest Crown Constable, who places her in the holding cage on her knees until her master is summoned. If she is compliant, she is sent to the Constable without correction. Her master pays the three Zarims fixed for the unescorted woman, and the five Zarims of the Appraiser’s fine besides if she was found non-compliant and then administers the correction the unescorted rule requires.

The fine is entered against the master’s name on the warrant and is paid at the nearest Revenue Office or to the nearest Crown Constable within seven days. The Appraiser keeps no fine and handles none. The correction is a statutory measure of the Sumptuary Statutes, laid on the Appraiser’s finding alone; it is not a criminal sentence, and no Magistral’s judgment precedes it. The master’s own duty under the Fourth Pillar stands beside it, and the Appraiser’s strokes do not discharge it.
Audit Procedure

During any public audit, an Appraiser may require an unmarried girl or woman under guardianship to bend forward, feet slightly apart, and touch her toes so that the marked cheek may be inspected and, where a breach of decorum, dress, speech, or the Lowered Tongue is found, may administer up to six strokes of the cane. Refusal of inspection is itself a summary offence and draws an automatic six strokes, administered at once. The strokes are recorded against the guardian’s household and do not require a Magistracy hearing unless the underlying breach is more serious.
Kneeling is reserved solely for the measurement of hem length. The bending position serves both inspection of the training glyph and the delivery of summary correction.
Limits and the Master’s Remedy

rows.t: Six at most for each woman in each audit, across the seat only, laid by the Appraiser or Inspector himself and never delegated to a Constable, a servant, or the master.

The Appraiser and the Bureau of Weavefire’s Inspector are the only men in the Commonwealth, other than her own master, permitted to strike a woman, and within his own charge a male instructor. They alone may strike another man’s wife. Every other man (a Constable, a Warden, a parish steward, a Magistral, a Marshal, a soldier) who lays a hand upon a woman not his own commits an offense against her master.
A stroke beyond the sixth, a stroke elsewhere than the seat, or a hurt beyond the passing mark of the Cane.

A master (or guardian) who holds that the correction was excessive may sue the Office of the Appraisers before the Municipal Court of his district, with appeal to the Regional Court and the Grand Bench. The suit is his, brought in his name, and the woman is never a party. The finding of non-compliance is not before the Court. The measure of the correction is.

The fine is paid first and recovered with the damages if the suit succeeds. The Court awards damages against the Bureau as it sets them, and the judgment is entered on the Appraiser’s Roll. Repeated entries, or one for injury, bring the Appraiser before the Registrar for removal.

The Commissioner reads every Audit Roll, and an Appraiser whose findings depart from the norm of his district is audited in turn. An Appraiser who makes findings for gain or spite, or who takes any gift, is tried as any officer for oath-violation.

Professed Sisters and every woman claimed by the Church (to touch a professed Sister is sacrilege, and the Church governs her dress entire; an Appraiser who sees one in fault reports it to her Confessor, who handles it); the Closed Naval Cities and the Servitor Quarters, which lie outside any civil circuit; and the Royal Household, which the Commissioner of Decorum for Kaervast reads at the Palace threshold (see The Royal Gown).
Crown Constables and Wardens assist an Appraiser when he asks (to summon a master, to collect a fine). They do not strike, and he has no power of arrest.

blocks.text: The Crown Administrative Service

Civil servants of the Commonwealth — clerks, auditors, record-keepers, and the working administrators who staff a Satrap’s or Marshal’s office — are installed entirely through meritocratic examination followed by a sworn oath of service. Hereditary appointment to the civil service is explicitly and categorically banned by Commonwealth law, the one bureaucratic office in the realm where lineage carries no weight whatsoever. The Archivist Lyceum is its principal feeder school, though the examination itself is open to any male citizen who can pass it.
Foundational Principle, Oath, and Offices

The CAS ensures the Commonwealth functions regardless of the virtue, vice, brilliance, or failure of any ruler. Where the Crown commands, it executes; where law is written, it applies; where institutions endure, it remembers. It is non-political and oath-bound to lawful continuity, not to personal loyalty.

rows.t: By examination and oath. Hereditary appointment is forbidden.
By merit, service record, and legal review.
Only by judicial ruling or by royal decree for cause.
The Magistracy (legal compliance); the Joint Treasury Commission (financial audit).

blocks.text: I serve the Crown by serving the law, and I serve the law by serving the people sworn beneath it.

rows.t: Provincial census and population rolls; oversight of tax assessment and collection; coordination among Satraps, Marshals, town councils, and the Crown; emergency authority during disaster or siege
Acts through the Crown’s lawful delegation
Roads, bridges, rail, ports; town water mains and well-houses; ever-lamp lighting, sanitation, and public bathhouses
May not alter military installations without the approval of the relevant Marshal, or ecclesiastical structures without Church consent
Regional granaries stocked to feed a family of five one meal a day for six months; rotating stock; emergency rationing authority
Audited jointly by the CAS and the Church
Staffs the Royal Chancellery: collectors, customs officers, assayers, accountants, and Mint officials
Acts through the Chancellor; audited by the Joint Treasury Commission

blocks.text: A hungry citizen is a failure of governance, not fate.
The Royal Chancellery of the Treasury
The Assembly sets the purse. The Commission unlocks it. The Chancellery counts what is collected and pays what is released.

The Chancellery is the Commonwealth’s fiscal executive: a Crown administrative body, staffed through the Crown Administrative Service, that collects the revenue the Assembly sets, keeps the Treasury’s accounts and reserves, disburses what the Joint Treasury Commission releases, and directs the Royal Mint. It sets no rate, makes no appropriation, and holds no legislative power.

rows.t: Nominated by the Assembly; confirmed by the Crown; personal oath of accountability to the Crown sworn before he acts (the same double gate as Satraps and Mayors)
The Privy Council, with voice and no veto. The Chancellor provides finance where others provide policy, strategy, judgment, or force
By judicial ruling of the Magistracy, or by royal decree for cause on the Assembly’s petition
Crown Administrative Service: examination and oath; hereditary appointment banned
Joint Treasury Commission (financial audit); Magistracy (legality); annual accounts laid before both chambers

May not levy or alter a tax (Assembly); may not appropriate (Assembly); may not release any sum above 500 Sol (50,000 Zarims) without the Commission; may not direct the Royal Bank; may not touch the King’s private estates, which are a separate book from the State’s
Collects the land-and-harvest levy, hearth-levy, and duties. The Satrap continues to oversee collection in his satrapy and does not collect
Port dues and caravan tolls (including the garrisoned Shimmerwind track); works alongside Guild Concordance inspectors
Master of the Mint; strikes Thals, Zarims, and Sols under the Mark of the Anvil & Sol; assay; exchange or re-striking of foreign bullion
Custody of the Zarim Reserve and the Blood Quartz Stockpile; Blood Quartz is released only jointly with the Warden of the Oath (and, for the Church orders, the Warden of the Flame)
Prepares the annual estimates for the Assembly’s Treasury Office; keeps the ledgers the Commission audits
Liaison to the Court of Governors of the Royal Bank; the Lockwright Reserve facility; the Tidemark Reserve; Ashfall Compact dues and Tidemark settlements

blocks.text: The fiscal cycle

rows.t: Absolute veto or assent; Royal Assent

blocks.text: Emergency liquidity. When urgent expenditure cannot wait for the fiscal cycle, the Chancellor petitions the Court of Governors of the Royal Bank for an advance against future appropriations or expected revenue. The advance is reported at once to the Joint Treasury Commission, entered as a charge against the next appropriation, and repaid from Assembly-appropriated funds. The Bank lends; it never spends Treasury funds.

Classified lines. A few lines, chiefly the engines contract, are heard only in closed session by a sworn subcommittee of the Joint Treasury Commission and paid by the Chancellery through a sealed sub-account (see Section IX).

The reserves. The Zarim Reserve, the Tidemark Reserve, and the Blood Quartz Stockpile are inviolable against ordinary appropriation. They are drawn only in a declared crisis (a war certified by Parliament, a general levy, a blockade, a famine, or a disaster the Commission certifies) and then only on release by the Commission with Royal Assent; every draw is reported to both chambers.
Sovereign borrowing. Any borrowing in the name of Zeythariaeth, including the Lockwright Reserve facility, requires Assembly authorization and Royal ratification, and is audited by the Commission.
The Magistracy: Rule of Law in the Commonwealth
The Magistracy, the Crown, and the Church

rows.t: The Church sanctifies and does not adjudicate crime. Trials of heresy are ecclesiastical and end in censure, excommunication, and loss of sacramental standing, never in a criminal sentence. Only the Magistracy may declare a man criminal. Worship of the proscribed powers is prosecuted before the Magistracy.
The Crown commands enforcement and holds capital appeal; it does not interpret law.
Subject to Commonwealth law in civil and criminal matters.

blocks.text: Constitutional Character of the Magistracy

The Magistracy stands within the sovereign order of the Commonwealth and not above it. Its purpose is not to rival the Crown, Parliament, or Church, but to preserve lawful order among them. It judges without fear or favor, but never without allegiance.
The Magistracy interprets, applies, and enforces the Constitution, the statutes, and lawful oaths without fear, favor, or faction. It stands within the sovereign order and not above it.

rows.t: Not itself a religious body and not a foreign tribunal. Crown-owned and staffed by ordained clergy (the Magistrals), with a Harmonist of the Circle of Memory leased to each sitting to keep the record; consecrated jointly to Aequitus (Law) and Sophisra (Wisdom) as a matter of doctrine and oath, not divine jurisdiction.
The Constitution, the Oath of the Standard, and lawful delegation by the Crown.
None recognized in law. No judgment issues in the name of any god; no miracle determines guilt. Faith is permitted; divine authority is not.
All lawful judgment derives from the Magistracy. No sentence binds unless rendered in its name.

Interpret law independently of Crown and Parliament; try all civil and criminal cases; rule laws unconstitutional; enforce property rights and contracts. Any person (a male citizen) may sue anyone, including the Crown. A woman is never a party; any suit touching her is her guardian’s, brought and answered in his name.

Citizens who have sworn the Oath of the Standard and renounced foreign legal authority. They remain subject to Commonwealth criminal and civil law and are not exempt from prosecution, removal, or judgment by their peers.
Contractors, not members. Swear no civil oath and stand outside the Magistral’s chain entirely. Accountability runs through the Circle of Memory: the Amma of Harmony and the Archivist.

blocks.text: Structure of the Courts
The Magistracy is organized in three tiers, each pairing Magistrals who judge with a leased Harmonist who records.

rows.t: 15 Magistrals, with 4 leased Harmonists; sits in benches (the full 15 for constitutional rulings), one Harmonist recording each bench
Constitutional matters; final appeal in all cases except capital sentences; may rule laws unconstitutional; may remand, reduce a sentence, or order retrial; keeps judicial uniformity
50 courts, each sitting a single Magistral with a single leased Harmonist per hearing
Major criminal trials; civil cases; property disputes; appeals from municipal courts
A single Magistral with a single leased Harmonist for recordkeeping
Minor civil disputes; minor criminal matters; guardianship and indenture review

blocks.text: Procedure

rows.t: Filed with the court. The Harmonist records the filing into the Lore.
Evidence and testimony are heard. The Harmonist observes in silence, speaks only when the Magistral asks her to read back the record, and never questions witnesses.

The Magistral deliberates alone (in the municipal and regional courts; a bench of the Grand Bench deliberates together and rules by majority, each Magistral bearing his share of the burden). He may ask the Harmonist to read back any part of the record — a prior statement, an objection, a ruling — and she reads what was recorded and nothing more. She researches no precedent, offers no counsel, and volunteers no opinion on the outcome. The burden of judgment remains wholly the Magistral’s.
Rendered by the Magistral alone, in the Magistracy’s name. The ruling is his burden.
The Harmonist enters testimony, reasoning, and judgment into the Lore, and the original record is surrendered to the Cathedral vault and a fair copy of the transcript passes to the Royal Archive.

blocks.text: The Magistral and the Harmonist

rows.t: Fully ordained cleric of Aequitus, trained in the Aequiten legal tradition at the Aequiten Center of the University of Concordia (Scholar’s Rest, Republic of Concordia), returning home on graduation
Ordination, plus secular legal training in Crown-recognized law schools; twenty years of combined service
Formation in the Order of Harmony (House Sophisran)
Nominated by the Arbiter; appointed by the Crown; confirmed by Parliament
Leased by contract with the Circle of Memory; assigned by the Amma of Harmony
Records the whole proceeding verbatim, in Côr-Llaw; reads back the record when the Magistral asks, and answers nothing else
Robed, elevated, the scales of Aequitus displayed
Plain habit and deepest veil, seated below the bench and to the side, with the lyre of Sophisra present
Serve as advocate before any court

blocks.text: The Commonwealth’s courts are staffed by two offices with entirely different functions, one that judges and one that records. The Magistral is set out in the table above; the Harmonist is described in full here:
Harmonists

Vowed women of the Sophisran House, leased to the Magistracy by long-standing agreement between Crown and Church. A Harmonist is a contractor and not an officer of the court: she stands outside the Magistral’s chain entirely, and neither he nor the Crown holds her. She is Church property in the full legal sense Commonwealth coverture gives that word, held by the Circle of Memory, and her fee for a given court term is paid not to her but upward, to the Circle. She sits below the bench and to the side of the Magistral — in the municipal and regional courts, one Harmonist to one Magistral; on a bench of the Grand Bench, one Harmonist records for the whole bench — silent, fully veiled in a plain habit unlike any other vowed woman’s dress — even a professed Sophisran Devota outside the courtroom wears the House’s ordinary habit; a Harmonist in her seat below the bench wears the deepest veil the Church permits any woman to wear in public — and records the whole proceeding word for word in Côr-Llaw, a shorthand the Order has refined over centuries for exactly this purpose. She takes no oath to either party, and neither plaintiff nor defendant may address her or expect an answer if they try. She speaks only when the Magistral asks her to read back the record, and what she reads is what was recorded and nothing more. She is no clerk and no counsel to him: she does not research, advise, or interpret. At the close of every trial or hearing her original record is surrendered whole to the Cathedral vault of the Circle of Memory. The Magistral’s judgment is the entire ruling, binding the moment he renders it, whether or not a Harmonist happened to be present to record it — she has no judicial role, no vote, no veto, and no bearing whatsoever on a trial’s outcome or validity. She is a recorder. Nothing about the Magistracy’s authority runs through her. The Magistracy is her largest lessee but not her only one: Harmonists are leased to any body that wishes its proceedings remembered, and the record she keeps belongs to the Circle of Memory (see below).

The Magistracy handles constitutional matters, civil litigation, and criminal trials alike, and its jurisdiction reaches the Crown itself — any person (a male citizen, in the law’s sense), of any station, may sue the Crown before it. Its budget is constitutionally fixed and cannot be altered, delayed, or withheld by either Crown or Assembly, precisely so that a court that might one day have to rule against either has no reason to fear doing so.
Judicial Ethos

The Magistracy holds that law exists to serve justice rather than replace it. For this reason, a Magistral’s formation proceeds in a deliberate order: justice first, obedience second, and law third. The Commonwealth teaches that law without justice becomes cruelty, while justice without discipline becomes chaos. The purpose of judicial training is therefore not merely to produce learned jurists, but men capable of carrying the burden of judgment without surrendering either compassion or restraint.

The Magistracy’s duty is not to create law, nor to govern in law’s place, but to render lawful judgment faithfully and consistently across generations. Precedent is respected because memory preserves fairness; procedure is respected because power unrestrained eventually becomes arbitrary.
Capital Sentences and Royal Appeal

rows.t: Men only. No woman is sentenced to death; the sentence for a woman’s crime falls on her guardian.
Any man sentenced to death may appeal directly to the King.
Execution is automatically stayed. The appeal is filed through the Magistracy.
Refuse to hear the appeal (the sentence proceeds), or grant an audience.
Speech before sovereignty, not mercy. The accused may speak, counsel may argue, and the King listens or does not.
Royal justice without spectacle; mercy without a flood of precedent; sovereign authority without judicial collapse.

blocks.text: The Arbiter
The Arbiter serves as the Commonwealth’s senior legal conscience. He advises, but does not command; warns, but does not rule from council.

rows.t: By the Crown; confirmed by Parliament.
Life, subject to removal for cause.
The Privy Council, with voice and no veto.
Heads the Grand Bench; nominates Magistrals; guards the Magistracy’s independence and its uniformity of precedent.
Speaks for the Magistracy and does not command it.

blocks.text: The Arbiter’s presence upon the Privy Council exists to provide judgment where others provide policy, strategy, finance, or force.

He possesses voice and not veto, influence and not command. He advises on constitutional risk, lawful authority, and the probable consequences of proposed actions, but neither governs nor legislates. His purpose is not to direct the Commonwealth’s course, but to ensure that those directing it understand the legal ground beneath their feet.
Budget, Advocacy, and Accountability
The Commonwealth holds that to judge and to argue are incompatible oaths. For that reason no member of the Magistracy may ever serve as an advocate before a court.

rows.t: Constitutionally fixed and independent; audited for misuse, not negotiated for favor. The provision exists for a single reason: justice must never beg.
Represent the Crown as a party before the Magistracy, and are counsel only; they never sit in judgment.
For corruption, falsification, breach of oath, or conviction of crime; by the Grand Bench on petition.
For falsifying the Lore or breaching procedural integrity; recalled by the Circle of Memory on the Arbiter’s petition.
May be sued. The Magistracy’s ruling binds it.

blocks.text: The Commonwealth recognizes a strict separation between judgment and advocacy.

A Magistral may never serve as counsel in any court. Likewise, an advocate may never sit in judgment over a matter in which he has argued. This division exists to preserve public confidence that judgment is rendered independently of interest, loyalty, or personal investment in a particular outcome. The principle is frequently summarized by jurists of the Magistracy:
To judge and to argue are incompatible oaths.
The Scale Hall
Before the Magistracy you are not accused or defended. You are known.

The Magistral sits raised and robed with the scales of Aequitus displayed. The Harmonist sits below the bench and to the side, fully veiled, with the lyre of Sophisra present. No voice interrupts without cause.
Visible Order
The Commonwealth holds that justice must not only be done, but be seen to be disciplined.

For this reason, the arrangement of the Scale Hall is not decorative. The elevated bench of the Magistral, the veiled station of the Harmonist, the paired symbols of Aequitus and Sophisra, and the ordered progression of proceedings all exist to instruct the public in the proper relationship between judgment, wisdom, and authority.
Justice speaks. Wisdom remembers.
The citizen who enters the Scale Hall is meant to understand immediately that the law will proceed neither by passion nor spectacle, but through ordered deliberation under oath and precedent.
Cultural Understanding

Among ordinary citizens, the Magistracy is admired less for mercy than for permanence. Kings die. Assemblies dissolve. Ministries rise and vanish. Laws are amended. Churches may argue doctrine. The Magistracy remains, and its reputation rests on consistency and inevitability. Its authority rests not upon fear alone, but upon the widespread belief that rank, wealth, office, military distinction, and noble birth ultimately provide no shelter from lawful judgment. The peasant expects a Magistral to hear him. The noble expects a Magistral to hear him. Both expect the law, rightly or wrongly, to be applied by the same institution. For that reason, the Magistracy enjoys a reputation rare among great institutions: not beloved, but trusted. The common saying remains:
You may beg a priest and bargain with a lord. Before the Magistracy, you stand only as you are.
The Circle of Memory: The Order of Harmony
The Commonwealth keeps law and record in two separate hands. The Magistracy judges. The Circle of Memory remembers.

The Circle of Memory is the Order of Harmony, a dedicated Order of the Church devoted to the preservation of knowledge, memory, and truth. Its women are the Harmonists, Sisters of House Sophisran within the Roselight Circle. Its men are monks of the Church’s Order of the Sworn Flame, who keep the Order’s archive in the monastery of Kaervast Cathedral. Its sacred duty is not governance, legislation, judgment, or advocacy, but the faithful preservation of what has been said, written, agreed, and recorded throughout the Commonwealth. The record they keep is called the Lore.

The Order serves Sophisra, Goddess of Wisdom and Judgment, and teaches that wisdom cannot exist without memory. What is forgotten cannot be studied; what is altered cannot be trusted; what is lost cannot instruct future generations. The Magistracy is consecrated to her wisdom beside the Law of Aequitus; the Order serves her through memory. The Harmonists therefore regard preservation of the historical record as a sacred obligation and one of the highest forms of service.
Constitutional Character of the Circle of Memory

rows.t: A dedicated Order of the Church. Not a court, not a legislature, not an office of the Crown.
None legislative, executive, or judicial. Its influence derives not from power over others but from universal trust in the integrity of its records.
The Archivist, then the Amma of Harmony, then the Harmonists.

A high-ranking priest drawn from the monastic Order of the Sworn Flame. Heads the Circle, keeps the Lore, and commands the Amma of Harmony and, through her, every Harmonist. Answers to the Archsworn directly.
Senior Sister of the Order and head of its Harmonists. Assigns Harmonists to leases and answers to the Archivist, not to a Praesul. Her authority is over women only, as every Amma’s is.

A vowed woman of House Sophisran, Church property in the full legal sense Commonwealth coverture gives that word. A contractor to every lessee and a member of none of their chains. Her fee is paid not to her but upward, to the Circle.
The fees paid for the lease of its Harmonists.
The whole preserved record of the Commonwealth: what has been said, written, agreed, and recorded.
Falsifying the Lore or breaching procedural integrity is cause for recall by the Circle, on petition of the Arbiter where the fault is in a court.

blocks.text: Origins

Before the Royal Archive was founded under King Alexi, the Commonwealth’s record was kept by the monks of the monastery at Kaervast Cathedral. The Order of Harmony grew out of that cloister, and the Cathedral Archive remains its mother house and the keeper of the Lore. The Royal Archive is a Crown institution and a separate one; it is a lessee of the Circle like any other.
Role in Society
The Harmonists are custodians of the Commonwealth’s collective memory.

They preserve treaties, census records, land grants, genealogies, parliamentary proceedings, judicial transcripts, royal decrees, guild charters, scholarly works, and countless other records upon which the realm depends.

No major institution exists independently of their work. The Crown governs through records they preserve. The Magistracy relies upon precedents they maintain. Guilds depend upon contracts and negotiations they record. Historians, scholars, and officials alike must petition the Circle when they seek the memory of the Commonwealth.
Côr-Llaw

Over centuries the Order developed Côr-Llaw, a sophisticated shorthand system designed to capture spoken language at the speed of conversation. It is among the Order’s most closely guarded and demanding disciplines. A trained Harmonist can record legal proceedings, negotiations, assemblies, speeches, and testimony almost verbatim as events unfold.

The original Harmonic record is the primary source document. Following an event, the original shorthand record is surrendered to the Cathedral vault at Kaervast, where other Harmonists transcribe it into formal Zeylara, catalogue it, cross-reference it with related records, and preserve both the original and the transcription. The original never leaves the vault. A fair copy of every court transcript passes to the Royal Archive.

The Harmonist present at an event concerns herself with faithful capture; her sisters at the Archive concern themselves with preservation and organization. See Appendix C: Côr-Llaw Reference Manual for more details on how the shorthand works.
The Lease

Because of their reputation for accuracy and neutrality, Harmonists are leased to any body that wishes its proceedings remembered: the Magistracy first among them, by long-standing agreement between Crown and Church, and beyond it the Crown, Parliament, the Assembly, guilds, noble houses, merchant houses, universities, town councils, and any chartered body able to meet the Circle’s fee. The lease is made with the Circle of Memory, through the Amma of Harmony, for a sitting or a term, and the fee is paid to the Circle.

rows.t: One Harmonist to every Municipal and Regional court; one to every bench of the Grand Bench. The standing lease and the largest.
Proceedings, councils, treaty negotiations, and decrees.

blocks.text: A lessee may end a lease. He may not direct her pen. She stands outside the chain of every body she serves, and answers for her record to the Circle alone.

Her presence does not grant legitimacy to a proceeding, but her absence often invites suspicion. Many guildmasters and officials refuse to begin important negotiations without a Harmonist present, stating simply:
“I will not begin without Memory.”
In such circumstances the Harmonist serves neither party. She does not advise, interpret, negotiate, advocate, or participate in the discussion. She merely records. Her duty is memory.
Harmonists in the Courts

When assigned to a court, a Harmonist sits below and to the side of the bench, veiled and unobtrusive. She does not serve the litigants. She does not serve the advocates. She does not serve the Magistral. She is a contractor outside his chain entirely, and she serves Memory.

The litigants are forbidden from addressing her directly. She neither questions witnesses nor offers opinions. During proceedings she remains silent unless directly addressed by the Magistral. A Magistral may ask:
“Sister, please read back the defendant’s statement.”

The Harmonist then reads precisely what was recorded and returns to silence. She offers no interpretation, emphasis, or judgment. The Magistral determines what the law means. The Harmonist preserves what was said.
Preservation Rather than Judgment

The Commonwealth recognizes an important distinction between law and memory. The Magistracy determines which evidence is admissible, which arguments are persuasive, and what judgment shall ultimately be rendered. The Circle of Memory determines none of these things.

rows.t: Recorded. He may order it disregarded; he may not order it forgotten.

blocks.text: The record is preserved in its entirety. There is no equivalent within the Commonwealth of striking words from the record. The legal significance of a statement may change; the fact that it was spoken does not.
Institutional Philosophy
The Order teaches that memory belongs to no ruler, court, assembly, or generation.
The Crown may govern. Parliament may legislate. The Magistracy may judge. The Order remembers.

Harmonists therefore regard themselves not as participants in the events they record, but as custodians standing witness on behalf of future generations. Their highest virtue is fidelity. Not wisdom alone. Not knowledge alone. But the faithful preservation of truth, whether flattering or embarrassing, noble or shameful.
Among the Order, a common saying endures:
Justice speaks. Wisdom remembers.
Local Law Enforcement: Crown Wardens & Constables

The Magistracy decides, the Crown commands, and enforcement officers sworn to both execute. Crown Wardens and Constables are Crown-appointed civil officers funded directly by the national Treasury. They answer neither to Mayor nor to Satrap, and they are judicially answerable to the Magistracy alone. They investigate crime, execute warrants, and keep public order. They hold no judicial power of their own and may neither declare guilt nor impose punishment—that authority belongs to a Magistral alone.

rows.t: Every major city and provincial capital

Execute lawful warrants, arrests, seizures, and sentences; keep custody of the accused pending trial; oversee investigations, the city watch, detention facilities, and evidence handling; coordinate with military authority only when civil order has collapsed or invasion is imminent
May not judge guilt or innocence, interpret law, punish on his own authority, or act in the name of any god or religious body
Every town, village, and rural district
Preserve order; investigate minor offenses and disturbances; detain suspects pending transfer; serve summons, fines, and warrants; escort the accused to a regional court or Warden custody
May detain and not condemn, restrain and not punish. Reports administratively to the regional Warden, never to local nobles, guilds, or clergy
All enforcement is reviewable by the Magistracy. Unlawful detention, excessive force, or action without warrant is prosecutable. An officer acting without lawful authority commits oath-violation.
Wardens and Constables do not enforce doctrine, sacrament, or theology. Church discipline stays ecclesiastical unless civil law is broken.

Does not conduct civil enforcement except under a declared emergency, and in the frontier marches, where the Marshal holds combined military-civil authority. One standing exception: a Constable or Warden summoned by a Quartermaster under the Indenture Statute enters a Servitor Quarter at any hour, and no commander may refuse him.
No sacred police, no private law, no armed justice.

The Appraisers of the Bureau of Civic Decorum are Crown officers outside the Warden and Constable service. They hold no power of arrest. Constables assist them on request and do not strike (see The Bureau of Civic Decorum).

blocks.text: How Officials Are Installed

rows.t: Hereditary succession within the recognized Houses of the Maenari, the Satyrim, and the Maestrai (descended from unions between the other two), plus military-order courtesy seats
Universal male suffrage among male citizens age 20+, service completed

Elected by the male citizens of the satrapy (age 20+, service completed, Oath of the Standard sworn), then formally confirmed by the Crown and required to swear a personal oath of accountability to it before taking office
Crown-appointed from the senior officer corps of the Crown Regulars or the Order of the Standing Wall — a military command, not an elected office, given the frontier march’s standing war footing
Elected directly by the male citizens of the town, under the same civic qualification as provincial elections
Nominated by the Assembly; confirmed by the Crown; personal oath of accountability sworn before he takes office
Aequiten Center formation (Concordia), twenty years’ combined clerical service, and secular law training, nominated by the Arbiter, appointed by the Crown, confirmed by Parliament
Meritocratic examination, followed by a sworn oath of service; hereditary appointment banned by law
Crown Administrative Service: examination and oath; hereditary appointment banned
Examination in the sumptuary statutes and the Rule; two years’ probation under a senior Appraiser; oath sworn before the Office of Public Oaths
Chancellor (Keeper of the Seal), Spymaster, Royal Steward, Admiral of the Navy
Crown appointment; the Chancellor is confirmed by Parliament

blocks.text: A Satrap or Mayor elected by his satrapy or town is not thereby installed — the Crown’s confirmation and the officeholder’s personal oath of accountability are both required before he may act with any Crown authority at all. This double gate (popular election, then royal confirmation) is deliberate: the Commonwealth wants its provincial administration popularly answerable and centrally loyal at once, and sees no contradiction in demanding both.
The Ceremonial Inscriptions of the Commonwealth
As recorded by order of the Assembly and inscribed upon the principal halls of governance, justice, and crown.
I. The Magistracy
Law of the Commonwealth · Keeper of the Oath‑Canon
Zeylara Inscription (Monumental Script)
Zeythariaeth ei Vathis “The Commonwealth in Its Voice.”
Common Speech Motto
“Where the Joined Speak as One.”

This inscription is carved above the eastern arch of the Magistracy, where petitioners enter to place their cases before the Grand Bench. It signifies that judgment is rendered not in the voice of any people, but in the unified voice of the Commonwealth itself.
II. The Assembly Hall
Elected Chamber of the Nine Peoples · Seat of Civic Mandate
Zeylara Inscription (Formal Script)
Caer Zeythariaeth “The House of the Commonwealth.”
Common Speech Motto
“By Mandate, We Govern.”

This inscription stands above the public portico of the Assembly, marking the chamber where the Zeythari speak through their chosen delegates. It affirms that the Assembly is not merely a hall of debate, but the dwelling-place of the Commonwealth’s civic will.
III. The Parliament of Lineage
Hereditary High House · Custodians of Tradition · Keepers of the Line of Stewardship
Zeylara Inscription (High Poetic Register)
Lorathar ei Caerthira “The Hall of Memory and Stewardship.”
Common Speech Motto
“What Was Given, We Guard.”

Inscribed above the marble lintel of the Parliament’s ancestral gate, this phrase binds the hereditary houses to their ancient charge: the preservation of continuity, lineage, and the long memory of the Commonwealth.
IV. The Royal Palace — The Great Hall of Audience
Seat of the Crown · Hall of Petition · Throne of the Joined
Zeylara Inscription (Royal Register)
Vaethor Zeylan ei Mirenath “Where the Joined King Hears the Future.”
Common Speech Motto
“All May Speak Before the Crown.”

This inscription crowns the public entrance of the Great Hall, where the King receives petitions each seventh-day for six hours. It affirms the ancient covenant: that the Crown stands not above the people, but among them, hearing their voices without barrier or privilege.
V. The Circle of Memory — The Cathedral Archive
Order of Harmony · Keepers of the Lore · Witness for Those Not Yet Born
Zeylara Inscription (Cloister Register)
Sophira Mnaemar ei Vathis “Wisdom Keeps the Voice.”
Common Speech Motto
“What Justice Speaks, Wisdom Keeps.”

This inscription is cut above the door of the Cathedral Archive in the monastery of Kaervast, where those who seek the memory of the Commonwealth come to petition the Archivist. It is repeated, small, upon the lyre of Sophisra that stands in every Scale Hall, beneath the seat of the veiled Sister. It affirms that the Order judges nothing and forgets nothing: the Magistracy speaks, and what it speaks is kept for those who come after.
The King’s Bench (The Great Hall of Audience)
As recorded in the civic annals of the Royal Commonwealth of Zeythari

Every seventh‑day at the eighth hour of morning, the doors of the Great Hall of Audience are opened to the people of the Commonwealth. This tradition—older than the Parliament, older than the Assembly, older even than the Magistracy—remains the most beloved ritual of the Crown. It is known simply as the King’s Bench, though no vote is taken there and no law is passed. It is the hour when the Joined may speak directly to the throne.
Purpose and Tradition
The King’s Bench exists for one reason: to allow any Zeythar to place their plea, grievance, petition, or hope before the Crown without barrier or privilege.
No appointment is required. No noble intermediary is needed. No fee, writ, or sponsorship is demanded.
A farmer from the Ashward March stands equal to a merchant of Solmara. A Duraken guildsman stands equal to a Maenari lord. A Vykril caravan‑master stands equal to a Satyrim scholar.
This is the living expression of the Commonwealth’s founding principle: Zeyla thira — “All are joined.”
Hours of Audience
The Assembly is held every Saturday from 0800 to 1400, without fail.

The Crown’s heralds strike the First Bell of Joining at the eighth hour, and the King takes the Seat of Petition beneath the great skylight of the Hall. Citizens enter in order of arrival, forming a line that often stretches through the palace courtyard and down the Avenue of Oath‑Gold.
Though the formal hours end at the fourteenth hour, it is well‑known that:
The King will not rise while a petitioner remains unheard.
On days of crisis, celebration, or heavy need, the Assembly has extended:
to the fifteenth hour during the Grain‑Short Winter
to the seventeenth hour during the Shimmerwind refugee influx
past the eighteenth hour during the Great Concordance Strike
and once, famously, until nightfall during the Oath‑Fire Vigil
These extensions are remembered with affection and pride. They are cited often as proof that the Crown remains a servant of the Joined, not a master.
Process of Petition

A petitioner steps forward, kneels or stands according to custom, and speaks plainly. No ceremonial language is required; Common Speech is preferred. The King listens without interruption, then responds in one of four ways:
Immediate Judgment — when the matter lies within the Crown’s direct authority
Referral to the Magistracy — when the matter concerns justice or legal dispute
Referral to Parliament — when the matter concerns lineage, stewardship, or ancestral rights
Referral to the Assembly — when the matter concerns civic mandate or public policy

A woman may petition the King only with the written permission of her master or, if she has none, her guardian. She presents the permission to the herald and is announced by her relation (“wife of,” “daughter of,” “ward of” the man who holds her), and the petition is entered under his name. Her master or guardian may also present a written petition touching his household himself. She does not swear the Petitioner’s Oath.
In all cases, the King’s response is recorded by the Royal Clerks and delivered to the appropriate body before the next sitting day.
Political Significance
Though the Commonwealth is not yet a republic, the King’s Bench is widely regarded as the moral heart of the realm. It is the ritual that binds Crown, Parliament, Assembly, and citizenry together.

The Elder Minister attends each Bench in the upper gallery, observing the petitions that may shape the agenda of Parliament. Many reforms of the last century began not in debate chambers but in the Great Hall, spoken by ordinary Zeythari whose voices carried upward into law.
The public adores this tradition. It is said that:
“A King who hears the Joined remains joined.”

And so the Bench continues, week after week, year after year, as the Commonwealth slowly evolves toward a distant future, some 150 years off, when a Prime Minister will hold executive power—but the King’s Bench will remain, a cherished covenant between Crown and people.
Opening Words of the King’s Bench
As spoken each seventh‑day at the eighth hour, beneath the skylight of the Great Hall of Audience.
The herald strikes the First Bell of Joining, and the Hall falls silent. The King steps forward, places his hand upon the Oath‑rail, and speaks:

“Zeythari, children of the Joined Commonwealth — the Hall is open. By the covenant of our forebears and the charge laid upon the Crown, all may speak before me. No voice is too small, no burden too heavy, no plea unworthy of hearing. I sit not above you, but among you, as the Joined King of a Joined People. Come forward, Zeythar, and let your words be known.”
The herald then calls the first petitioner, and the Assembly begins.
Closing Words of the King’s Bench
As spoken at the end of the Saturday Audience in the Great Hall of Audience.

When the final petitioner has been heard—or when the hour grows late and the King must rise—the herald strikes the Last Bell of Joining. The Hall quiets. The King stands from the Seat of Petition, places his hand once more upon the Oath‑rail, and speaks:

“Zeythari, Joined Ones of the Commonwealth—your voices are carried. What you have spoken here will not fade. By oath and by charge, I bear your words to the halls where judgment is made and to the chambers where law is shaped. You have been heard in full, and you will be answered in full. Go in strength, Zeythar, and stand in the unity of the Joined.”
The herald then proclaims the Assembly closed, and the King departs through the western arch toward the Parliament galleries, carrying the day’s petitions with him.
Petitioner’s Oath for the King’s Saturday Audience
As spoken by any citizen stepping before the Seat of Petition in the Great Hall of Audience.
The petitioner steps forward, places a hand upon the Oath‑rail, and speaks clearly:

“I stand as Zeythar, joined in duty and truth. By my voice and by my honor, I speak without falsehood. What I place before the Crown is my need, my burden, or my hope. I ask to be heard in the unity of the Joined Commonwealth.”
The herald then announces the petitioner’s name and place of origin, and the King gives leave to speak.
A woman does not swear this oath.
III. RELIGION & IDEOLOGY
Church of the Sworn Flame

The Church of the Sworn Flame is the recognized regional church of the Royal Commonwealth of Zeythari and of the lesser kingdoms of its march (a principality, a duchy, and a march-kingdom , each of which seats its own Praesul under the Archsworn) and the institutional embodiment of the Covenant of the Living Flame within them. It stands in full communion with the Holy See of the Church of the Living Flame, under the Solaeliel as Supreme Pontiff, as a regional church recognized by the High Council and bound by the conditions of that recognition and by the Thirteen Articles of the Covenant of the Living Flame.

The Church of the Sworn Flame is not a separate religion, nor a divergent sect. It is a regional church — a localized, fully orthodox expression of the Covenant of Living Flame — adapted to Zeythari’s culture, law, and historical circumstances while remaining bound to the universal Canon of the Living Flame.

Origins. The Crown took the Living Flame in Realm Year 512, and for the next eleven centuries the Church in Zeythari was the official Church of the Living Flame, ordinary in rank, rite, and structure. Over those centuries it drifted, in custom and then in practice, into an expression of its own, and about four hundred years ago (Realm Year 1603) the Holy See authorized the creation of the Church of the Sworn Flame as a regional church of the Living Flame. It has been one ever since.

All sacraments administered by the Church of the Sworn Flame are valid—their validity derives from proper administration before Kairon and Seraphiae, in accordance with the Thirteen Articles, not from any external recognition. The Holy See recognizes this validity under the conditions of its recognition of the regional church.
Despite the integrated civic identity of the Commonwealth, any citizen accused of worshipping the following creeds will be prosecuted by the Magistracy:
Golden Imperative
The Sovereignty Dominion
Any Abyssal Cult
What the Church Is

The Church of the Sworn Flame (Domwevar Veoratha) is the regional church of the Royal Commonwealth of Zeythari and of the lesser kingdoms of its march, in full communion with the Church of the Living Flame. It is not a new faith wearing old vestments. It is the Living Flame, held nearest the fire: the Covenant of Kairon gathered up, with its first-named obligation, the First Oath, set at the center of a realm that learned on its walls that a kingdom of nine peoples survives only as long as its word does. Its watchword is Veoreth Darnath Ethar, “The Oath binds the man,” spoken at the close of every Confirmation, every muster, and every crowning.

Zeythari is made of nine people with no blood, tongue, or origin in common. What holds them to one banner, one law, and one field of battle is the Oath. A soldier of one people, sword-sworn beside a soldier of another, held a wall neither was born on, and what the Commonwealth discovered on its walls, its churches later set down: if the wall holds because the oath holds, the oath must be made sacred, uniform, and unbreakable, sworn the same way by every child of every people before the same Flame. For its first centuries, the Church in Zeythari was the ordinary Church of the Living Flame. It drifted, in custom and then in practice, into an expression of its own and never in doctrine. About four hundred years ago the Holy See examined a frontier realm already faithful and already orthodox, found nothing to correct, and authorized the Church of the Sworn Flame.
Standing within the Living Flame Communion

The Codex of the Sworn Flame is a companion volume to the Codex of the Living Flame and never a rival to it. Where it is silent, the Living Flame’s Codex governs without exception. Where the two appear to differ, the difference is one of emphasis and never of doctrine. The Church is a regional church under Part IV of the Living Flame Codex, bound as every regional church is bound to all eight conditions of its recognition, among them:

rows.t: He is Supreme Pontiff over Zeythari exactly as over Kyrielvar Insula. No Patriarch, Council, or Crown stands outside his final judgment
The Pattern and the Testimonial of the Visitation are held unaltered. Zeythari has not softened a single Article of Heavenly Order to suit frontier custom
Clergy formed under the Holy See
Clergy are formed at the Seminary of the Sworn Flame, accredited by and answerable to the Holy See on the same footing as the Seminary of Truth
Same form, number, and Seraval sealing as anywhere in the Communion. Confirmation in Kaervast Cathedral and in the smallest palisade chapel of the Ashward March are the same rite
The Patriarchate remits its tithe annually to the Sacred See and sends its Patriarch, or an empowered delegation, to the Decennial Conclave

blocks.text: Within these conditions Zeythari was granted its own leadership structure, its own devotional emphasis, and its own Creed of local confession, provided none of it touches the Pattern.
The Creed of the Sworn Flame

Recited at every Confirmation, every coronation, and every ordination, standing where the Living Flame’s own Creed stands in the ordinary liturgy and spoken alongside it as Zeythari’s own confession of the same faith.

We hold, as the whole Communion holds, that Kairon is Truth, and Seraphiae is Grace, and that neither stands complete without the other; that Aequitus is Law and Sophisra is Wisdom, and that the four together are the Living Flame, and no soul, no household, and no kingdom may stand upon one alone.

We hold, as the whole Communion holds, that the Pattern is not custom but creation: that men are ordained to govern and women to devote and to submit, that neither office may be traded for the other, and that a kingdom which forgets this forgets the shape of the world itself.

We hold that the Pattern admits no exception for ability, for virtue, for necessity, or for any reason a mortal mind may advance. A woman who governs better than the man set over her has not earned his office. She stole it.

But we confess this above all and confess it first among the Articles, as the ground the rest are built on: that the Oath is Truth made binding across time and that a man is worth exactly what his word is worth, and no more.

A crown does not make a king. A blade does not make a soldier. A ring does not make a wife. The Oath makes them sworn once before Kairon and never sworn again, because Truth does not need repeating to remain true. What a man swears at sixteen; he owes at sixty. What a woman swears before the Flame, no master, no war, and no grave releases her from it early. We do not ask whether an oath was convenient to keep. We ask only whether it was kept.

We confess that nine people, holding nothing else in common, hold this in common: that the word given before the Flame does not bend to blood, tongue, or birth. The Oath does not ask what a man is. It asks only what he has sworn. This is why nine people stand as one Commonwealth and why the wall has never yet fallen for want of unity, however often it has fallen for want of numbers.

We confess that Kairon judges every soul first by its Truth, and that no Truth is tested so completely as an oath tested by cost. A man who keeps his word when keeping it is easy has sworn nothing yet. We confess, therefore, that the Final Reckoning weighs a broken oath heavier than almost any other sin named in the Covenant, for it is Truth’s own wound, dealt by the one soul who swore to guard it.

This is the Creed of the Sworn Flame, held in full communion with the Living Flame, under its Patriarch and subordinate to the Solaeliel, and confessed by every child of the Commonwealth and of every people in the same words before the same Flame.
Veoreth Darnath Ethar. The Oath binds the man.

The Closing Confession, spoken at the close of every Confirmation after the sealed Oath and before the Oath of the Standard: Veoreth Darnath Ethar. Kyrason Lorasath; Aelyr-mirath unmiret. “The Oath binds the man. Truth rules; the Living Flame does not divide.”
The Doctrines of the Sworn Flame
Doctrina Veoratha, the Kyreth Veoratha: the Formal Articles of Faith.

The Articles are not a new confession. They are the Living Flame’s own confession, stated with the precision a frontier church has earned the right to demand, and grounded in the Pattern revealed to Arkanos at the Living Flame, in the Four Pillars of Sacred Femininity set forth by the Holy See, and in the doctrine of Darlorath established in Canon II of the Living Flame Codex. They are read aloud at every ordination of a priest, at every installation of a Praesul, and at the Archsworn’s own enthronement, and they are taught at the Seminary of the Sworn Flame as the foundation of every other subject of formation. They add no Article to the Covenant, alter no Sacrament, and loosen no line of the Pattern; where any word of them conflicts with the Pattern, that word is void, and the rest stands. The Church holds that the Pattern is most clearly seen in its enforcement and that a doctrine believed but not enforced is a preference. The Commonwealth enforces the Pattern. The Church teaches it. The Articles are the bridge between the two.
Article I: On the Pattern

The Pattern is creation, not custom: the structure of reality itself, established by Kairon at the making of the world and revealed in its fullness to Arkanos. Men govern. Women submit. Neither may trade the other’s office for their own. It repeats at every scale, and authority descends in an unbroken chain from Kairon to the Solaeliel, from the Solaeliel to kings and Praesuls, from kings and Praesuls to fathers and husbands, and from fathers and husbands to the households committed to their care. No man governs in his own right; every office is borrowed. No woman stands anywhere in the chain. She is governed by it.

rows.t: The Crown commands; the Commonwealth obeys
The Priest teaches; the parish obeys
The husband governs; the wife submits

blocks.text: The Pattern admits no exception for capability, demonstrated virtue, or frontier necessity. It assigns offices, not rewards; capability is the servant of the office and never its master. To govern where submission was given is rebellion against creation, and so against Kairon himself. In Zeythari the civil code restates what canon teaches: no woman holds any office over any man in Crown, bench, altar, muster, guild, or household, and what a woman rules she rules by lent or delegated authority, revocable at a word. A man’s authority phases in, since he swears at sixteen and stands a citizen at twenty. A woman’s submission does not phase out. She passes from girlhood to womanhood by marriage alone, and no degree of proven competence carries her out of it.
Article II: On the Oath

An oath sworn before Kairon is Truth made binding across time, owed in full until death. A man is worth exactly what his word is worth. Four corollaries govern it: the oath does not lapse; it is not measured by ease; it is sworn once, since to ask a sworn soul to swear again is to say the first oath failed; and it binds by the swearing, regardless of the swearer’s understanding of its cost, her liking of its terms, or her opinion of the one it is sworn toward. A broken oath is Truth’s own wound and weighs heavier at the Final Reckoning than almost any other sin. The Oath does not bend blood, tongue, or birth, and the Church holds this as doctrine and not merely as civic policy. The oaths of the Commonwealth are these:

rows.t: Sacramental; the oath itself is the sacrament

One rite in every satrapy of the Communion; binds the swearer to Kairon for life. The boy swears the Oath of the Crowned (in Zeythari, the Vow of the Flame) before Kairon and Aequitus; the girl swears the Vow of the Faithful before Seraphiae and Sophisra
Civil: confers no grace and creates no covenant with Heaven
Confirmed men only, immediately after the sacrament, before the parish Priest and the gathered garrison or township

To answer the Crown’s summons, stand where set, keep faith with the men beside him, and not abandon his post while breath remains: What I swear at sixteen, I shall owe at sixty. The Church witnesses and records it; the Crown holds the claim. Cowardice at the post is reckoned near kin to perjury.
Sworn to Heaven in her own voice

To remain faithful and chaste in body and word; to obey the man placed to rule over her, husband, father, or master, as Seraphiae obeys her Lord Kairon; to devote her life to righteousness and to the wisdom Sophisra grants; and, if she errs, to submit to correction and judgment. It binds unto death and is not released by the unworthiness of the man it is sworn toward.
A public declaration, not a sacrament, not a binding oath, binds nothing at law.
Every confirmed woman, kneeling before Seraphiae’s image in the same hour as her Confirmation, witnessed by the parish Priest

Her obedience to her father until she is given in marriage, to her master from that day until death, and to any master set over her thereafter; faithfulness in the keeping of her household, modesty in bearing, dress, and speech, and steadfastness in the duties the Pattern assigns her. It puts her obedience on public records. A woman who later refuses her master’s lawful governance has gone back on her public word and broken her Vow of the Faithful
Sealed in Seraval, the one word of a woman’s law of the realm acknowledges the instrument of transfer.

blocks.text: A woman’s declared and sworn word is these three acts, the Faithful, the Hearth, and the Marriage Vow, and she swears no other oath in any court, on any matter, at any age; the State takes no oath from a woman. The Church’s liturgy adds the Vow of the Rose, a vow of the Church and not an oath, made at her Veiling at twelve and recited again in the Confirmation Rite. A woman obeys because she swore, and her obedience rests on her oath and not on her nature. The Order of Sisters keeps a parallel vow of the Church, not of the State: that a professed Sister will not abandon her post in the war-hospitals, granaries, or garrison households for fear, as her brothers are sworn not to abandon theirs.
The Order of the Confirmation Muster
Common declaration of all candidates:
I accept Kairon as my God and Domar Solael as the Radiant House into which I am sealed
The boy swears the Oath of the Crowned and the girl the Vow of the Faithful, two oaths before two pairs of gods.
The Priest seals each oath in Seraval.
All say:
Loriel Oikethra Ethrason, “So stands the Rightful Order”
The Vow of Flame, recited by every confirmed man, and the Vow of the Rose, by every confirmed woman
The Closing Confession, Veoreth Darnath Ethar
Men swear the Oath of the Standard before the garrison or township.
Women make the Vow of the Hearth, standing behind her father or guardian.
Article III: On the Governance of Men, Guardian’s Debts, and Honor

Governance is a sacred vocation entrusted exclusively to men, and the Pattern exacts a price of the man who bears it. That price is Honor (Eldrath), a standing among men and a debt to Kairon at once. The man who bears rule answers at the Final Reckoning for five duties:
Protection and Provision;
Instruction and Guidance, teaching her the Creed, the prayers, the oaths, and the household arts
Correction: to discipline her faults by any reasonable means he judges fit, short of permanent injury
Direction and Honor, directing her bearing, speech, dress, company, and labor without reducing her to chattel
Sacrifice and Answer, rendering the whole account of her conduct before Kairon, the Crown, and the men of his parish.
Authority survives its abuse, and honor does not survive automatically. A master who abuses what is his keeps Darlorath, but his honor falls, and it is judged by his equals and by the Priest.

rows.t: Conduct of a man toward his dependents
Provision made, household ordered, wife visibly obedient
Wife’s bearing excellent in public; household praised
Wife publicly disobedient or without her Band or covering; household disordered
Diminishes; her fault is his shame
Cruelty beyond all measure; persistent abuse of dependents
Diminishes sharply; the Priest summons him; where injury made permanent, the Magistracy prosecutes
Forfeit entire; heresy and capital charge
Indenture of a daughter for a his debt
Diminishes for life; entered in the Municipal Court’s registry and the parish record. The shame is his and never hers

blocks.text: Shame disciplines men; obedience disciplines women. The Church does not govern the internal discipline of a household. A master may correct, restrict, or discipline his wife as he judges necessary so long as he does not injure her permanently, and no Priest, Praesul, or tribunal in the Commonwealth, civil or ecclesiastical, hears a wife’s complaint against the measure of it (Canon II §2). The Church disciplines the man’s honor through the Right of Correction (Canon II §4), and the Priest acts on the report of the parish stewards or on his own sight, never on the complaint of the wife. The Pattern binds the man as surely as the woman: the man who abdicates governance sins against Truth as the woman who usurps it sins against Grace, and the Priest may summon him to return him to his chair.
Article IV: On the Station of Women and the Darlorath

In Commonwealth usage the man who holds Darlorath is the woman’s master. “Husband” is the relational title that arises from the Marriage Rite; “master” is the legal and practical office. Where the two coincide, the text prefers master except in ceremonial or purely marital contexts.

Submission is a permanent spiritual office, as permanent as the office of governance assigned to men. A wife is her husband’s property in civil law and a soul before Kairon, and the Church holds both truths together. She is held by one man, held in common by none, and owned as his hearth and his blade are owned: her person, her labor, her obedience, her silence, her body, and her bearing are his in the full weight of civil law. This is the Darlorath, the dominion, and it is not a metaphor. It is not diminished by her virtue, her intelligence, or her service. Yet she is not goods and not chattel, and she cannot be sold. Slavery is heresy in the Commonwealth and has been since its first law; the wife was never a slave to begin with, being a soul in the keeping of one man, and a soul may be kept but may not be traded.

Darlorath transfers once, from father to master at the Marriage Rite, and never again by act of man. A mastery held in trust for a term, under indenture or under a Crown or Church charter, is not a transfer of Darlorath. On the master’s death it descends to his heir and does not return to her father. The Forbidden Alienations are sale, trade or barter, pledge or surety against a debt, stake or forfeit at wager or at arms, lease, hire, or loan of the woman's person or mastery for any term. The contract of her labor or services by her master, wife or daughter, to the Crown, the Church, or a private party is not an alienation: Darlorath and the mastery stay with him, gift to another man as property, bequest as goods to anyone but the lawful heir, and surrender as blood-price. Two exceptions stand, and neither is a sale. The first is the indenture of an unmarried daughter by her father, approved by a Municipal Court under the Indenture Statute (Section VI). The second is the fixed-term service of an unmarried daughter, contracted by her lawful guardian to the Crown or the Church under charter. Each conveys a mastery in trust for the term and never the Darlorath (see Mastery in Trust, below). No plea of hospitality, necessity, or the woman’s assent serves in defense, since she has no assent to give. A plea of debt serves only as the ground of a petition under the Indenture Statute and never as a defense to sale. Whoever sells and whoever buys stands guilty of the heresy of the chattel: excommunication, delivery to the Magistracy, and execution under the civil code, the buyer hanged beside the seller. The recovered woman passes by ordinary descent, and no stain attaches to her.
Marriage Cultural Settlement

The Veyrathi and the Rimborn place their daughters by payment between men. The Commonwealth does not recognize that payment as a sale. It recognizes it as a Settlement: a bride price paid to the father (or, among the Veyrathi, to the head of the household, his eldest brother serving in his stead) as the price of his consent and of the transfer of Darlorath at the Marriage Rite. The woman is not goods and is not conveyed. The Forbidden Alienations stand unchanged.

rows.t: Placement before her twentieth year: she is offered to suitors and shows condition, skill, martial prowess, and instant obedience.
Sale at the village auction or by private sale, within a month of the trial
The Presentation, with the martial display kept as part of it. Offers are betrothal petitions to her father or eldest brother
The Betrothal Gathering, held after Hearth Training. Offers are betrothal petitions to her father. No bidding platform, no open auction
Bride-price to the head of household, entered in the parish record as a marriage settlement
Bride-price to the father, entered in the parish record as a marriage settlement. Rimborn settlements run higher, as the dossier records
An advantage between men, in return for consent. Not the price of her person
No dowry is paid. The bride-price stands in its place; payment runs one way only, to the father
Once, at the Marriage Rite, by a Sworn Flame priest
Same. A Threshold-Speaker's blessing may accompany it and carries no civil standing
Any payment for a woman outside a Marriage Rite is the heresy of the chattel: capital for seller and buyer
The chain of mastery transfers entire to the husband, as the dossier states

blocks.text: Mastery in Trust
A daughter held under indenture, or leased under a Crown or Church charter, is never held as a wife is held. The rules below govern every such term.

rows.t: Stays with her father, whole, for the whole term. He remains her master in law and the injured party in any wrong done to her.
Full mastery for the term: her service or labor, residence, movement, dress, correction, and conduct, and, where she casts, the glyph’s phrase. He answers for her as a guardian answers.
Carnal use. He is not her husband and holds none of a husband’s rights. Any carnal use is despoilment, and her willingness is no defense.

None. He may not lend, hire out, sublease, or assign her to any other man, house, or body. Any such act voids the lease at once and returns her to her father with her dowry paid in full. The Magistracy censures the holder.
The father may not recall her during the term, except as the instrument or charter allows.
The term ends by operation of law. The mastery lapses and she returns to her father’s household marriageable, intact, and unmarked.

blocks.text: A woman of the Commonwealth holds no independent legal personhood at any age, rank, or circumstance. She holds no title to land, goods, coin, or livestock; no claim against any man or house; no suit at law, as plaintiff or defendant; no contract; no testimony in any court, her guardian testifying to what she saw; no oath beyond the Faithful and the Marriage Vow; no office, civil, military, or ecclesiastical, over any man; no House name or arms; no representation of herself before any tribunal; no trade or profit in her own right, what she makes under her master’s direction being his; and no culpability as a principal in crime, her guardian answering for her conduct before the Crown. The dowry is the whole of any claim she will ever make on her natal house.

The wife’s whole person lies within her master’s hand, saving Five Boundaries. These do not belong to her. They are the lines Heaven drew around what a man may do with what belongs to him, and they give her no standing before any court.

rows.t: Her life is not his to take, and his discipline may not injure her permanently. A master who kills his wife forfeits the Darlorath, loses his standing among men, and stands before the Crown for a capital offense

He may not command her to murder, to renounce Truth, or to destroy an unborn child. A wife so commanded refuses, by silence and stillness and not by word or flight, and declares the command to her Priest. The burden of proving the command lies with her, and a false declaration is a graver offense than the disobedience she sought to avoid
What she says to her Priest within the seal may not be used by any man against her. No master may demand what she confessed or punish her for having confessed
The Final Reckoning holds her. She answers for her obedience, and her master answers for his governance of her
