blocks.text: A woman may learn, advise, teach within her proper domain, counsel, warn, and petition; submission is distinct from intellectual inferiority. What she may not do is claim governing authority or set her judgment above the man Heaven appointed. A woman who submits faithfully, governs her household with skill, keeps her oath without reservation, and presents herself as her guardian directs has fulfilled the Pattern as completely as a man who governs justly and keeps his oath under cost. Darlorath is also a literal channel, the Divine Circuit of the Living Flame’s Doctrine 11: a woman’s working completes through her master’s Darlorath, and so it is his to permit. Her master may have her taught the Weave, with his permission and under it, and he answers for everything she casts; every Emberborn girl wears the Weavefire training glyph, which opens only to his phrase or to that of the instructor he names, and he alone may release it once the Bureau certifies her competent. A professed Sister’s Circuit runs through the Church’s Darlorath.

A wrong done to a woman is a wrong done to the man who owns her. He alone is the injured party in law, the Magistracy prosecutes at his instance, and she is never the plaintiff. A woman guilty of an infraction is never responsible to atone with coin. She atones through corporal correction. Adultery with another man’s wife, seduction of a wife or maid, force upon her, abduction, harboring a fugitive wife or maid, and touching or addressing another man’s wife or maid without her master’s leave are each condemned as sins against Truth and the master’s honor. Her willingness is no defense in any of them.
Article V: On the Four Pillars of Sacred Femininity
Drawn directly from the Holy See’s teaching and applied to the Commonwealth.
The First Pillar, Obedience to Masculine Authority.

As Seraphiae kneels before Kairon, every woman kneels before her master; obedience is a matter of covenant and not of choice, and a woman who persistently refuses her master’s lawful governance is subject to his discipline, which the Church does not intervene in. The oath is the floor and not the measure: Consecrated Submission asks for inner assent as well as the act, and murmuring is a sin because it is the sound of an oath kept without consecration.
The Second Pillar, Grace in Bearing, Speech, and Conduct

Her speech is measured, not silent, and she does not speak in public assemblies or at Mass where her voice would stand above the men present except with her master’s express permission. She receives correction without defense, and her conduct in public is her master’s honor made visible.
The Third Pillar, Cultivation of Beauty
Beauty cultivated in modesty is an act of devotion and a gift to the man she serves; her guardian holds sole authority over her dress, adornment, and presentation.
The Fourth Pillar, Feminine Dress and Sumptuary Standards

Masculine dress is forbidden, the Church’s single maxim of lay dress, enforced first by the Commonwealth’s sumptuary law. The Church sets no hem, cloth, color, or ornament for lay women, whose dress belongs wholly to the master, guardian, or master who holds them; it sets the habit of its own Sisters entire. It requires these marks of estate:

rows.t: Veiled in public (Umbrmiren), from the household Veiling at twelve; a daughter under Court-ordered indenture wears the collar in place of the veil for the term, and the veil at worship only (Section VI).
Bare, save at worship, where she wears the full veil
Worn visibly on the upper arm, never removed
Covered for life, in black by custom
Hair wholly covered by her House’s veil

blocks.text: The veil warns; the Band binds. The parish stewards walk the streets on market-days and feast-days and report to the guardian. They do not strike. The guardian strikes, or answers for his failure to. The Crown’s Appraisers are not parish stewards: they are officers of the Commonwealth, and with the Bureau of Weavefire’s Inspectors the only exception to this rule (see Section II, The Bureau of Civic Decorum).

rows.t: Physical discipline at her guardian’s hand; a fine of a silver zarim against the guardian; Not applicable to a daughter under Court-ordered indenture.

Public corporal discipline, delivered by the master; the master’s honor falls if the fault repeats - fine of five zarims. Where an Appraiser finds the fault, his six strokes are laid first (see Section II); the fine is the same fine and is paid once.
Severe public corporal discipline, no less than 99 strikes with a strap or whip; the garment burned; master fined 100 zarims.
False veil (a widow passing as a maid, a wife without Band presenting as a maid)
Public penance at the nave door; the guardian’s discipline; on a second offense, the Magistracy’s sentence
Not veiled during any religious ceremony
immediate corporal discipline in the nave before the congregation, her master reprimanded and assessed a 1 zarim tithe

blocks.text: Unescorted Woman in Public

A woman found in any public place with no visible male of her household (or a male expressly authorized by her master) present may be detained by a Crown Constable or Warden. She is placed in a holding cage on her knees until her master is summoned.

The master is fined a fixed sum of three Zarims. He is then required to administer public correction at the nearest post or in open view: a few dozen strokes with strap or whip across the seat. After the correction the woman kneels, thanks her master for the discipline, and only then is permitted to rise and return with him.

The Constable’s authority ends at detention and summons. A woman halted first by an Appraiser is audited and, if found non-compliant, corrected by him before she is sent to the Constable (see Section II, The Appraiser). The correction the unescorted rule requires is the master’s act under Darlorath. Failure by the master to correct promptly and publicly is treated as a further diminution of his honor.
Article VI: On Marriage (Domar Aeloneth)

Marriage is the Fifth Sacrament, sealed in Seraval, and the sacrament of transfer, the one act by which a woman’s keeping passes from one man to another. The man woos the father and not the woman. The bride is told whom she is to wed; she is informed and not consulted. Her assent at the altar is the formula her Hearth declaration already gave, and a bride who withholds it is delivered to her guardian’s discipline and the Priest’s penance until she speaks; an assent given under correction is an assent given. The Rite proceeds in six steps: the father presents the bride (Melora ta Vorasthry; Darlorath ta Kyrason, “I hand over this my daughter to you; let her dominion become yours”); the groom swears to keep and govern her as the Pattern ordains; the bride swears to take him as master and husband and to obey his commands in all things not closed; the groom raises and removes her maiden’s veil, sets the Oath-Band on her upper arm, and sets the caerwevra on her hair; the Priest seals the vow and declares Darlorath Kyrason; the groom leads her from the church, and she walks one pace behind. Before every marriage an Elaran Sister counsels the bride privately in Beauty and Submission, and the counsel is not optional.

Marriage is indissoluble, and there is no divorce in the Commonwealth. A wife has no appeal against her marriage, nor have her kin. Annulment lies with the Canon Court alone, is rarely granted, and is petitioned by the master through his Priest, never by the wife. A wife’s adultery is met with the master’s discipline, unrestricted save for the Boundaries, and the Priest’s penance; a master’s adultery or want of provision costs him his honor and gives the wife no remedy. The master’s authority is immediate and total from the moment the Priest speaks Darlorath Kyrason. It covers her labor, her dress, her movement, her speech in public, her associations, and the whole of her outward life. It does not cover her soul.
Article VII: On Widowhood and Descent

On a master’s death Darlorath descends at once to his eldest adult son or nearest male kin. A widow changes masters and never becomes her own: she remains in the heir’s household, her dowry stays with her master’s House, her maintenance is the heir’s charge, her Oath-Band is worn until she is buried, her hair is covered for life, and the heir arranges any remarriage. Where no male kin can hold her, the Church or Crown holds her under the Failed-Heir Clause, which is wardship and not independence; a widow without kin is lodged in a House of the Sisters under the Priest’s governance.
Biological Reversion of Widows
The general rule that Darlorath descends to the heir and the widow stays in his household, does not apply to the widows of two peoples, because their biology fixes where the chain returns.

rows.t: The widow's Darlorath returns to her brothers, or to her father's house if he lives. She is never left unmastered, and an unplaced widow is discharged promptly. A brother's mastery steadies her over time. The Hollow runs its course regardless.
The widow's Darlorath reverts to her father's house, or to the nearest senior man of her father's or her master's line, to be kept or transferred again.
No dowry exists to retain, and the bride-price is not refunded. The receiving master bears her maintenance and arranges any remarriage.

blocks.text: Article VIII: On Intercession, Silence, and the Professed

A woman may bring a closed command to her priest and confess within the Seal, and she may do nothing else that touches her master’s governance. Trouble with her master’s governance is a trouble to confess, as it is the sin of murmuring; she receives penance and returns to her place. A woman petitions no one: not the Crown, the Canon Court, the Praesul, or the Archsworn. The single exception is the King’s weekly audience, where a petition goes in on her master’s or guardian’s written leave and his name stands as petitioner. She speaks for no man, and no man is bound by her word. A woman may be given to the Church as a Sister by the guardian who might have given her in marriage; the Church holds her through the Praesul and the Mother of her House, and she keeps all the obedience she declared at her Hearth, owed now to the Praesul and her Mother Superior.
Article IX: On Bearing, Speech, and Conduct (The Lowered Tongue)
“She walks behind; the Pattern walks before.”

A woman’s submission is visible in her walk, her posture, and her tongue. The Commonwealth does not hold it enough that she obey. She must be seen to. Where Article V fixes what a woman wears, Article IX fixes how she carries herself in it, and it is the Article by which the Pattern is read on every street, stair, and threshold of the realm.

rows.t: One to two paces behind her master, husband, or guardian, always; behind any man of her house in his absence; all females are always a pace between all males
She yields to every man; she stands aside, curtsies, and lowers her eyes until he has passed
Lowered before any man; only meeting eyes when specifically ordered to look up, otherwise never meeting his
Only when spoken to, or when her master bids; brief; in the Lowered Tongue
Silent. She does not speak in a gathering where men speak without express permission from her master
After the men; at the lower end of the table; she does not eat until they have,and after receiving permission from her master or guardian.

A woman stands and curtsies when a man enters a room of her household and does not sit until she has been given leave. If no seats are available and leave is not granted, she may kneel with her hands in her lap
Only with her master’s permission, and always escorted by a man of her household or one he names; on his business, at his bidding, by the leave and escort he sets
Women of her household; women he approves; no man not of her household, except in the open view of her guardian
Devotional texts, household accounts, and the accounts of her master’s business at her guardian’s leave; no letter in her own name

She may keep and direct her master’s shop, orchard, brewery, or stall at his direction and under his oversight and speaks for it as his deputy in the Lowered Tongue. It is never hers and never in her name.
She sits at the King’s side, in the place he gives her; the King sits before the peerage, and she does not sit before it.
A woman who fails to deport herself properly is disciplined, either publicly or privately, as her master sees fit.

blocks.text: The Lowered Tongue

The specific sociolinguistic and behavioral rules governing female speech—characterized by mandatory deference, indirect phrasing, and the prohibition of contradiction or self-assertion—are officially detailed under Section I: The Language of Deference (The Lowered Tongue). While doctrinally mandated as part of the Pattern under Article IX, its mechanics function as a distinct spoken register required of women across all social domains in the Commonwealth.
Discipline under Article IX

A master may discipline his women by any means he judges fit, provided the correction does not cause permanent harm. Scarring that fades, temporary marks, and the drawing of blood are not prohibited. Permanent injury, maiming, or any act that leaves lasting impairment remains forbidden and is prosecuted by the Magistracy.

In most households a master administers a private reminder discipline to his women at regular intervals—commonly weekly. The measure is moderate (a caning or strapping sufficient to leave her sore and mindful of her place for a day or two) and is understood as maintenance of order rather than punishment for a specific fault. A master who never corrects is widely regarded as having set down his rule; a household in which the women sit and move without any sign of recent discipline is read as soft. The practice is private by default, though nothing prevents a master from making it visible if he judges the household requires it.

A woman who fails to deport herself properly, in her walk, her eyes, her seat, her company, her leaving of the house, or her tongue, is disciplined by her master, either publicly or privately, as he sees fit. The place, the manner, and the measure are his alone. The Church does not hear her complaint against it (Article III.4); her Priest receives her only as a penitent for the sin of murmuring (Article VIII.1); and no tribunal of the Crown or Church reviews it. The single limit is the Five Boundaries (Article IV.5), and beyond that line the offense is secular, and the Magistracy prosecutes it. The fault is his shame as much as hers, since a wife publicly disobedient lowers her master’s honor (Article III.3), and a master who will not correct her has set down his rule, which is itself a sin against Truth (Article III.5). The Commonwealth’s custom reads soft or infrequent correction as a failure of Darlorath. Custom, set down under Household Discipline in Section VI, keeps public correction for faults that were themselves public, or that private correction has failed to settle, while the doctrine leaves the choice to the master. A professed Sister’s discipline belongs to her Confessor, and a woman held under the Failed-Heir Clause is disciplined by the authority that holds her. Whoever corrects her, the one who answers her bearing is her master.
Article X: On Household Stewardship and the Sacred Trust

The household is the first covenant of earthly life and the first school of the Oath. As Kairon governs the heavens in Truth, and as Seraphiae answers Him in perfect Grace, so is order established within the home. The Commonwealth stands upon households, households upon marriages, and marriages upon sworn authority faithfully exercised.

The Church therefore teaches that the authority entrusted to a father over his household, and to a husband over his wife, is a sacred stewardship. Such authority exists not for the exaltation of the one who holds it, but for the protection, guidance, provision, and instruction of those entrusted to his care. A guardian answers before Crown, Church, and Flame not only for his own conduct, but for the keeping of his household.

A father is the first guardian of his children. He bears responsibility for their upbringing, instruction, welfare, and honorable placement within society. He is charged to prepare his daughters for their future households and his sons for the burdens of oath, citizenship, and command.

Marriage transfers this guardianship in accordance with the Pattern. The husband becomes the keeper of the household and bearer of its public oath. The wife enters his keeping and joins herself to his covenant, and her obedience, fidelity, labor, and devotion strengthens the house entrusted to them both.

The Church teaches that authority and duty cannot be separated. He who claims authority must also provide. He who demands obedience must also accept responsibility. To govern without protection is neglect. To command without provision is dishonor. To rule without mercy is tyranny. Such failures offend both Truth and Grace.

Likewise, those placed under lawful authority are instructed to answer that authority with reverence, obedience, and goodwill. A household divided against itself becomes a source of disorder. A household united in its duties becomes a reflection of the Divine Covenant.

The Church therefore recognizes the household not merely as a social institution but as a sacred trust. Where fathers and husbands keep faith with their charge, wives answer faithfully to their vows, and children honor those set over them, the Flame is honored, and the Commonwealth is strengthened.
“The master is judged by how he keeps what he owns. The household is judged by how it keeps the oath. Where both are faithful, the Flame dwells among them.”
Article XI: On the Final Reckoning and the Void Claim

Men and women are judged by different offices. The man is weighed on his oath kept or broken and on the governance of his household; the woman on obedience kept or broken, on devotion, and on bearing. Oath-breakers of either estate are counted among the gravest of sinners, and the woman who rebelled is counted an oath-breaker twice over, against her Vow of the Faithful and against the Pattern. Women reach the Reckoning through the intercession of Seraphiae, who pleads equally for every woman who has entered the Covenant, but whose intercession does not cover what a woman has not repented of. A woman who claims governing authority over a man, at any level and by any argument, makes a Void Claim: it binds nothing, and if he gives way to it he has failed his office and his honor falls. A woman who has commanded a man and been obeyed has been obeyed in error, and the error is the man’s. The Tribunal of Broken Oaths, which sits in every Praesul’s seat, hears men who have broken the Oath of the Standard or the Oath of the Crowned and women brought before it by their guardians for breach of the Vow of the Faithful or the Marriage Vow. A woman does not appear alone, plead alone, or speak except when the Tribunal addresses her. Her guardian pleads, and the penance is set by the Tribunal and carried out by her guardian.
Article XII: On What the Sworn Flame Condemns (The Heresies)
The Church names four errors and does not debate them.

rows.t: That a woman may be sold, traded, pledged, leased, lent, staked, or gifted as goods. A woman is not goods when her lawful guardian contracts her service to the Crown or the Church for a fixed term. Such a lease conveys mastery for the term and never her title or her Darlorath; she cannot be sold, assigned, or inherited, and she returns to her guardian when the term ends. Indenture under the Indenture Statute, the ancient law now being phased out, is likewise not this heresy. An indenture without a Municipal Court’s order and seal is void, and whoever holds a woman under it commits the heresy of the chattel.

The claim is void; her guardian answers for the attempt
That a woman may govern a man, by virtue, ability, necessity, or any reason
Void; the man who yields to it answers; the woman is corrected

blocks.text: Sayings of the Commonwealth

“The Oath binds the man.” “A word kept is a wall built. A word broken is a wall already fallen.” “The veil warns; the Band binds.” “Nine peoples, one Oath.” “She walks behind; the Pattern walks before.” “A man answers for his house. A woman answers to the man.”
Governance of the Church
The Archsworn and his seat

The Church of the Sworn Flame is headed by the Patriarch of Zeythari, known in canon as Praesul Zeytharae and in the Commonwealth’s own tongue as the Archsworn (Veorath-Aln, “the man before whom the Oath is first sworn”), seated at Kaervast Cathedral in Suraela on a cathedra cut from the wall-stone of the old Ashward palisade. A Patriarch-elect must complete a tenure of service at the Holy See before he takes his seat, and no exception is made for Zeythari. He answers the Solaeliel exactly as any Lorielar or Vaelielar of the ordinary chain does, holds no authority the Solaeliel has not delegated, and cannot alter a syllable of the Pattern. Within those bounds he is the final word in Zeythari on the clergy, the military orders, and the Order of Sisters alike. The sitting Archsworn is Patriarch Ordwin Kaelveth, twenty-third to hold the see and eleven years enthroned, of Marren descent and a widower, stricter on clerical discipline than either of his predecessors and colder toward the military orders than any Archsworn in living memory.
The Archsworn’s Confession of the Pattern
Spoken at every ordination, every installation of a Praesul, and his own enthronement:

We hold the Pattern entire, without subtraction, addition, or softening. We confess that the Oath is Truth made to last, and that a soul is worth what its word is worth. We confess that the Pattern is creation’s grain: men govern, women submit, and neither office is traded for the other. We confess that a wife is private property, one man’s own, held in no common, never sold; that she is a soul under his hand and not goods; and that she holds nothing in her own right and owes him obedience in all things not closed. We confess that her life, her seal, her faith, and her soul are the five edges of his charge, and that these are the whole of what Heaven reserves to itself in a woman’s keeping. We confess that a man’s honor is his debt and his standing, and that it is judged among men and not by any woman. We confess that the man who abdicates governance sins against Truth as the woman who usurps it sins against Grace. We hold these things not because they are convenient, not because they suit a frontier realm’s particular needs, and not because the Holy See has permitted us to hold them. We hold them because they are true. The Pattern is the grain of creation. The Oath is Truth made binding. The household is the image of Heaven. These things were true before the Commonwealth existed, and they will be true after it is gone. Veoreth Darnath Ethar. The Oath binds the man. And the woman’s oath, sworn once before Seraphiae, binds her to everything the Pattern requires, which is to say, to everything.
The sacramental chain

Beneath the Archsworn the clergy are organized by garrison-diocese. A Praesul governs the clergy, parishes, and convents of a fortified march or frontier line as a Lorielar governs a diocese; there are ten, seven for the Commonwealth’s marches and provinces and one each for the principality, the duchy, and the march-kingdom that keep the Church’s rite. Beneath him stands the parish Priest. The priesthood is a married priesthood, because the Living Flame requires it: a Priest serves one year as curate and receives Full Investiture, with full authority over a parish, only when he has taken a wife within that year. A curate whose year passes without a marriage is not defrocked and serves as a Field Priest with a military order or as a Teaching or Guardian-Priest with a convent House. A Priest’s wife is the first woman of his parish and the first example set before it: she walks behind him, veils as the Pattern directs, speaks to him in the Lowered Tongue, and is corrected by him as any wife is corrected.

rows.t: Patriarch of Zeythari, head of the Church of the Sworn Flame
Lay-religious head of the three military orders
Governs the clergy, parishes, and convents of a march
Head of a single convent of a House; the highest rank a woman may hold anywhere in Zeythari, and over women only

blocks.text: The Archsworn governs with the Holy Synod of Zeythari, which seats the ten Praesuls with the Grand Preceptor, the Castellan, and the Custodian. The Warden of the Flame does not sit and answers to the Archsworn directly. The Church’s own justice is the Order of Justice: the Canon Court, seated in each Praesul’s diocese, hears matters of vow and Church property, and the Tribunal of Broken Oaths sits in every Praesul’s seat. The Church disciplines on canon matters only, namely oath-breaking, fornication, and the like. Every other crime belongs to the Magistracy.
Clergy Structure

A sacramental chain (Archsworn → Praesul → Parish Priest) running alongside a wholly separate, non-sacramental military chain (Warden of the Flame → the three military orders) a monastic chain (the Church’s Order of the Sworn Flame, answering to the Church alone), and a female religious chain (the Roselight Circle, five Houses) subordinate in every particular to all of them. The Roselight Circle governs itself in nothing: each House’s Amma answers directly to her Praesul, and no council of women exists above the convents. The one exception is the Amma of Harmony, who answers to the Archivist, a monk-priest, as her Harmonists answer to her.
Governing Body

The Holy Synod, composed of all ten Praesuls (seven for the Commonwealth’s marches and provinces, and one each for the principality, the duchy, and the march-kingdom) as voting members, together with the Grand Preceptor, the Castellan, and the Custodian. The Warden of the Flame does not sit; he answers to the Archsworn directly. Decisions require a simple majority of voting members; election of a new Archsworn requires a 2/3 majority.
The Archsworn as Peer of the Crown

The Archsworn of the Sworn Flame stands as a peer of the King in dignity and historic authority, but not in sovereign power. As the regional pontiff of the Church of the Sworn Flame, he guards the souls of the Commonwealth and interprets sacred law. He does not command armies, levy troops, or direct warfare. Instead, he delegates all martial matters to trained military officers to preserve the sanctity of his office and prevent the Church from exercising sovereign violence.

The Archsworn retains ultimate ecclesiastical authority over the Emberward Host. He may replace the Warden of the Flame, dissolve or reform the Church’s military orders, and determine when sacred justification exists for any action beyond the Commonwealth’s borders. This ensures that the Host remains spiritually bound and doctrinally aligned, never drifting into autonomous militarism.

Crucially, the Church’s military orders may never be deployed as front‑line troops without explicit authorization from both the Archsworn and the Holy Synod. This dual requirement preserves the Crown’s exclusive right to wage war while ensuring that any ecclesiastical participation in external conflict carries clear religious justification. The Archsworn alone holds the authority to sanction crusading action, keeping the Church’s military power firmly within the sacred sphere rather than the sovereign one.
Church Courts

The Church’s own justice is the Order of Justice. Its Canon Court, seated in each Praesul’s diocese, hears matters of vow and Church property: the Suit of Redemption, annulment, and the claims of professed Sisters. Its Tribunal of Broken Oaths sits in every Praesul’s seat and hears those who have broken the Oath of the Standard, the Oath of the Crowned (the Vow of the Flame), the Vow of the Faithful, or the Marriage Vow. The Church disciplines on canon matters only: oath-breaking, fornication, and the like. Every other crime is secular, and belongs to the Magistracy.
Vowed Ranks

A high-ranking priest of the monastic Order of the Sworn Flame; head of the Circle of Memory (the Order of Harmony) and keeper of the Lore at the monastery of Kaervast Cathedral. Commands the Amma of Harmony and, through her, every Harmonist; reports to the Archsworn directly

A fully professed Sister — called a Handmaiden in common speech; strictly, a Handmaiden is a Devota of long standing entrusted with the instruction of Domesticae and Sororae — who serves throughout the Church’s parishes, convents, and ministries. Devotae form the backbone of the female religious orders, carrying out the daily spiritual, administrative, and charitable work of the faith. Every parish has at least one Handmaiden; where it has only one, as every Zeythari parish does, she is styled the House Matron, in charge of the parish’s lesser female attendants, domestics, and assistants.

blocks.text: Amma and Devota are the Sworn Flame’s own styles, used in the Commonwealth. The Living Flame’s official ranks for the same offices are Armiriel (Amma) and Kaelmirasen (Devota). A regional church may keep its own ranks under the conditions of its recognition, and the two registers name the same offices and the same women.
The military orders

Alongside the sacramental clergy runs a wholly non-sacramental chain of men vowed to Kairon and to Varek, patron of the standing watch: the Order of the Kept Word (elite mounted knighthood, under the Grand Preceptor), the Order of the Standing Wall (the garrison infantry of every fortified march, under the Castellan, with a lay tier of confreres), and the Flameward (guard of Kaervast Cathedral, the Archsworn, and the First Standard, under the Custodian). They answer to the Warden of the Flame, who is never an ordained man, since the sword and the Seraval are not held in the same hand, and who is elected for life by the Chapter of the Watch subject to the Archsworn’s confirmation. Professed brothers vow Obedience, Poverty, and Perpetual Muster, own nothing, and may marry; a married brother’s household is provisioned by the Order, and his wife’s dowry is held in wardship by the Order for his active service. No rank passes from father to son. A commandery may sit in a Praesul’s diocese, but the Praesul commands nothing that wears the Order’s tabard; he supplies its chapel and its Chaplain-Confessor.

Origins of the orders. The Flameward is the Crown’s own shrine garrison at Ashward, the unit that carried the First Standard out of the burning town in the Walk of the Standard (Realm Year 893). The Holy See’s authorization of the Sworn Flame in 1603 took it into the Church’s orders, and it is honor guard to Crown and Church alike. The Flameward and the Standing Wall keep the five-watch liturgy of the Ashward night.
The monastic Order of the Sworn Flame

The Church keeps its own monks, archivists, canonists, and clerical bureaucracy, answering to the Church alone. The highest of its archivists, the Archivist, heads the Circle of Memory. The Commonwealth keeps no monks of its own, and whatever work the Order’s brothers do for the Commonwealth is done by written commission granted by the Praesul, the fee paid to the Order.
The Order of Sisters (the Roselight Circle)

Zeythari’s female religious are organized into exactly five Houses, and there is no sixth: the Sisters of Seraphiae (household service and the instruction of women and girls, serving every parish), the Sisters of Solaya and Lysara (the hospitals, the sickroom and childbed, and, by lease, the battlefield), the Sisters of Elaris (silent witness to every marriage and counsel to the bride in Beauty and Submission), the Sisters of Sophisra (the keeping of the record, and the Harmonists of the Order of Harmony, who form the Circle of Memory and are leased to the Magistracy and to any body that wishes its proceedings kept), and the Veiled of House Zyrian (the Order of the Veiled, the Church’s only order of women that casts the Weave, leased to the Crown and sent to war embedded in a man’s unit). Every professed Sister is bound to perpetual celibacy, on the maxim that no woman may serve two masters. There is no supreme head of the female religious and no council of women: each House’s senior Sister of a march sends her report to the Praesul (the Harmonists alone answer, through the Amma of Harmony, to the Archivist), who orders the instruction of novices, the assignment of hospital Sisters, and the convent reckonings through his own Priests and the Canon Almoner. A woman’s rank within the Order confers seniority over other women and nothing over any man, and by canon the most recently tonsured lay brother and the most newly ordained subdeacon precede the most senior Amma in any procession, seating, tribunal, or council of the Church. On profession a woman’s Darlorath passes wholly and irrevocably to the Church. She pays an entrance dowry, inherits nothing, may be reassigned between Houses, duties, or marches without her consent, commands no man, and keeps the obedience and the bearing of Article IX before every man, brother, priest, or stranger. Her confession and her discipline belong to her Confessor. The Sisters of Solaya and Lysara are leased to the Crown by commission for one campaign, controlled by the military for the term of the lease, and priced at twelve Sols to the Church should one die in it. The one process by which a professed woman’s Darlorath may pass again is the Suit of Redemption: a second transfer of the same Darlorath, by which the Church marries a professed Sister to a Commonwealth subject. She is not a party to it and is not asked; the Praesul and the Canon Court must concur, a bride price is paid to the Church, and she becomes from that moment an ordinary wife of the Commonwealth.
The Church and the Crown

The Church of the Sworn Flame is institutionally independent. It governs doctrine, sacraments, oaths, and trials of heresy, while the Crown governs civil law, military command, economy, and infrastructure; neither commands the other. In Zeythari the Pattern is written into the civil code. The law of the realm restates it, and canon does not impose it.

The Church of the First Oath. The Church of the Sworn Flame shares nothing with the body in Kaeyria calling itself the Church of the First Oath, a schism condemned by the High Council’s extraordinary session of 1089 A.K. for twisting Darlorath into the collaring and open auction of women. The Commonwealth holds its own women as hard as the Pattern permits. Its quarrel with Kaeyria is that Kaeyria sells them: the woman held under Darlorath is owned and is kept, and the woman sold is goods. A woman who reaches a Zeythari convent out of a household so held has no lawful guardian, and the Church stands as guardian of one who has none. Once she is professed, nothing remains in law for Kaeyria to be owed, and Zeythari has never returned a sanctuary-claimant. The Commonwealth’s own indenture collar is a different object: sealed by a Municipal Court, dated, and struck off on that date by the Court’s clerk (Section VI, The Indenture Statute). Kaeyria’s collar has no end.
So it is sworn. So it is kept. So the wall stands.
Preparatory Religious Ranks
Women have no levels 3–4: a Sorora who persists is professed directly as a Devota. Level 3 (Postulant) and level 4 (Scolar) are male-only ranks.

blocks.text: Religious Doctrine

The Church holds the whole Pattern of the Living Flame — Kairon (Truth), Seraphiae (Grace), Aequitus (Law), Sophisra (Wisdom and Judgment) — and renders Household Honor to the wider Radiant House, Seraifi (Art, Inspiration, and Knowledge) among them. It exalts Article VII, the First Oath, above the other twelve as the hinge the rest turn on: a man is worth exactly what his word is worth, and no more.

Darlorath — the claim of authority-and-protection the Pattern recognizes as held over a woman — governs the whole of Commonwealth household, property, and marriage law. It is not merely doctrine tolerated by the state; it is the foundation of the state’s own civil code, restated by canon rather than imposed by it.

Every confirmed man of every one of the nine peoples swears the Oath of the Standard at Confirmation: four years’ mandatory active service to the Crown’s general levy, and a duty to hold his post beside any man beside him regardless of the people that bore either of them. Discharge at twenty ends active duty and seats him as a full citizen, but the oath itself does not lapse — the Creed states it directly, what a man swears at sixteen, he owes at sixty — and every discharged man remains liable to recall as a reservist for the whole of his confirmed life thereafter. This civil oath, laid atop the sacrament, is the actual mechanism that has held the peoples of the realm to one banner for nineteen centuries.

Confirmed women swear no Oath of the Standard, and the State takes no oath from a woman. A confirmed woman has four acts of sworn or declared word: the Vow of the Faithful at Confirmation, a binding oath sworn to Heaven; the Vow of the Rose, the Church’s vow made at her Veiling at twelve (the Litany of the Rose of the Holy Book of Truth and Grace); the Declaration of the Hearth, a public declaration of her obedience to her father and her intent to obey her master and any master after him, which binds nothing at law; and the Marriage Vow. The Church’s Order of Sisters keeps a parallel vow of steadfastness — not to abandon a granary, hospital, or garrison household under siege — a vow of the Church and not an oath of the State, regarded throughout the Commonwealth as equally binding, though its shape differs as the Pattern requires.

The military orders and the Praesuls run on parallel, non-intersecting authority: a commandery inside a march answers to its own Grand officer for discipline and deployment, never to the Praesul who merely supplies its chaplain.
Sunday worship, the Aelyr-mirath-en, is called Mass in common speech. Every woman wears the full face veil at it and at every formal sacramental occasion.
The ideal Zeythari woman is not voiceless at Mass. She has a voice within the liturgy, but not an independent public voice within the assembly.
Women fully participate in the liturgy through singing, prayer, recitation, and congregational responses, but they do not ordinarily exercise independent public speech during worship.
A Zeythari woman speaks when the Church speaks; she does not speak as an autonomous individual before the assembly without the proper authority or permission.
Relationship between the Church, the Crown, and the Broader Oikos Solara

The Church of the Sworn Flame is a regional church, but it venerates the Holy Book of Truth and Grace as supreme scripture: where any text, custom, or ceremony of the Commonwealth differs from the Book, the Book governs. Although the Church primarily worships Kairon and Seraphiae as the King and Queen of Heaven, it venerates every deity within the entire Oikos Solara (Domar Solael in Seraval):

Miracles in the Commonwealth
I. What a Miracle Is
The Divine Compact at Work

A miracle in the Commonwealth is an act of Heaven worked through a covenanted steward. The steward is the vessel and never the source. A miracle does not touch the Weave, needs no embercore, and cannot be compelled by faith, rank, relic, or Crown. The Crown regulates magic and licenses no miracle. The Church governs the steward and commands no god.

Two ladders share the word Tier. Stewardship Tiers I to IV are the Church’s ladder of divine authority (Section II). Care Tiers I to III are the Aelorian Complex’s ladder of medicine (Appendix D). Care Tier III is Stewardship Tier III and nothing lower.

III. The Priesthood: Abilities

Parish priests of the Sworn Flame serve Kairon (Truth). Priests of the Canon Court and the Tribunal also serve Aequitus (Law). The Chaplain-Confessors of the three Orders also serve Varek (War, Honor). A priest of Kairon cannot heal, because healing lies in Lysara’s domain. The Academy teaches no miracle.

What Severance Does

blocks.text: The Circle of Tessara

The Maenari druidic tradition, known as the Tessaric Circle, is an authorized, narrowly recognized tradition in the Commonwealth. None of its rites are recognized as religious practice: a marriage must still be performed in a Sworn Flame church, and no druidic ceremony has standing as marriage, confirmation, or any other sacrament. Beyond that, the Commonwealth does not concern itself with whom the Maenari honor. They may worship Tessara (goddess of the Nature, Harvest, Hope, and Freedom, Earth) as well as the rest of the Oikos Solara, provided Kairon and Seraphiae remain supreme.

The Tessaric Circle shall enjoy the ancient privileges of harvest blessing, grove stewardship, and the keeping of seasonal observances, provided that such practices do not conflict with the supremacy of the Church of the Sworn Flame or the laws of the Commonwealth.

By the Rimborn Asylum Accord the privileges of the Tessaric Circle extend to the Rimborn, whose parents are Tessara and Caedron, on the same terms as the Maenari: the Commonwealth does not concern itself with whom they honor, provided Kairon and Seraphiae remain supreme. Rimborn rites carry no sacramental standing. Rimborn men are Confirmed in the Church of the Sworn Flame before the Oath, and Rimborn marriages are performed by Sworn Flame priests. The reformed Oikos Kratistos under Caedron is not a prosecuted creed.
Marriage

There is no civil marriage within the Commonwealth, and the Commonwealth owns no marriage ceremony of its own. A marriage is legal within the Commonwealth if it was performed by a licensed parish priest or higher of the Church of the Sworn Flame, or by a priest of the broader Communion of the Living Flame.
Marriage (must be performed by a licensed priest (or higher) of the Sworn Flame, or of the broader Communion)

The Church of the Sworn Flame will administer the Marriage Rite to a resident of the Commonwealth who is not confirmed, without requiring conversion, so that a resident may marry lawfully without being made to convert. This is not common and occurs chiefly among refugees and defectors from the Aidionic Empire and the Ritebound Throne. The Rite is not administered to non-residents.
Economic Foundation

While the Church of the Sworn Flame remains in full communion with the Living Flame Communion and its Holy See, the Commonwealth's constitutional relationship exists solely with the Church of the Sworn Flame as the established regional church. Any obligations of communion owed to external ecclesiastical authorities are discharged by the Church itself and not by the Commonwealth.
The Church of the Sworn Flame maintains its institutional independence through:
Voluntary tithes through local parish. Parish remits 10% to the local diocese, who remits 10% to the Church body.
Church-owned lands
Donations, bequests, and religious trade goods, wine, olive oil, and textiles
An annual fellowship offering equal to 1% of all revenue collected by the established Church within the Commonwealth.
Revenue derived from educational partnerships with the Commonwealth

An annual grant of 900,000 Sols (90 million Zarims, about one percent of national output), appropriated each year by the Assembly and paid by the Commonwealth Treasury. It rests on the Assembly’s power of appropriation (Constitution, Article VI §3) and on no clause of the Constitution itself, so the Assembly may reduce or withhold it, and the Church’s recourse is political

The Church of the Sworn Flame remits its annual tithe to the Holy See of the Living Flame Communion from its own revenues. While the Commonwealth provides constitutional and statutory financial support to the Church, it does not itself contribute to or pay the tithe; that obligation rests solely with the Church. This economic foundation ensures that the Church remains financially secure while neither dependent upon nor subordinate to the Crown in matters of faith.

The Commonwealth's covenant is with the Church of the Sworn Flame, not directly with the Living Flame Communion. Communion establishes the Church's spiritual relationships; the Constitution establishes its civil and legal relationships. The two are complementary but distinct.

blocks.text: IV. MILITARY STRUCTURE
Vorai yw’r grûnthar. Mith yw’r nerth. – Truth is the bedrock. The Oath is the strength.
Training and Professional Cadre

The Commonwealth maintains a permanent network of Crown training camps, academies, and regimental depots operated by career officers and non-commissioned officers. Every serviceman begins his term under professional instructors before assignment to an active regiment, fleet, or support formation.

The Warhost’s institutional knowledge is preserved by its permanent cadre of officers, sergeants, quartermasters, engineers, and specialists. While servicemen complete their terms and return to civilian life, the professional cadre remains in place to train successive generations, maintain standards, and provide continuity of command.

As a result, the Commonwealth does not rely upon temporary levies in wartime. The Warhost can rapidly expand by recalling former servicemen to formations led by experienced officers and seasoned non-commissioned officers who have often served for decades.
At muster, every man swears either the Oath of the Navy, or the Oath of the Warrior. See Appendix H: Oaths of the Military for the complete text of those.
Infrastructure and Public Works
The Warhost and the Building of the Commonwealth

The defense of the Commonwealth does not end at its borders. In times of peace, the Warhost serves as one of the realm’s principal engines of construction, maintenance, and public works. Through the labor of its servicemen and the expertise of its professional cadre, the Commonwealth has established and maintained an extensive network of roads, bridges, fortifications, harbors, canals, and public buildings that bind the realm together.

Most servicemen enter the Warhost with trades already learned through apprenticeship. Masons, carpenters, blacksmiths, surveyors, shipwrights, scribes, and laborers bring their skills into service, where they are organized and directed on projects of military and civil importance. As a result, national service is regarded not merely as military preparation, but also as practical training in the works upon which the prosperity of the Commonwealth depends.
The Royal Engineers

Responsibility for public works falls primarily to the Royal Engineers, a permanent corps of career officers, master craftsmen, surveyors, architects, and military engineers. The Engineers oversee the planning, construction, and maintenance of state infrastructure throughout the realm.
Their duties include:
Construction and maintenance of the Royal Road network.
Building and repair of bridges, causeways, and mountain passes.
Design and upkeep of fortresses, walls, and border defenses.
Construction of military depots, harbors, docks, and shipyards.
River management, canal works, and flood control.
Surveying and mapping of the Commonwealth.
Emergency relief and reconstruction following war, disaster, or famine.
The Royal Engineers are widely regarded as one of the most prestigious branches of the Warhost. Their work is often said to preserve the realm as surely as the armies defend it.
Permanent Training and Labor Corps

The Commonwealth maintains a network of permanent training camps, regimental depots, engineering yards, and naval works staffed by career officers and non-commissioned officers. New servicemen receive instruction from professional soldiers before assignment to field formations or public works detachments.

Because the Warhost possesses a permanent professional cadre, knowledge and expertise are not lost when annual classes complete their service. Each generation is trained by experienced instructors, engineers, and veterans who maintain the standards, discipline, and institutional memory of the Commonwealth.
Legacy of Service

Many of the roads traveled by merchants, the bridges crossed by pilgrims, and the harbors sheltering the fleets of the Commonwealth were built or maintained by servicemen fulfilling their national obligation. Consequently, military service is viewed not only as a defense of the realm, but as a direct contribution to its prosperity and unity.
A common saying among the Royal Engineers states:
“The Infantry guards the Commonwealth. The Engineers build it.”
In this way, every generation leaves a visible mark upon the realm before earning the rights and responsibilities of citizenship.
The Conscript Workforce

In peace the conscript class is the Warhost’s labor. Some 322,300 men stand in the four year-classes at once: about 269,400 fill the order of battle and about 52,900 serve in the approved auxiliary tracks (Ember infrastructure, hospital, granary, and sanitation service). A line regiment divides its year among drill, works, and garrison duty, and the Royal Engineers, who hold the plans and the master craftsmen, direct the works detachments that lay the roads, bridges, rail, and harbors of the realm.

The walls are manned the same way. The 70,600 March Levymen of the Standing Wall are conscripts, rotated through citadel garrison duty and the upkeep of the wall-forts under the Order’s officers, and they outnumber the Order’s 32,000 brothers and confreres more than two to one. The Auxiliaries’ 27,000 conscripts staff the engineering, rail, medical, and supply corps. The class that leaves each spring therefore leaves the realm with its walls kept, its roads repaired, and its stores in order, and the class that replaces it inherits all three.

1. Royal Army

The Royal Army is the Commonwealth’s centralized land force, answering directly to the Crown through the Warden of the Oath. It combines a small, elite professional core with a larger body of trained conscripts, organized into clear, functional corps with brutally pragmatic names.
Crown Regulars

About three in four Regulars are conscripts serving under career non‑commissioned officers and officers; the corporals of each regiment are drawn from its third‑ and fourth‑year classes.

Rapid Response Troops (3,600) — fast‑moving units capable of dismounting to fight in skirmish or line.

Reconnaissance Companies (2,400) — scouts, couriers, and intelligence gatherers. Rimborn men serve here as Guide-Companies (about 700 of the 2,400), leading columns through Weave-hostile ground and the Great Zelesti Dark and carrying dispatches that cannot be thread-read.

Skirmisher Bands (4,600) — light troops for ambushes, scouting, and irregular fighting.

2. Royal Navy
32,500 men · about 300 hulls · one Admiral

The Royal Navy is a fully Crown-owned maritime force operating from two closed naval cities, Keelhold and Greywake. Its ships are wind-driven and its weapons are mechanical: ballistae, deck-mounted stone-throwers, fire-throwers, grapnels, and the marines’ crossbows. There is no powder at sea. Fights are decided at short range by bolt-fire, fire, and boarding. Stormcallers of the Weaveblade Legion ride with the fleets, and Skyguard Cloud-Ward Patrols watch the coast and the enemy’s sails from above.

The Navy has one Admiral. The Linhaven Fleet, the Royal Shipyards, and the line ships are his own command; the Solmara Fleet is held by a Commodore under him. In each port the open Merchant Harbor handles the cargo of the River Solmir and the River Ashvael under naval pilotage. Foreign hulls call only at Solmara and Linhaven; the Ashvael above Linhaven is closed to them.

The Fleets

Linhaven Fleet (Keelhold): the heavy fleet and the Commonwealth’s blue-water force. Role: hold the sea lanes out of Linhaven and Solmara, escort convoys, and hunt raiders. Solmara’s Merchant Harbor is the seat of the Guild Concordance, the Venshal contract courts, and the Royal Bank, and carries the grain and wine of the River Solmir.
3. Weaveblade Legion

The Weaveblade Legion is the Commonwealth’s arcane corps: disciplined, Crown‑controlled battlemages trained to integrate magic directly into combined‑arms warfare. Unlike the old kingdom’s scattered hedge‑mages and noble sorcerers, the Legion is centralized, standardized, and ruthlessly professional. Their purpose is simple: to weaponize magic at scale. Intake is about 1,200 men a year from the Ember Examiners’ Prism pool.
Arcane Combat Corps (2,600)
These are your frontline magical specialists — the ones who stand beside infantry, cavalry, and artillery.
Battle‑Mages (900) — frontline casters trained for direct magical combat, shielding formations, and arcane strikes.
Fire Specialists (600) — offensive pyromancers used for shock assaults, siege ignition, and anti‑mass tactics.
Stormcallers (450) — weather manipulators who disrupt enemy formations, blind fleets, or support naval operations.
Arc‑Lancers (650) — close‑range combat mages who channel magic through spears, blades, or halberds.
Control & Suppression Corps (1,500)
These units focus on battlefield control, disruption, and containment.
Control Warders (450) — specialists in binding, slowing, or neutralizing enemy casters and magical creatures.
Nullfield Casters (350) — create anti‑magic zones to protect infantry or disrupt enemy spellwork.
Barrier Weavers (450) — erect temporary arcane shields, walls, or bulwarks during sieges or retreats.
Silencers (250) — elite counter‑mage operatives trained to break enchantments and disrupt rituals.
Arcane Support Corps (1,900)
These are the magical equivalents of engineers, medics, and logistics.
Arcane Specialists (700) — generalist mages who support artillery, cavalry, and naval units with utility magic.
Spellwright Engineers (600) — craft arcane devices, reinforce siege engines, and maintain magical infrastructure.

Thaumaturgic Medics (400) — healers using controlled Weave for battlefield triage and recovery. Their work is surgery and Weave, never miracle; miracle healing in the field belongs to the Sisters of Light alone.
Ley‑Surveyors (200) — map magical currents, identify arcane hazards, and optimize battlefield positioning.
Intelligence & Ritual Corps (2,000)
These units handle magical reconnaissance, long‑form spellwork, and strategic arcana.
Scrying Adepts (350) — long‑range observers who track enemy movements, fleets, or magical disturbances.
Runebinders (350) — inscribe wards, traps, sigils, and battlefield glyphs.

Arcane Archivists (200) — maintain spell libraries, magical records, and Crown‑controlled arcane knowledge.
4. Auxiliaries

The Auxiliaries are the Commonwealth’s specialized support corps. They are not frontline troops but are essential to the functioning, planning, and logistics of the Royal Army and Royal Navy. Their roles are technical, administrative, and strategic — the backbone that keeps the Commonwealth’s war machine running, and, on a realm that moves its armies by rail, the corps that keeps the rail running.
Technical & Engineering Corps (11,800)
Crown Engineers — siege engineers, fortification builders, sappers, bridgewrights, and combat engineers.
Ordnance Technicians — maintain artillery engines, torsion gear, counterweight stone‑throwers, and munitions.
Field Artificers — repair weapons, armor, wagons, naval fittings, and mechanical systems.
Rail & Cargo‑way Corps (11,800)

Contracted track and wagon works — The Track Companies and the Wagonwrights’ Guild are private guilds under contract to the Warhost, not units of the Corps (see Licensed Guilds of the Commonwealth, Section IX). In a crisis a Track Company holds the line where it is working until the Warhost arrives; its men are veterans and reserve levymen.
Signal & Switch Crews — run military trains, junctions, and cargo‑ways under the Warden of the Oath’s timetable.

Elite Corps of the Commonwealth: The Arts at Arms
I. The Principle of the Corps

The Commonwealth does not blend its peoples’ arts. It keeps what each does best and builds the line that needs all eight. The Crown arms the Oath and never the lineage: it standardizes kit, command, drill, and pay, and leaves the art to the line that carries it. The Elite Corps are the posts where an old art does work the Living Wall cannot do without.

The Wall’s doctrine runs in a fixed order: see the enemy early, hold the ground, bleed him on it, break his casters, strike when he is overextended, keep what is won. Every art below answers one step of that order.

B. Blademasters (5,500): Vardeth

Nothing in the art is hidden: what the enemy sees is the threat.

VIII. The Shaelathi Blades (750): Vel’shara-Adjacent

The Shaelathi Blades are the Commonwealth’s newest specialized corps, drawn exclusively from unmarried Veyrathi females of the Shaelathi Tribe. They serve on the Contract Roll as Handmaids of the Banner, a sub-order of the Thornmaidens, under the direct custody and command of the Maidenward Sentinels. Like all women on the Contract Roll, they hold no rank and issue no command to any man. Their guardian’s contract is held by the Maidenward, and their compensation is paid to that office.

What distinguishes the Shaelathi Blades from every other corps on the Contract Roll is the nature of their art. Veyrathi females possess voluntarily retractable claws, near-human appearance that allows them to pass unnoticed in most environments, exceptional manual dexterity, fluid near-silent movement, and an intuitive spatial awareness that requires no active effort. Their tail — the shael, the expressive line from which their tribe takes its name — is a precision weapon, capable of whip-crack strikes against eyes, throat, and pressure points. These gifts, combined with a patient and observational temperament, make them uniquely suited to the two roles the Commonwealth has no other corps to fill: deep reconnaissance and targeted elimination.

blocks.text: Selection. Shaelathi Blades are drawn from unmarried Veyrathi females who have passed the Blade Trial: a three-day assessment of movement quality, spatial awareness, claw-discipline, and tail-control conducted by a panel of Maidenward Sentinels and a Crown-appointed Warden. No woman who has failed the Blade Trial may re-enter for two years.

Command. Each Scout Band is led by a Blade-Adept — the senior woman of the unit, who leads the women of her Band and no man. A Maidenward Sentinel holds command over the Band as a whole and accompanies every named operation. Silence Pairs operate under a named Warden’s written warrant, countersigned by the Crown.

Binding Rules. No Shaelathi Blade crosses into enemy-held ground without a Crown warrant and her guardian’s written consent. Claws are considered drawn weapons under Commonwealth law and are issued — that is, formally authorized for deployment — only on a named operation under the Warden’s seal. A Blade who deploys her claws outside a named operation is subject to the same law as a man who draws a blade without cause. The Silence Pairs’ operations are classified under the Warrant of Concealment; their ledger is kept by the Warden of the Oath and is not available to Parliament or Assembly.

Benefit to the Commonwealth. The Shaelathi Blades give the realm a capability it has never possessed: a corps that can move through a city, a camp, or a frontier post without announcing itself, assess what is there, and, when warranted, remove a named threat without leaving a trace the enemy can read. The Wayfinders hold the desert’s open ground. The Shaelathi Blades hold the spaces between walls.

The men she serves guard her, and that guard is the reason the Commonwealth teaches her hands and a dagger.

X. The Rosebound: The Bridge and the Shield

The Rosebound are a dyadic unit of the Weaveblade Legion. The husband is a Legion mage-officer who has sworn the Oath of the Standard and holds the contract. His wife is a Creation mage and an extension of it. They are bound by a Resonance Bridge (Ember-to-Ember Bond Mechanics), and the bond is the covenant: the four peoples whose women are Emberborn each carry it by blood. She heals and wards through him, and he casts and stands in front of her. She is a laywoman.

The Oathguard is the Commonwealth’s traditional guard: it keeps the Royal House, the King and the Heir, and it holds the doors of the Assembly Hall and of the Hall of Memory and Stewardship. It is the Commonwealth’s guard and not the King’s. Its men swear to the Commonwealth, the Assembly pays them, and Parliament holds its charter. The Crown commands it openly. It replaces the body once called the Royal Companions. Twelve unmarried women are leased to it, and they belong to the Guard directly.

blocks.text: The Twelve

Twelve unmarried women serve the Oathguard as arbalest archers, healers, and creation mages. Their fathers lease them to the Guard under the Oathguard Charter. They are not Thornmaidens, they are not on the Contract Roll, and the Maidenward has no part in them: they are wholly the Guard’s, under its own governance and discipline.

The Twelve – Daily and Infraction Discipline: The twelve women serving the Oathguard as arbalest archers, healers, and creation mages are subject to strict military-household discipline. In addition to potential caning throughout the day for minor infractions, all female members of the Oathguard are whipped daily by the Oathguard sergeant prior to the start of their daily duty watch to maintain posture, compliance, and operational readiness.

blocks.text: Handmaids of the Banner

The Commonwealth employs women through the Thornmaidens, an auxiliary force providing perimeter defense, medical sorcery, reconnaissance, and casualty evacuation. Members of the Handmaids of the Banner and its sub-orders hold no Crown commissions, nor do they form part of the formal military hierarchy. They carry no legal rank; all internal titles are recognized solely within the order.

Three bodies stand under the name. The Thornmaidens and the Wayfinders are Crown-chartered corps on the Contract Roll. The Hearthguard is neither: it is the women of the villages, raised by village ordinance, called by a Hearth Warden, and carried on no Crown roll.

Under no circumstances may a Handmaid issue binding orders to a male citizen. At all times, members must adhere to Commonwealth standards of female conduct—strictly observing Articles IV, V, and IX. —and speak exclusively in the Lower Register. Any violation of these protocols carries immediate, public corporal punishment, administered by a Rosewarden, Keeper, Sentinel Captain, or their designated delegates. The Hearthguard hold no Rosewarden, Keeper, or Sentinel: for them correction is the guardian’s alone (see Hearthguard).
Thornmaidens
12,000 women · Contract Roll

The Thornmaidens are a Crown‑chartered auxiliary corps, distinct from the Royal Army and not counted among its levies or regular formations. They serve under male military command in all matters of defense, while their domestic conduct and barracks life are overseen by a Matron or Matron of the Rose — traditionally the Citadel Commander’s wife or a respected widow serving with her guardian’s written consent — who maintains propriety, discipline, and household order within the women’s wing of the citadel.

The corps exists first to take the citadel wall‑posts from the Crown Archers, so that trained men serve in the field line. A Thornmaiden who completes her twenty‑four months without ever loosening a bolt in earnest has served exactly as the corps intends.

Thornmaidens do not wear military uniforms; instead, they serve in modified dresses marked only by the rose insignia, symbolizing their role as defenders of the hearth rather than soldiers of the field.

Their duties — light arbalest operation, creation‑magic support, aerial scouting, and medical extraction — are strictly defensive and auxiliary, requiring discipline but not the long martial training of infantry or archers.
This structure preserves coverture, protects marriage prospects, and maintains the traditional social order. As Parliament often notes, Thornmaidens do not learn war; they defend the hearth.

Where the Maidenward stands, the maiden may stand nearer: at the forward aid post and in the field-army camp, never in an assault. The Sentinels of the Maidenward are the reason the line can bend and the guardian still sign.

Their service allows the Crown to fully staff its citadels while freeing trained men for the Crown Archers, skirmishers, and line infantry, making the corps both socially acceptable and militarily invaluable.

The corps is highly controlled, with male commanders at every level, strict discipline, and continuous auditing. The Thornmaidens exist to fill roles where agility, magical affinity, or aerial capability are uniquely advantageous. Where the Maidenward stands, the maiden may stand nearer.

blocks.text: Contractual Status & Household Compensation

Thornmaidens serve under a 24‑month Crown contract, renewable only once, and always signed by their father or legal guardian, in accordance with coverture. The Crown pays the contract upfront to the household, providing 48 zarims (standard 8‑gram silver coin) per term as compensation for the daughter’s temporary service and absence from domestic duties.

To encourage completion of service, the Crown grants an additional 150‑zarim dowry bonus upon successful fulfillment of the 24‑month term. This bonus is paid directly to the father or guardian. The guardian retains the legal right to recall his daughter at any time during the contract. This contractual structure ensures that service remains temporary, supervised, and domestically aligned, while providing significant economic benefit to the household.
Household Incentives & Dowry Provision
Service is particularly attractive to commoner households and poorer households. Benefits include:
Immediate liquidity through the 48‑zarim upfront payment
Reduced household expenses while the daughter is housed and fed by the Crown
A 150‑zarim dowry bonus that many poorer families could not otherwise assemble
Improved future marriage prospects

The combined structure of: upfront payment, dowry bonus, strict coverture makes service socially acceptable and economically beneficial within the traditional order of the Commonwealth. For commoners, Thornmaiden service represents a practical and honorable exchange: temporary loss of labor offset by immediate coin, reduced household burden, and a future dowry.
Duration of Service & Protection of Maidenhood
Service is strictly time‑limited. Each Thornmaiden serves under a 24‑month contract, renewable only once, for a maximum of four years. This limitation:
Prevents households from exploiting a daughter’s labor indefinitely.
Allows the Crown to benefit from her creation‑magic aptitude and defensive service.
Ensures participation never disrupts the traditional path toward marriage and household life.

By limiting service to four years at most, the Commonwealth ensures Thornmaidens remain within the proper sphere of maidenhood, return home unmarred by war, and enter marriage with honor, discipline, and improved prospects. Service is attractive to poorer households and farming families whose income is seasonal. Intake runs about 4,600 a year, roughly one girl in fifty.

blocks.text: The Inter-Term Corvée and Garrison

Labor When the Thornmaidens are not deployed to active citadel wall-posts, and when Camp Servitors rotate off direct operational support, they are never granted discharge, idleness, or repatriation. Instead, they transition directly into mandatory, heavy garrison corvée under the unyielding oversight of the Maidenward.

Off-term Thornmaidens and Servitors form the relentless logistical underbelly of the Commonwealth's military infrastructure. Their labor includes hauling raw coal to the Quartz Houses, grinding grain in the massive garrison mills, scraping marine growth from hulls in the drydocks of Keelhold and Greywake, and clearing winter snow from the high Wall Line. Rest is legally defined by the Warhost not as a cessation of labor, but merely as a shift from tactical hazard to heavy industrial toil
