The Skyguard pair flies at her wing. The escort commands the sortie in the air
Only Sun‑Veil Screens cast, with the guardian’s consent and the Crown’s authorization. A Zerii girl’s innate Umbral manifestations are not used on duty
Held by a Maidenward Oath. A Sentinel does not fly
A sortie slip, signed by the Flight‑Master, entered in the Rosewarden’s ledger and read against the return‑lamp log

blocks.text: Lifewings (1,500)

Elite Luminari female creation‑mages trained to evacuate wounded soldiers from the wall‑side recovery line and, under Maidenward escort, from the field itself, to the citadel’s hospital‑works or the forward aid post.

rows.t: Luminari girls who use specialized harnesses to lift wounded soldiers and carry them to the hospital‑works
Rig the harness and stabilize patients mid‑flight, prevent shock, and maintain altitude under load; they fly the second place of a pair‑lift
Extraction specialists on the ground who coordinate with ground medics at the recovery line for the transfer. Wingless Luminari may serve here
Creation‑mages who hold the shock‑dampening field around the casualty during evacuation

blocks.text: The branch holds 100 Flights of 15, about four to a citadel. Each Flight has a Flight‑Master.
Role: Rapid evacuation of the wounded from the foot of the wall and, under Maidenward escort, from the field, especially where stretcher parties cannot reach quickly.
The Lift‑Harness (Rose Pattern)

rows.t: Leather over ash‑wood stays, sitting on the collarbones and across the back below the shoulder pocket. Cut with wing‑ports so the wings open and retract clear of every strap
Four load rings, a quick‑release at each

The casualty hangs face‑up in a cradle of ash‑linen and leather with a head‑rest and leg loops, so he is carried below and in front of the flyer. His hands are strapped across his chest. He does not touch her wings
A 2.2 m ash‑wood bar for the pair‑lift. The casualty hangs from its center between two flyers
Two 6 m lines for a pick‑up from ground with no landing room. A line lowers and never drops
A blood‑quartz plate at the sternum, under the yoke. It carries the lightening working so the flyer’s Ember goes to the load and not to her own lift
Sewn to the cap, read by the citadel’s Ember Veil
A single red cord at the cradle. The casualty is freed by the flyer, never by the casualty
About 12 km to the aid post, speed about 40 mph under load
Pair‑lift on the spreader bar, two flyers
Six lifts a day to a flyer; then relieved

blocks.text: Mission profiles

rows.t: From the recovery line at the foot of the wall to the hospital‑works. Short hops under the Ember Veil on her ward‑token

From a landing ground held by a Maidenward Oath to the forward aid post. The Field‑Recovery Maidens meet the casualty at the line and bring him to the ground. She never lands where the Oath does not hold
A Skyguard Cloud‑Ward patrol flies overhead on every field lift. Wall lifts need none
She does not lift during an assault. She lifts when the line is relieved or the assault is spent
Lower, never drop. A flyer who cannot hold the load sets it down on the nearest friendly ground and signals. The Oath recovers him
Over enemy‑held ground; in an assault; unveiled; without the Oath at the landing ground

blocks.text: Uniform and kit

rows.t: As Farwings: minimal‑strap two‑piece, gored weighted hem at mid‑thigh, cap with veil sewn, harness worn over it
Harness as above; dressing roll; triage tags; tool‑knife; water‑skin; flight bar; hand ever‑lamp
The lightening working, the shock‑dampening field, and the Creation workings of the branch, under the guardian’s consent and the Crown’s authorization

blocks.text: Supervision

rows.t: The Skyguard Flight‑Master (100). Launch, recall, and the lift ledger
At the receiving post, the Army Surgeon or Sister of Light. The Flight‑Master has no say in the case
A Maidenward Oath holds the landing ground and the post’s rear. The Sentinels escort the Flight to and from it
Ember Fever stand‑down by the surgeon. The Rosewarden’s ledger
Every lift is entered in the lift‑ledger: casualty tag, class, flyer, hour. The Commander reads it weekly against the surgeon’s case‑ledger

blocks.text: Wayfinders
3,500 women · Vykril · Contract Roll

The Wayfinders are Vykril women trained in desert infiltration, reconnaissance, deception, and covert warfare. Although commanded by a male Vykril commander, they are not part of the Royal Army or counted in the Bloodwind Brotherhood. They serve under 24‑month contracts arranged and signed by their guardians (renewable once), and remain legally bound to them. All compensation earned in service is paid directly to those guardians, on the Thornmaiden schedule. Minimum age is eighteen, and no wife or widow serves. Intake runs about 1,350 a year, roughly one Vykril girl in twenty‑three.

rows.t: 380 lead a unit; 20 instruct at Kharvesh Hold
Masters of desert movement, camouflage, and heat‑mirage deception
150 Scout Bands of nine (an Adept and eight Scouts)
Specialists in blending into terrain, using light‑bending techniques to vanish at close range
130 Posts of eleven (an Adept and ten Wardens)
Defensive specialists who hold chokepoints, dunes, and ravines with minimal manpower
100 Teams of seven (an Adept and six Knives)
Small infiltration teams trained for assassination, sabotage, and night raids

blocks.text: Role: The Wayfinders excel in reconnaissance, infiltration, and defensive holding actions in harsh terrain. Notes: Their doctrine emphasizes precision, misdirection, and psychological disruption rather than brute force.

Dress and the Warrant of Concealment. At base a Wayfinder wears the Thornmaiden dress and keeps the same rules of deportment and discipline. She must still wear the standard dress, but with darker clothing. The Warrant of Concealment is the second page of her guardian’s contract. A contract without it is void.

rows.t: The guardian’s separate signature on the contract’s second page, held by the Waywarden

The darkened dress; the shade‑veil in place of the sheer veil; the Sand‑Knife, from the Hold chest, on a Writ; operation where no Commonwealth man will see her face; the face veil lowered beyond the line where concealment needs it, each occasion recorded by the Waywarden
Anything carnal; any labor or errand outside the Writ; any correction past the Waywarden’s; a blade worn where a Commonwealth man can see it; unveiling before any Commonwealth man
The sheer veil and the standard dress resume before any man of the corps sees her
Remains the injured party in law and keeps his recall

blocks.text: Mission profiles

rows.t: A Band moves well to well, about 35 km, between dusk and dawn. The Shadow‑Meld word works in real shadow and fails in full light, so the work is done at night and at the edges of the day. The season is the cold nights, the season of raids
Mirage‑cloth on a staff frame throws false shapes at 300 to 800 m. The Adept lays them to draw a raiding column off a well or a fort

A Post holds a well, a pass, or a ravine in the Wastes by trap, misdirection, and observation, not by standing. It delays, bleeds, and falls back to the fort. It sends word by mirror to the nearest citadel

A Team of seven works the Wastes against raiders, smugglers, and slave‑takers: night strikes on camps and caches, sabotage of water, assassination of leaders. It operates only on a Writ, and beyond the line only under the crossing rule in this table

Aidion, Kaeyria, and the Ritebound Throne enslave captured women. No Wayfinder crosses the border without the express permission of the Crown and of her master or guardian, both in writing. The Crown’s permission is a Writ naming the crossing. The guardian’s is his countersignature on the Warrant of Concealment for that crossing. Neither stands for the other, and either may be withheld

blocks.text: Uniform

rows.t: The two‑piece in charcoal and dusk‑brown ash‑linen; mid‑thigh hem; oxblood trim instead of flame‑crimson
The rose badge in blackened iron thread, worn on the left breast at the Hold and the release point and carried in the pouch beyond the line
Ash‑dark dust‑gauze, which serves as the sheer veil at the Hold and as the shade‑veil in the field
Plain iron skull‑cap, blackened, under a dust‑cloth; hair in a plain cord. The Vykril habit of covering the ears is kept
Leather bracers and padded jerkin, blackened. A Vykril woman’s light, strong bone and her speed do the rest. No plate
Soft‑soled sand‑boots, wrapped to the shin
A shade‑cloak, charcoal on one face and mirage‑cloth on the other
The standard iron‑grey dress and the sheer veil
As Thornmaidens. The Oath‑Band is reserved to wives and widows

blocks.text: Kit

rows.t: A single‑edged knife with a blackened 18 cm blade. Held in the Hold chest; issued on a Writ; returned at the release point and counted
The Shadowleaf pattern, kept in the Post’s cache for Wardens. Not carried on patrol
Two skins and a cache at every release point. A Vykril woman’s need runs about half a human’s
Dried meat, no cook‑fire. Vykril digestion takes it raw or spoiled
One to a Band; Adepts carry the staff
One to a Band, for the Post‑to‑citadel line

blocks.text: Mounts

rows.t: None. A Wayfinder does not ride in operations. A beast needs water the Wastes do not give; wells stand about 35 km apart; a Vykril woman is faster and more agile afoot than a Vykril man, and silent

The Shimmerwind Spur carries a Band 110 km from Kharvesh to the first caravan‑track fort. From the fort a Pack‑Beast Handlers’ mule string of the Animal & Transport Corps lays water and ration at the release points. The Band walks from the cache
Waywardens ride the Crown’s horses. Bond‑Wardens ride to their release point and no further

blocks.text: Supervision

rows.t: A male Vykril officer of colonel grade, seated at Kharvesh. Answers to the Marshal of the Sundral March for operations and to the Warden of the Oath for the roll

A male Vykril officer of captain grade, one to each 250 women (14 in all). Records duty and conduct. Holds each woman’s mastery in trust by her father’s delegation; the father keeps the Darlorath. Holds the Warrant of Concealment. Corrects, or delegates the correction

A male Vykril veteran of the Reavers, one to each Band, Post, or Team (380). Receives the Writ from the Waywarden, gives it to the Adept, keeps the release point and the clock, and receives the unit’s return report. He is her call and not her correction
The senior woman of her unit. She leads the women of it and no man. She takes the Writ in the Lowered Tongue
One to each 250. A widow serving with her guardian’s written consent, who keeps the women’s quarters and acts their “mother”
One to each Hold, leased from the Praesul as at the citadels
Issued by the Marshal of the Sundral March, or the Warden of the Oath, naming the unit, the ground, the task, the return‑hour, and the release point. No unit moves without one

A unit returns to its release point by the return‑hour. At the hour and one watch the Bond‑Warden reports it overdue to the Waywarden. He does not go after it. A recovery by a Reaver detail goes only on the Marshal’s written order

Kharvesh Hold (headquarters and school), a wing at each of the two caravan‑track forts, and the Posts’ own walled holds. Each is walled and gated, with the key held by the Matron and the gate held from outside by Reaver veterans of the Waywarden’s hold‑guard
Wayfinders are outside it. The Reaver hold‑guard and the Bond‑Warden stand where a Sentinel would, without his Warrant’s two blows
The Waywarden’s Writ‑ledger, read against the Bond‑Warden’s return‑log, is read monthly by the Commander

blocks.text: Hearthguard
Village rolls · No Crown roll · Unpaid

The Hearthguard are the women of a village, armed and called by its Hearth Warden to keep the village while its men are away, and to take small game for its tables. They are not a corps. They hold no Crown charter, no Crown commission, no Crown device, and no Crown pay, and they appear on neither the Contract Roll nor the Service Roll nor in the Order of Battle. The Oath of the Standard takes a village’s men to the levy; the Hearthguard are what stays behind with a bow.

Raised by village ordinance under the town council’s ordinary power over the watch, the Hearthguard are the household’s affair and the Warden’s, and the Crown tolerates them and does not fund them. They are defensive only. They arrest no one, judge no one, and pursue no one.

Usage. “Hearth Warden” is a village office and is unrelated to the Crown Warden, the Warden of the Oath, or the Warden of the Flame. “Quiver” is the Hearthguard’s one echelon. The Army’s Hearth (128 men) is another thing.
Standing

rows.t: Informal village defense of women. Not a Crown force, not a Church order, not a militia. Outside the Maidenward and outside the Contract Roll
Wives (with their master’s consent), unmarried sisters of sixteen and over, Presented and veiled, and mothers and widows (with the consent of their guardian: the eldest son, or the nearest male kin)

Girls under sixteen. Any woman under a Thornmaiden or Wayfinder contract or an Oathguard lease (her membership is suspended for the term and resumes at release). Any woman under indenture. Any professed Sister. A woman in the last four months of pregnancy or nursing a child under one year, who stands off the roll and returns

One Quiver to a village, of eight to twenty‑four women, not more than one woman in forty of the village’s adult women. A large town raises one Quiver to a ward. The Crown keeps no count; the Assembly’s estimate is about 120,000 women
None. No payment to the household. The household bears her absence
None. She makes the Declaration of the Hearth‑Watch before the Warden and the parish Priest, once and kneeling. It is a public declaration, not a sacrament, and no court receives it
Keeps full Darlorath. He may withdraw her at any time, without notice or penalty
Guardian, then the Warden’s call, and nothing above the Warden for the Hearthguard’s work. The Constable keeps the law

blocks.text: Offices

rows.t: Appoints the Hearth Warden by written commission; may suspend or remove him. Holds no command in the field and no military jurisdiction. May consent to a Lamp Watch

A male citizen of forty‑five or over, service completed, in good standing; usually a veteran, never a serving Crown soldier. One to a village. Keeps the roll, the Rack keys, and the Warrants; calls the activation; names the Hearthmen; issues the slips. His orders to the Quiver pass through the Quiver‑Mother

An elder man of the village whom the Warden names to walk with a party. He is the male the unescorted‑woman rule asks for. He carries the Warden’s slip. One of them is the Bowmaster, who trains the Quiver

The eldest wife or mother of the Quiver. Seniority among women only, not an office. She keeps the women’s roll and passes the Warden’s call to the Quiver in the Lowered Tongue. She holds no authority over any man
Keeps the village’s law. Holds the second key to the Rack. May stand an activation down for cause and reports to the regional Crown Warden
May restrict or stand the Hearthguard down within his March (see The Marches, below)
Commands no soldiers and cannot activate the Hearthguard. He may consent to a Lamp Watch
The only man who corrects her. See Command and Conduct

blocks.text: The Warrant of the Hearth
Her guardian’s leave, given once a year at the spring muster and in writing, filed with the Warden.

rows.t: Her name on the roll; arms drawn from the Rack; ordering her where she stands, sits, or goes for the term of an activation, a hunting leave, or a Lamp Watch; and the naming of the Warden and his Hearthmen as the male expressly authorized by her master for the unescorted‑woman rule
Any touch. Any correction. Any labor or errand. Any arms kept in her house. Any order from any man but the Warden or the Hearthman he names
He answers for everything she looses as he answers for any act of hers (The Guardian’s Liability). A shot outside the Warden’s order is his offense

blocks.text: Activation

rows.t: Arms on the Rack. Monthly muster. Hunting leave by day‑slip
The Quiver assembles at the Hearth Hall (the parish hall). Bows are issued; war‑points are not. Posts at the gate and the lanes
War‑points issued from the Warden’s chest. Posts held day and night in three watches. No woman alone. Lamps and fires checked each watch
The Quiver withdraws to the Hearth Hall with the children, shuts the doors, and holds it
The Warden, the Mayor, the Constable, or the Marshal
Arms returned to the Rack and counted

blocks.text: Triggers: a wolf or other beast on the flock, fire, flood, bandits, the levy called away, a raid on the rare occasion one gets past the frontier, or the Warden’s judgment. The common activation is the levy called away, and the common use is the hunt. He reports the activation to the Mayor and the Constable the same day.
Scope and Limits

rows.t: Exactly three: guard the village; hunt small game; and, when authorized, the Lamp Watch

The gate, the lanes, the bounds, the well, the granary, the Hearth Hall, and the flocks and fields inside the radius. She rings the bell and lights the alarm lamp. The call to the levy is the Warden’s

She issues no order. She holds an intruder at bowpoint and sends for the Warden or the Constable. She does not bind, search, strike, or question him. She looses on a man only on the Warden’s order, or when he is in the act of violence against a person of the village
Five kilometers from the village bell‑stone, in any direction. Beyond it only on the Warden’s express written leave, naming the women, the purpose, the route, and the hours
None. She does not follow past the Bound

Small game only: hare, coney, fowl, wildfowl, pigeon, squirrel, and vermin, nothing over ten kilograms. By day‑slip, in a party of three or more with a Hearthman, back before the dusk bell. The kill is her guardian’s; any sale is his
The men’s. A beast on the flock or in the lane is met under Guard, not hunted
None. Detention, search, and judgment belong to the Constable and the Magistral. No private law, no armed justice

blocks.text: Arms

rows.t: A short recurved composite of ash, horn, and sinew, cut first by the Maenari bowyers of the Threnwood for their women. Draw about 35 lb at 28 inches, which a woman of ordinary build holds steady. Effective to about 50 m, extreme range about 150 m. It takes small game cleanly and holds a lane; it does not pierce mail. About 12 Zarims. The pattern is issued to the women of every people
Twenty‑four to a woman. Field points and blunts only on the Rack. War‑points are the Warden’s, issued at Full Watch

A single‑edged hunting knife, 15 cm blade, plain wood or horn grip wrapped in cord, a leather sheath on the right hip, stamped with the village mark. It dresses game and serves as the last defense. About 1.5 Zarims. It bears no Flame sigil and no First Oath glyph, and no hair is bound in its hilt
None. No jerkin, bracers, or cap. She hunts and guards in the dress her status requires
Any sword, spear, crossbow, or thrown weapon

The Hearth Rack, in the Hearth Hall, under two keys: the Warden’s and the Constable’s. Arms are drawn at Muster or on a hunting leave and returned the same day, counted by the Warden. The Rack is the village’s, stocked by household subscription; a household that cannot buy a bow borrows one

A bow or knife missing from the Rack is reported by the Warden the same day. Arms found on a woman without the Warden’s slip are seized by the Constable, and her guardian is fined as for the unescorted woman (three Zarims)
The butts at the village’s green, monthly after Mass on the feast‑day. The Bowmaster tests her yearly: eight of twelve arrows in the ring at 40 m

blocks.text: Dress and Mark

rows.t: Unchanged. A sister wears the face veil, the mid‑thigh two‑piece, and the plain cord. A wife or mother wears the caerwevra and the Oath‑Band on the upper arm, unveiled. A widow wears her own cut
A flame‑crimson sash at the waist, knotted on the right, with the village mark stitched at the knot‑end. Worn on activation, a hunting leave, and a Lamp Watch only
The bow in its case on the back, unstrung until the post. The quiver and the Hearth‑knife on the right hip
The rose badge. The Flame sigil. The First Oath glyph. The Oath‑Band’s place on the upper arm is never taken by any mark of the Hearthguard

blocks.text: Command and Conduct

rows.t: Article IX in full toward every man of the village. On post she speaks only when the Warden or Hearthman speaks to her, and signals alarm by bell, horn, or lamp without speech. The Warden’s order is the leave
Her guardian alone. The Warden reports a fault to him and may stand her off the roll. The Warden does not strike her. No man other than her guardian and an Appraiser may
A Hearthguard woman halted by an Appraiser shows her slip and is audited like any woman. Arms are no exemption from audit
A party with the Warden’s slip is released at once. A party without it is an unescorted woman and is dealt with as such
Credited to her guardian and her household, as for any woman

blocks.text: The Marches

rows.t: The rules above in full, with the Lamp Watch. Fall‑Back stands against the rare pirate landing
March villages within about 60 km of the Aidionic, Kaeyrian, or Ritebound frontier

Local custom governs, and it is old. The frontier is among the best defended in Virelia, and its villages have kept their women out of slavers’ reach for centuries by their own arrangements: the Hearth Hall as a keep, the Fall‑Back drilled each year, the women inside before the bell finishes. The Hearthguard there musters against beast, fire, and flood and keeps the Fall‑Back. It does not hold a post against a human enemy; the wall and the Marshal’s patrols do. The Marshal may restrict it further in writing

blocks.text: The Lamp Watch
When the Hearth Warden authorizes it and the Mayor or the Satrap consents, the Hearthguard may man a lighthouse, a beacon, or the village’s lamps, and see that every fire and lamp burns as it should.

rows.t: Three keys, in writing, posted at the light: the Warden’s express leave (the light may lie beyond the Hearth Bound); the consent of the Mayor where the light is within his bounds or of the Satrap where it is not; and the license of the Office of Maritime Safety, whose lights they are
When the light’s Keeper is absent (the levy, sickness, a death). The Lamp Watch stands in for him. The light is never dark

Six women of a Quiver, in three watches of two. No woman alone. The lamp‑room never holds fewer than two. A Hearthman, as Lamp‑Warden, lodges at the light with his household; the women lodge in the Keeper’s house under his wife or a mother of the party

Light at the dusk bell and put out at dawn. Trim and refill. Check the crystal’s glow against the gauge. Keep the beacon fire and the fuel. Keep the log. Show the standing signal. Report any dimming, flicker, or color shift at once to the Lamp‑Warden
The lamp round each dusk: the ever‑lamps at the gate and lanes, the Hearth Hall’s hearth, the watch‑fires. The same tampering prohibition applies
She never opens a crystal housing. A failing crystal is replaced by a licensed Lamp‑Wright of the Office
She shows the standing alarm only, the colors the Office assigns, and only on the Warden’s or the Lamp‑Warden’s word, or on sighting raiders where no man is within reach. She sends no other signal
The Watch shows the alarm and falls back to the Keeper’s house. The light is lost before a woman is
None. The Keeper’s wage stays the Keeper’s

blocks.text: Camp Servitors in the Warhost
4,000 women · about 40 postings · Service Roll

The Camp Servitors are the Crown’s regulated domestic labor in army and naval establishments. Each is an unmarried daughter ordered into indenture by a Municipal Court under the Indenture Statute (Section VI) to a Keeper of the Maidens, who holds the Crown’s contract for the posting. The corps takes labor that would otherwise exist informally and dangerously and places it under law, budget, and an accountable officer. It is not a martial institution. It is a domestic one, extended to the scale of the realm. It stands outside the order of battle and outside the Contract Roll, and it is the one body of the Warhost built on a relic: indenture is lawful in the Commonwealth, though not honored, and the Assembly’s fee on it is the means by which the Commonwealth intends to price it out of existence by degrees.
Standing

rows.t: Non-combatant. Bears no arms and swears no oath of the State. Indentured under the Indenture Statute (Section VI), in continuous guardianship.

The indenture instrument carries the Warrant of the Ward, and the Keeper’s Crown contract names it. The Warrant is the Keeper’s standing leave, given once, for the Sentinels of the Maidenward to address, restrain, lift, and carry her, and to strike her no more than twice on one occasion. It gives no leave for any labor or any carnal use. See The Maidenward (the Sentinels).
The Keeper of the Maidens, one per posting. The Keeper is the master under the Statute.

The Keeper holds mastery in trust for the term (Article IV, Mastery in Trust). Her father keeps the Darlorath. The Keeper is not her husband, and any carnal use is despoilment. He may not lend, hire out, or assign her to another posting, Order, or household. Doing so voids the instrument and returns her to her father with her dowry trust paid in full, and the Court censures the Keeper.
All pay goes to the Keeper. The Keeper pays the father’s debt into the Court and the Indenture Fee (125 Zarims) at registration.
Four years, or until her twenty-second birthday if that comes sooner.
As the Statute fixes. Collar always. Veil at Mass only, issued by the Keeper.
The Keeper answers for her conduct before the Magistracy, as a guardian answers.
Ordinary adult cut: mid-thigh, two-piece, undyed ash-linen, apron and cap. No Oath-Band, caerwevra, dagger, or rose badge.

blocks.text: Servitor and Thornmaiden Compared

rows.t: Keeper holds. Father may not recall
Citadel women’s wing, under the Matron of the Rose
150 Zarims from the Crown to the father on completion
125 Zarims from the master’s fee, in Court trust for her husband1

blocks.text: 1 The 125 Zarim release fee is paid directly into a Municipal Court trust, held strictly in reserve as a dowry for her future husband upon her marriage. The father is barred by law from receiving, claiming, or accessing any portion of these funds.
Posting

rows.t: One Keeper, one Stewardess, about 100 Servitors, and two Maidenward Oaths (sixteen Sentinels), who hold the gate and the tents and escort the Quarter. Serves roughly 2,500 men.
Executed between the Crown, through the Quartermaster, and the Keeper. The Quartermaster holds it.

The Order of the Standing Wall and the other Orders contract their own postings on the same Statute. The Crown’s Quartermaster has no part in them. Servitors under one contract do not work for the men of the other.
Allots work-sites and posts the Provost guard on the work-routes. Issues no order to a Servitor. Requests go through the Stewardess to the Keeper.
Keeps the work-routes. The gate and the tents are the Maidenward’s. May discipline a Servitor at will.
An Army Surgeon examines monthly, in the Stewardess’s presence.

blocks.text: Scope of Duties

rows.t: Galleys, messes, and ration stores of the establishment.
Billets, tents, corridors, and ships at berth.
They attend the camp or installation and do not belong to its social or martial life. Their presence is functional and deliberately unobtrusive.
The establishments to which a posting is assigned, about one man in ten of the Warhost. Conscript service tracks and the Medical & Welfare Corps’ Sanitation Wardens carry the rest.
Arms, guard duty, the wall-line, the line of battle, nursing, or any labor outside the instrument.

blocks.text: Employment in the Army

rows.t: Kitchens, laundry, billets, corridors, lamps, sanitation
Where most Servitors are posted. Servitor Quarter inside the walls, apart from the Thornmaidens’ women’s wing. Never on the wall-line.
As above, at the Warden of the Oath’s seat
Depots, garrison towns, year-class muster and training camps
Ration preparation, laundry, tents, waste handling
Fenced Quarter at the camp’s rear, one gate, held by the Maidenward.
Inside the camp’s ground, behind the line, under a Maidenward Oath, including beyond the marches. Never in the line.

Aidion, Kaeyria, and the Ritebound Throne enslave captured women, and a Servitor cannot be returned marriageable from capture. On any alert the Oath carries the Quarter to the nearest citadel or camp wall.

blocks.text: Employment in the Navy

rows.t: Crown Naval Basins (Solmara, Linhaven) and the Royal Shipyards
Victualling yards, barracks, laundry, galleys, sanitation
One or more postings per basin. Linhaven takes the most.
Hulks, tenders, transports, and warships at berth
Aboard by daylight only, by the gangway, in pairs, with a Sentinel at the gangway head.

At a berth, no Servitor sleeps aboard or below decks after the dusk bell. On a ship whose roll carries her section she sleeps only in the screened compartment, under the Maidenward door-watch, and never in the crew’s quarters.
Cooking, laundry, and cloth care, as at berth

Only on a ship the Admiral’s order names, with the section entered on the ship’s roll and a Maidenward Half-Oath aboard. The Quarter musters ashore, certified by the Keeper and the Provost, before any hull not so named casts off. The captain answers for any Servitor found aboard a ship under way who is not on the roll.
Servitors are Crown labor in Crown establishments only.

blocks.text: Bearing in Camp

rows.t: First light to the dusk bell. Gate locked from dusk to dawn, key held by the Keeper.
In pairs, never alone. Escorted by a Sentinel between Quarter and work-site.
Never alone with a man, her Sentinel aside.
Article IX in full: one pace behind, eyes lowered, yield every door and stair, speak only when spoken to, in the Lowered Tongue.

No soldier or sailor addresses or touches a Servitor without the Keeper’s leave. The Sentinels of her Oath hold that leave in the Warrant of the Ward. For the term the Keeper is her master. The Sentinel his Steward. A man needing her work speaks to the Stewardess.

blocks.text: Command Structure

The Commonwealth keeps a dual but non-competitive hierarchy. The Crown commands all sovereign military force; the Church commands its own three orders under the Warden of the Flame (unchanged, see Section V). On the Crown side, three apex commanders sit as peers: the Warden of the Oath (Army), the Admiral of the Navy, and the Weaveblade Legate. Each answers to the Crown directly, and none commands another. A fourth officer, the Captain of the Oathguard, commands for the Crown alone; his charter is Parliament’s and his pay the Assembly’s. The Crown is the only joint commander, acting through the Council of War.

The Servitor Quarters and Routine Disciplinary Regimes
The Servitor Quarters and garrison barracks are entirely sealed compounds within the broader military infrastructure, locked and governed strictly by the Maidenward Sentinels.
The Standing Audit: The Maidenward conducts routine, bi-weekly inspections of the quarters and work details.

Standardized Correction: Minor infractions—such as a poorly scrubbed flagstone, a frayed seam in a garrison uniform, or a failure to instantly execute the Lowered Tongue before a Sentinel—are met immediately on-site with standardized caning administered by the guard.

Total Isolation: When not marching or laboring under the eye of the Maidenward, women on the Contract and Service Rolls are locked in communal holding barracks with zero contact with ordinary conscript servicemen or the civilian populace.

Communication Ban: All incoming or outgoing communication must pass through the Quartermaster's censor office. Any sign of psychological fracture, exhaustion-induced slowdown, or discontent is logged as "insubordination of the Indenture" and punished by extended terms of service. Every disciplinary fine or administrative penalty is charged back directly as debt-extension to their guardians' accounts, ensuring that service terms are perpetually prolonged.
The King’s Reckoning

Four years into his reign, King Theron Karaya issued the King’s Reckoning (the Reckoning of Suraela), a standing decree covering the entire military apparatus — Crown Regulars, Navy, and, by the Crown’s own assertion, the rank structures of the three Church orders as well. Its terms:

Precedence in active service is suspended from title. A commoner captain outranks a lieutenant who happens to be a duke’s son. Precedence within a grade is set by commission date, demonstrated competence, and seniority — never by birth or peerage — for the duration of active service.
The purchase and sale of commissions is abolished outright. Commissions are granted by examination and Crown or Marshal appointment only.

Titles are suspended, not stripped, while in service. A peer’s rank and lands are untouched at home; within the ranks, they carry no weight at all. The distinction is deliberate — the King has been careful to frame this as a wartime discipline rather than an attack on the peerage as an institution.

Entry requirements are unchanged. The Reckoning governs rank and precedence only. The Order of the Kept Word, for instance, still draws its full brothers from minor nobility or from rankers raised by the Warden’s own writ — the Reckoning does not touch who may join, only how he is ranked once he has.

The King has invoked the decree under his existing constitutional authority as supreme commander of the armed forces, reasoning it directly from the Church’s own doctrine of the Reckoning — that an oath is judged by what it costs the man who swore it, not by the blood he swore it with. Parliament has not yet voted the Reckoning into permanent law; the King has openly challenged the peers to do so. Until they act, the decree holds by executive authority alone. Its extension to the three Church military orders is the more contested piece: the Warden of the Flame answers to the Archsworn, not the Crown, and neither the Patriarchate nor the Chapter of the Watch has formally conceded that a royal decree can reach into an internal precedence the Church has always governed on its own. Compliance there is, for now, uneven and unresolved rather than settled either way.

This is the first concrete step toward a larger, longer-term ambition of the reign: the King intends, in time, to consolidate every branch of the Commonwealth’s military — Crown, Navy, and the three Church orders alike — under a single chain of command at its apex. The Reckoning does not accomplish this by itself; it establishes the principle of merit across the whole apparatus first, and leaves the harder structural fight — one Crown, one Marshal, one command — for later in the reign.
Military Doctrine
The Living Wall
Defense‑in‑Depth

The Commonwealth’s doctrine—known formally as The Living Wall—is deliberate, disciplined, and wall‑centered, descended from the founding legend of a held line rather than a won field. Zeythari’s armies prefer fortification, attrition, and coordinated combined‑arms response over open‑field risk. Infantry, artillery, Emberborn cadres, and citadel garrisons are trained to absorb and blunt assaults, then counterstrike only when the enemy is overextended.

Cavalry, desert rangers, and frontier scouts remain fully capable of aggressive action when ordered, but the strategic identity of the realm is the held line, not the decisive charge. Every element of the doctrine assumes that Zeythari must endure the pressure of a numerically superior predator—the Aidionic Empire—and survive.
Professional Standing Army

Zeythari fields one of the largest and most professional standing armies among frontier realms, supported by knightly orders, clerical hosts, and Emberborn formations. This reflects both the Commonwealth’s wealth and the seriousness with which it treats the Oath of the Standard as more than ceremony.

The Crown Regulars drill year‑round, maintain permanent logistics and engineering corps, and operate under a unified command structure capable of rapid mobilization without reliance on feudal levies or ecclesiastical musters. Universal male service (ages 16–20) places some 80,600 men in the ranks each year and fills the reserve rolls with about three million trained men, some 800,000 of them within ten years of discharge, while roughly one man in seven continues into professional service.
Integrated Magic

Emberborn forces are embedded at every echelon of the Warhost. Male Emberborn serve a mandatory term in the Weaveblade Legion; female Emberborn are encouraged into the Thornmaidens or, by Church vocation, the Roselight Circle. Specialized pipelines train arcane artillery, ward‑mages, battlefield weavers, and citadel‑bound defensive specialists.

Integration doctrine ensures that Emberborn units operate seamlessly with infantry, cavalry, artillery, and engineers—multiplying the effectiveness of every conventional arm and giving Zeythari a force quality advantage over Aidion’s massed conscripts and penance legions.
Merit Over Blood

The King’s Reckoning embodies the scale of the threat this doctrine is built to meet. A hereditary officer corps, however brave, is not the instrument that holds a line for nineteen centuries against an empire fielding slave legions and mass conscription from a population of fifty million.

The Crown’s view is blunt: competence must outrank blood, or the wall eventually fails to a better‑led enemy rather than a stronger one. The Reckoning enforces this principle across the entire apparatus—Crown, Navy, and, by royal assertion, the Church orders—ensuring that the Living Wall is commanded by officers chosen for skill, not lineage.
Citadel Network

The Commonwealth maintains twenty‑four citadels across its territory, concentrated along the three borders and the frontier marches. These fortresses form the backbone of the realm’s defense‑in‑depth doctrine, each serving as a permanent garrison, supply hub, and rally point for both Crown Regulars and Church auxiliaries.

rows.t: Threnwood March (two on the Kaeyrian border)

blocks.text: Each citadel’s garrison is drawn from the Order of the Standing Wall, with Crown Regulars, the Artillery’s Fortress Companies, and the Thornmaidens quartered within: some 4,300 Standing Wall men and about 500 maidens to the average citadel. The Standing Wall’s March Levies rotate through under Church oversight. Camp Servitors are posted to most citadels, in Crown postings serving the Crown units quartered within, in a Servitor Quarter apart from the Thornmaidens’ women’s wing. The Standing Wall contracts its own postings separately.

The largest of these, Hearthwall, stands as the final line before Suraela and serves as the Seat of the Warden of the Oath. Hearthwall is effectively a citadel‑city, capable of housing an entire field army and coordinating the defense of the capital. Its presence anchors the Commonwealth’s strategic identity: a realm built not to win fields, but to hold lines.

The citadel network is the physical expression of the founding legend — a defensive system designed to absorb invasion, bleed momentum, and deliver coordinated counterstrikes. It is the infrastructure that makes the Commonwealth’s doctrine possible, and the reason its armies can sustain a defensive posture against far larger foes.
Strategic Logic of Survival

Taken together— universal service, Emberborn integration, Duraken industry, meritocratic command, and the citadel network—these elements explain how a smaller, wealthier realm has endured for nineteen centuries beside a predatory empire.
Zeythari cannot conquer Aidion. Aidion cannot afford to conquer Zeythari.
V. INSTITUTIONS
The Royal Archive of Zeythari
Knowledge, Record, and Strategic Memory of the Realm
Zeythari does not endure by strength of arms alone. It endures because it remembers what others forget.

The Royal Archive of Zeythari, housed in the capital city of Suraela, serves as the realm’s central repository of law, history, foreign doctrine, and preserved knowledge. Founded during the reign of King Alexi, the Archive reflects a foundational Zeythari conviction: that ignorance is not piety, and that truth—properly ordered—is a form of defense.

The Archive exists not to disseminate all knowledge freely, nor to practice every art it preserves, but to understand the world as it is, rather than as enemies or rivals would prefer it to be misunderstood.
Purpose and Philosophy
The Royal Archive is founded on three settled principles of Zeythari statecraft:
Truth transcends borders. Knowledge itself is morally neutral. Its virtue or danger lies in how it is used. The First Oath demands truthfulness, not blindness.

Understanding precedes judgment. A Magistral who knows foreign law judges more precisely. A commander who understands enemy doctrine defends more effectively. A diplomat who knows custom avoids catastrophe.
Scholarship is not endorsement. To study a belief, law, or magical tradition is not to practice it. The Archive preserves knowledge for comprehension, comparison, and defense—not devotion.

For this reason, Zeythari maintains one of the most comprehensive sanctioned archives in Astraia, while simultaneously enforcing some of the strictest access and oversight regimes known among lawful realms.
Structure and Oversight
The Archive is a Crown institution, funded through royal appropriation and administered independently of both Parliament and the Church, though subject to lawful inspection by each.
The Archive is overseen by the Royal Archivist, a Crown-appointed office responsible for acquisition, preservation, access control, and internal discipline.

The Archive is a lessee of the Circle of Memory (see Government & Authority), as any body is. Harmonists are leased to it to transcribe, catalogue, and cross-reference incoming records, but they remain the Church’s and answer to the Archivist, not to the Royal Archivist. Before the Archive’s founding, the realm’s records were kept by the monks of the monastery at Kaervast Cathedral.
Archive staff consist of professional archivists, scribes, translators, and security wardens, selected for loyalty, discretion, and scholarly competence.
The facility itself is purpose-built, combining public reading halls with restricted vaults, preservation workshops, and secure underground chambers.
The Archive is physically adjacent to the Palace Complex, but maintains a separate public entrance, symbolizing its service to the realm as a whole rather than to the Crown alone.
Public Collections
The Public Archive is open to all male citizens of Zeythari (age twenty and over, service completed) and serves as a critical civic institution.
Its collections include:
Foreign legal codes and comparative jurisprudence
Trade law, guild standards, and commercial practices
Agricultural, engineering, and medical treatises
Naval charts, maritime law, and navigation records
Historical chronicles and cultural studies of other realms
Language dictionaries and translation guides

These collections are heavily used by students, merchants, Magistrals, military officers, and scholars. Works of high demand are maintained in multiple copies, and scribes are available to reproduce materials for lawful use.
The Public Archive exists to educate without endangering, providing broad access to practical and historical knowledge while excluding materials that pose strategic, theological, or security risk.
The Restricted Collection
Beneath the public halls lies the Restricted Collection, a secure vault accessible only by authorization and monitored continuously.
This collection contains materials of strategic, arcane, theological, or diplomatic sensitivity, including:
Foreign military doctrine and campaign analyses
Advanced magical theory across lawful Threads
Comparative theology (stored strictly as academic material)
Intelligence reports, diplomatic correspondence, and political treatises
Seized materials obtained during lawful defensive wars

Access is granted only for demonstrated need and is tightly regulated. All research is logged, supervised, and subject to review. Materials do not leave the vault, and unauthorized copying is forbidden.
The Restricted Collection exists to ensure that Zeythari is never surprised by ideas, whether they arrive as armies, laws, or doctrines.
Theological and Legal Safeguards
The Archive operates under strict doctrinal boundaries:
No Umbral or proscribed materials are permitted under any circumstance.
Comparative theological works are clearly marked as non-devotional and are subject to regular inspection.
The Church of the Sworn Flame conducts scheduled audits to ensure theological integrity.
The Magistracy relies on Archive materials for precedent and foreign legal understanding, but no judgment is ever rendered on the authority of foreign doctrine.
The Archive does not override Church teaching or Crown law. It exists within them.
Strategic Importance
The Royal Archive is one of Zeythari’s quiet advantages.
Because of it:
Military commanders train against real foreign doctrine rather than conjecture.
Magistrals anticipate legal arguments before foreign courts make them.
Diplomats negotiate from knowledge, not assumption.
Emberborn innovators refine native practice through comparative understanding.
Refugee cultures are preserved rather than erased.
Rival realms often mistake Zeythari’s restraint for ignorance. The Archive ensures that such mistakes are costly.
Cultural Understanding
Among the people, the Archive is neither feared nor romanticized. It is regarded as necessary.
A common saying holds:
“Steel defends the border. Law defends the realm. Memory defends the future.”
The Royal Archive is that memory—ordered, guarded, and sworn to the Commonwealth.
The Aelorian Healing Complex
Where Virelia Sends Its Incurable

The Aelorian Healing Complex at Suraela is the finest medical institution on the continent of Virelia, and the Commonwealth’s most effective instrument of foreign goodwill. Nobles, officers, refugees, and commoners from nearly every lawful realm travel to it, by the Commonwealth’s rail network, for conditions that other realms call incurable. It is a Crown institution that the Church staffs where only the Church can: the Sisters of the Lily, Lysara’s faithful within the Solayan House, carry its sickrooms, its childbed, and its highest healing. Detailed figures and rules are in Appendix D.
Origin

The Complex began as a refuge. The Ritebound Throne descends from the Drazek tribes, human tribes who went north some thousands of years ago, before the human tribes fractured and the Satyrim ceased to be purely human. The Drazek rejected every “weak” deity and kept Varek alone, god of war. To the Throne, the worship of any other god is heresy, and the worship of a female god is treason as well. It enslaves every people that is not human. It therefore had no place for the Aelorian Maenari, and none for Lysara’s faithful among them, who could not stay and live. Some three centuries ago it expelled them, and seventy-three Sisters of the Lily crossed the border with the exiles, were examined and received by the Church, and set up a sanctuary in Suraela. The Throne, having cast out its own Lysarans, is left with mundane and magical healing alone and no miracle-work at all.

The Commonwealth was not without healers when they arrived. The Sisters of Solaya and Lysara already kept its hospitals, sickrooms, and childbeds. What the exiles brought was the high discipline of Lysara’s rite, the long working that regrows what has been lost, which the native House did not practice. In the border crises that followed, the Sisters treated thousands of wounded soldiers and civilians with survival rates no other house could match, and public memory of that work made the sanctuary permanent. The Commonwealth’s medicine is an old tradition; the Complex’s excellence is the product of its asylum.

Twenty-seven years ago the Crown, on an appropriation by the Assembly, chartered the sanctuary as the Complex. The charter also formalized the sanctuary’s centuries-old apprenticeship of physicians into the School of Merciful Arts.
Structure and Oversight
The Complex is Crown-funded, Crown-administered, and Church-staffed at its highest tier. It is governed by a seven-seat Administrative Council:

rows.t: The Chirurgeon, an elected physician and president of the Complex
Sisters of the Lily, as observers

blocks.text: The Sisters sit as observers because the Amma holds authority over other women but none over any man, and a vote on the Council would be authority over men. They answer to their Amma and their Confessor, never to the Council, and the Council may ask the Praesul to withdraw a Sister but may not direct one. The Royal Chancellery of the Treasury audits the Complex annually, independent of the Council, and the Canon Almoners audit the Sisters’ own ledgers. The Complex has passed all twenty-seven audits since its charter.
The Three Tiers
Medicine in the Commonwealth escalates through three tiers, centered on the Complex.

rows.t: Acolytes of the Lily (men), with Domesticae on the women’s side
Assessment, stabilization, routing. Present in every regional facility.
Physicians (men), midwives (women), Weave-healers and Ember-healers under Crown regulation
Resolve about 95% of cases, including surgery, disease suppression, and childbirth.
Regrowth of limbs and organs, and restoration of what lesser medicine cannot reach.

blocks.text: Tier III is the Complex’s defining power and its governing limit. A rite of regrowth takes days of prayer, fasting, and vows of purity, and it cannot be done in the field. That is why the Complex exists as a hospital rather than a doctrine: the patient is stabilized by Tiers I and II, held alive through the preparation, and brought to the Sisters. It is also why the Warhost sends its worst-wounded to Suraela by rail.
Education

The School of Merciful Arts, beside the Complex, trains the Commonwealth’s physicians and surgeons and is the sixth Royal Institution (see Higher Education). It is male only, as are the other five. The School is old in practice and young in title: it grew from the sanctuary’s apprenticeship of physicians, and the charter gave it a name, a curriculum, and a seat among the Royal Institutions.
See Appendix D for capacity, staffing rules, consent and guardianship, the refugee wing, and the Universal Access Doctrine.
VI. ORDERS
Order of the Sworn Flame

The Commonwealth keeps no monks of its own. The monastic and canonical clergy of the Church of the Sworn Flame, its monks, archivists, canonists, and the bureaucracy that runs the Church, belong to the Church’s own Order of the Sworn Flame and answer to the Church alone. Whatever work the Order’s brothers do on the Commonwealth’s behalf is done through the Church, by written commission granted by the Praesul with jurisdiction over the brother, and the fee is paid to the Order. The Commonwealth cannot raise a monk, and it cannot command one.
The Three Orders of the Sworn Flame
Overview

Non-sacramental military orders vowed to Kairon and to Varek, patron of the standing watch. Founded from the legend, as the liturgy tells it, of five soldiers of the five peoples who held the collapsing Ashward palisade through a single night, swearing to one another that none would leave while another stood.
Structure

rows.t: The Order of the Kept Word
Minor nobility, or a ranker raised by the Warden’s own writ
The Order of the Standing Wall
Garrison infantry, the bulk standing force of every march
Any confirmed man of the nine peoples, low birth expressly welcome
Full brothers: Obedience, Poverty, Perpetual Muster; confreres: single Vow of Muster
Guard of Kaervast Cathedral, the Archsworn, and the First Standard
Nomination only, twelve years’ prior service, clean record
The above, plus a fourth vow of Silence

blocks.text: Equipment
Plate and mail forged in Duskhearth’s Duraken guild-halls, resonance-warded against Ember effects
The Kept Word ride Maenari- and Satyrim-bred coursers; lances and long blades
The Standing Wall equips pike, crossbow, and the fixed engines of the wall-forts
The Flameward alone carries the First Standard’s honor-guard blades, never drawn outside Kaervast Cathedral’s grounds except by the Archsworn’s own word
Unique Abilities / Training

Full professed brothers own no personal property; a married brother’s household is provisioned by the Order itself, and any dowry his wife brings is held in trust for the duration of his active service rather than passed to him directly — a deliberate check against any Order officer becoming an independent landed rival to the Crown or the Church.
No rank or standing within any of the three orders passes from father to son; a Grand Preceptor’s own son petitions and trains exactly as a stranger to the Order would.
The Roselight Circle

The Roselight Circle includes all female religious within the Church of the Sworn Flame. Each Sister is assigned to one of five Houses, each devoted to a patron goddess and a specific sacred vocation. There is no sixth House. The Circle is the body of these women and not their government: they are ruled by men, through the Praesul, in every House and at every rank, and no council of Sisters decides anything of the Order’s.
House Seraphian: devoted to domestic and pastoral service. Dedicated to Seraphiae, Goddess of Grace and Femininity.

House Solayan: devoted to healing in all its forms, under two goddesses. Dedicated jointly to Solaya, Goddess of Light, Forgiveness, and Deliverance, and Lysara, Goddess of Life, Family, and Motherhood. Lysara governs childbirth and sickness throughout the Commonwealth: the hospitals, the healing houses, and the care of the sick and the lying-in at home. Solaya governs battlefield-adjacent healing, which is not as complete a healing but enough to save a man and carry him to the hospitals.
House Elaran: devoted to marriage and maiden virtue. Dedicated to Elaris, Goddess of Beauty and Sacred Submission.
House Sophisran: devoted to harmony and wisdom. Dedicated jointly to Sophisra, Goddess of Wisdom and Judgment, and Seraifi, Goddess of Art, Inspiration, and Knowledge.

House Zyrian: devoted to courage in service and to the yielding that carries it. Dedicated to Zyri, Goddess of the Moons and Courage, the Yielding Lady, slave-wife and twin of Varek, God of War, who stands as the House’s anchor. Her tested devotion to him is the model of the bond. Zyri and Varek are children of Kairon and Seraphiae and of the Oikos Solara by blood, and they keep a cult of their own. The House is tied to the Church loosely, through the two of them, and not through the parish chain.
The Sisters of Light

The Sisters of Light, practitioners of the Solayan Discipline, are the only miracle healers permitted to serve on or near a battlefield. The Army’s own healers — Army Surgeons, Thaumaturgic Medics, and the healing Thornmaidens within the citadel walls — practice surgery and Weave, never miracle. They are Sisters of House Solayan, sent into the field by lease, and they alone are entrusted with miracle healing in times of war.

House Solayan keeps two disciplines under its two goddesses. The miracles of Solaya are swift and practical. Through prayer and divine light, a Sister of Light may close wounds, steady the dying, purge curses, or return a wounded soldier to fighting condition within moments. Such miracles are less comprehensive than the works of Lysara, but they are what saves a man in the field and carries him to the hospitals, where speed decides whether a life is saved or lost. The miracles of Lysara are among the most powerful known to the Church: the mending of shattered bones, the repair of damaged organs, the healing of injuries that would otherwise leave permanent disability, and the delivery of children. They require ritual preparation, extended prayer, and strict adherence to vows of purity and non-harm, and so the Lysaran discipline is practiced in hospitals, healing houses, sanctuaries, and the homes of the sick and the lying-in throughout the Commonwealth, behind the front lines.

Even the Sisters of Light operate under strict oversight. Military commanders and ecclesiastical authorities closely monitor their movements, patients, and use of divine powers. A Sisters-of-Light company is guarded by a Temple Guard, a named file of the Order of the Standing Wall under its Guard-Captain, who commands the guard and has no hand in her discipline. Her Confessor keeps her soul and her discipline.

The Church leases a Sister of Light to the Crown by commission, by name and in writing, for one campaign. If one is killed during the lease, whether by an enemy, by fire, by plague, or by the fault of the Crown’s own men, the Crown owes the Church twelve Sols (twelve hundred Zarims), the Church’s price for its asset, fixed in canon and not open to bargaining. It is not blood-price, and her kin are owed nothing.

All other priestesses are prohibited from battlefield service. Their duties are confined to convents, sanctuaries, hospitals, and healing houses behind the front lines, where they care for the wounded after evacuation, provide long-term treatment, and oversee the recovery of soldiers and civilians. The daughters of Solaya preserve life amid war; the daughters of Lysara restore it afterward and bring it into the world. Together they embody two complementary expressions of divine healing within one House.
House Elaran
An Elaran Sister has no authority to approve, reject, evaluate, or testify regarding a marriage.

A marriage petition is made by the man who holds authority over the woman: her father, brother, guardian, or, if none exists, her local Praesul. The decision to grant the petition rests entirely with him.

During the marriage rite, the Elaran Sister stands veiled and silent. Her role is purely ceremonial. She witnesses that the rite occurred but does not judge, correct, or validate it. She does not speak Seraval and therefore could not examine the priest’s words even if her office allowed her to do so.
Her duties instead focus on the bride. Before marriage and again shortly afterward, she provides instruction in the two virtues governed by Elaris: Beauty and Submission.

Upon taking her vows, a Sister’s Darlorath passes entirely to the Church. She holds genuine authority over other women, but under no circumstance possesses authority over any man, regardless of his rank or station.
House Sophisran

The Sophisran House trains the Church’s scholars, archivists, illuminators, and its most visible contribution to secular society: the Harmonists of the Order of Harmony, who form the Circle of Memory and are leased to the Magistracy and to any body that wishes its proceedings kept. A Harmonist answers through the Amma of Harmony to the Archivist, a monk-priest of the Church’s monastic order, and not to a Praesul.

A Sophisran Devota neither counsels households nor tends the sick. Her vocation is to read, record, preserve, and remember. The Church regards these pursuits as sacred disciplines deserving their own patronage and their own House.

Within her convent, she also serves as a tutor in advanced literacy for the daughters of affluent families. She maintains the convent’s libraries and records, and, where gifted, illuminates manuscripts and liturgical texts. This work falls under the patronage of Seraifi as much as that of Sophisra.
House Zyrian: The Veiled

House Zyrian keeps one Order, the Order of the Veiled. It is the Church’s only order of women that casts the Weave, and the only one it sends to war embedded in a man’s unit. A Veiled Sister is a Creation mage and not a miracle-worker. She is professed to Zyri with Varek as her anchor, owned by the Church, and leased to the Crown.

rows.t: The Order of the Veiled, House Zyrian, Roselight Circle. Its Sisters are the Veiled. No more than 200 at any time.

Professed Sisters, celibate and perpetual, veiled, unringed, wearing no Oath-Band. Women of the Satyrim, Maenari, Maestrai, and Luminari. Mid Emberglow, Creation Thread. A Luminari woman qualifies only where her Prism reads Creation. Weave, not miracle.
By Church vocation (Roselight Circle), after the Hearthcoming.
Passes entirely to the Church on profession, as for every Sister. She holds authority over other women and none over any man.
Her Confessor keeps her soul and her title.
While she is leased, the commander of the unit she is attached to holds operational and practical mastery of her and holds her discipline. Darlorath stays with the Church.
By commission, by name, and in writing, to the Crown, in the form of the lease of a Sister of Light.
Struck on her Weavefire License. The Church, as her guardian, lodges the release. She is inspected by her Confessor or her Praesul alone.
The Church’s lease, a fourth door into service beside the Contract Roll, the Warrant of the Pair, and the Handmaiden’s Hour. Open to the Veiled alone.
Healing by Creation, embedded with the men she serves. Field miracle remains the Sisters of Light’s alone.
Unarmed work and the dagger. Nothing greater than a dagger.
The unit that holds her mastery is the unit that guards her. Licensed academies are forbidden to teach combat, and no other woman of the Church is taught it.
The Roselight habit in the convent. The Aurelian Veil System (Appendix O, M) in the field.

blocks.text: Discipline of a Roselight Circle Sister

A professed Sister stands under the most complete form of Darlorath the Commonwealth recognizes. Because she is held up as the living ideal of beauty ordered by submission, physical discipline is applied more frequently and more routinely than in any ordinary household.

The Confessor (or designated male clerical superior) administers it as a normal instrument of formation. Correction occurs inside the convent—chapter room, the Sister’s cell, or a designated discipline chamber. The habit, a one-piece dress whose hem sits an inch above a laywoman’s, is raised for it. Discipline is firm, frequent, and thorough: open hand, strap, or light rod across the backside and upper thighs for faults of speech, posture, attention, or any lapse from the expected standard of perfect submission. Sessions are more common and often more extended than civilian practice, because the standard itself is higher.
Softness on the Confessor’s part is itself subject to superior review. The Amma holds authority over other women but none over any man, so the corrective office remains exclusively male.

The Sister’s dress, bearing, and the higher rate of discipline under which she lives are understood as the Church’s public statement of what ordered feminine beauty under full Darlorath looks like. To touch her remains sacrilege; to correct her is the Confessor’s ordinary duty.
VII. SOCIETY & CULTURE
Cohesion Across Nine Peoples: The Parish, the Oath, and the Cohort

Nineteen centuries of standing against the Aidionic Empire and Kaeyria’s vassals has not been held by treasury and steel alone. It has been held because the Commonwealth built, deliberately, the machinery that turns nine peoples with no blood, tongue, or origin in common into men who trust the stranger beside them on the wall — and that machinery runs through the parish school, the Confirmation Rite, and the muster roll, in that order, long before it ever reaches a battlefield.

The parish school. Every child of a Confirmed household of any of the nine peoples enters the same parish school around age six, taught by the local clergy of the Sworn Flame in Zeylara and no other tongue. Home languages are never suppressed — Lórenei still governs Maenari lineage and courtship, Saelkyr remains the tongue of the Satyrim temple and household, Khor’dal is still shouted in Vykril war-bands, Durakhtûn still runs a Duraken forge-floor, Avesai still carries Avesari enclave ritual, and a Luminari household keeps both Saelkyr and Avesai as private inheritance rather than a tongue of its own — but Zeylara, the Council of Tongues’ deliberately forged common tongue, is the sole language of instruction, catechism, and law from the first day of school onward. A Duraken boy and a Maenari boy learn their letters from the same primer, in the same room, a decade before either swears anything to anyone.

Confirmation and the Oath of the Standard, at sixteen. The Creed of the Sworn Flame states the age directly: what a man swears at sixteen, he owes at sixty. Every confirmed boy of every people — Maenari, Satyrim, Duraken, Vykril, Avesari, Maestrai, Luminari alike — swears the Oath of the Standard in the same words, before the same Flame, in his own parish, on the day of his Confirmation. This is the moment ten years of shared schooling becomes four years of shared mandatory service, sworn identically regardless of which people bore the boy swearing it, and a reserve liability that outlasts the service itself by four decades.

The mixed cohort. Crown Regulars and the Order of the Standing Wall muster by year-class and garrison need, never by people — a matter of deliberate Crown and Church policy rather than incidental mixing. The founding legend the Commonwealth itself keeps is read, in barracks and in doctrine alike, as a mandate rather than a story: five soldiers of five peoples held one wall, and no fortified march since has been permitted to raise a single-people line regiment on the strength of that legend. The only single-people formations are the volunteer corps raised for a people’s distinct art — the Bloodwind Brotherhood’s martial traditions (the Vykril Reavers, the Satyrim Blademasters, and the Maenari Fangs), the Avesari and Luminari Skyguard, and the Duraken Siegewrights — recruited by contract and never levied by year-class. The women’s Contract Roll, the Thornmaidens and the Vykril Wayfinders, and the Service Roll of Camp Servitors stand outside the muster altogether. A Vykril recruit out of the Shimmerwind Wastes trains, messes, drills, and eventually holds the same shield-line as a Maenari recruit out of the Threnwood from his first muster onward, and neither transfers out of that cohort by request.

The shared civic calendar. The Council of Tongues Day, kept identically by all nine peoples without local variation, and the parish Confirmation Musters held every spring across every satrapy at once, give the Commonwealth’s civic year the same unifying rhythm its schooling and muster already provide.

None of these institutions arose by accident. Every element was designed during the Commonwealth’s first centuries by Crown, Church, and Council alike. The goal was not merely peaceful coexistence among nine peoples, but the creation of a single civic identity strong enough to survive generations of frontier war. The Commonwealth regards this project as its greatest political achievement, equal in importance to any military victory.

rows.t: Shared literacy and catechism in Zeylara, before any oath is sworn
Confirmation Rite + Oath of the Standard (age 16)

The Oath of the Standard is identical in vow and wording for every confirmed man regardless of people, and opens an identical four-year term of mandatory service for every confirmed boy alike. The sacramental oaths beneath it are two: the Oath of the Crowned (in Zeythari, the Vow of the Flame) for the boy, the Vow of the Faithful for the girl
No regiment or garrison raised along racial lines; postings assigned by year-class and need
One register for law, market, muster, and parish — home tongues survive intact at hearth, temple, and guild, never in competition with it
Council of Tongues Day and the Confirmation Musters observed identically, realm-wide

blocks.text: This is why the Commonwealth’s frontier holds the way it does: not because nine peoples have learned to tolerate each other under pressure, but because every confirmed man of the Commonwealth passed through the same schoolroom, swore the same oath at the same age, and has stood a muster roll built, on purpose, so that he never faced that pressure beside only his own people in the first place.
Social Structure

rows.t: Maestrai dynasty; executive sovereignty and supreme military command
Hereditary Houses — Maenari lineage-lords, Satyrim clan-lords (the Marren-descended clans foremost), Grand officers of the military orders by courtesy seat, Maestrai Houses
Sworn the Oath of the Standard and serving their mandatory four years; not yet enfranchised, may not yet own property or hold guild rank
Confirmed men who have completed their mandatory service; hold the Assembly franchise, may own property, eligible for guild membership (at journeyman standing) and higher education
Duraken guild-masters, merchant-guildsmen, Venshal- and Tesshare-speaking traders

Cultural Values — Honor and the Oath

Honor (Eldrath) in Zeythari is read as a debt scaled to dominion: the more a man holds — land, rank, a household, a wife, a garrison — the more he owes those beneath his hand. A man who holds Darlorath over a woman and abuses it does not lose the authority the Church recognizes in him; he simply fails the debt Honor attaches to it. The Commonwealth does not regard this as a contradiction requiring resolution. A broken oath is judged, at the Final Reckoning, more heavily than nearly any other sin named in the Covenant — Truth’s own wound, dealt by the soul that swore to guard it.

Most men hold many loyalties simultaneously: to household, guild, parish, people, satrapy, Church, and Commonwealth. Zeythari political thought does not seek to eliminate these lesser loyalties. Rather, it teaches that each must ultimately yield when it comes into conflict with a sworn obligation to the Commonwealth itself.
