blocks.text: Cultural Values — Gender Roles, Property, and Law (Darlorath)

rows.t: Held in trust under Darlorath — vested in her father, then her master, then (if professed) the Church of the Sworn Flame; never self-held, at any age or rank. Church or Crown wardship of a wife or widow arises only under the Failed-Heir Clause

Women hold no land, title, or office in Commonwealth law, of any of the nine peoples, without exception. A woman’s dowry, rendered at marriage or at religious profession, is the whole of any claim she will ever hold on her natal household’s estate
Passes through the male line without exception; this is Commonwealth civil law antecedent to Church doctrine, which ratifies rather than imposes it
Assembly suffrage is restricted to male citizens who have completed their mandatory four years’ service (age 20+). Parliament seats and the Crown are hereditary in the male line exclusively

Petitioned by the man who holds her — father, brother, or guardian, or her local Praesul if she has none — and granted or refused by him alone. No court, testimony, or third-party approval attaches to the decision. At the altar each party’s assent is formally asked, as in the old rite; either may technically refuse, but the stigma falls on the refuser and his or her house for life, and refusal almost never occurs

Confirmed men swear the Oath of the Standard at sixteen: four years’ mandatory active service, followed by reserve liability to the general levy until sixty. Confirmed women swear no oath of the State. The Church’s Sisters keep a parallel vow of steadfastness — not to abandon a hospital, granary, or garrison post under siege

Profession is total, irrevocable transfer of Darlorath from household to Church. Reversal exists only through the Suit of Redemption — a Commonwealth national only, requiring the concurrence of the Praesul and the Canon Court, and rarely granted

Darlorath reverts to the eldest adult son or nearest male kin-guardian; a widow may be remarried at her guardian’s arrangement. The Church or Crown holds a widow only under the Failed-Heir Clause (see below)
Applied uniformly to Maenari, Satyrim, Duraken, Vykril, Avesari, Maestrai, and Luminari households alike under Commonwealth civil law, regardless of each people’s own inherited customs

blocks.text: Darlorath in Civil Law: Capacities and Incapacities

rows.t: A woman is not a “person” in the statutory sense (see Terms of Law); she holds personhood in trust and is protected by law from violence and theft. Her personhood is held by her guardian and is never self-held.

Cannot own property in her own name. May manage property on behalf of her guardian. May run her master’s business, never in her own name and never without oversight; the profits belong to her guardian.
Cannot contract in her own name. May execute instruments under her master’s seal (see Contractual Authority Under Seal).
Does not testify in her own right. What she saw is carried into court as her guardian’s testimony, given through her with the guardian present and speaking for it.
Is never a party. Any suit touching her is her guardian’s, brought and answered in his name.

Upon her Confirmation, a woman swears the Vow of the Faithful, affirming her place within the spiritual order. Yet the law does not recognize this as a legal oath, and the Declaration of the Hearth she then makes before her father and the parish is a public declaration of obedience, not an oath, and no court receives it. Under the Crown’s jurisprudence, the marriage vow alone constitutes a woman’s binding oath, and no other sworn undertaking carries legal force. Consequently, a woman may not swear civil oaths, represent herself directly before the Crown’s courts, or assume independent legal culpability. Responsibility for legal obligations rests instead with the authority under whose protection she stands, most commonly her master, father, or guardian.
May enter the Roselight Circle. On profession her Darlorath passes to the Church, and she stands under male clergy in every particular.

Violence against a woman, or violation of her visibly marked status, is an offense against her master, and will be prosecuted before the Magistracy at his instance and in vindication of his oath and the Crown’s peace.

blocks.text: The Guardianship Chain

rows.t: Her father, or her lawful guardian
The Church of the Sworn Flame
The Church, through her local Praesul; or the Crown (see Widows and the Failed-Heir Clause)

blocks.text: Wives, Property, and Personhood
Legal ownership does not negate personhood, and lack of autonomy does not imply enslavement. The Commonwealth holds both principles together.

rows.t: I. Property in law, not in soul

A wife is property in civil law: she exists under the legal authority and guardianship of her master (before marriage, her father or a religious House). Property status governs legal responsibility. She is never a thing, a commodity, or a tool. She is a full moral and spiritual person before the Church and the gods, and personhood governs spiritual dignity.

She is not an independent legal agent. Justice follows oath-capacity: because she cannot swear, she cannot be punished as a principal. Every legal consequence of her public acts, honorable or criminal, falls upon her guardian. She is shielded from direct punishment, never treated as a criminal subject, and never abandoned to vulnerability; a man answerable to Crown and Church for her stands over her.

All praise, penalty, and liability for a wife’s public actions rest on her guardian. Her valor in war increases her master’s honor. Her unlawful act or disruption of order is held against him as a failure of proper mastery. Justice follows the chain of oath, not the hand that struck the blow.

Custom may judge a wife’s appearance or conduct; law judges only her guardian. A woman who violates norms may endure social discomfort, which is cultural pressure and not legal sanction. Shame disciplines men, not women.
Those who wield authority must bear responsibility; those who cannot swear must be protected, not punished. Ideal chivalry is male accountability and not female independence.
As a dependent, as a duty
Removed from any sacred household order
Integrated into a sacred household bound by oath

blocks.text: Slavery dehumanizes; marriage sanctifies a covenant.
The Guardian’s Liability

Doctrine of Guardianship: A woman possesses personal dignity, standing, and protection under the law, but does not bear independent legal liability. Honor earned by her actions and penalties arising from them attach to her lawful guardian, who is answerable for her governance before the Crown and the Magistracy.

rows.t: A woman performs an honorable act (valor in war, public service, notable achievement)
The honor is credited to her guardian or household. She may be praised, but legal and civic distinction accrues to the guardian.
A woman commits a minor offense or disturbs the peace
She is not prosecuted as a principal. Her guardian must answer before the Magistracy for failure of governance and may be fined, censured, or otherwise punished.
A woman casts under her guardian’s permission

The guardian answers for everything she casts, as he answers for any act of hers. Every Emberborn girl wears the Weavefire training glyph, which opens only to her guardian’s registered phrase or that of the instructor he names.
A woman commits a capital offense
No woman may be sentenced to death. The full legal penalty, including death where prescribed, falls upon her guardian.
A guardian is executed or otherwise dies as a consequence of her offense
She immediately enters widowhood status and is governed under the Widowhood Provisions.
A master or guardian sells, attempts to sell, barters, pledges, or otherwise transfers a wife or ward as property, other than by indenture approved under the Indenture Statute

The accused is arraigned before the Magistracy and afforded the full protections of trial. If convicted, the court must impose the sentence of death. No judge, lord, priest, or royal officer may commute the penalty. The man who buys or knowingly receives her is tried and, on conviction, likewise executed; no plea is a defense in law. A recovered woman passes to her eldest adult son, failing him to her nearest male kin or a convent.
A woman under indenture commits an offense
She is not prosecuted as a principal. The master answers as her guardian before the Magistracy
A guardian is cruel to or neglects a woman in his charge

A master may discipline his wife by any reasonable means; the only line is permanent injury. Past that line the offense is secular, and the Magistracy prosecutes it as oath-violation. The Church’s own concern is limited to canon matters and to his honor. A master may not kill his wife; killing her is homicide.
A wife requires correction or discipline under law or custom
This remains exclusively the responsibility of her master, by any reasonable means short of permanent injury. Neither Crown nor Church assumes custody of a wife as punishment for her own misconduct.
A woman has no living guardian
Legal responsibility passes to the authority holding her under the Failed-Heir Clause. The Church, Crown, or appointed steward answers in place of a private guardian.

blocks.text: Household Discipline
Public Discipline (Ordinary Woman)

Public discipline is lawful but uncommon. It is used when private correction has failed to produce lasting order, or when the fault itself was public (disrespect shown in the market, insolence toward a superior in the street, open failure of deportment that reflects on the household).

The guardian (master or father) administers it himself. The woman is ordinarily required to stand or kneel in a place of ordinary traffic—doorway, market edge, parish courtyard—while he delivers a measured series of open-handed smacks or strokes with a light domestic implement (strap, light rod, or the flat of the hand) across the backside or the upper thighs. The short adult hem means the target is readily accessible without further undressing. The correction is brisk, purposeful, and ends when the guardian judges the point made. It is never prolonged into spectacle, and never aims at permanent injury.

Bystanders treat it as the restoration of household order rather than entertainment. A man who makes a prolonged display of it risks social comment for excess; a man who never corrects publicly when the fault was public risks comment for softness. The woman’s status markers (caerwevra, Oath-Band) remain fully visible throughout. Once finished, she is expected to resume her duties at once, the matter closed.
Private Discipline (Ordinary Woman)
Private discipline is the ordinary and far more frequent form. It occurs inside the home and covers the full range from minor maintenance to serious correction.

Minor faults—failure to curtsey, speaking without permission, lagging in household tasks, a sharp tone—are met at once with a swift open-handed smack across the backside. This is treated as routine, unremarkable, and expected. More substantial correction follows the same principle: the woman is required to present herself (often bent over a bed, bench, or the guardian’s knee), the short hem is raised if necessary, and a longer session with hand, strap, or light rod is delivered. The intensity and duration are at the guardian’s judgment, always stopping short of permanent injury.
Any use of discipline for the master’s personal satisfaction or “entertainment” remains strictly private, confined to the home, and is never performed in public or outside the household.

A well-ordered household is expected to show the results: quiet speech, prompt obedience, and the absence of public lapses. Soft or infrequent private discipline is itself regarded as a failure of Darlorath.
Household Reception and Daily Service

When her master returns to the house, a wife meets him at the threshold on her knees. She whispers, reverently, “Welcome to Your home, Master,” then lowers herself further and kisses his feet. She remains in that position until he raises her. If he does not raise her, she stays on her knees or crawls after him as he moves through the house. She never rises without his express permission.

Once permitted to stand, she takes his cloak, his tools or weapons, and any other burden he carries. She waits while he seats himself in his chair, then brings whatever he orders—whiskey, water, the crop, or any other thing—without being told twice. At table she serves him first and remains kneeling beside his place until he grants her leave to sit and eat. If no such permission is given, she stays on her knees throughout the meal and eats only after he has finished and left the room.

These acts are ordinary household custom, not extraordinary displays. They mark the continuous reality of Darlorath: the house is his, she is his, and her place is at his feet until he orders otherwise.

rows.t: Merges with the master’s. He is her legal guardian and representative.
Personhood in trust; protection under law; moral and spiritual standing.

blocks.text: Contractual Authority Under Seal

rows.t: A master may entrust his wife with his signet ring, authorizing her to execute contracts, guild instruments, and commercial agreements under his seal.
A document so sealed binds as if the master had signed and sworn it, with full force before Crown courts, guild tribunals, and ecclesiastical review.
It transfers no ownership, citizenship, or personhood. It is representation, not independence.
The master remains fully liable for all obligations entered under his seal.

Most common when the master is absent for long periods (military service, reserve call-up, diplomatic travel, long-distance trade) and traditionally granted while heirs are young and continuity of the household is paramount.
A mark of profound trust and respect: she acts as steward of her master’s oath, reputation, and economic standing.
On the master’s return, death, or legal incapacity, the seal is surrendered to the lawful guardian or heir.
Unauthorized retention or misuse of a man’s seal is fraud and oath-violation under Crown and Church law.

blocks.text: Divorce and Annulment

rows.t: Extremely rare. Only by the Church’s Canon Court, which rarely grants it. A woman has no legal channel of any kind, and the Crown grants none.
The impediments of consanguinity and prior bond; in the rarest case, a wife’s proven adultery or desertion. Failure to provide is a matter of the master’s honor and no ground.
Brought by the master, through his parish Priest. Never by the wife, and never by her kin on her behalf.
The marriage is annulled; the hair-lock may be removed from the hilt; her guardianship returns to her father or nearest male kin. If none, the Failed-Heir Clause applies.

blocks.text: The Indenture Statute

Indenture is lawful. It is not honored. The Commonwealth permits it as the lesser of two failures, and fixes the law so that the shame falls on the man who failed and on no one else. It is a relic of the Theocratic Kingdom of Zeythar, kept on the books through the Constitutional Settlement and shunned by every house that has had to use it.
Parties and Grounds

rows.t: An unmarried daughter of eighteen or over, Presented. Never a wife, widow, professed Sister, or son.
Her father alone. He may not indenture her himself. Only a Municipal Court may order it. Any arrangement for a daughter’s service on a father’s own authority is void and is the heresy of the chattel.

A catastrophic debt of the father: the failure of his mortgage, the loss of his holding, or ruin of that order. Ordinary debt, arrears, and hardship are no ground. The debt must be real, recorded, and owed.
A male citizen of good standing (twenty or over, service completed, Oath sworn) who pays the debt.

The master pays the debt into the Municipal Court, which discharges it to the creditor and enters the discharge in the Registry. No part of the debt payment passes to the father at any time. Nor does any part of the Indenture Fee: it is her dowry, held in trust for her husband.
By a Municipal Court only, after review. The Magistral may refuse. An indenture without a Magistral’s order and seal is void, and whoever holds a woman under it commits the heresy of the chattel.
Written in Zeylara, sealed by the Magistral, and entered in the Registry of Indenture. Names father, daughter, master, creditor, debt, posting or household, term, and the date of release.

rows.t: The father’s petition, the creditor, the debt, and the master are examined in open court. The Magistral may hear the father’s kin and may refuse the petition.
Catastrophic in the sense above. Real, recorded, and not dischargeable by the father’s means or his kin’s.
Eligible under the table above, and not previously indentured.
Qualified, and not himself a party to the debt’s creation.
She will be housed and governed under a married woman of the master’s household, or under the Stewardess of a Crown posting.
Four years. Fixed in the instrument.
The instrument contains every safeguard below, or the seal is refused.

blocks.text: Master’s Right

rows.t: An asset the master has paid for across a set period, and not property. A term interest created by the Court. It returns to the father by operation of law on the date of release. It cannot be conveyed, assigned, or inherited.

Held in trust. She remains listed in her father’s household. His Darlorath stays with him, whole, throughout. The master holds mastery in trust for the term and not the dominion, and he is not her husband.

Full mastery for the term, carnal use excepted (he is not her husband): her labor, residence, movement, dress, the collar, her correction, and her conduct. He answers for her before the Magistracy as a guardian answers (Guardian’s Liability). He may not sublease, lend, or hire her to any other man.
He may not despoil her. He may not beat her excessively: the Five Boundaries (no permanent injury, etc)

May not recall her. Holds no claim on her labor or on any pay for her during the term. Remains the injured party in law, with recourse in the Municipal Court for any mistreatment, during the term or after her return.

blocks.text: The Indenture Fee

rows.t: 125 Zarims, levied on the master at registration, over and above the debt.
The whole 125 Zarims is held by the Municipal Court in a dowry trust for her future husband and paid to him on her marriage. The father receives no part of it, and the Court takes none.

The 125 Zarims is her dowry and is earmarked for it. The Registry enters the trust. The father is barred by law from receiving, claiming, or reaching any part of it, and no creditor of his may touch it. Her husband draws it from the Court on her marriage.
Entered in the trust on every release: the term’s end, redemption, or the Court’s order of release. A master released for failing forfeits the fee all the same.
The master recovers none of it.

Set by the Assembly’s Treasury Office with the Commonwealth’s other rates, subject to Parliament’s veto and Royal Assent. Raising it is the slow means by which the Commonwealth makes indenture unprofitable.
All other fines and fees under this Statute go to the Court.
The fault is the father’s debt and not the girl’s. The fee penalizes the master and secures her dowry.

blocks.text: Safeguards

rows.t: The master has paid a catastrophic debt and the fee for an asset he must return sound, unmarked, and marriageable. An injured, scarred, or despoiled girl costs him the asset, the price, and his standing. The law makes her care his interest.

An instrument for a Crown posting carries the Warrant of the Ward: the master’s standing leave, given once, for the Sentinels of the Maidenward to address, restrain, lift, and carry her, and to strike her as needed. The Warrant creates no right to her labor and gives no leave for any carnal use. An instrument for a Crown posting without it is refused the seal.
Four years, or age 22, whichever comes first, non-renewable by any master in any form. No woman is indentured twice. The Registry refuses a second entry.
Sale, trade, pledge, assignment, or transfer of the woman or of the instrument is the heresy of the chattel. Capital for seller and buyer (Article IV). The instrument is void.
Any carnal use of her by the master, or by any man of his household with his leave or through his neglect, is a crime. Her willingness is no defense.

She is returned to her father marriageable: intact, sound, and unmarked. On the date of release the clerk removes the collar and the Harmonist records the release. A Sister of the Solayan House may be asked to review her condition. Her review is information for the Magistral and certifies nothing.

A prudent master has a Sister of the Solayan House assess her at entry and at release, and has the assessment attested by the Quartermaster or another officer. It has no standing as certification. The Magistral weighs it with the rest of the evidence, as he weighs any record.

The father or his kin may redeem her at any time by paying the master, through the Court, the debt the master paid, less a credit for the months she has served. The fee is not refunded. The Court orders the release, and the fee is entered in her dowry trust as on any release. The bar on a second indenture stands.

Plain ash-steel band, fixed by the Court’s clerk at registration. Struck with the Court seal, instrument number, master’s mark, and date of release. Removed only by the Court’s clerk on that date or on a Magistral’s order of release. The master may not remove it. A collar without a seal and a date is Kaeyria’s and Aidion’s, and is evidence of sale.
Suspended for the term. The collar replaces it as her mark of guardianship. Worn over the collar at Mass and sacramental occasions only. Restored at her father’s door on release.
Her unveiled face during the term is not an offense. No fine falls on father or master.

The Registry records the term as service to her household. No stain attaches to her or to her prospects. No suitor may cite it against her in negotiation. The Registry’s entry of release is accepted by Priest and parish as proof of her standing.
The Registry and the parish record name the father’s failure. In her village the collar reads as his failure and her service.
Her father alone negotiates it, as for any daughter. The master holds no right in it whatever: he may not propose, grant, withhold, or take a price for it. Marriage follows release.
Master’s death, bankruptcy, or loss of his Crown contract
The Court releases her to her father. The instrument does not pass to a successor.

blocks.text: Complaint and Release

rows.t: Any failing may be reported by the daughter, her father, or any male citizen to a Crown Constable (a Crown Warden in a city). Where she is held in a Crown posting, the chain in Part C applies. A report is information and not a suit.
The Constable investigates and informs the Municipal Court within three days. He judges and punishes nothing.
Within ten days. The father is the injured party, the master is respondent, and the Constable’s report is the evidence. The Magistral rules alone.

On a finding of failing the Magistral releases her from the bond. The clerk removes the collar, her veil is restored, and she returns to her father. The price is not refunded. The father’s debt stays discharged, with no claim against him for the unexpired term.
The Constable may remove her to her father’s house or, if he cannot receive her, to the parish House Matron.
During the term the father may bring a complaint of mistreatment at any time. After her release or return he has thirty days and no more. The failing table applies.
Neglect of food, dress, billet, or medical care
Release. Fine. Crown audit where the posting is Crown.
Release. The Magistracy prosecutes as oath-violation. His honor falls.
Release. Fine. Posting or household forfeit.

Release. Tried before the Regional Court as a major criminal matter at her father’s instance. The release does not wait on trial. Barred for life from holding any indenture. The Church tries him as well: fornication before the Canon Court, and breach of the Oath of the Standard before the Tribunal of Broken Oaths. Whatever the verdicts, the charges alone ruin him socially.
Sublease, loan, or hire to another
The lease is void at once. She returns to her father with her dowry paid in full. The Magistracy censures the master, and he forfeits the fee.
Capital under Article IV. Instrument void.

Widows and the Failed-Heir Clause

rows.t: Her nearest male kin holds Darlorath.
None. A widow’s Darlorath passes to a new guardian; it is never released to her.

In Maenari communities a widowed mother is commonly kept by her eldest daughter, in the household of that daughter’s husband, who has the shelter and care of her and draws her dower directly from the heir’s estate. The Commonwealth and the Church permit it as custom and neither requires it. The heir remains owner of the estate and holder of Darlorath; the dower remains his charge, drawn from his estate rather than carried under his roof. No shame attaches to either household

Applies only where the master’s line has failed (no son, no male kin able to hold Darlorath) and she has no father, brother, or kin to receive her. She then passes to the Church through her local Praesul or, where the extinct House held a peerage or Crown office, to the Crown.
The State and the Church never hold a married woman or a widow.

blocks.text: Names and Lineage
Naming is patrilineal.

rows.t: A child bears the father’s surname. A wife takes her master’s surname at marriage.
Kept in genealogical records, temple records, and formal lineage recitations. Nobles recite both names on formal occasions; commoners rarely use it outside legal documents.
Personal name, optional lineage marker, patrilineal surname. Markers: ben (son of), sae (daughter of), vaen (child of; neutral, ceremonial).
Ancient Lórenei or Saelkyr roots, masculine in form; unchanged except by extinction or royal decree.
Drawn from professions, places, ancestral traits, or guild affiliation.
Satyrim priests and scholars adopt sacred-gender (luminal) temple names, used only in temple contexts.
Some male citizens adopt a collective, gender-neutral oath-name on taking the Oath. It never replaces the surname.

The bride’s lineage recedes at marriage: her legal identity, surname, and inheritance rights transfer to her master’s House, and her children belong to it. She is not cut off socially, and her natal House keeps her in its records.

A Maenari wife who has borne her House its eldest son and heir. Not every wife earns it, and it outranks the Naeva (lady of the house). It is hers for life, widowhood included, and precedes her name and rank in every introduction, queens among them: Vaeva Queen Sarena, or Her Majesty, Vaeva Sarena. The Queen and the Queen Mother both insist on it. Where two Vaevas share a House, the wife of its current head is senior: Queen Sarena outranks the Queen Mother, Queen Ilyara.

Agricultural villages (volcanic-soil advantage); mining settlements (Thaldrin); fortress towns (marches); more racially homogeneous but not segregated; strong community bonds; veteran leadership

Patriarchal household under Darlorath; extended families common; women manage household operations; children educated in service preparation; high value placed on daughters, the flame the household protects

VIII. EDUCATION & THE LIFE-CYCLE OF THE OATH
Foundational Doctrine

Education in the Commonwealth is a civic-ecclesiastical obligation flowing from the Confirmation Rite and the Oath of the Standard, rather than a personal entitlement. Knowledge is treated as an instrument of truth, order, and endurance—shaping children of the nine peoples into capable, literate citizens who understand their place and duties within Darlorath, household, Church, and Crown.

Foundational schooling is universal, compulsory, and subsidized, ensuring that even a rural farmer or village artisan receives a robust, practical education. Because access is tied to the Faith and the sacraments, instruction is seamlessly shared between the Crown and the Church:

The Parish Network: On the frontier and in rural regions, children are educated directly within local parish houses by clergy and lay-scholars, saving the Crown administrative overhead while embedding civic duty into spiritual life.
Urban Academies: In larger towns and cities, formal civic academies manage the larger student bodies.
Curriculum: Instruction emphasizes functional literacy, practical numeracy, local civic law, and oath-ethics.
Sex-Differentiated Formation
Foundational instruction begins at approximately age six for all Confirmed children:
Boys remain under formal instruction until Confirmation at sixteen, followed by mandatory service until twenty.
Girls remain under formal instruction until age ten.

Following this foundation, education diverges sharply by sex. This differentiation does not stem from a perceived disparity in intellect, but from the settled doctrinal ground of the Pattern, which assigns distinct obligations to men and women. A school preparing a child for the wrong set of obligations serves neither the individual nor the Commonwealth.
The Gated Upper Tiers

While foundational literacy and civic competence are universal for the obediently Confirmed, advanced learning is strictly regulated. Higher education—comprising royal universities, technical institutes, military academies, and sanctioned arcane colleges—is gated by a combination of rigorous merit, sponsorship, and social standing.
Specialized Training: Dedicated institutions train high-tier administrators, engineers, master healers, jurists, and Emberborn practitioners to maintain the governance and defense of the realm.

Institutional Permanence: Educational governance, accreditation standards, and advanced curricula are treated as permanent, enduring institutions rather than experimental programs, preserving the traditional order.
Governance of Instruction

rows.t: Both (separate instruction within the same parish)
Church of the Sworn Flame — parish clergy (boys), Sisters of the Seraphian House (girls)
The Crown (Crown Regulars, Order of the Standing Wall, or an approved auxiliary)

blocks.text: The Civic School is a Crown institution and a Crown expense, and it exists for boys alone. A girl’s formation after the Hearthcoming returns entirely to her mother’s authority and her father’s roof; the Crown does not maintain schoolrooms for daughters, on the settled reasoning that a household, not a civil institution, is where a woman’s obligations under Darlorath are actually exercised and are therefore best taught. This is not read within the Commonwealth as a lesser provision. It is read as the correct one: the Crown spends where the Crown will later collect — the levy, the bench, the guild hall — and does not spend to form a citizenship a woman will never hold.
Civic Literacy & Public Order

Independent of the parish-and-civic school track, every child of the Commonwealth — boy and girl of every people alike — receives instruction in the practical grammar of lawful society, delivered through parish teaching, town drills, and guild-hall demonstration rather than confined to any single schoolroom. This is treated as public safety, not civics for its own sake.

Recognition of lawful authority — the insignia and jurisdiction of Satraps, Marshals, Crown Wardens and Constables, and Magistrals; the limits of who may command whom; the obligation to comply first and contest later through lawful channels.
Emergency signaling — bells, horn-calls, ever-lamp color shifts, and beacon towers; when to shelter, when to evacuate, when to clear a thoroughfare, when to render aid.
Public infrastructure — sanitation, ever-lamp maintenance and tampering prohibitions, rail and cargo-way right-of-way, water rationing and contamination reporting.

Reporting obligations — the duty to report violent crime, unlicensed Ember manifestation, structural corruption of civic works, and abuse of office, through channels taught as service rather than betrayal; vigilantism and mob action are taught, explicitly, as unlawful.

Because this instruction is universal and lifelong, Commonwealth towns run with fewer constables per head, faster crisis response, and higher compliance with lawful orders than the scale of the frontier would otherwise predict. A Commonwealth town is not quiet because it is watched. It is quiet because every soul in it, confirmed or not yet confirmed, man or woman, knows what is expected of her or him, and why.
The Education of Boys
Early Childhood (Birth to ~Age 6)

A boy remains fully under his father’s household authority. Formal instruction has not yet begun; what a child learns at this stage he learns within family and parish life — prayers, obedience, family duties, and the basic social expectations of a Confirmed household. This period is not considered educational in the formal sense. It is considered formative in the truest sense, and the Church holds a household that neglects it responsible for whatever the parish school must later struggle to undo.
The Parish School (Ages ~6 to 9/10)
A boy of a Confirmed household enters parish school around age six, instructed by the ordained clergy of the Sworn Flame alongside every other boy of the parish regardless of people.
Subjects:
Literacy through sacred texts
Basic mathematics
Catechism and doctrine
Theology
Daily prayer and ritual observance
Purpose: The goal is not intellectual freedom but moral formation. A boy at parish school is taught, specifically and by name:
Truthfulness
Obedience
Oath-keeping
Religious identity
Respect for authority
The Church’s long-held position — never seriously contested by the Crown — is that spiritual formation must precede civic formation.
The Civic School (Ages 10 to 16)
At ten, instruction passes from the Church to the Crown. Professionally trained, Crown-employed instructors take over in a dedicated Civic School.
Academic:
Advanced reading
Formal writing
Mathematics
Accounting
History
Civic:
Law
Governance
Constitutional structure
Public responsibilities
Practical:
Trade introductions
Guild exposure
Basic military training

The Crown treats this whole curriculum as an investment with a fixed maturity date: a boy who leaves the Civic School at sixteen is meant to be ready, in the same year, to swear the Oath of the Standard and begin his four years’ mandatory service — prepared for it, not merely aged into it.
The Training Dagger (Age 12)

At twelve, every boy of a Confirmed household receives a small training blade. It carries no authority, is not oath-bound, and confers no status of any kind. It exists for one purpose: to remind the boy, and everyone who sees it at his belt, that adulthood and service are approaching and that he is expected to begin preparing for them in earnest. A boy who treats the training dagger carelessly is, in most households, corrected sharply and immediately — not because the blade itself matters, but because the lesson it is meant to plant does.
Confirmation, the Oath of the Standard, and the Oath Dagger (Age 16)

At sixteen, a boy receives the Confirmation Rite before Church and Crown alongside every other boy of his parish’s year-class, at the spring Confirmation Musters. Immediately following the sacrament, he swears the civil Oath of the Standard and receives his Oath Dagger: a plain blade marked with the Flame sigil and the glyph of the Standard, presented by the parish or, in the wealthier holds, forged by the boy’s own household through a licensed smith.
The Oath Dagger is not decorative. It is:
a visible declaration of Confirmed, oath-bound status;
a legal instrument recognized by Crown and Church alike as proof of citizenship-in-progress;
worn openly — belt, sash, or harness — for the whole of a man’s unmarried life.

A confirmed man found in public without his Oath Dagger is presumed unbound, in violation of civic duty, or under disciplinary sanction. There is no defense of forgetfulness recognized in Commonwealth law.
Swearing the Oath of the Standard is what begins mandatory service, not what completes citizenship. That distinction matters, and the Commonwealth is exact about it.
“A man does not speak his oath. He carries it.”
Mandatory Service (Ages 16 to 20)

Every confirmed young man serves four years, posted to the Crown Regulars, the Order of the Standing Wall, or an approved auxiliary according to Crown need and his own aptitude as tracked through the Civic School.
Purpose:
Military training
Civic discipline
Social integration
Demonstration of loyalty

A boy of any of the nine peoples serves this term beside boys of every other people, never in a regiment raised along racial lines — the same cohesion doctrine that governs the Crown’s mixed-muster policy generally applies with full force to the four years of mandatory service, since this is precisely the age at which the Commonwealth intends a Duraken recruit and a Maenari recruit to become men who trust one another, not merely men who were taught to.
Exemptions.

rows.t: Certified by Crown physicians; service is then rendered in a form suited to the man (see below).
Must be accepted into Church service. Exempted men serve as scribes, chaplain assistants, temple guards, or administrative support. No man avoids service entirely; it is military or ecclesiastical.

blocks.text: Citizenship for the exempt. An exempt man becomes a citizen by serving the State in another form, usually a civil project or other work assigned for the Commonwealth’s benefit. The point is service: no man is a citizen who has not given the State his labor.

Failure to complete service. A man who does not finish his term remains a non-citizen. He cannot own property, marry, vote, or hold office; he pays special taxes; he bears social stigma. Fewer than one man in a thousand fails.
Civic Adulthood (Age 20+)
Completion of the four years’ mandatory service — not the sacrament of Confirmation four years earlier — is what grants full civic standing. Upon completion, a man gains:
Full Assembly voting rights
Property ownership
Guild membership at journeyman standing, and eligibility for eventual mastery
Higher-education eligibility (pending competitive examination)
Eligibility to stand for civic office
The right to marry

This marks complete male adulthood in Commonwealth law. What a man swears at sixteen, the Creed of the Sworn Flame states, he owes at sixty — the Oath of the Standard does not lapse with his discharge at twenty. Completion of the fixed term retires him from active duty and seats him as a full citizen, but he remains liable to recall to the general levy as a reservist for the whole of his confirmed life thereafter, precisely as the Creed’s own reckoning implies. Most men marry between twenty and twenty-five, establishing a new household — the smallest and most vital unit of the Commonwealth.
The Education of Girls
The formation of daughters proceeds through named ceremonies marking each developmental stage, and a fourth passage — marriage — that is the culmination of all that precedes it.
The Parish School (Ages ~6 to 9/10)
A girl of a Confirmed household attends the same parish school as the boys of her age, in separate instruction under the supervision of the Sisters of the Seraphian House.
Subjects:
Literacy
Basic mathematics
Theology
Household records
Needlework
Domestic arts

Unlike many neighboring realms, literacy is expected of Commonwealth girls as a matter of course — a girl is expected to read the Creed herself and understand the prayers she recites, not merely repeat them.
The Hearthcoming (Age 9/10)

When a girl completes her parish schooling, the Hearthcoming is held at the parish itself. The presiding priest blesses her and formally returns her to her father, who receives her before the congregation with a spoken affirmation of guardianship. The Devota of the Seraphian House who served as her primary instructor — a Handmaiden, in common speech — places a hearthstone — a palm-sized piece of polished volcanic stone from the Kaelvash Valleys, marked with the Flame sigil, the First Oath glyph, and Seraphiae’s own emblem — into the girl’s hands. She keeps it for life.

Meaning: the Church’s formal role in her upbringing ends here; her father’s household resumes primary authority; and the ceremony marks, at once, formation completed, return to family life, and preparation for womanhood.
She was given to the Flame to be formed. She is returned to the hearth to be prepared.
Home Education (Ages 9/10 to 16)
From the Hearthcoming, a girl returns fully to her mother’s authority and her father’s household.
Subjects:
Household management, including the direction of servants
Household accounting and the ordering of food and supplies
Textile work, domestic production, and practical craft
The instruction of younger children
Domestic and social conduct

Wealthier households may additionally provide private tutoring in music, literature, the arts, and advanced literacy. A girl identified as suited to religious life may instead remain, or be returned, to Church authority to train within the Roselight Circle.
The Veiling (Age 12)

The Veiling is conducted on or near the girl’s twelfth birthday, before the altar of Seraphiae in the parish church, at which she receives her face veil. Per the Holy Book of Truth and Grace, the rite is administered by the Elder Sister or Matron of the house — in Zeythari, the parish’s House Matron, its single Devota, who is ordinarily the girl’s own Handmaiden — and the girl, in white, carrying no flowers and no ornament, speaks the Litany of the Rose, her Vow of the Rose. The parish priest attends, and the family and household are present as witnesses.

After the Litany, the mother prepares the veil and places it over her daughter’s face, speaking words that name what is being covered — beauty, youth, promise, and the right of her father to present her in his own time. If the mother is dead or absent, the duty falls to the nearest female relative. The father then formally declares his guardianship before those present.

Meaning: from the Veiling the girl is, at once, socially protected, legally unavailable for courtship, and visibly under paternal authority. She begins wearing the face veil and knee-length dress of protected girlhood. The veil remains until marriage.
There is no public feast; the family shares a private meal, and gifts are modest and domestic.
The Presentation (Age 16)

The Presentation is the largest ceremony of a girl’s formation, and the only one held at the community level. It falls at the same Confirmation Musters at which the young men of her year swear the Oath of the Standard — the Church’s own Confirmation Rite, identical in sacramental form for both sexes, is common to both events; what follows the sacrament diverges sharply by sex, as Darlorath requires. For the young men it is the civil Oath of the Standard. For the girl it is the Litany of the Veiled Rose, spoken over the year’s confirmed girls as the Holy Book of Truth and Grace provides, and, in the same hour, her Declaration of the Hearth: a public declaration, made before her father or guardian and the parish Priest, of her obedience to her father and her intent to obey her master and any master after him. It is not a binding oath, and no court receives it.

At the parish hall or public square, each girl is presented by her father before the assembled community, who announces her name, her household, and her readiness for courtship. The priest blesses her; a Sister of the Seraphian House anoints her hands. Then, publicly, the girl lifts her veil for the first time since age twelve — briefly, before the community — and lowers it again.

Meaning: the Presentation marks entry into adulthood, eligibility for courtship, and public recognition of maturity. Her dress transitions that same day to the mid-thigh hem and two-piece garments of adult women. The community feasts; the Presentation is a genuine and joyful public celebration, not a solemn one.
She was covered to be protected. She is shown to be sought. She will be veiled again only when she is found.
Courtship

Following the Presentation, a young woman becomes eligible for courtship, but a man does not approach her directly. He approaches her father, her guardian, or her household, and a man who is yet a son under his father’s roof is matched by his father, who approaches on his behalf. A successful courtship is understood, in Commonwealth law and custom alike, as a negotiation between households rather than merely between individuals — the covenant itself is negotiated by the men who hold authority on either side, and neither the girl nor the boy is a party to the negotiation. Consent is what it was in the traditional household: each spouse’s assent at the altar to the match made for them, a son’s as much as a daughter’s. In theory either may refuse; the refusal brings a stigma upon the refuser and his or her house that lasts a lifetime, and nearly every bride and groom assents and moves on. A daughter under indenture is courted as any other: through her father alone. The master holds no voice in it.
“A man woos a woman. A master petitions a household.”
The Three Ceremonies of Daughters: Reference

The Devota (Handmaiden) who taught her places the hearthstone in her hands: polished volcanic stone marked with the First Oath glyph and Seraphiae’s flame. Her father formally receives her before the congregation
Modest; the family celebrates privately afterward
Completes Church schooling; formal return to her father’s guardianship. The hearthstone is personal, kept for life, and is proof of formation, blessing, and lawful return

Parish church, before the altar of Seraphiae, on or near her twelfth birthday. Administered by the parish’s House Matron (its single Devota, ordinarily her primary Handmaiden); the parish priest attends

She speaks the Litany of the Rose (her Vow of the Rose) in white, without flowers or ornament; then her mother prepares the veil and places it over her face, speaking words that name what is being covered; her father formally declares his guardianship before those present. If the mother is dead or absent, the nearest female relative
None public; a private family meal; gifts modest and domestic
Knee-length dress and face veil of protected girlhood. Not marriage-eligible; approaches to her father are not appropriate

Parish hall or public square, annually at the Confirmation Musters (the Festival of First Oaths), the same day the young men swear the Oath of the Standard, the local lord standing witness for the Crown. The morning belongs to oaths; the evening belongs to presentation

Her father walks her before the assembled community and announces her name, household, and readiness for courtship; the priest blesses her; the Handmaiden anoints her hands; she lifts her veil for the first time since twelve, briefly, and lowers it
Community feast; a genuine public celebration
The public lifting is the signal. Courtship inquiries to her father are now appropriate; mid-thigh hem and two-piece garments from this day

blocks.text: Religious Vocation and Completion

A girl identified as suited to service may remain under, or return to, Church authority beyond the Hearthcoming to train within the Roselight Circle, most commonly toward the Solayan House if she shows healing aptitude, or the Seraphian House otherwise. For every other girl, formal education concludes with the Presentation. Civic adulthood for a man arrives only at twenty, on completion of his mandatory service; a woman passes from girlhood to adult status through marriage alone.
Magical Instruction & the Regulation of Ember
The Commonwealth treats magical education chiefly as public safety, not personal empowerment, and applies it identically across sex, people, and station.
Universal Ember Literacy (Ages 7 to 12)
Every child of the Commonwealth receives basic Ember-awareness instruction, delivered through the parish and funded by the Crown, regardless of sex or people. It is not spellcraft.

Instruction is held on Sundays, some dozen sessions across the five years, and administered on the Church’s side by the Sisters of the Seraphian House on behalf of both Church and Crown; the parish is reimbursed by the Crown for running it.
Subjects:
What Ember is — a natural property of the Weave, not a divine miracle and not a curse
How to recognize Ember manifestation in others
What suspicious or uncontrolled magic looks like, and why it is dangerous
How and where to report a magical incident
The difference between magic (the Weave) and miracle (divine compact)
Legal obligations regarding magic — why Emberborn are registered, and why concealment is a crime

This instruction exists to prevent panic and false accusation, ensure accurate reporting, and acclimate every child, from the first, to a Commonwealth in which Ember is a regulated civic resource rather than a rumor. It does not teach casting of any kind.
The Volcanic Glass Prism (Ages 12 to 16)

Each year between twelve and sixteen, every child is tested by a Crown-appointed Ember Examiner using a Volcanic Glass Prism — an obsidian resonance instrument, formed in the Kaelvash Valleys’ own dormant vents, tuned to detect Ember presence. Testing continues annually until the child turns sixteen, tests positive, or has already tested positive in a prior year.

rows.t: Minor Ember present; enrolled in the Vraenhari; may later serve in infrastructure roles
Significant Ember; enrolled in the Vraenhari; tracked for possible Collegium training
Rare and heavily regulated; enrolled in the Vraenhari; subject to immediate Crown oversight

blocks.text: A positive result triggers mandatory enrollment in the Vraenhari. Concealment of a positive result by any household is a criminal offense under Crown law, prosecuted without regard to the people or station of the household concerned.

Registration and record. A positive result is recorded jointly by the Bureau of Weavefire, and the household is notified under an oath of confidentiality binding both institutions. Registration confers no privilege and no status — it is a household record, not a mark of distinction — though completion of the Vraenhari is separately logged as a civic duty fulfilled.
The Vraenhari — The Ember Hearth
A one-year, Crown-mandated course in magical control and safety — not a school of magic, not military instruction, and not itself considered higher education, any more than weapons discipline is.
Structure:
Duration: one year
Schedule: four hours each morning, the child returning to ordinary schooling or household duty thereafter
Attendance: co-educational — with Universal Ember Literacy, one of only two points in Commonwealth instruction where the ordinary separation of the sexes does not apply

Administration: locally organized, funded by the Crown — the town or village bears the cost of running its Vraenhari and is reimbursed by the Crown Treasury — staffed by licensed mages, Ember Examiners, or other qualified local practitioners
Location: facilities exist in every town of meaningful size throughout the Commonwealth
Subjects taught:
Recognition of Ember manifestation and its emotional triggers
Emotional regulation and suppression technique
Safe dissipation of excess Ember
Summoning and holding a small, controlled flame
Minor wound closure through basic Creation touch
Elementary crop augmentation
Absolute prohibition on unsupervised casting, kept by the boy’s oath and by the girl’s glyph in its place
Subjects explicitly forbidden:
Thread theory or specialization
Combat application of any kind
Weave manipulation beyond a controlled cantrip
Independent casting outside supervised environments
Any Umbral instruction whatsoever

Because Ember manifests across puberty rather than at a fixed age, the Vraenhari is triggered by detection rather than calendar: a boy detected mid-Civic-School pauses and resumes; a girl detected mid-home-instruction does the same. If detection falls in the same year as Confirmation or the Presentation, the ceremony may be delayed one year pending completion, which the Crown and Church both regard as a reasonable accommodation rather than a disruption. A girl who completes the Vraenhari is regarded, without exception, as having demonstrated both exceptional nature and civic responsibility — a distinction that improves rather than damages her standing at the Presentation.

The glyph (girls): a boy keeps the prohibition on unsupervised casting by his oath, and a girl, who cannot swear one, wears the Weavefire training glyph in its place from enrollment. The glyph is a magical, painless, non-punitive safeguard, unlike the collar, which degrades the Ember and is reserved to law enforcement. It leaves the Ember whole, lets her form and practice every working, and diverts a working into containment unless the instructor of record opens it. It is struck when the Bureau certifies her and her guardian releases it (see Why the Commonwealth Uses a Glyph, Not a Collar, in Magic in the Commonwealth).
The flame that is not mastered will consume the hand that bears it. Control is obedience. Obedience is safety. Safety is truth.
Advanced Magical Education
For most citizens of either sex, the Vraenhari is the end of magical instruction. Advancement beyond it is a controlled exception, available only through:

Crown-sponsored service — assignment to an approved magical division such as the Weaveblade Legion, or the Thornmaidens, state-funded and closely supervised, and bound by oath (for men) or by guardian’s contract and sacramental vow (for the Thornmaidens);
The Arcana Scholium, part of the United Colleges of Zeythari system.
Licensed private academies, fee-based, and forbidden from teaching combat or experimental spellcraft;
For a woman specifically, explicit written consent of her guardian under Darlorath, in addition to Crown authorization, who may then apply for admission to the Royal Nexus Academy.
Unlicensed advancement, unsanctioned casting, or concealment of Ember ability carries confiscation of implements, mandatory, imprisonment, or, for repeat offenses, indefinite magical suppression.

A woman’s casting. Teaching a woman magic with her guardian’s permission is contrary to neither Church canon nor Commonwealth law. The law requires only that the permission exist, and that the teaching and every working be done under it. Her guardian answers for everything she casts. The embercore is the metaphysical organ that gives access to the Weave, and an active embercore is what defines a person as emberborn. From her first day of the Vraenhari she wears the Weavefire training glyph, which stands in the place of the oath she cannot swear and answers to the harmonics of her guardian’s voice. The inhibitor crystal of Ironweave Works, the Duraken and Maenari engineering firm, was invented a century ago for law enforcement, and the Commonwealth keeps the collar for that use alone.
Higher Education

Higher learning in the Commonwealth exists to serve the realm, not the scholar. It produces officers, administrators, jurists, mages, and engineers whose loyalty is bound by oath and demonstrated merit, and it is deliberately exclusive, centralized, and doctrinally supervised throughout.
Eligibility
Sex: male
Age: 20 or older

Standing: Confirmed, and in full civic standing — meaning the mandatory four years’ service is complete. There is no exception. A young man who has not finished his term does not sit the examination, whatever his aptitude.
Selection: competitive entrance examination
Length: four years
Tuition: roughly 15 Zarims per year, with Crown scholarships available on examination merit
Enrollment: some 5,000 students across all six institutions at any time
The Six Royal Institutions
Below is a summary of the Royal Institutions and the schools of Higher Education within the Commonwealth. Please see Appendix I: The United Colleges of Zeythari for complete details.

Arcana Scholium (Suraela) — pure magical theory and metaphysics: arcane law and resonance theory, spellcraft principles, Weave metaphysics, and magical ethics under the Oath. Produces court mages, senior ritualists, and magical theorists.

Magitek Arcaneum (Duskhearth) — applied magic and engineering, run alongside the Duraken guild-halls that already dominate the town: steam-arcane systems, lightning capture and distribution, water purification, arcane weaponry, and resonance-ward fortification. Produces military engineers, infrastructure architects, and weapons designers. It is a polytechnic and not a theory school, and it is the Commonwealth’s research-and-development engine: its students learn magic at the guild bench, as a craft and a discipline of engineering.

Etherforge University (Duskhearth) — non-magical engineering: mechanics, structural engineering, roads and aqueducts, mining and industrial systems, siege and logistics engineering. Produces civil engineers, industrial planners, and Crown infrastructure officials.

Archivist Lyceum (Suraela) — scholarly and civic disciplines: history, philosophy and ethics, law and jurisprudence, literature and rhetoric. Produces Satraps’ administrators (the principal feeder school for the Crown Administrative Service), diplomatic aides, canon lawyers, and scholars.

Royal Military Academy (Ashward) — officer formation, divided between the Host (ground warfare, logistics, fortress doctrine) and the Navy (fleet operations, maritime law, out of Solmara and Linhaven). Produces commissioned officers of the Crown Regulars and Naval Fleet — the Academy trains for the Crown’s own forces specifically, not for the three Church military orders, which raise and train their own officers under the Warden of the Flame.

Magic as engineering. The Commonwealth’s particular strength is that it treats magic as a science and integrates it with engineering. Pure theory has two seats: the Arcana Scholium at Suraela, and the Maenari mage tower of Zelesti, which teaches theory in the manner of the classics. They are two options for the same thing. The Magitek Arcaneum is something else, the Commonwealth’s research-and-development engine, which teaches magic as a trade at the forge and the loom of the Duraken guild-halls, with Maenari theory supplying the design. It is a quiet symbol of why the Commonwealth, and Ironweave Works in particular, can build things like the Arcano Cannon and the paired crystal: a realm that teaches theory alone does not produce them, and a realm that teaches a trade alone does not design them.

School of Merciful Arts (Suraela) — medicine, surgery, and the theory of healing, co-located with the Aelorian Healing Complex (see Section V). Four years: secular medicine, Weave-healing theory, and the theory of Lysaran miracle-work, which the School teaches to men as doctrine and never as practice. Requires 1,200 or more clinical hours at the Complex, written and practical examinations, an original thesis, and the swearing of the Healer’s Oath. Produces physicians, surgeons, and Army Surgeons. Its graduates serve throughout the Commonwealth and in allied realms abroad.

All six institutions are Crown-run but doctrinally reviewed by the Church of the Sworn Flame throughout: theology is embedded across every discipline, magical instruction is monitored for heresy, and Oath-ethics are a mandatory component of every course of study. None operates outside ecclesiastical sanction.
Women and Higher Learning

Women are forbidden, as a matter of settled doctrine under Darlorath, from attending any of the five Royal Institutions. The great majority of Commonwealth women receive no education beyond the Presentation: basic magical control where applicable, domestic education, and religious instruction. Advanced education for a woman is treated as exceptional rather than normal, in any form it takes.

The Royal Nexus Academy is the sole domestic exception: a female-only institution under direct Crown ownership, seated at Aerendal in the Threnwood March. Sisters of the Solayan House serve in its residential halls and teach the theology of Seraphiae and the Four Pillars of Sacred Femininity; a Confessor seconded from the Church serves its spiritual welfare; but governance, discipline, and administration are wholly Crown offices. The Academy’s Finishing College is open to any woman of suitable standing whose guardian has consented and committed to tuition and board; no magical gift is required for admission to the Finishing College. The Creation College, which trains licensed practitioners of the Creation Thread, requires the guardian’s written consent, a Prism of Aurivelle result of Mid Emberglow or higher, and the Bureau of Weavefire’s license review before instruction begins. No parish recommendation is required for admission. Its graduates in healing magic serve in the Complex’s women’s wards and as its midwives, under the Sisters of the Lily.

The Foreign Education Exception is the Commonwealth’s one acknowledged inconsistency, and it knows it. Commonwealth law recognizes degrees earned at the following foreign institutions: Harborlight University at Reefhaven Commonwealth — the same institution Crown Prince Asyre himself attended, and, the University of Concordia at Scholar’s Rest in the Republic of Concordia, for religious, classical, and legal study. The University’s Aequiten Center, which accepts many foreign students, is where the Commonwealth’s Magistrals are trained in the Aequiten legal tradition; they return home on graduation. The Republic’s own justice department is the Lyceum of Justice.
The Guild Apprenticeship System

A parallel path to the five Royal Institutions, chiefly the Duraken model of craft-pact instruction, adopted in modified form across most Commonwealth trade guilds: part-time apprenticeship from sixteen to twenty alongside a young man’s mandatory service, full apprenticeship from twenty to twenty-seven, journeyman status from twenty-seven to thirty-five, and mastery by examination thereafter. Women may not hold rank or mastery within any guild, consistent with the Commonwealth’s uniform bar on female office-holding under Darlorath.
Educational Philosophy
The central goal of Commonwealth education is not self-expression, wealth, or personal achievement. Its schools — parish, civic, home, and the five Royal Institutions alike — are built to produce:
Literate citizens
Disciplined men
Competent household managers
Controlled Emberborn
Loyal servants of Church and Crown

In the Commonwealth’s own words, education exists not for aspiration but for endurance — a society built, deliberately and at every level of its schooling, around oath, duty, authority, and social continuity.
Church Formation

Those who dedicate their lives to the Church enter one of two sacred vocations. Men called to Holy Orders undertake the long course of seminary formation, preparing them for the priesthood and the governance of the Church. Women who take vows are received into the Rose Spire, where they are formed for lives of service within the Ladies’ Houses.
The Seminaries of the Living Flame

The Communion of the Living Flame recognizes three seminaries authorized to educate and ordain clergy: the Seminary of Truth on the Isle of Truth, the Seminary of the Flame in Concordia, and the Seminary of the Sworn Flame in Solmara. Each operates under a Writ of the Flame, a charter granted by the Holy See that authorizes the formation and ordination of clergy. No institution lacking a Writ of the Flame may lawfully prepare candidates for Holy Orders, and ordinations performed outside a recognized seminary are not acknowledged by the Church.

Foremost among them is the Seminary of Truth, founded beside the Holy See and regarded as the mother seminary of the Communion. Though each institution possesses full authority to train and ordain priests, the Seminary of Truth serves as the doctrinal center of clerical education. The Rector Legatus of the Seminary of Truth bears ultimate responsibility for the formation of the clergy and conducts a formal audit of each regional seminary every decade.

Men may pursue their studies at any of the three seminaries. The course of formation is long and demanding, encompassing theology, philosophy, liturgy, canon law, Church history, and pastoral administration. Upon ordination, a priest may lawfully administer the sacraments of the Church and serve within its parishes, monasteries, military orders, and governing institutions. Each seminary submits reports regularly, but every decade the Rector Legatus conducts a formal visitation and audit.

The Rector Legatus of the Seminary of Truth bears ultimate responsibility for the formation of the clergy and conducts a formal audit of each regional seminary every decade. Following each visitation, the Rector Legatus certifies the seminary’s continued good standing under its Writ of the Flame. In cases of grave doctrinal error, persistent negligence, or disobedience to Church authority, a seminary’s Writ may be suspended or revoked by decree of the Holy See.

All seminaries teach the same faith, confer the same ordination, and prepare men for the same priesthood. Although every seminary produces fully ordained priests, each is known for a particular specialty:
Seminary of Truth: Canon law, theology, and ecclesiastical administration.
Seminary of the Flame: Monastic traditions and contemplative discipline.
Seminary of the Sworn Flame: Missionary service and the military orders.

Although all three seminaries possess equal authority to ordain clergy, the Seminary of Truth enjoys special prestige as the mother seminary of the Communion and the seat of the Council of Seminaries.
The Rose Spire
Hidden within a forest glade in Kaelvash stands the Rose Spire, where every woman who takes vows within the Church begins her religious formation.
Over three years, each Sister studies the language of Zeylara, the foundations of theology, and the traditions of one of the three Ladies’ Houses: Seraphiaen, Solayan, or Sophisran.

Life within the Spire is governed by service, obedience, and the Pillars of Femininity. Alongside their religious instruction, the Sisters are trained in the practical arts expected throughout the Communion, including weaving, textile production, husbandry, agriculture, winemaking, record keeping, and accounting.

Upon completing her formation, a Sister enters her chosen House and is assigned wherever her service is required. Though senior Sisters oversee much of the community’s daily instruction, the Rose Spire itself is governed by a Confessor, who maintains discipline, administers the sacraments, and serves as the Church’s spiritual authority within the institution.

This version treats the seminary as the Church’s elite clerical academy while presenting the Rose Spire as a centralized convent school and house of formation, which feels much closer to the medieval model you’re drawing from.
Dress, Status, and the Visible Oath
Foundational Principle

In the Commonwealth, a person’s legal and social standing is never meant to be ambiguous. Dress is a public language of law, guardianship, and oath, not ornamentation alone — a doctrine the Church reads directly out of Article VII: truth must be visible, and obligation unmistakable. A woman’s face marks her public boundary; her form does not. The veil signifies presence, status, and lawful separation — the body, though visible, is not thereby public property, and to violate that boundary is crime, not mere impropriety. The state treats a violation of a woman’s visibly marked status as an offense against her master, and the oath alike, not merely against household honor, and recognizes no defense of ignorance: a woman’s standing is always visible, and failure to recognize or respect what her dress declares is willful defiance of law, not confusion. The underlying doctrine, stripped to its foundation, has nothing to do with modesty in the sense a foreign visitor might expect, and everything to do with visible truth. A Commonwealth citizen should be able to determine, at a glance, whether a woman is married, whether she stands under paternal or marital guardianship, whether she is widowed, whether a man is a confirmed citizen, whether he is married, and whether he holds lawful authority. The entire clothing system is an extension of the Oath itself — not fashion, not piety, and not, in its intent, status competition (though custom competes in every margin the law leaves open; see The Caerwevra), but the plain conviction that truth should be visible, that status should not be hidden, and that an oath must be seen as well as spoken.
“Truth should be visible. Status should not be hidden. An oath must be seen as well as spoken.”
Male Dress: the Oath Dagger

Foundational principle: the oath must be carried. Manhood in the Commonwealth is defined not by authority but by obligation. Where a woman’s status is made visible through dress and guardianship, a man’s is shown through the bearing of oath-bound responsibility. A man’s oath is not abstract. It is carried.

Every Confirmed man carries an Oath Dagger openly from Confirmation onward. It signifies acceptance of lawful violence when the Crown commands it, willingness to risk his life for Commonwealth and Crown, and submission to judgment should the Oath of the Standard be broken. Unlike a sword or spear, the dagger is always present, always personal, and always intimate — the weapon of last resort, and for that reason the most honest one a man carries. A man who claims protection, authority, or marital standing without the proper dagger markings is guilty of fraud, and Commonwealth courts recognize the dagger itself as evidence of oath, proof of marital bond, and indicator of standing in any dispute where it is relevant.

rows.t: Visibly marked with the Flame sigil and the First Oath glyph (the glyph of the Standard)
A legal instrument recognized by Crown and Church
A visible declaration of oath-bound status and a reminder of mortal obligation
The man is presumed unbound, in violation of civic duty, or under disciplinary sanction
Claiming protection, authority, or marital standing without the proper dagger markings is fraud

blocks.text: Male Dress: the Hair-Bound Hilt

Upon marriage, a man binds a lock of his wife’s hair into the hilt or pommel of his marriage dagger — a practice universal, codified, and legally recognized throughout the Commonwealth. The hair-lock signifies that the man bears not only his own oath but a second, living trust; that his wife’s safety is bound to his honor; and that his failures endanger more than himself. The lock must remain visible upon inspection and protected from damage, and it is never removed except by death, annulment, or Church decree. To lose or damage the hair-binding through negligence is a serious social disgrace; to remove it unlawfully is treated as oath-violation outright. The parish’s pair-mark, struck on the pommel and on the wife’s Band before the Rite, joins the two objects in the registry (see The Band-Bed and the Pair-Mark).
A hair-bound hilt immediately tells any onlooker:
“This man speaks for a household.”
This system deliberately mirrors, without duplicating, the female status markers described below — a woman displays who protects her; a man displays what he must protect.
Male Dress: Mandatory Trousers and Required Bearing

Freedom of movement and exposure belongs to women in the Commonwealth, not to men — a deliberate asymmetry. Women are protected; men are burdened. Women are the flame; men are the stone that endures heat without yielding. Accordingly, every adult man of the Commonwealth is required, by both law and unbroken custom, to wear trousers in public — loose or fitted according to labor and climate, breathable fabrics permitted, short trousers ending below the knee acceptable, bare legs not. This applies without exception to citizens and peers, soldiers and civilians, married and unmarried men, clergy and laymen alike, saving only medical necessity or formal punishment. Male dress is governed by restraint rather than comfort: freedom of movement and exposure is granted to women, not to men, and men are constrained through obligation.
Her status is seen. His duty is borne. Together, the Oath endures.
Noble Luxury Restrictions

Rather than forbidding wealth outright, Commonwealth sumptuary law regulates symbols. Certain metals are reserved to specific ranks; certain gemstone arrangements are restricted to office-holders; official Crown insignia is protected by statute against imitation, regardless of the wearer’s actual wealth. A merchant may become fantastically rich. Wealth of any size still cannot impersonate office. A guild-master’s wife may drape herself in more gold than a baroness owns outright, provided none of it is cut, set, or marked in a pattern reserved by law to the peerage or to Crown service — the moment it is, the offense is not vulgarity but impersonation, and the Magistracy treats it as such. The caerwevra is the most closely watched object under this law.
Female Dress: the Veil, the Hem, and the Oath-Band
Every woman’s dress communicates her exact standing at a glance, so that no man may plausibly claim not to have known it.

Girls, ages 12–15 (Protected Girlhood): face veil; single-piece dress mandatory; hem to the knee or just above; arms and shoulders may be bare, the climate being what it is. Two-piece garments and any adult silhouette are forbidden. The dress itself says: not yet for courtship. Authority: the guardian’s rule over his ward’s dress under the Fourth Pillar of Sacred Femininity (Holy Book of Truth and Grace, Part Nine), enforced publicly as status-marking under the Crown’s law against falsification of status.

Women, age 16+ (post-Presentation): face veil continues until marriage; hem rises to the cultural standard of mid-thigh; two-piece garments, sleeveless or minimal-strap tops, and exposed arms, legs, and midriff are all culturally neutral rather than immodest. Fabrics favor lightweight, breathable ash-linen, light wool blends, or, among the wealthy, enchanted silks. A full-length skirt on a woman of this age is confined, in practice, to funerary rites and rare ceremonial reenactment; anywhere else it draws immediate and specific notice, since it obscures markers of status the Commonwealth expects to be legible. A married woman wearing a face veil in ordinary public life is, likewise, actively discouraged — it creates exactly the ambiguity the whole system exists to prevent. A daughter under Court-ordered indenture is the one exception: the collar replaces the face veil for the term, and the veil is worn at worship only (Section VI, The Indenture Statute).

Married women: no face veil; the caerwevra required (its form distinguishes married women, widows, and professed religious; see The Caerwevra); Oath-Band worn visibly on the upper arm at all times. Only married women and widows may lawfully wear an Oath-Band at all — for anyone else to wear one is treated, without qualification, as marital fraud. Given the climate, long sleeves are rare, so any concealment of the band is read as deliberate and treated as legally suspect.

The transition at sixteen is legal communication, not fashion: a man who approaches a girl still in knee-length dress commits a status violation regardless of his claim to ignorance, because her dress itself warned him away.
Zeythari’s volcanic terrain, persistent heat, ash-laden air, and labor-intensive daily life have shaped female dress toward minimal, breathable, and mobile designs.
Belts, sashes, or girdles secure tools, pouches, or ritual items. Shorter hems are common and unremarkable at sixteen and after. Beauty is not suppressed; it is ordered by age and status.

Service dress. The Thornmaidens and the Wayfinders wear the dress every other unmarried woman of sixteen and over wears — face veil, mid-thigh hem, two-piece garments, plain-corded hair — and add only the Crown-chartered rose badge. No band is worn on the upper arm, no caerwevra, and no dagger. The full specification is in Section IV. Camp Servitors wear the same adult cut in undyed ash-linen with apron and cap, collared, and unveiled outside worship. The full specification is in Section IV. The Royal Rangers’ Overwatch wear the same cut in field green; the full specification is in Section IV.
The Logic of Age-Based Modesty
Commonwealth clothing law distinguishes developmental protection from adult availability.

rows.t: Single-piece, knee-length dress: “not yet for courtship”
Protects girls from premature marriage pressure; allows physical development without sexual visibility; marks a protected transitional stage
Shorter hem and two-piece garments: marriage eligibility
Does not imply availability without guardian consent; allows courtship negotiation to begin lawfully; the veil continues to enforce guardian authority

blocks.text: Constants across all ages

rows.t: Knee-length or longer skirts on women 16+
Effectively confined to funerary rites, rare ceremonial reenactments, and foreign visitors
Regarded as impractical or concealing: they trap heat and ash, restrict movement, and obscure legally significant markers of status
A woman 16+ in a skirt below mid-thigh in public
Assumed to be engaged in a specific ritual, constrained by rare medical or occupational need, or intentionally signaling nonconformity; such cases are uncommon enough to attract attention
Exempt from the hem by the master’s leave, on the Lysaran cord. See Expectant Women: the Longer Hem

blocks.text: Status Markers by Life Stage

rows.t: All unmarried girls are veiled in public. The face veil signifies familial guardianship; single-piece dress required, hem to the knee or just above; two-piece garments prohibited; marks the wearer as legally protected and not yet marriage-eligible; removes all ambiguity of developmental status

Face veil continues (guardianship persists); hem transitions to the mid-thigh standard; two-piece garments permitted; marks the wearer as marriage-eligible; signals the transition from childhood protection to adult courtship availability

Only on marriage, formal consecration, or, for the term of a Court-ordered indenture, by the Court’s order. On entry into a recognized female order the face stays veiled, but the veil is now the Church’s and not her father’s.

Marriage replaces concealment with oath-bound clarity. Forged of iron, ash-steel, silver, or gold according to station; engraved with the First Oath glyph and the sworn guardianship mark; legally required to remain visible in public. It signifies sworn protection, not ownership. To violate a married woman is to violate an oath: an offense against Crown, Church, and gods alike. Long sleeves are rare in this climate, so concealment of the band is intentional and legally suspect

Court-sealed ash-steel band, dated, replaces the veil for the term; veil at worship only; mid-thigh adult dress; no band, caerwevra, dagger, or rose badge. Marks her as held in trust for a term and her father as having failed. Struck off on release

A distinct and inviolable category: veiled, unringed, wearing no Oath-Band, only the Sister’s token.
