Status is declared through the habit of her House: a high-collared, sleeveless, solid one-piece dress of undyed grey-brown linen (boiled wool in the northern winter; see Regional Turning), the upper arm bare and unbanded, a cloth cuff of the same grey-brown at each wrist, its hem an inch above a laywoman’s and the shortest in the Commonwealth, the same cut for all five Houses and distinguished only by the veil and a thread at the collar and cuff. No familial or marital marker. Their dress proclaims institutional claim: they belong to the Church alone. To touch a Handmaiden is sacrilege; the prohibition binds the laity, and her Confessor, acting for the Church that holds her, is not bound by it

blocks.text: The Caerwevra: the Married Woman’s Covering

The caerwevra (Zeylara: caer, “house” + wevra, “weave”; plural caerwevrai) is the netted headband of the married woman: a fine net of cord worn across the hair and strung with bead, gold, or jewel. It is the form the Covenant Covering has taken by custom. The Church requires a covering and has never prescribed the net.

rows.t: Married women and widows. No unmarried girl and no professed Sister wears one.

Made, or commissioned, by the bride’s mother and the women of her household; given by her mother into the groom’s hand and set on the bride’s hair by him at Step Four of the Church’s Rite. If the mother is dead or absent, the nearest female relative gives it.
The Oath-Band, always. The band is the master’s labor and means; the caerwevra is the bride’s household’s.
Uncovered. The caerwevra does not veil the face.
Worn beneath the full face veil; its workmanship stays visible.
Wearing one while unmarried, or as a professed Sister, is falsification of status, like the Oath-Band.

blocks.text: Workmanship by station.

rows.t: Plain twisted cord; a few glass or clay beads; mended rather than replaced
Waxed cord or silk thread; bone, coral, or polished obsidian beads; small silver fittings
Silver wire net; pearl, garnet, or amber; a heavier fall at the nape
Gold thread and gold beads; cut stones in the arrangements reserved to her House
Gold net; precious stones in the Crown’s reserved arrangements

blocks.text: A woman’s station can be read from her caerwevra at twenty paces.

Sumptuary law. Metals and stone arrangements reserved to the peerage or to Crown service (see Noble Luxury Restrictions) are barred to any caerwevra outside that rank. A merchant’s wife may wear more gold than a baroness owns, provided none of it is cut, set, or patterned in a reserved arrangement. The moment it is, the offense is impersonation, and the Magistracy treats it as such.

The margins custom contests. The law holds every married woman to one frame and leaves its workmanship open, so women’s competition runs through what the frame leaves: the caerwevra’s beadwork, the whiteness of the linen against ash-grey air, and the sweep of the skirt at mid-thigh. Women read one another at a glance and rank one another without a word. The Appraisers of the Bureau of Civic Decorum enforce the frame (the covering, the Band, and the hem) and never the workmanship; the competition itself needs no enforcement from above.

Where the reading lands. Custom judges a woman’s appearance; law judges only her guardian. A caerwevra poorer than her master’s means is read as a measure of his provision, and the whisper attaches to his name and not to her person. The ill-provided wife of a wealthy man makes him maethak (house-shame). Failure to provide is a matter of his honor, and it gives the wife no remedy (see Divorce and Annulment).
By status.

rows.t: Caerwevra of her household’s station, with the Oath-Band
Black caerwevra beneath the black veil; Oath-Band retained
Face veiled; hair wholly covered beneath her House’s veil, without net or bead

blocks.text: The Reproach. The netted band is named in the Reproach of Ishvael (the Book of Warnings), which lists the ornaments the Flame will strip from the daughters of the proud:

In that day the Flame shall strip from the daughters of the proud the netted bands of the head and the crescents of the brow; the pendants, the chains, and the bracelets; the sashes, the girdles, and the vials of scent; the rings of the hand and the jewels of the nose; the mantles, the mirrors, and the fine linens. In place of scent, ash. In place of the girdle, a cord. In place of the netted band, a shorn head.

Commonwealth canonists hold that the Reproach condemns the gold and not the net, and that the covering is required while the ornament is merely permitted. The market holds that the Reproach names the one object every married woman in the Commonwealth wears. Both readings are current, and the goldsmiths of Solmara supply the difference.
Cloth as Ledger: the Weave Ladder

The law holds the frame and leaves the cloth open, and the Commonwealth reads a household’s means in the weave. The Appraisers audit the headgear, the hem, and the Band, and never the cloth. The cloth is where a master’s provision is seen, and it is read at a glance, as the caerwevra is.

rows.t: A household that works and keeps its women decently; mended, not replaced
A household that can spare the labor of the wash
Double-gauze, the trade pattern woven into the selvedge
A house with its own looms, or a standing account with a weaver
Enchanted silk, Weavefire-worked under Concordance license: it sheds ash, runs cool against the skin, and keeps its white in ash-laden air (60 Zarims typical; range 40 to 200)
A master whose wife is the cleanest woman on the road

blocks.text: Open weaves (rungs two and three) carry heat and sweat away. The whiteness of the linen against ash-grey air, the contest named under The Caerwevra, is a contest of cloth: whiteness costs water, soap, and the hands to use them, and enchanted silk wins it by shedding the ash the others must wash out. A cloth woven in a pattern reserved to the peerage is impersonation, as a caerwevra cut in one is. The selvedge of enchanted silk carries the stamp of the Guild Concordance, and a forged stamp is fraud before the Market Division of the Bureau of Civic Decorum.
The Household Braid

Every woman of a household wears the household’s braid on her hem: a narrow woven edge-braid in the pattern of her master’s trade or guild. It is repeated on the strap of her sandal (see The Master’s Leaves). Seen from the street, the household files behind its master as one house. At the threshold audit, where the master brings out every woman of the household, the women stand together under one pattern.

rows.t: The master’s trade or guild pattern, entered in the Register. A peer’s household carries the reserved arrangement of his House
The wife, the unmarried daughters of the house, and the widowed mother
A daughter under Court-ordered indenture (collared: held in trust, not of the house); a Camp Servitor; a daughter in Crown or Church service, who wears the service dress entire for the term
The Rule is laid to the lower edge of the braid. A braid that carries the hem below the notch is a non-compliant hem, and the master pays
A braid in a pattern the household does not hold is falsification of status; in a reserved arrangement, impersonation
The Academy’s ribbon is a finger-wide stripe-count of college and year. The braid is the pattern of a house

blocks.text: The braid makes the hem edge plain to the Rule, which is why lighter, fuller skirts are safe to audit under it. The sweep of a skirt is judged standing and the Rule is laid kneeling: a skirt cut so full that it falls below the notch when its wearer kneels fails the hem, and the fault is the master’s.
The Band-Bed and the Pair-Mark

The band-bed. Between the Band and the skin a wife may wear the band-bed: a ring of boiled linen one thread thick, of the thickness the Register fixes. The Band-measure is taken over the bed, so the bed never fails the audit, and a thicker or padded bed does. It is the wife’s relief against chafe in the High Heat, in wet work, and at the loom, and it is hers by her master’s leave, as every comfort is.

The pair-mark. When the groom brings the Band, and the bride’s household brings the marriage dagger, to the parish for blessing before the Rite, the parish registrar strikes the household’s registry number with the parish die on the inner face of the Band and on the pommel of the dagger, and enters both in the parish register. A later band is struck with the same number by the parish, on the master’s petition. The pair-mark is the Commonwealth’s registry custom and no part of the Church’s Rite, like the Dagger and the hair-lock. It lets an Inspector of Insignia match a Band to its dagger, and a household to its register, at a glance: the man displays what he must protect, the woman displays who protects her, and the registry says they are one pair. An unmatched pair is cited for inquiry and not for fraud, since Bands are re-struck on succession and households re-entered on remarriage. In widowhood the mark stays on the Band, as the Band stays on the arm.
The Logic of the Hem Lengths: Environment, Labor, and Inheritance

The Commonwealth’s hem-length customs did not arise to serve religious modesty. They arose from three realities working together, and the symbolism the Church and Crown later overlaid grew out of those realities rather than replacing them.

Environment comes first. Most of the Commonwealth’s populated heartland — the Kaelvash Valleys above all — is hot, humid, agricultural, and volcanic, and physically demanding to live in. In that environment, a floor-length skirt makes very little sense: it traps heat, collects dust and volcanic ash, restricts movement, becomes soaked through in mud and irrigation water, and raises the real risk of heat exhaustion. The average Commonwealth woman is not sitting in a salon. She is working orchards, carrying produce, managing livestock, operating machinery, supervising laborers, and walking long distances in a day. A practical hem becomes normal well before it becomes fashionable.

Labor shapes fashion. Commonwealth women work constantly and always have — as weavers, brewers, potters, orchard managers, textile workers, market operators, domestic producers, and warehouse supervisors. Long garments around belts, wheels, shafts, looms, pumps, and machinery are genuinely dangerous. A culture with extensive arcano-steam systems, mills, workshops, and rail infrastructure develops clothing that minimizes snagging hazards as a matter of course. Shorter hems, in that light, are not merely tolerated. They are sensible.

Maenari inheritance runs beneath both. The Commonwealth’s founding culture carries heavy Maenari influence, and the older Maenari tradition of shorter, mobile garments suited to woodland and frontier life did not vanish at the founding — it became foundational rather than foreign. An outsider tends to assume the short hems are a concession to heat alone; a Commonwealth historian would say the heat merely reinforced what Maenari custom already favored, which is the richer and more accurate account.

Why long skirts would be the strange choice. Given the climate, the agricultural and guild labor, and the Maenari inheritance together, a mid-thigh adult hem is the culturally normal garment in the Commonwealth — the unusual clothing is not the short hem, but the knee-length girlhood dress, which is not practical clothing at all. It is status clothing, worn specifically because a twelve-year-old girl occupies a protected developmental category. At sixteen she transitions to the clothing already worn by every working adult woman around her — not to a more revealing style, but finally, to the ordinary dress of a Commonwealth adult. A duchess and a farmer’s wife may wear the same silhouette; what separates them is the cloth, the embroidery, and the metal of the Oath-Band, never the hemline.
Modesty Redefined: What Is and Is Not Improper
Because bodily exposure is not the operative concern, “modesty” in the Commonwealth is measured by truthful presentation rather than covered skin.
A married woman in a short working dress, caerwevra on her hair, Oath-Band visible, is entirely proper.
A girl disguising herself as a presented woman is improper.
A married woman concealing her Oath-Band is improper.
A widow pretending not to be a widow is improper.
The concern in every case is status deception, not exposed knees.
Expectant Women: the Longer Hem
A woman with child is exempt from the mid-thigh standard by her master’s leave. The exemption is from the hem and from nothing else. Every other mark of her estate stays where it is.

rows.t: A wife, or a widow carrying her late master’s child. An unmarried girl has no exemption: her condition is her guardian’s affair, and the status rules stand on her unchanged

The master’s, or for a widow her guardian’s (the eldest son, or the nearest male kin). Granted or refused by him alone. She does not petition. A master who refuses leaves her at the standard hem, and no one asks him why

The Lysaran cord: undyed linen with a single gold knot at the left hip, bound on her by the parish Priest on the master’s petition once the child quickens, under the patronage of Lysara. The cord is her warrant. It is the mark an Appraiser or Constable reads first

Any length to the ankle, at the master’s choosing. Never past it. A single loose piece of ash-linen or light wool. Black only for a widow of working age. The full-length hem of the widow beyond working age is not hers
The caerwevra. The Oath-Band on the upper arm. The widow’s black. The full face veil at Mass. She is still plainly a wife
From the binding of the cord to her churching, the first Mass after the birth, where the Priest unbinds it and she returns it to the parish. The standard hem resumes within the week
She may keep the standard hem throughout, and in the High Heat many do. A master’s leave is a permission and not an order
The unescorted-woman rule. Article IX. The Oath-Band’s visibility. The bar on male clothing. A long hem is never a license to wear any garment of male cut

An Appraiser who finds a long hem reads the cord. With the cord and the master’s leave, she is audited as any compliant woman and no fault is found. Without it, the hem is non-compliant, the fault is the master’s, and the Appraiser’s fine of five Zarims falls on him as for any non-compliant woman
A cord worn by a woman who is not with child is a false status, treated as the false veil: penance at the nave door, the guardian’s discipline, and on a second offense the Magistracy’s sentence
A woman in the last four months of pregnancy stands off the Hearthguard roll and returns after the churching. Wives and widows do not serve under a Thornmaiden or Wayfinder contract in any case
The dress declares what the law requires every dress to declare: she carries her household’s child, and the man who holds her has granted it to be seen

blocks.text: The Church Hem

For church services only, every woman of sixteen and over may wear a dress that reaches the top of her boots or shoes, with her master’s or guardian’s permission. The permission is his alone to give. The exemption is from the hem and from nothing else.

rows.t: Every woman of sixteen and over: a sister, a wife, a widow. A girl of twelve to fifteen keeps her knee-length single piece. A professed Sister keeps the habit of her House entire and is outside this rule

The holder of her Darlorath: her father or guardian, her master, her eldest son or nearest male kin if she is a widow, and for a Thornmaiden the Rosewarden. A Servitor’s is the Keeper’s. Granted or refused by him alone. He may give it for a year, for a feast, or for a single service
To the top of the boot or shoe, no lower. A loose single piece or a two-piece with a long skirt, in the cloth her master chooses. Black only for a widow

At a church service: Mass, a sacramental occasion, a funeral, a wedding. She wears it to the service and from it by the shortest road. On a service morning on the church road, a long hem is presumed lawful and an Appraiser reads it as such. At any other hour or on any other road it is non-compliant and audited as such
The face veil of an unmarried woman, the caerwevra and Oath-Band of a wife, the widow’s black, and the full face veil at Mass over all of it. The long hem hides nothing the law requires to be read
The unescorted-woman rule. Article IX. The bar on male clothing. No long hem is cut as a man’s garment
She may attend in the standard hem. The permission is a leave and not an order. Many do in the High Heat
The Lysaran cord and the Longer Hem apply throughout the week. At a service she may wear either
A long hem outside the service rule is a non-compliant hem. Her master pays the Appraiser’s five Zarims, as for any non-compliant woman

blocks.text: The Royal Gown: the Crown’s Exception
“The Queen’s gown is a year of cloth.” / “The Queen has no orchard.”

The Commonwealth makes one exception to a woman’s dress by reason of rank. It is made for the Queen Consort and for the daughters of the Crown, and for no other woman: not the Queen Mother, not the wife of the Heir, not a Duchess, not a Duke’s daughter. Every other long hem in this section belongs to a condition or an occasion: the Longer Hem of the expectant woman, the Church Hem of the service morning, the long black of the widow past the marriage market. The royal gown belongs to the woman, and it is worn on every road and in every hall she walks.
It is an exemption from the hem, the sleeve, and the collar. It is an exemption from nothing else.
“Her sleeve clears the Band.” / “To the finger. They measure.”

rows.t: The Queen Consort, and the unmarried daughters of the King and Queen Consort from their Presentation at sixteen. It ends for a daughter on the day she is wed, when she leaves the Crown’s household and takes a wife’s dress of her master’s station. It ends for a Queen on her widowhood, when she becomes Queen Mother and takes the widow’s dress under the ordinary rule.

None. A Princess of twelve to fifteen wears the single-piece knee-length dress and face veil of protected girlhood, as every girl of the Commonwealth does. The exception does not reach girlhood. The gown is first worn on the evening of her Presentation, in the hour her dress would otherwise rise to the mid-thigh standard.

A standing clause of the Sumptuary Statutes, entered in the Register of the Bureau of Civic Decorum under the Royal Household. A woman in the royal gown is read as lawful on sight, as any registered garment is. The clause is the law’s. The gown itself is the King’s leave under the Third Pillar: he is master and guardian of every woman who wears it, he grants it, and he may withhold it. A Queen or Princess whose gown he withholds wears the standard dress and is audited as any woman.

Floor-length: the hem clears the floor by a finger’s breadth, and the household braid runs its edge. Bodice fitted, waist defined, skirt full, and for state a train. The sleeve is short, ending on the upper arm. The collar is low and open across the collarbones, and the throat is bare.

The sleeve is cut to end a finger above the Band’s upper edge. On the Queen the Band shows below the sleeve. On a Princess the arm below the sleeve is bare, and the bare arm reads as it reads on any unmarried woman: no husband’s Band is on it. A sleeve that covers the Band is concealment of the Band, and a gown so cut fails the Register.

Enchanted silk, rung four of the Weave Ladder, Weavefire-worked under Concordance license. On state days the Queen’s is cloth-of-gold, above the top of the Ladder’s range. The Queen wears the national colors, flame-crimson and oath-gold, on state days. The Princesses wear storm-silver, ivory, and pale gold, and never the Queen’s crimson.

The household braid of House Karaya, the Standard Flame quartered with the Silver Storm-Crown of Zelesti, runs the hem of every gown, and the sandal strap repeats it. The arrangement is reserved. Woven or cut by any other house, it is impersonation.
The caerwevra, gold net with precious stones in the Crown’s reserved arrangements, at all hours. The Oath-Band on the upper arm, visible, never removed. The face bare. The full veil at Mass.

The face veil (Umbrmiren) in public, the same plain ash-linen gauze every maid wears, from the Veiling at twelve until her husband lifts it at the Rite. No caerwevra. No Band. Hair at the King’s discretion. The full veil at Mass.

Articles IV, V, and IX. The Lowered Tongue. The bar on male clothing. The unescorted-woman rule: a royal woman does not walk the road without the Household Escort of the Oathguard and a man of the House or one the King names.

A district Appraiser does not halt the Crown’s carriage or kneel a royal woman on the road, and the Rule is not laid to her hem. The Commissioner of Decorum for Kaervast reads the household at the Palace threshold at the turning of each season, the Royal Steward bringing out the women of the house, eldest first, against the Register’s entry. A finding is entered against the King’s name, and the correction of it is his.

Rank, not estate. The long hem says whose house she belongs to. The net and the Band say who holds the Queen, and the veil says who holds a Princess. The street is not confused: the gown shows the Crown, and the marks on the head and the arm show the master.

The Princesses are Maestrai. The Lumen Affectus shows on the bare arm and collarbone and, through the gauze, on the face, and the cut makes no attempt to dim it. Court custom treats it as the plainest case of the principle that truth should be visible. Queen and Princesses alike carry Azyrra’s Sheen, and the evening cloth of the court is cut to hold candlelight.

blocks.text: The Master’s Leaves: Footwear and Climate Comforts

Under the Third Pillar the guardian holds sole authority over a woman’s dress, adornment, and presentation. Her footwear and every comfort beyond the frame therefore reach her as her master’s leave, and the leave is part of the display: the street reads what he grants, what he withholds, and what he provides. None of it touches the three points an Appraiser audits (the headgear, the hem line, and the Oath-Band), and an Appraiser audits no leave.
Footwear. Sandals are the standard footwear of every woman and girl of the Commonwealth, in every station.

rows.t: A woman under her master’s discipline, or in a poor master’s keeping. The sight is uncommon and the street reads it at once; the shame attaches to him in either case (maethak)
The standard: a household that keeps its women properly

In bad weather, and for the farmwife in the field and the orchard, by a standing leave given for the working year. A master who sends a woman into mud, ash, or frost in sandals is read as a poor provider

blocks.text: Sandal work is a margin the law leaves open, like the caerwevra’s beadwork, and it is ranked in the same way. A clean foot against ash and mud joins the whiteness contest: the sandal shows what the dress shows.

rows.t: Plain cord strap; thin hide sole
Dyed leather strap bearing the household braid; pegged leather sole
Silver-fitted or tooled strap; doubled sole
Strap fitted in the arrangements reserved to her House

blocks.text: The ladder of leaves.

rows.t: Sun and ash on the nape and shoulders
Hangs from the lower edge of the caerwevra, never over the net; the face stays bare; rolled and pinned up at Mass
None. A boot-top never changes the hem
Knitted hose to mid-thigh, worn below the hem, as in the Academy’s registered uniform. A hose cut with a waist or joined at the crotch is a trouser and is male clothing
Provides cloth and lining, and permits it

blocks.text: The shade-fall. A fall of ash-gauze hung from the lower edge of the caerwevra to the shoulders, weighted at the hem with the household’s beadwork. It turns sun and ash from the nape and shoulders and leaves the arms and the Band bare. The merchant’s wife’s “heavier fall at the nape” is the same object in silk and silver; the shade-fall is its light form, open to every station. The caerwevra is the most closely watched object under the sumptuary law, so the fall hangs below the net and never over it, and carries no reserved arrangement. At Mass it is rolled and pinned up, so that the net’s workmanship shows above the full veil.

The woman’s cloak. The cloak is the male garment a wife takes from her master at the threshold (see Household Reception and Daily Service), so the woman’s cloak is cut so that it cannot be mistaken for it: hip-length, hemmed no lower than the dress beneath it, in boiled wool for the cold and oiled linen for the Threnwood damp, and open at the upper arm in a window through which the Oath-Band is seen. A cloak cut or hung as a man’s is male clothing, and the bar under the Fourth Pillar applies to it as to any garment. At audit the Appraiser reads the Band through the window, lifts the cloak at the hip, and lays the Rule on the dress hem beneath. A cloak that cannot be opened over the arm (laced or pinned shut) conceals the Band, and the fault is the master’s.

Where the weather is hard. In the Thaldrin, the Ashward and Duskhearth winter, the Threnwood cold and damp, the Sundral passes, and the desert nights, boots, hose, and cloak pass from comforts to the plain provision of a competent master. A wife sent into snow in sandals is the master’s fault, and every neighbor reads it. In the valleys, on the seaboard, and through the High Heat the ladder reads the other way: the shade-fall, the clean sandal, and the open weave are his care.

Register entries. Each of the following is entered in the Register of the Bureau of Civic Decorum: the household braid, the shade-fall, the woman’s cloak with its window, the hose, the band-bed, and the pair-mark. A registered garment is read as lawful on sight. An unregistered garment is audited as it is seen, and the finding is the Appraiser’s alone.
Full Veils During Mass

Outside the Cathedral, status, age, and marital standing all matter and are all visible. Inside, during Mass, every woman present — married or unmarried, noble or common, Handmaiden of the Order or farmer’s daughter — wears the full face veil, regardless of what she wears, or does not wear, the rest of the week.

On a feast day at Kaervast Cathedral, the Queen herself may arrive in cloth-of-gold, a jeweled Oath-Band, precious stones, and a gold-and-jeweled caerwevra, taking her place beside the King, who sits before the realm’s assembled peerage. Before Mass begins, she lowers the same plain face veil worn by every other woman in the nave — not because she ceases, for that hour, to be Queen, but because Crown authority yields to divine authority the moment the rite begins. A Commonwealth observer finds nothing strange in this at all:
“Outside the Cathedral she is our Queen. Inside the Cathedral she is a woman before Seraphiae.”

Rank, family, and wealth remain fully visible in every other particular — the dresses, the jewelry, and the fabrics all still declare exactly what they declare on any other day. Only the face is covered, uniformly, across the whole congregation. The caerwevra stays in place, its workmanship visible above the lowered face veil. A widow in her black veil lowers the plain face veil like every other woman; her black veil lies over her caerwevra. The message is theological, not egalitarian: before the realm, women occupy many stations; before the gods, all women stand covered. The plain face veil is one cloth for every woman: ash-linen gauze in a single weave, from the Cathedral to the village parish, so that no veil can rank its wearer.
The Church Regulates Symbols, Not Clothing

It bears stating plainly, because visitors from less exacting realms often assume otherwise: the Church of the Sworn Flame regulates the dress of its own women, the Sisters, entirely, and for every other woman it does not regulate hemlines, fabrics, or cut. Dress is left entirely to the discretion of the master, guardian, or master who holds her. That discretion is itself the Church’s teaching: the Fourth Pillar of Sacred Femininity (Holy Book of Truth and Grace, Part Nine) places a woman’s dress under her master’s authority and forbids masculine dress without exception. For lay women it holds three symbols and one maxim.
Is she unmarried? Then she wears the face veil in public.
Is she married? Then her hair is covered (by custom in a caerwevra, though the Church prescribes no form), and her Oath-Band is worn.
Is she standing before the gods? Then she wears the full veil, regardless of any other status.
The maxim: a woman may not dress in male clothing. This is chiefly the Commonwealth’s sumptuary law, which enforces it before the Church does.

Everything else — hem length, fabric, ornamentation, color, cut — is culture, economics, climate, and fashion, and the Church has no doctrine on any of it. The Church does not care whether a married woman wears an orchard dress, a merchant’s outfit, a guild-work garment, or a noble gown, provided her hair is covered and her Oath-Band is visible. It does not care whether her skirt reaches the knee, the mid-thigh, or the ankle. Those are social decisions, not religious ones.
Summary:

rows.t: Unmarried girls wear the face veil. Married women wear a hair covering and visible Oath-Band. All women wear the full veil at Mass. No woman wears male clothing (the Fourth Pillar). The Church sets the habit of its own Sisters entire.

Status markers must not be falsified. Oath symbols must remain visible where required by law. Women may not wear male clothing. The Crown’s Appraisers audit the veil, the caerwevra, the Oath-Band, and the hem at random, to the knee-line for girls twelve to fifteen and the mid-thigh line for women sixteen and over (see Section II, The Bureau of Civic Decorum).

Hem lengths, fabrics, ornamentation, colors, cuts, footwear and outer garments (see The Master’s Leaves), and the form and workmanship of the caerwevra, are determined by climate, occupation, wealth, people, and local fashion, and, within the Crown’s standards above, by the master, guardian, or master.

blocks.text: Widowhood: Dress and Standing
Black is not worn in ordinary Commonwealth life; a woman in black is recognized immediately as a widow, and the particular form of her black dress communicates her exact standing without ambiguity.

A widow still within the marriage market wears the standard dress of adult women, in black, with her Oath-Band still visible and her caerwevra in black — her guardianship having passed, on her master’s death, to her eldest son, who may in time arrange a remarriage. She is not disgraced; the bond was not broken, only the man who bore it has passed, and she remains protected under it.

A widow past the marriage market, by age or by her household’s judgment that no further match is practical, is distinguished instead by a long black dress, a black caerwevra, and a black veil — the sole Commonwealth woman permitted a full-length garment in public without remark, since her dress declares plainly that she stands outside the active order of the household, honored and cared for rather than working.

Black is the color and not the weight. A widow’s black is cut in gauze-lawn, dyed through, over a cool slip, and the long black of the widow past the marriage market is the same lawn, side-gored for the walk, and never wool in the valleys. She does not go out unescorted: her eldest son, or the man he names, walks before her as Article IX requires and, in the High Heat, carries her parasol, a black gauze canopy held back over her at the one-pace interval. She never carries it herself; no woman of the Commonwealth handles a cane, rod, or whip, and what is carried for her is carried by her escort. The son’s household is seen to provide for his mother, and that is the display.

In both cases the Oath-Band is never removed. The Church holds that the marriage covenant, once sworn before the Flame and the Crown, is not unmade by death — only completed. At her burial, her daughter (or whoever prepares her body) places her original Oath-Band on her; if she remarried, the band of her current marriage is laid on her chest.

rows.t: In the marriage market; under the guardianship of her eldest son. Standard adult dress in black; Oath-Band worn on the upper arm; black caerwevra. Her son, if prudent, seeks a suitable remarriage in due course. She is recognized as a woman whose marriage was lawful and honorable: the bond was not broken, only the man who bore it has passed. She is not disgraced. She is protected

Passed from the marriage market by age or by the absence of practical remarriage prospects, as determined by her household. Long black dress, black caerwevra, and black veil in public; Oath-Band retained. The sole woman outside the Royal Household who may wear a full-length garment in public without remark. Her dress declares: I am no longer in the active order of household. I have been lawfully wed. I am honored. I am cared for. Most sons do not seek remarriage for their mothers and keep them within the household until death

Never removed. The marriage covenant, once sworn before the Flame and the Crown, is not unmade by death, only completed. The band remains because the oath was real, the man honorable, and the woman lawfully defended; to remove it would deny the truth of what was sworn. At her burial, her daughter (or whoever prepares her body) places her original Oath-Band on her; if she remarried, the band of her current marriage is laid on her chest.
A widow in black wearing her Oath-Band declares, in a form recognized by all Zeythari: I was found. I was wed. He is gone. I endure.

blocks.text: The Sisters of the Church: Oath-Claimed Attire

Every professed Sister of the Order — Seraphian, Solayan, Elaran, or Sophisran alike — is veiled, unringed, and wears no Oath-Band, her dress carrying no familial or marital marker whatsoever. In its place, the Church’s own habit proclaims institutional rather than household ownership. It is set by decree of the Archsworn and kept, diocese by diocese, as regional custom: a high-collared, sleeveless, solid one-piece dress of undyed grey-brown linen, its hem an inch above a laywoman’s, the shortest hem in the Commonwealth. The Church does not hide the women it holds. It shows them more fully than any master shows his own, because a woman wholly claimed is the plainest statement of the claim, and the Order holds her up as the living ideal of beauty ordered by submission (see The Roselight Circle, Section VI). Her upper arm is bare and unbanded, which declares as plainly as a wife’s Band that no household holds her. At each wrist she wears the Church’s cuff, a band of the same grey-brown cloth, which is the Church’s mark upon the arm. All five Houses share this cut; they are distinguished only by the veil and a thread at the collar and cuff.

rows.t: A small open flame, the hearth

blocks.text: Construction. One piece, one hem, no front closure. The collar stays high, the Church’s claim at the throat, but stands loose off the neck on an open-lace stand. The back-yoke is vented beneath the veil-fall, the underarm gusseted, the gores closed. The single hem and the absence of any front closure keep the habit raising as one piece, as the Confessor’s correction requires (see The Roselight Circle, Section VI, under Discipline of a Roselight Circle Sister).

The veil. The House veil rides a light split-reed frame off the head and shoulders, over an inner gauze sewn to the cap. The hair is wholly covered and the face veiled always. The weight follows the duty: in the ward and the childbed, fine boiled gauze changed after every case; in court, the Harmonist’s deepest veil; at a marriage, the Elaran Sister’s deep rose in double-gauze.

The Sister’s token. The Sister’s token is the Tier II mark of a professed Devota, issued by the Praesul and replaced on loss, as the priest’s stole is his. It is worn on a cord at the right hip or at the right collar-point, outside the habit and never on the skin. The left breast belongs to the rose badge, the left hip to the Lysaran cord, the upper arm to the Band, and the throat to the collars, so the token takes the right side. Like the stole it proves standing and powers nothing; the House is read in its device.
The convent selvedge. Each convent weaves a thread of its own into the selvedge of its cloth, so the convent reads at the hem and the cuff, where a laywoman’s household braid sits.

Regional turning. The sleeveless linen habit is the habit of the valleys, the plain, the seaboard, and the desert. In the Thaldrin, the Ashward and Duskhearth winter, the Threnwood cold, and the Sundral passes the Cold habit is worn: the same cut, collar, hem, and cuffs in undyed boiled wool, sleeved to the wrist, the cuff worn over the sleeve. The Praesul of each diocese sets the dates of the turning, at the Greening and the Gathering, and the whole convent changes cloth on one day. A Sister’s footwear and cloak follow the same ladder as a laywoman’s, with the Church as grantor: sandals as the standard, boots and the cloak in the Cold turn and in the field by lease.

No professed Sister wears a caerwevra; her hair is wholly covered by her House’s veil. To touch a professed Sister is not merely criminal under Commonwealth law. It is sacrilege; the prohibition binds the laity, and her Confessor, acting for the Church that holds her, is not bound by it. The professed Sister, a Devota and called a Handmaiden in common speech, occupies a distinct and inviolable category: she belongs to the Church alone, and her dress says so.
Voices of the Realm
Ordinary Commonwealth women are not, in practice, quietly impressed by extra cloth. They may respect a duchess without envying her wardrobe, and market conversation reflects it plainly:
“Pretty dress.” / “Pretty useless in an orchard.”
“That’s six months of cloth.” / “I’d rather buy another mule.”
“The Lady looks lovely.” / “Aye. Let her try loading fruit carts in it.”
“Look at Marta’s caerwevra. All silver.” / “Aye. Her master’s a better provider than mine.”
“Her cord’s worn thin.” / “Then it’s her master they’ll be talking about, not her.”
“Her master’s put her in boots.” / “Aye. Frost’s early.”
“Bare feet on the market road?” / “Either he’s corrected her or he can’t clothe her. Neither’s a thing to be proud of.”

None of this challenges noble authority; it simply reflects frontier practicality. The noblewoman, for her part, has an equally valid answer: “I manage three estates and five hundred workers. Why would I dress for harvesting pears?” She is not wrong. Her clothing reflects a different role, not a different standard of virtue, and the Commonwealth is entirely comfortable with both being true at once.
Legal Doctrine: No Ignorance Defense

Whether by veil, hem, Oath-Band, or sacred insignia, a Commonwealth woman’s standing is always visible in law as well as custom, and no court will entertain a claim of ignorance. Her dress is open to the Crown’s inspection at any hour: the Appraisers audit the veil, the caerwevra, the Oath-Band, and the hem at random, without notice or complaint (see Section II, The Bureau of Civic Decorum).
The veil warns. The band binds. The Oath endures.
Marriage: The Exchange of Covenant

Marriage is the Commonwealth’s central covenant, witnessed by Church and Crown, sealed by objects both spouses will carry for the rest of their lives. For a man, marriage is understood not as personal fulfillment but as an expansion of his oath obligations — the household he now leads is a second, living extension of the Oath he swore at Confirmation, not a private matter set apart from it.
The Three Daggers
A Zeythari man carries three daggers across his life. Each is distinct in meaning, and the progression marks the stages of his formation.

rows.t: Four inches, plain, serviceable. The dagger of preparation: you must now begin to think about what is coming
Age 16, on swearing the Oath of the Standard
The parish, a licensed smith engaged by his household, or, where his father kept faith, his father’s own retired Oath Dagger
Personal and significant, but inherited, not earned: the blade of a son at the threshold of a man’s life
His bride’s household: her labor, her father’s connections, her brother’s effort. She places it in his belt with her own hands

A family sacrifice: a smith engaged through her father’s contacts, hours of domestic labor converted into value, a brother’s time freely given. Her labor belongs to her household, so the gift is the household’s. It is the first object in his life that belongs entirely to him, given by no authority above him but by the one who will stand closest to him. Her hair is bound into the hilt that same day; he touches that lock every time he draws it

blocks.text: When he dies, the marriage dagger passes to his eldest son with the lock of his wife’s hair still inside. The son carries his father’s covenant until his own marriage, at which point he receives a blade of his own.
The Oath-Band

Prior to the wedding, the groom must provide the Oath-Band — one of the heaviest obligations of the entire marriage process. Traditionally he forges it himself, assists directly in its making, or commissions it through his own labor and sacrifice. The point is not luxury. The point is effort. A poor farmer’s plain iron Oath-Band, made by his own hand, is considered more honorable in the Commonwealth than a wealthy man’s extravagant band purchased outright, with no labor of his own in it at all. The band becomes proof that the man has invested something of himself into the covenant, forged of iron, ash-steel, silver, or gold according to his station, and engraved with the Flame sigil, the First Oath glyph, and the sworn-guardianship mark. A man who cannot provide the band cannot provide the protection it represents.
The First Band

The Oath-Band placed on a bride’s arm during her wedding vows is uniquely sacred, and is known in some provinces simply as the First Band. Later bands — silver, gold, jeweled, engraved, ceremonial — may follow across a marriage as the household’s fortunes allow, but they are replacements or adornments only. Only one band was ever placed upon her arm as the vows were actually sworn, and that band is never sold, never altered, never melted down, and never gifted away. A wife may wear a later band publicly for daily life; the First Band remains the true covenant token, and most women preserve it within a household shrine, a dowry chest, or a family reliquary rather than wearing it day to day. At her death it is retrieved and placed on her for burial.
“The second band is wealth. The first band is oath.”
The Oath Dagger’s Successor

A man carries the plain Oath Dagger he received at Confirmation until his marriage. His bride’s household — her own labor, her father’s connections, a brother’s effort — produces the marriage dagger that replaces it: a dagger belonging entirely to him, given by no authority above him but by the household that will stand closest to him from that day forward. A lock of his bride’s hair is bound into its hilt during the ceremony itself; he will touch that lock every time he draws the blade for the rest of his married life.

The retired Oath Dagger does not vanish. A father who kept faith with his own oath customarily passes it to his eldest son at that son’s own Confirmation — so that an old, well-carried Oath Dagger changing hands at a Confirmation Muster is, without a word said, a small public accounting of the father’s record.
The Ceremony

The marriage ceremony proceeds in a fixed order, and every element carries legal and spiritual weight. It is witnessed by a priest of the Sworn Flame before the couple’s households and invited witnesses. Its first six steps are the Church’s own Rite. An Elaran Sister attends throughout, standing behind the priest, veiled and silent. The Dagger and the hair-lock that follow are the Commonwealth’s custom, and no part of the Church’s Rite.

One — The Presentation. Her father, or whoever holds Darlorath over her, gives her in the fixed formula (Melora ta Vorasthry; Darlorath ta Kyrason). The Church solemnizes and does not give the bride, for it holds no title to her; it presents only a woman it already holds, such as a professed Sister married under the Suit of Redemption.

Two — The Husband’s Oath. The groom swears first, to keep and govern her as the Pattern ordains: to cherish, support, guide, and protect her, to provide for his household, and to bear his oath before Crown, Church, and Flame without flinching. The Commonwealth reads his oath as one of responsibility, and the Church reads it as the oath of the man who governs.

Three — The Bride’s Oath. The bride kneels and swears the only oath Commonwealth law will ever receive from a woman’s lips: to take him as master and husband; to obey, honor, and submit to him in all things lawful; to govern his household faithfully; and to bear her station with dignity before the gods and the realm. She may not swear before a court, vote, hold property in her own name, or stand as a citizen in her own right — yet this vow, which places her under her master’s Darlorath, Crown and Church receive with full solemnity, as the most consequential legal act she will ever perform. In theory either party may refuse; in practice marriages are arranged, and a refusal carries a lifelong stigma. After her oath of obedience and fidelity, she kisses her master’s feet and waits for him to lift her from her knees.

Four — The Unveiling, the Band, and the Covenant Covering. At his leisure, the groom raises his bride up to her knees. The groom’s own hand raises her maiden’s veil and removes it permanently. The veil represented girlhood, paternal protection, and familial guardianship; its removal signifies that stage has ended. He places the Oath-Band on her upper arm. Vow and gift arrive together; a Commonwealth priest would say the oath entered the band the moment it entered her arm. Her mother then gives into his hand the first caerwevra, made by the women of her household, and he sets it upon her hair: the hair covering appropriate to married women. She is not left unveiled. She is differently covered. From this day she wears the full veil only at Mass on Sundays and at formal sacramental occasions.
“The father’s veil falls. The wife’s covering remains.”
Five — The Seal. The priest seals the vow in Seraval and declares Darlorath Kyrason, confirming the marriage complete. Darlorath passes from father to master.
Six — The Departure. The groom leads her from the church, and she walks one pace behind him.

The Commonwealth’s Custom — The Marriage Dagger and the Hair-Lock. After the seal, the bride draws the marriage dagger her household provided and places it in her master’s belt with her own hands, arming him before she is fully standing. The gesture is deliberate: she gives from a position of giving, and rises having given it. “I give you this from a position of giving, and I rise having given it.” The priest witnesses it, and the groom binds a lock of the bride’s hair into the new dagger’s hilt with his own hands, completing the exchange.
Her veil was the promise of a future. The band is the proof of a present. The dagger is the weight of what he has sworn to carry.
Death and the Funeral Rite

In the Commonwealth, death is the closing of an account. A man who swears the Oath of the Standard at sixteen opens a covenant before Crown, Church, and gods; a woman who swears her marriage vows opens the only covenant the law will ever receive from her. The funeral is the moment at which the Church formally declares how that covenant was kept.

Funerals are community events of genuine weight: not only occasions for grief, but a public rendering of verdict, not legal judgment but social and spiritual accounting. The community that watched a man bear his oath gathers to hear whether he bore it well.

The priest’s declaration. At the graveside, after the prayers of mourning and before the burial is sealed, the presiding priest makes a formal declaration. These are not eulogies; they are formal pronouncements, spoken in the voice the Church uses to witness oaths and bless marriages. The covenant opened at sixteen, or at marriage, is now declared closed.

rows.t: A man who bore his oath faithfully
His oath has been discharged. He has earned honored rest with the Radiant King, Kairon.
A woman faithful to her marriage vow
She was faithful to her oath of marriage. She has found faithful rest with the Radiant Queen, Seraphiae.

blocks.text: The Church witnessed the beginning. The Church declares the end.
The passing of the dagger and the keeping of the band

rows.t: Drawn from the man’s belt by the priest and placed in the hands of his eldest son; the lock of the wife’s hair remains bound in the hilt. If his wife lives, she watches the blade she provided, which bore her hair, pass from her master’s hands to their son’s

Never passed to another. It was placed on her arm as her master swore his vows and belongs to that covenant alone. She wears it, or a later band in its place, until her own death. At her burial, her daughter (or whoever prepares her body) places her original Oath-Band on her; if she remarried, the band of her current marriage is laid on her chest. The covenant is completed, not unmade; she takes the proof of it into her rest

rows.t: A man who kept his household in order, served faithfully, and died honorably, in battle or in bed
A man who abandoned his family or lived in evident dishonor
Burial is not withheld, but the declaration is absent, and the community understands why
Most of ordinary life; the community must judge, imperfectly, as communities do. What lies beyond human sight belongs to Kairon and Seraphiae alone
