blocks.text: X. FOREIGN RELATIONS
Commonwealth commercial treaties are negotiated in accordance with the Trade Doctrine, balancing strategic openness with economic independence and the preservation of sovereign decision-making.
Major Allies

rows.t: Formal alliance sealed by dynastic marriage — Princess Ilyara Thessandrion of Zelesti, a Maenari, to the Satyrim-blooded King Alexi Karaya, whose union produced the current, first-generation Maestrai sovereign. Zeythari holds a citadel-city on Zelesti’s frontier, ceded as part of the marriage settlement, guarding the forest road; Zelesti itself is a five-million-strong Maenari (high-elf) forest realm, magic-rich and steel-poor, whose rangers, archers, and mages are without peer on the continent but who cannot match a legion for numbers or a smith’s forge for steel. Its mage tower teaches pure magical theory in the manner of the classics, a counterpart to the Commonwealth’s Arcana Scholium; the Magitek Arcaneum, the Commonwealth’s research-and-development engine, has no equivalent in Zelesti.

An uneasy trade alliance rather than a friendship — functional, mutually profitable, and shadowed by the standing theological rupture between the Church of the Sworn Flame and Kaeyria’s own Church of the First Oath. Kaeyria is a feudal fortress realm holding the mountain passes north of the Great Zelesti Dark, connecting through to the Aidionic Empire on the far side; it borders Zeythari’s northwest borderland directly.

blocks.text: Rivals / Enemies

rows.t: The Commonwealth’s major rival and the largest power on the continent — an ancient, slave-legioned imperial theocracy of some fifty million, expansionist by doctrine and untroubled by what it burns to take ground. Contested along the Shimmerwind Wastes frontier to Zeythari’s south, at sea along the shipping lanes out of Linhaven and Solmara, and, increasingly, against Zelesti from the far side of the Great Zelesti Dark.

The Throne descends from the Drazek tribes, human tribes that went north thousands of years ago, before the Commonwealth’s founding; it is a schism from the old worship of the human tribes, not from the Church. It rejects every deity but Varek, treats the worship of any female god as treason and heresy together, and enslaves all non-human peoples. Its expulsion of the Aelorian Maenari and their Lysaran Sisters founded the Aelorian Healing Complex (Section V).

blocks.text: The Financial Order

The Commonwealth is a signatory of the Ashfall Compact and a borrower from the Lockwright Reserve, a neutral financial nation-state on Ashfall Isle (see Section VIII). Its state-level trade with every power, hostile or allied, settles through the Reserve’s Tidemark network.
Visible Wonders
A foreign lord who crosses the border sees a realm that has already left his own century behind. What he does not see is the one thing the Commonwealth has built to be used only once.
What a foreign visitor sees

rows.t: What it looks like to an outsider
A train linking every major city and most of the citadel garrisons: the single most astonishing sight in the realm, and openly advertised as proof of the Commonwealth’s prosperity
Piped, aqueduct-fed, purified wells in every town (a tap in a private house is a rich man’s luxury)
Sewers and drains in the cities, and public bathhouses; a visitor from a feudal realm sees the absence of the plague-streets he knows at home
Ever-lamp lighting on the streets and in the halls
No horseless carriages, no engines on the roads: the Commonwealth is a realm of the older age in everything except the systems its engineers have built

blocks.text: The Cost of Wonder
Foreign visitors often mistake the Commonwealth’s railways for a sign that the realm has entered some new mechanical age. This is not so.

The rail network is not powered by coal, steam, or any common fuel. Each locomotive relies upon destruction-threaded arcana sustained either by trained mages or by carefully prepared blood-quartz crystals encoded with the required spellwork. Both are expensive. Neither is abundant.

The Commonwealth’s railways exist not because rail transport is cheap, but because the Crown, the Duraken engineers of Ironweave Works, and the Maenari arcane houses judged the immense cost worthwhile. Every mile of track represents years of engineering, magical labor, and political cooperation.

As a result, the network serves primarily as state infrastructure. Trains carry freight, mail, military supplies, officials, and strategic cargo. Passenger travel exists, but remains secondary. A foreign merchant marvels that the Commonwealth possesses railways at all. A Commonwealth treasurer knows precisely what they cost.
The rail system is therefore less a transportation service than a declaration of national capability: proof that the realm can sustain projects whose expense would ruin most kingdoms.
What a foreign visitor does not see
The Arcano Cannons

rows.t: Ironweave Works, the Duraken and Maenari engineering firm (“Ironweave”), under a standing Crown contract.
Twenty, to date; the allocation is classified, and one of them stands in the Zelesti citadel.
Huge, fixed engines mounted on citadels, crewed by small squads of mages clustered around them.
None. They have never been fired in war. The Crown’s standing order is that they are not fired except in a declared war, so even the Shimmerwind skirmishes are fought without them.

A foreigner who reaches a citadel wall may see a squad of mages gathered around a large mounted engine: unusual, but not evidently a weapon. The Magitek Arcaneum’s curriculum says only that “arcane weaponry” is taught.

Twenty engines in sixteen citadels; eight of the twenty-four citadels hold none. Ashward March: 6 engines in 5 citadels; Sundral: 5 in 4; Threnwood: 4 in 3; Zelesti: 1; the two Shimmerwind forts: 2; Hearthwall: 2 in 1.

About 26 Weaveblade to an engine: eighteen operators in three watches of six (Ritual Conclaves), four Spellwright Engineers, two Runebinders, and two Silencers, plus four Ordnance Technicians of the Auxiliaries. Total strength is approximately 520 Weaveblade and 80 technicians, about 6.5% of the Legion.

Each engine stands in a sealed, Crown-only precinct inside the citadel. Only career Weaveblade and Ordnance personnel enter; conscripts and Church brothers never do. The Ward-Yard answers to the commander of the Weaveblade Legion and the Warden of the Oath, not to the citadel Commander or the Castellan.
Officially a “resonance-ward battery.” Citadels already carry resonance-ward fortification and mage squads, so a cluster of mages at the wall draws no comment.

Ironweave test-fires every engine at its Duskhearth proving ground before mounting, using only its own staff; the Duraken insist on it. After mounting, crews drill dry on a low-draw crystal and never fire. The engines are land-mounted only; none is yet installed aboard a ship.
Anyone who serves in a citadel knows there is a walled yard of mages and a large covered engine, much as they know the rail and the clean water. Almost no one knows what it does.

blocks.text: Two names for one engine.

The Army calls it the Arcano Cannon. Ironweave, meticulous in its terms, calls it a Resonance engine, after the Weavefire term for the control spell that establishes the connection. The spell can join mage to mage, and in the crystals it joins crystal to crystal. Ironweave’s innovation was to offload that process into a crystal, which made it far more portable and usable by people who are not mages. The same word names Ironweave’s paired “resonance crystals,” whose whole function is that connection. Engineers correct the generals and the generals do not change: “It is a Resonance engine. Arcano is what the Army calls what it does not understand.” The divide is the usual one between those who build the thing and those who command it.
State Secrets
A Strategic Project

The Arcano Cannons were born from the same magical and engineering traditions that created the rail network. Like the railways, they are not products of mass manufacture, private enterprise, or common military procurement. Each engine incorporates rare materials, specialized spellcraft, custom engineering, and personnel whose training takes years. Their operation depends upon resources available only to the Commonwealth and its closest partners.

For this reason, the Arcano Cannons are not regarded as ordinary weapons. They are strategic assets. Responsibility for them lies not with local commanders but with the highest military authorities of the Commonwealth. Their numbers are limited, their locations classified, and their use restricted by standing Crown order. To foreign observers the railways are the Commonwealth’s greatest wonder. To the Warden of the Oath, the Arcano Cannons are simply another very expensive infrastructure project, one built for a contingency that the realm hopes never comes.
Ironweave’s other secret: the paired crystal
The crystal operation below is planned for the near future and has not yet been fielded; Section XIII is the projection of how it unfolds.

rows.t: A small resonance crystal, invented by the same firm, that carries the Resonance connection in the crystal itself, so that a carrier who is not a mage can use it, and speaks with a single paired crystal from up to 800 km away
Twelve in the world, six pairs, all currently in Ironweave’s vault. The Crown plans to issue one pair, the agent’s crystal and its twin at the Zelesti citadel; ten would remain in the vault

Planned: one field agent, a Maenari woman serving under a ten-year lease authorized by her father, the Admiral of the Navy, a stubborn Maenari lord, the twin to be held by her handler at the Zelesti citadel

Ironweave believes it can encode the pairing itself by voice harmonics, building on the voice-keyed valve of the inhibitor crystal, and a Maenari inventor leads the work. If it succeeds, the crystals could be made far more quickly. None has yet been made, and the present crystals are encoded by hand
To be set into the collar the Empire forces its enslaved women to wear, which the agent’s cover requires. The Empire’s own mark of bondage is the last thing an overseer would examine
By the carrier’s own voice alone, in a whisper, in a few phrases of Saelkyr, a language the Empire outlawed centuries ago. The agent is to be trained to use it only in isolation
Why the Empire is unlikely to notice

Aidionic mages are capable but have never seen such a device, and the Empire does not innovate: its magic is owned by the state and its doctrine leaves no room for a new kind of device, so a crystal that fits no category is likely to be read as something it already understands, not as something new. The crystal would sit in the collar of a Maenari woman, a class and sex their doctrine discounts as irrelevant. Saelkyr, outlawed there for centuries, is a tongue almost no one in the Empire would recognize, though anyone who heard it would know it was foreign. The Commonwealth is banking on timing: the secret has to outlast the invasion
Intended to give the Crown real-time intelligence from inside the Aidionic Empire, without couriers

blocks.text: How the secret is kept

rows.t: Citadels are military installations; foreigners are turned back at the outer gate. Duskhearth, where the engines are built, is a restricted district
Ironweave splits the work: casting hall, ward-work, and fire-control crews each know only their own part
Crews and citadel garrisons are under military vow (the Standing Wall’s confreres and brothers under their Vows of Muster); Ironweave’s engineers are bound by their craft-pacts and by Crown oath
The Church reviews all magical work; the Archsworn and the Warden of the Flame sanctioned the engines, which keeps the Church chain inside the secret rather than outside it
Mages on the walls are ordinary sights in the Commonwealth; the engines do not stand out from the wards
Heavy components travel by covered car on the Crown’s own rail lines
Disclosure is treason; the Magistracy hears such matters in a closed docket

blocks.text: The money

rows.t: A classified sub-line in the wall-forts and engines budget, about 100,000 Sol (10 million Zarims) a year, paid to Ironweave Works as a standing research-and-development contract
A closed session of a sworn subcommittee of the Joint Treasury Commission, with Magistracy review; the Assembly and Parliament vote the wall-forts figure as a whole
The Chancellery pays it through a sealed sub-account

Ironweave Works is a private research-and-development firm kept alive by Crown contract and subsidy. Its civilian revenue (steam-arcane systems, rolling stock, water works) is audited in the ordinary way by Concordance inspectors and its own auditors; its military sub-accounts are far less visible to the Assembly than a state office would be
The arrangement is lawful, but it sits at the edge of the Assembly’s control of the purse. It is a live constitutional question, and a political hook

blocks.text: Who knows

rows.t: The King and his Council; the Warden of the Oath; the Chancellor; the closed-session Commission members; Ironweave’s senior engineers; and, because the Church sanctions all magical work and the Order of the Standing Wall garrisons the citadels, the Archsworn and the Warden of the Flame
Citadel commanders (Crown and Standing Wall) and the engine crews
Zelesti: the Crown told its allies when a cannon was first mounted in the Zelesti citadel-city, the old dowry gift from the marriage settlement of ~1548 A.K.
Aidion, Kaeyria, and every other power; the Assembly at large; the public

blocks.text: Where the secret could leak
Zelesti’s front line. Aidion presses Zelesti from beyond the Great Zelesti Dark; a captured Zelesti officer is the likeliest leak.
Kaeyria’s possible alliance with Aidion (unproven; see Section XIII). A Kaeyrian lord who notices mages clustered around unusual engines is the visitor most likely to report them.

A discovered crystal. If Aidionic mages learned to read a paired crystal, the collar would expose both the agent and her handler. The protection is their contempt for the carrier and their ignorance of the device, and both fail if the collar is replaced, inspected, or taken, or if a whisper in a foreign tongue is overheard.

The Imperial Inquisitors. If a whisper were overheard, the Inquisitors would be called in. They would know the tongue was foreign, and a determined inquiry could trace it to Zeythari, whose Satyrim still keep Saelkyr as the tongue of temple and academy. It would be a high-risk operation, and she will know it.
A foreign-educated official or engineer with a source abroad.
The Lockwright facility. The Reserve knows a military buildup exists, though not what it consists of.
The first use. The secret expires the first time the cannons are fired in war.
The Policy of the Open March

Beyond the Ashward, Sundral, and Threnwood Marches lie two realms the Commonwealth has never annexed: the Margravate of and the Principality of . Each is feudal, each holds under a million subjects, and each keeps the Flame in the communion of the Sworn Flame. Parliament has declined to take either. Annexation would put their sixteen-year-olds under the Oath of the Standard, their households under Darlorath law, and their walls on the Crown’s ledger, and it would buy the Commonwealth nothing it does not already have. A faithful neighbor that holds its own frontier is the cheapest line the realm owns. Parliament’s name for this is the Open March: the two realms are left their sovereignty, and the Commonwealth is left its choice of war.
The Open March draws one line, and it falls between people and territory.

rows.t: Rescue of women and children taken by the Aidionic Empire or its raiders
Duty. Darlorath does not stop at a border or wait on a margrave’s leave. Rangers and the Warhost go, and the Hearthwatch follows.
Passage of Rangers and the Hearthwatch through either realm
Right, asserted by the Crown and tolerated by both courts
Defense of the realms’ own walls and levies
Discretion. The Commonwealth owes neither realm a garrison, a march, or a levy.
Parliament, with the Assembly funding any campaign
Direct invasion of the Great Dark of Zelesti
Treaty. The Marriage Settlement makes the alliance mandatory, and the Warhost marches at once.
Aidionic invasion of the Marches proper
Duty, as the realm’s own soil

blocks.text: The line is held on purpose. A man who swears the Oath of the Standard owes the women of the realm authority and protection, and so does the realm that rests on his oath. Neither realm has sworn anything, so the Commonwealth owes their lords nothing beyond what the Flame asks of any neighbor. But Parliament has never claimed that a Zeythari rescue waits on a foreign lord’s consent. When the Empire takes women, the Rangers cross the border, and whatever the margrave says of it afterward, he says to a realm that has already acted.

What follows an invasion of either realm is argued in Parliament, and the argument turns on cost: whether a feudal levy can hold, whether the Warhost risks men for walls it does not command, and whether the realms’ own lords will keep faith with a defense they did not pay for. The Chapter of the Watch is divided. The Hearthwatch and the Rangers press for action. The Standing Wall prefers a line it can see. The Church answers that a debate costs days the women taken do not have, and that is the argument the Archsworn brings to Parliament every time it sits on the matter.
Diplomatic Strategy

Defensively postured but not passive — the Commonwealth negotiates from a position of genuine military and economic strength, and treats its uneasy alliance with Kaeyria as leverage rather than dependency.

On matters the Crown and Church regard as settled — chiefly the standing question of Kaeyrian sanctuary-claimants professed into Zeythari’s convents — the Commonwealth has never once altered its position across three reigns, and states plainly that it is content to let the matter be resolved by whatever means the other party prefers, having never yet lost that argument by either force or law.

Zeythari’s spymasters read Kaeyria’s recent fortification of its own passes as defensive preparation against Aidionic pressure from the far side — the reasonable, institutional conclusion, and the one the Crown currently acts on.
XI. HISTORY
Founding

The realm began as a Satyrim frontier kingdom under House Marren, the Kingdom of Zeythar, ruled in the old tongue as Pākāra Rājyā and founded at Suraela by King Vaethar Marren I in Realm Year 1. For eighteen centuries House Marren held its Crown without a break, and the realm gathered peoples as it gathered borders: the Duraken of the Thaldrin, bound by the Thaldrin Compact; the Vykril of the Shimmerwind, by the Compact of 331; the Avesari of the Linhaven coast, from about 350; the Maenari of the Threnwood, from about 420. Five peoples stood under one Crown by the fifth century. The Maestrai were born of the Army of Light and the Great Compact of 738, and the Luminari of Satyrim and Avesari unions on the Linhaven coast; seated beside the five in the Great Parliament of the Seven, they made the seven peoples of the Commonwealth. The Shaelathi Veyrathi joined by petition in 1996–98 and the Rimborn by asylum in 1998, making nine.

The Commonwealth is the younger thing. When the male line of House Marren failed in 1743, Parliament, after nine years of regency and argument and without a battle, elected a Maenari lord, Aldric Karaya, to the throne. His dynasty has intermarried for some four centuries with the surviving Marren lines and is counted Satyrim by blood in all but name, though it remains, and is still called, House Karaya. The extinct royal house’s lines and lands were subsumed into House Karaya and the other Houses of the peerage; its descendants include the foremost Satyrim clan-lords in Parliament and the sitting Archsworn, who currently holds the Patriarchate as well. King Aldric proclaimed the Commonwealth in Realm Year 1780. Zeythar is therefore about two thousand years old, and the Commonwealth about two hundred and twenty.

A History of the Royal Commonwealth of Zeythari: Two Thousand Years is the companion volume. Where the two works differ on chronology, causation, or the names of events and persons, the History governs; where they differ on the present structure of the realm, this volume governs.
The Constitutional Settlement of Zeythari

Before 1780 Zeythar was a hereditary kingdom, first under House Marren and then under House Karaya, governed through a partnership of Crown, Church, and noble Houses. As the realm expanded, tensions emerged between the wealthy interior provinces and the distant frontier regions. The marches bore the burden of defending the realm against raiders, monsters, undead, and demonic incursions, yet many frontier lords believed their concerns were routinely ignored by the royal court in Suraela. King Aldric I had convened the Great Parliament of the Seven in 1768 to rebuild the realm’s constitution; for eleven years it argued the structure of the realm while the frontier’s defense stood unaddressed.

The crisis came in the autumn of 1779, when a powerful Vykril March Lord, frustrated by decades of neglect, forged an alliance with several influential Duraken clan-chiefs. Together they marched on the capital, not to overthrow the monarchy, but to compel it to recognize the interests of the frontier and the clans. After defeating loyalist forces, the coalition encircled Suraela and laid siege to the city, the Great Parliament still sitting inside the walls.

The siege lasted a month. Food shortages spread, disease followed, and civilian deaths mounted. Faced with the prospect of civil war and the collapse of the realm, King and rebels agreed to negotiations. Two weeks of deliberation produced what became known as the Constitutional Settlement, which the Great Parliament adopted that winter and the peoples of the realm swore before the First Standard at Ashward on the Day of the New Oath, in the spring of 1780.

The old Kingdom of Zeythar was formally dissolved and replaced by the Royal Commonwealth of Zeythari. The Crown was preserved, but its powers were defined and limited by a written Constitution. Parliament, once largely advisory, was elevated into a coequal governing institution with the authority to restrain the Crown. A new elected Assembly was created to represent the citizenry and to control taxation and public expenditure. The frontier marches received permanent representation and constitutional protections against future neglect: the Satraps lost their commands, and the frontier passed to Marshals appointed by the Crown.

No faction achieved complete victory. The Crown retained its dignity, military command, and central role in government. Parliament secured the rights of the great Houses and clans. The Assembly gave ordinary citizens a voice in governance. The Church remained an independent pillar of the Commonwealth while surrendering its former role in direct temporal rule.

The resulting system was neither monarchy nor republic, but a compromise between both: a Constitutional Dynastic Commonwealth, founded on the principle that no institution should ever again govern the realm alone. Two centuries later, the Commonwealth remains shaped by that settlement. Its constitution is still evolving, and many of its customs remain those of a kingdom adapting itself to constitutional rule. The Crown endures, but now reigns within a Commonwealth whose stability rests upon the hard-won balance forged outside the walls of Suraela.
The Three Eras
