“The Illuminated”: converted after the Vigil of 508; made the Living Flame the official faith in 512
Raised the Army of Light and presided at Kaelvash and the Great Compact
Flameward commander who led the Walk of the Standard in 893
Petitioned the Holy See for the regional church, authorized in 1603
Maestrai scholar whose Argument on the Nature of the Royal Line (1750) won Parliament for Aldric Karaya
First king of House Karaya; convened the Great Parliament; proclaimed the Commonwealth in 1780
Made the Zelesti alliance dynastic by his marriage (1948)

blocks.text: XII. SEASONS & FESTIVALS
Festivals of Daily Life

rows.t: The Confirmation Musters (popularly, the Festival of First Oaths)

Mass Confirmation and Oath of the Standard ceremonies held across every parish for that year’s confirmands; the year-class that swore four years earlier is discharged and seated as citizens; oath-songs performed throughout the realm; public feasts and military parades; popularly read as celebrating the founding of the Commonwealth. The morning belongs to oaths and to the girls’ Declaration of the Hearth; the evening belongs to the Presentation of the year’s sixteen-year-old girls
Harvest festival of the volcanic-valley wine trade, the Commonwealth’s largest secular civic celebration
Commemorates the night at Ashward; kept most solemnly by the Flameward and the Order of the Standing Wall
Honors the Emberborn of the Commonwealth: licensed public displays of Ember (Weave) and Luminari and Avesari aerial performances; recognition of Thornmaidens
Marks the completion of Zeylara; the one civic holiday observed identically, without variation, by all nine peoples
Duraken cultural festival celebrating the arrival of the Duraken refugees; forge-blessings and metalwork competitions; the Blessing of the Hammers
Honors the Satyrim’s ancestral homeland; commemorates the defenders who held the line; martial demonstrations (Vardeth); Crown Vigil ceremonies

blocks.text: Eight festivals of daily life follow below.

The great festivals of the Commonwealth belong to the Crown, the Church, or one of the nine peoples. These eight belong to the household, the village, the guild, and the road. Neither Crown nor Church proclaims them. Each parish steward fixes his own day within the season, and the Appraisers walk the feast-day streets as they walk any market-day. They honor the work that keeps the realm fed, lit, shod, and carried.

rows.t: Households, millers, bakers, the granary wardens

Each household bakes its first loaf from the rotated grain of the Royal Granaries, whose doors stand open for the day so that any man may see the stores. The wife bakes and the husband carries the first loaf to the parish table; the second loaf goes to the poor. A loaf costs a Thal, and on this day the bakers’ guild sells none, and gives
Carters, the Track Companies, rail crews, posting-house keepers

The roads are declared open. Each posting-house, about every 35 km, serves travellers a free meal and a mug of ale, and the keeper hangs a fresh ever-lamp. Locomotives are garlanded and run slow through the junctions; the semaphore towers fly their flags. The roadmenders’ names for the year are read at the first milestone

Every village shoots on its green. The men’s contests come first, for the Crown butts, and the Hearthguard’s yearly test follows on the same ground, before the village. It opens the season for small game. Wagers are taken in Thals. The winner’s guardian takes the prize
Summer, held at dawn and dusk against the heat
Wives and daughters of weaving, brewing, pottery, and orchard households; guild masters as judges

The household trades are shown under the guardian’s table and in his name: cloth, ale, ware, and fruit. The guild masters judge, and the prize and the sale are the guardian’s. It is the one day each year the whole village counts what its women make
Saltday and the Lighting of the Lights
Fishing villages, saltworks, smokehouses, the Office of Maritime Safety

The inshore boats are blessed and the first salt of the year is drawn. At dusk every lighthouse and beacon on the seaboard is lit in one hour, the Keeper at each light, or the Lamp Watch where the levy has taken him. The smokehouses feed the shore

Every child of six enters the parish school with a slate and a stick of chalk, the boys in one line and the girls in another, each at the hand of the father. The Priest writes the child’s name once on the slate, and the child writes it a second time beneath
Households, lamp-wrights, the parish, the Hearthguard where they keep a Lamp Round

The ever-lamps of the street and the hall are cleaned, and the crystals checked against the gauge. Each household lights its hearth-lamp from the parish lamp, carried home by the children. The Lamp Round is walked at dusk and the Weather Clerks hoist the storm signals
Winter, in the Thaldrin and the snowbound north
Miners’ households, the Track Companies, the Duraken guild-holds

The families wait at the pithead and the track-end with lamps through the shift change, and a hot meal is carried down to the men. The names of the miners and trackmen lost in the year are read. No man goes down or out on that night without his household’s lamp lit behind him

The sumptuary law holds on every feast-day. The hem, the veil, the caerwevra, and the Oath-Band are audited as on any other day, and an expectant woman wears her cord (Expectant Women: the Longer Hem)
Under the guardian, in his company or his named escort’s. The unescorted-woman rule is not suspended. A feast does not lift Article IX
A festival does not stand down a muster, a watch, or a Hearthguard activation. The Warden calls the Quiet Roll as any day
The household’s, or the parish’s. The Crown pays for none of them, and the Assembly has never been asked

blocks.text: Cultural Rituals

The Confirmation Rite (sacramental: the Oath of the Crowned for men, called the Vow of the Flame in Zeythari, and the Vow of the Faithful for women, in one rite) followed immediately by the civil Oath of the Standard for confirmed men, and by the Litany of the Veiled Rose and the public Declaration of the Hearth for confirmed women
The Divergence Knot and, where taken, the Thorned Rose — Avesari coming-of-age markings, tolerated as private custom rather than absorbed into Church rite
The Kaela-Velyr Thael and Vesyn-Syrael Kaer — Maenari communal and individual dance traditions, performed at bonding ceremonies and civic gatherings
XIII. THE LIVING ARTS
Martial and Performing Traditions of the Nine peoples
“The Commonwealth does not blend its peoples. It keeps what each does best and builds the house that needs all eight.”

Every one of the nine peoples entered the realm carrying an art: a way of using the body that its bodies, its gods, and its wars had taught it. The Commonwealth never replaced them. It standardized the instrument and left the tradition alone. A Reaver still fights as a Reaver, a Blademaster as his father taught him, and a Maenari girl still learns the wind-dance in her mother’s courtyard. What the Crown added is the frame: a common drill every confirmed man learns, a common dance every parish daughter learns, and a short list of posts where the old arts do work the realm needs done.
I. The Doctrine of the Arts
The Three Tiers

rows.t: The foundation every confirmed man carries out of service. The unarmed half is the Foundation’s Song of Kyrdryn Aethos: forty movements, four years, the same four years as the Oath of the Standard
Every confirmed man, of every people
The Civic School (basic military training, ages 10–16) and the year-class itself
The inherited men’s arts (Vardeth, Kyrdryn Aethos with Siralkaer Thyrn, Keth’draul, Kael Serathun, Vethrai Kael, the Pass-Hold), kept whole inside the Elite Corps
Men of the line that carries each art
Father to son; master to sponsored pupil. The Crown standardizes kit and command and never the art
The women’s arts and the dances: Thryss-Kaer Dryn, Velyrthryss Kaela, Shaekaer Vesyr, Vel’shara, the Long Hearth, the women’s forms of Kael Serathun and Vethrai Kael, and every dance in Section III
Women of the peoples that keep them
Mother to daughter, inside the household. In Crown service only by the Contract Roll or the Pairing Roll

blocks.text: The Five Rules

A man’s art is taught by men and enters service through the Oath. The Crown arms the Oath. It does not arm the lineage. A son is taught by his father. If the father is dead or gone, by the nearest kinsman of the father’s line; failing all of them, by his mother’s father, and the Crown’s roll records the exception and asks no more.

A woman’s art is taught by women and enters service by one of two doors: a maiden’s guardian signs the Contract Roll, or a husband holds the Warrant of the Pair. A wife never serves alone and never under another man’s command.

No art is taught outside its line against its own custom. Vardeth passes father to son and is never taught to a stranger. Siralkaer Thyrn is taught on the sponsorship of a House or a recognized teacher; for the Fangs, the Bloodwind Brotherhood stands as the recognized teacher. Keth’draul’s conditioning is built on the Vykril bone and is offered to no other body. What a custom permits to be shared is shared, and nothing else.
The Convention of the Household governs every woman’s art.

The Pattern is not amended. It is fenced. When the realm needs what a woman’s art can give and the law of Darlorath stands in the way, the Crown does not repeal the law. It draws a narrow instrument around the need, names it, and enrols no one it was not drawn for. The Contract Roll, the Warrant of the Ward, the Court indenture, and the Warrant of the Pair are one habit applied four times.
The Convention of the Household

In Commonwealth practice a woman carries implements, not arms. Arms belong to the Oath. The Maenari have always held that a woman’s hunting bow and hunting knife are not weapons. The Vykril wear the vel’keth as a work knife, explained by the day’s labor. A dance in a courtyard is a dance. The Crown took the convention into usage and never into statute: it does not ask what an implement was taught to do, and no man of any household names it. A woman’s art is therefore never an offense, never a rank, and never a boast. She is not praised for it and not punished for it. When raiders come and the men are gone, and the children are alive in the morning and the hold is standing, she did what was expected. The outcome is not told as a story.
II. The Ages of the Arts

The Commonwealth’s calendar of service was laid over the calendar of the arts, and the two fit better than anyone planned. Almost every tradition has its foundation complete by sixteen, and the Oath finds the young man trained.

rows.t: Satyrim sons begin Vardeth, the unarmed foundation
Satyrim daughters begin Eshara-Auria; parish school begins at six for every child
The parish school teaches every girl the Seraphian Dance
Maenari daughters begin archery (Velyrthryss Kaela, ages 7–10)
Maenari daughters begin Thryss-Kaer Dryn (ages 8–12); Vykril daughters begin Vel’shara
Civic School military training begins; Training Dagger at 12
Keth’draul full initiation; the Khor’vatha awakens
The Satyrim father gifts the vereth-blade
The Oath of the Standard; the Oath Dagger
Mandatory service: the Common Drill, the cohort
Contract Roll opens; eighteen is the lowest age at which a maiden may be wed; her father or guardian sets the age
The Contract Roll; the Wayfinder and Thornmaiden posts
Discharge; the Brotherhood selects; Vardeth specializes; the Duraken Kindling opens
The Bloodwind Brotherhood draws its men

blocks.text: III. The Nine peoples
The Maenari

The men: Kyrdryn Aethos and Siralkaer Thyrn. Every Maenari son learns Kyrdryn Aethos from seven or eight: stances, strikes, falls, breath. Blades come after eight or nine years, and Siralkaer Thyrn, the Twin Storm Dance, follows on sponsorship. About three in five of them reach it.

The Common Unarmed Course. The Foundation’s Song runs four years, and mandatory service runs four years. The Commonwealth set one against the other. A Maenari recruit swears the Oath with eight or nine years of Kyrdryn Aethos behind him. In the year-class he is the instructor, under a Fang non-commissioned officer, and the cohort learns the Song from the men who have already walked it. The Crown pays no master for the course. What the Song teaches is body mechanics and breath common to every man in a file. It is not the rest of the art, which a Maenari boy of a House may continue under sponsorship.

The Fangs (6,000). The realm’s fast blades and its teachers of the Song. Among the Fangs’ graduates, those the Prism marks Emberborn go to the Weaveblade Legion’s Arc-Lancers, where Siralkaer Thyrn’s thread techniques are trained beside the Silencers (250). The Velyr-Weaving that cuts a casting in the moment of its making is the Silencers’ second art.

The women: Thryss-Kaer Dryn, Velyrthryss Kaela, Shaekaer Vesyr. About ninety-five Maenari women in a hundred learn the wind-dance, from eight to twelve, in the courtyard before dawn, in a circle with the other women of the household. It is performed at weddings, births, and festivals as the Weaving Dance, seventy-two movements that every man in the room has watched since childhood and that none of them names as combat. Beneath it lies the whole of the art: the Eight Winds, throws, joint-breaks, and the multi-opponent footwork of the circle. Archery (Velyrthryss Kaela) is taught to two in five by their mothers, from seven. The Shaekaer Vesyr, the hidden blade, is kept by fewer than a hundred women in all Maenari lands. Its cover is the Dance of Seeming, twenty-eight movements that can be performed at any celebration without revealing what they are.

In service. The Shadowleaf Sentinels (4,000) take Velyrthryss Kaela. The stance, the breath, and the release carry from the bow to the arbalest, and the draw does not. Rampart Marksmaids are drawn from Maenari daughters who hold the Silent Storm, and Satyrim and Maestrai daughters are taken for the gift of the eye. Volley Crews count their fire in the Seraphian cadence, in the voices of the crew, and the crew’s mirrored timing is the dance’s. The wall-post is the bastion lord’s direction the art has always allowed. The Lifekeepers (4,500) hold the dawn circle of the hospital-works in the Kaela-Velyr Thael. The Shaekaer Vesyr is not enrolled. It is the quiet qualification of the Matron of the Rose: the wife who holds the wing from within has often danced the Seeming.
The dances: Kaela-Velyr Thael and Vesyn-Syrael Kaer.

Kaela-Velyr Thael, the Joyous Weaving Circle, is the Commonwealth’s civic dance. Its circles, spirals, and stars are danced at weddings, births, harvests, and festivals, to the harp, the flute, and the frame drum. In the Commonwealth the men’s circle and the women’s circle dance in turn in the same square on the same music, and the mixed forms of the Dominion are not danced here. They are kept by the Maen’varii. Three uses follow it:
The Vintage of Kaelvash. The largest secular celebration in the realm holds the largest dance: whole valleys dancing the Circle, harvest after harvest.

The Dawn Circle. The Ritual Conclaves (1,100) hold their practice in a dawn circle, facing east, men only. Velyr-Resonance, the near-telepathic coordination of a dancing circle, is what a large working asks of the men who share it. The Conclave’s mages are taught the Circle as their breath-drill, and the Lifekeepers keep the women’s.

The Oath-Song. At the Confirmation Musters the oaths of the young men are sung. Women’s voices carry the melody from the women’s side of the hall, perfect in pitch as their gift makes them, and the men lay the harmony beneath it. It is the Commonwealth’s one hymn that needs both sexes by design, and neither sex crosses to the other’s side.

Vesyn-Syrael Kaer, the Dance of Silk, is kept as the Threnwood households have always kept it: for family and invited guests, at weddings, in the celebration form: more coverage, brighter colors, the artistry of the veil and the turn. Teaching is private, mother to daughter. It is not offered for hire, because a woman under Darlorath does not contract and a fee would be her guardian’s. It is neither celebrated nor shamed. Some households forbid the radiant display of the Emberborn dancer as unseemly, and the Commonwealth leaves the decision with the household.

The Flame Displays. At the Festival of the Flame, licensed Emberborn dancers perform Lyraeth-Weaving: the light trails drawn in the air by the circle, visible to every observer and not only to the Emberborn. A guardian’s written consent and the Crown’s authorization are required, and the dancer must hold her License with her glyph struck, since a glyphed woman does not perform.
The Satyrim
The men: Vardeth. The Satyrim son’s sword is his father’s gift, taught from five and gifted at fifteen. The three paths are three posts.
Ekael, the Single Hand: the duelist, the judge, the ship’s captain.
Duorel, the Twin Hands: the shock, boarding, and palace-guard path, about three Blademasters in ten.

Tresael, the Integrated Weapons: spear, blade, shield, dagger, and the formations that join them. It is the one art in the Commonwealth that trains a man to command men of other arts. Its graduates fill the officer corps of the Standing Wall.

The Blademasters (5,500) are Vardeth under the Crown. A Blademaster’s vereth-blade is his father’s gift and stays outside the Crown’s inventory. The Crown holds his Oath Dagger and his rank, and the line holds the rest. Vardeth specializes around twenty, which is when service ends and the Brotherhood selects, so the Crown takes the man now the art asks him to choose a path.

The women. No Satyrim woman’s art is martial. A daughter inherits grace as a son inherits the blade: Eshara-Auria is the girl’s equivalent of the blade. Both train the same economy of motion, purpose, and control, one toward the sword and one toward beauty and devotion, and each passes down its own line, a son’s from his father and a daughter’s from her mother. The Satyrim teach them separately and do not teach either to be understood by the other sex. The Commonwealth does not try to make them counterparts in arms. It takes the daughter’s inheritance as a different instrument, and uses it where it is strongest.

The dance: Eshara-Auria, the Open Grace, called in the parish the Seraphian Dance. Every girl of the Commonwealth learns the Satyrim open dance: the Five Graces of invocation, blessing, joy, gathering, and closing bow (Orateth, Eshanel, Laetia, Kelena, Thareth). Among the Satyrim it is the girl’s equivalent of the blade, taught from age five or six by her mother and the women of her household. The Sisters of the Seraphian House teach it in the parish school to the daughters of all nine peoples, and the Satyrim mothers who taught it at home are the Handmaidens’ best allies. It is the Commonwealth’s common dance as Zeylara is its common tongue, the girls’ equivalent of the Common Drill. Both are the same economy of motion turned to different ends.

rows.t: Orateth, the opening stillness, danced by the Handmaiden as the girl is returned to her father
The feast that follows the lifting of the veil opens with Kelena, the year’s girls dancing in mirrored unison. The ceremony itself is unchanged

Eshanel, the blessing, danced by the bride with the women of her household in the open view of the fathers and husbands. Eighteen is the lowest age at which a maiden may be wed; her father or guardian sets the age
Eshara-Sanctum, the Covenant Dance, for the husband alone, behind sealed doors
The whole of the Five Graces, led by the Sisters
The schooling of bearing; see Section IV
The Five Graces in full, danced by Satyrim girls

blocks.text: The Covenant Dance: Eshara-Sanctum

Eshara-Sanctum, the Secret Grace, is the Satyrim bride’s offering to the husband she is betrothed to, and the Commonwealth counts it the fullest expression of the Fifth Sacrament that any people of the realm keeps. It is taught only to the betrothed woman, danced only for her husband once she is wed, and seen by no one else. The Church does not teach it, does not witness it, and does not record it. It recognizes it, as it recognizes the Pattern itself, by leaving it whole.

The wedding day. The Church rite is the transfer: the father hands over the daughter, the master raises her veil, sets the Oath-Band on her arm and the caerwevra on her hair, and she walks one pace behind. At the feast the bride dances the Eshanel with the women of her household, modestly and joyfully, in the open view of the fathers and husbands, with nothing in it of what the night will hold. Hours later, behind sealed doors, the same body and the same vocabulary are given the one meaning they were always being prepared to carry. The Commonwealth sets eighteen as the lowest age at which a daughter may be wed; the age itself is her father’s or guardian’s to set.

The instruction. It is given to the betrothed woman in the three months before the wedding, in absolute secrecy, by her mother or grandmother, or, where she has neither, by a Satyrim Sister of Seraphiae commended by her Handmaiden. It teaches the bride no new movement. Every isolation, wave, and descent is a form she has known since she could walk. The parish school taught them to her as devotion, the Handmaiden’s Hour as bearing, and the Presentation as grace. What the instruction adds is meaning: that this grace was never the community’s and is now given to one man for life. The Commonwealth’s schooling of its Satyrim daughters is, seen from the marriage chamber, a dozen years of preparation for a single night, and the Elaran Sister’s counsel in Beauty and Submission, which no bride may refuse, is the doctrine that the dance embodies.
The Seven Veils. The dance has seven stages, and the bride wears her veils to the first.

rows.t: She circles the seated husband, eyes lowered in respect
The first veil falls; she draws near
The second veil falls; her arms open like petals
The third veil falls; for the first time in the dance she lifts her eyes to his
The fourth veil falls; the rhythm quickens and the husband’s whip enters the dance as his hand
The fifth and sixth veils fall; he directs her where he will
The last veil falls; the dance ends at his feet or in his arms, and he claims her as his own

blocks.text: The husband keeps the drum, or the crack of the whip, as the dance’s pulse and directs its pace. The whip is braided with silk and small bells. It is the symbol of his authority in the chamber as the Oath-Band is on her arm, and it is never used to injure. Doors are sealed and the whole wing is cleared of servants.

The meaning. The Satyrim hold the dance to be Seraphiae’s gift of erotic grace and the divine glue of marriage: the wife’s surrender mirrors the soul’s devotion to Heaven, and the husband’s mastery mirrors Heaven’s authority over the soul. Each performance renews the covenant, and the Satyrim say that a wife who dances it with true devotion keeps her husband’s loyalty and desire and makes her body a living temple that only he may enter. The Church of the Sworn Flame, which teaches the Pattern as the order of Heaven, finds nothing in the dance to correct. A Commonwealth master’s authority is total from the moment the Priest speaks Darlorath Kyrason. In this one act the wife offers him, with joy, the whole of what he already holds.

The law of privacy. The dance is never performed for another’s eyes. A husband who lets family, servants, or guests witness it betrays his wife’s trust and the covenant, brings deep dishonor on her and on himself, and answers for it to the Magistracy as for any grave breach of a household’s honor. The dance is varied by the Satyrim’s regions: fluid and wave-like on the coast, fierce and athletic in the mountains, slow and trance-like on the plains. The Commonwealth keeps them all and ranks none.

Other wives. The Maestrai and Luminari daughters of Satyrim mothers inherit it as their mothers’ art. The Maenari wives of the Threnwood households keep the private form of the Dance of Silk for the husband, as Vesyn-Syrael Kaer’s oldest practice has always allowed. No private dance is recorded among the Duraken, Vykril, or Avesari wives, and the Church asks none of them for one. It asks Beauty and Submission of every bride, and a wife offers them as her people have taught her.
The Forbidden Dances

The Covenant Dance has two shadows, and the Commonwealth forbids both in the open. The Kingdom of Jyotirai does not: it tolerates the first and lawfully trades in the second. Kethghal and Therghal date from the five centuries in which the Kyrillic Empire of the Zheradim and the Zyssyn held the Satyrim in bondage, when captors took what the Satyrim held sacred and made it a spectacle: a dance performed before witnesses (Kethghal), or forced on a slave for the display of the man who owns her (Therghal). The Covenant Dance is the opposite in every particular. It is a wife’s free offering to the one man who holds her, under the sacrament, behind a sealed door, with no eye upon it but his.

The Subjugation is some sixty-five hundred years gone, and the Satyrim of the Commonwealth keep it as their people have always kept it: in the Remembrance, in the teaching of the Church, and in the Zhaorya, the living kin of that bondage whom the slavers’ markets still sell. The Satyrim who came to the frontier a thousand years ago, to join the older settlers of House Marren’s kingdom, brought their reason with them, and it is five lifetimes behind them and still named. When the old forms of the Subjugation began to surface again in the closed gatherings of the great houses of Jyotirai, the exiles accused the nobility of corrupting the Pattern. Their longevity, their wealth, and their long nearness to the Zheradim and Zyssyn states had made them soft where the Pattern required them hard. The Flame King offered exile in place of civil war, and was surprised at how many accepted. They do not hold the line between the Covenant and the slave-pit to be a matter of how much a woman submits. They hold it to be a matter of who stands over her, by what right, and who is permitted to watch. A lawful master, a sacrament, and a sealed door make a marriage. A collar, a crowd, and a man who wants a witness make a slave-pit. It is also why the Satyrim, of all the peoples of the realm, need no persuading of the Capture Rule. They know what the enemy does with the women he takes, because it was done to their own.

Neither dance is licensed, blessed, or performed in the open anywhere in the realm. Kethghal in public is vulgar and is fined against the man answerable for the woman who dances it; behind a man’s own door the Commonwealth does not police it, and his only limit is permanent harm. Therghal is still taught, quietly: in the back rooms of dealing-houses and traffickers’ halls, to the women who are made to dance it, by the men who profit from it. The Royal Rangers list the Seven Stages of Therghal in their manual of anti-slavery operations as the sign of a trafficker’s house, and a warded collar found at one is evidence of the slaving that the dated collar of a Court indenture is not.
The Duraken

The men: the Pass-Hold. The Duraken are defensive and attritional by temperament: they hold a pass and do not seek open war. The Pass-Hold is the art of holding a narrow place. It is fought with the tower shield, the maul, and the short pick, and its first discipline is the Receive: taking a charge on shield and bone. The Iron Bones are why a Siegewright can be thrown from a wall and stand. The art is built on that, and on its price.

The Quench. A Duraken feels pain hours late. After every engagement the men inspect each other, head to foot, by touch, before they eat or rest. A Duraken does not ask where he is hurt. His partner tells him. A man who skips the Quench is not punished. He is simply found, some hours later, standing in the pass with a cracked rib he was told nothing of.

The Kindling. From twenty a Duraken man may kindle once in a year: the blazing forged focus, perfect balance, and shock resistance that end in a delayed reckoning of every injury he suppressed. The Pass-Hold’s rule is that the Kindling is spent once a year at the one door that cannot be lost. Each Siegewright names his door at Hammer-Day, and the Crown posts a second man to hold it behind him while he pays the reckoning. It is the Relay of the Hymn again, in iron.

In service. The Siegewrights (5,000) are sappers, siege-train masters, stone-ward artisans, and the Tunnel-Cut Brigades, whose war is counter-mining: the gallery fight in the dark, where nothing can be flanked and everything is received. No Duraken serves afloat, because the Iron Bones sink.

The women: the Long Hearth. The Duraken woman is four to four and three-quarter feet tall, dense, with the same bones and the same late pain, and she is raised to be contained, deliberate, and unyielding. The Long Hearth has two halves. The Hold is close defense at the hearth-door and the stair, in the low planted stance of a body that cannot be lifted, with the hearth-iron, the tongs, and the bellows-pole. The Convention of the Household makes them implements. The Count is the war of the cellar: stores, water, fuel, and fire rationed so that a hold stays alive past the point where it should have fallen. The Crown’s siege-stores tables for the citadels were drawn from the guildwives’ hold-books, and the Quartermasters consult the guild-masters, who consult their wives.
The dances: the Anvil Round and the Banking. The Duraken have no dance of their own on file and a great deal of rhythm. The Commonwealth’s Hammer-Day gave it a form.

The Hammer-Count is the forge-rhythm every Duraken child learns at the anvil, and the Siegewright companies march, dig, haul, and brace to it. At Hammer-Day it becomes the Anvil Round. A ring of anvils, a man at each, the strikes passed around the ring in interlocked time, the stamp of boots on the beat. At its climax the guild-master’s voice calls the Ember’s Answer: the pitch that sets a blade ringing in the smith’s hand.

The Banking belongs to the women. At the Blessing of the Hammers a ring of women circles the forge-fire with the slow, breath-timed steps of a hearth being banked for the night. At the turn the first coal is carried from the woman’s hand to the man’s anvil. The fire passes from the Long Hearth to the forge, and the hammers are blessed after it.
The Vykril

The men: Keth’draul. Keth’draul is the Vykril art of the bone: the dense, scarred body turned into the wall. Drek’sol is the guard, Varakh the pressure, Keth’un the reading of the scars, Vrath’kel the Kill Tongue, the close-kill doctrine of bite, jaw-lock, and eye and ear work, taught last. Drek’voth is the art in cold stone, and Drek’sova, the Hymn, is the art in red.

The Relay of the Hymn. The Hymn buys thirty minutes at five times a man’s strength and costs one to two days of combat-ineffective collapse. The Crown therefore never sings a Reaver company without a second behind it. Companies sing in succession: one cracks the line, the next holds the breach, and the first falls back behind Shield Troops to recover. A Reaver who has not proven himself in Drek’voth for years is not released to the Hymn. The art amplifies what is already there. The Reavers (10,000), with the Blademasters and the Fangs, make up the Bloodwind Brotherhood (21,500).

The Fueled Hymn. A Reaver whose wife is in the field may take the Hymn in its fueled form: about seven times a man’s strength for about sixty minutes, with clarity kept. He brings her to pain and subspace by his own hand before the Hymn, and she is kept in a rear camp within hearing of it, about a quarter mile off. If she breaks from subspace the bonus ends at once and the base Hymn continues. The Commonwealth holds this to be a husband’s lawful management of what is his. The Crown does not regulate it, enrol the wife, or count it in the Relay’s planning figures.

The women: Vel’shara. Vel’shara is the Vykril woman’s art, taught by her mother from age eight, and it hides inside the day’s labor. Vel’kira is the knife, Nym’vel the scout’s and hunter’s art of silent running, tracking, and the unseen crossing, Kaen’vel the choosing and holding of ground, Mira’sheth the still mind and false compliance, Nesh’vel the last resort. Its doctrine is protection: every technique has a version, Vel’ura, that keeps her between the threat and what she guards. The hold is never undefended.

The Wayfinders (3,500) are Vel’shara on the Contract Roll, commanded by a Vykril man. Their branches follow the art: Sand-Knife Bands (Vel’kira), Silent Wardens who hold a chokepoint with minimal manpower (Kaen’vel), and Scouts (Nym’vel). Mira’sheth runs through every branch. Nesh’vel is not taught as a branch, and a Wayfinder who uses it has already failed.

The Warrant of Concealment. A Wayfinder’s contract carries the Warrant of Concealment: the guardian’s leave, given once and in writing, for her to wear the work-knife (vel’keth) at the hip or thigh and the wrist-spike (vel’dun) under the sleeve, in the darker cut of the Thornmaiden dress. The saber (shara’keth) is issued from the Wayfinder armory on a named operation and returned when it ends. The Warrant covers no other woman of the Roll.
The dances: Keth’sol, Sheth’kira, and Vera’sheth. The Vykril keep no dance of ceremony. They keep three of use.

Keth’sol, the Struck Wall. The men’s dance, danced in Drek’voth and never in the Hymn, because the Hymn is for killing and this is for remembering. A ring of men, forearm to forearm and shin to packed earth, strike bone on bone in the cadence of the Drek’sol guard until the ring sounds like a wall being beaten. Between rounds each man’s scars are read aloud, one by one, by the man beside him: the scar is the lesson. It is danced at Reaver regimental feasts, on the return from a hard march, and at the burial of a Keth’ra, when his initiates read his scars to the end.

Sheth’kira, the Still Dance. The women’s dance, danced at caravan halts and at weddings. Water-jars and loads on the shoulder and the head, a slow circle of carrying-steps, long stillnesses, and sudden turns in which nothing is spilled. The guests see grace. The men of the clan see the way a woman moves a heavy load while keeping her eyes on the room, and they do not say what else it is. The Wayfinders are drilled in it.

Vera’sheth, the Held Step. The Pair-Dance, danced by a husband and wife and by no one else, without music. A single drum is struck at intervals set by an elder; the pair meets each strike without word or glance, he planted and she moving about him, until the two read as one body in two. It shows the elders that his guard and her ground are drilled to each other. The Vykril do not take a pair on its vow alone: the pair is tried, as Zyri’s yielding to Varek is the pattern of every house, and the Vera’sheth is how the elders say so. A third dance exists, the survivor’s: danced alone, with the second place left empty in the circle, and no one else is permitted to see it.
The Avesari

The arts: Kael Serathun and Vethrai Kael. The Avesari keep two arts, divided by body and not by sex. Kael Serathun belongs to the Kaelii, the wingless three in four: the wide, low Rootform, the grip-strike that drives the claw and holds it, the tail as a third limb, the horn in the clinch. Vethrai Kael belongs to the Zerii, the winged quarter: never be where the strike lands, the stoop that turns altitude into velocity, the downbeat check at close range, and the Widow’s Descent that seizes a target and, with the release retained, removes a combatant from a fight without killing him. Avesari women practice both arts with the retractable claw, the false hand, and in the same grammar.

The Skyguard (8,000). The Zerii and the winged Luminari fly the Skyguard under Vethrai Kael. A candidate is passed by a Wind Trial, a mentor-and-student duel fought entirely in the air and ended only when one party is forced to land. The Luminari’s denser frame makes their stoop heavier and their feathered wing allows short hovers, and the Sunlancers fly to that strength.

The Rootform Cadres. Three in four Avesari men are wingless Kaelii, and the Skyguard has no place for them. Kael Serathun is the art of a body built to stand, and the Crown posts it where standing is the work: to the Shield Troops, where breach defense is the work; to the Marine Hearths and the Harbor Guard; and after eight years’ service to the Maidenward Oaths. The male ember-reflexes Korath-Heel, the ground rupture, and Zuthar-Claw, the armor-cracking strike, fall naturally to a planted stance. Where the Reavers crack an enemy line, the Rootform Cadres hold the breach behind them and cannot be moved from it.

The Farwings (2,000). Zerii and winged Luminari daughters on the Contract Roll, flown in escorted pairs with a Skyguard escort, never over enemy ground. Vethrai Kael reaches them as flight discipline: evasion, the break, the dive to cover. It is taught to a Farwing as the way not to be taken.

The dances. The Avesari spent a long time learning to speak without obeying, and the dances remember it. Their words are the softened forms of the Avesai (vraha for vrakh, kelta for qelth) so that the voice may call what the body will not do.

Tharun-sa, the Shared Sky. The Zerii pair-dance, danced in the air: two spirals, the catch and the release, the Widow’s Descent turned to an embrace. It is the display of an Avesari pair-bond, and the Zerii pair-bond is fierce enough that the loss of one shows in the other’s flight. A married pair dances it with the husband as escort, which is the Commonwealth’s rule for any wife in the air. Unmarried Farwings fly its escorted form. The Luminari dance it with the hover.

Ser-Kael, the Stone Round. The Kaelii dance, danced on bare earth: a ring of men, the stamp on the beat of Korath-Heel, the tail planted, the horns locked in the Thornlock by pairs at the turns. The callings are shouted in the softened tongue, and the ground rings and holds. The women dance it with the false hand shown at the turn, the claw coming out on the final beat. It is danced after a Combat Trial, at the pits, and at the Vintage.

Nai-Vraha, the Dark Round. The night dance, danced in total darkness in the last hours of the Vrath’kel, before the First Telling, and kept in the dark-halls the Crown built at Linhaven. The Avesari see by heat and by the eyeshine of the others. The hall sees only the eyes, a hundred lights turning in a ring. The Luminari, who see in both lights, are the only outsiders it admits.

The Ten Refrains. The women’s circle, ten figures named for the ten Fixed Manifestations: the Shadow Refrain, the Chain of Silence, the Grasp of Hollow Space, the Umbral Lance, the Echo Step, the Dissonance Field, the Nightcoil, the Abyssal Mirror, the Grave Whisper, and the Veil of Breaking. About one woman in ten ignites, and each of those shows her own manifestation in the dance’s climax: the dancer who vanishes from the circle’s eye, the one who blinks across the floor. The others dance the figure. The Grave Whisper is danced at funerary witness, to listen for the fading imprint of the dead. Casting under the Ten Refrains is licensed as any Ember display, with the guardian’s consent, and only by a licensed woman whose glyph is struck.
The Maestrai and the Luminari

The arts. A son is taught by his father, and the Maestrai and the Luminari are no exception, because the art comes down the father’s line. A Maestrai son of a Maenari father takes Kyrdryn Aethos; of a Satyrim father, Vardeth. A Luminari son takes Vardeth, Kael Serathun, or Vethrai Kael as his father’s line carried it. A Maestrai or Luminari father who is himself the fruit of both teaches what his own father taught him. The rare son with a dead father learns from his father’s kin, and failing them from his mother’s father.

A daughter learns her mother’s art as her mother’s people keep it. The Maestrai and the Luminari wives are the Commonwealth’s most various, and they hold their mothers’ arts in the household and carry them to the Roll or the Warrant by their mothers’ door.

In service. The Maestrai fill the officer corps by examination, and the best of the archers; Maestrai sons of the Satyrim line enter the Standing Wall as Tresael officers. The Luminari fly the Sunlancers, the Skyguard’s light-work, and the Lifewings (1,500), whose Creation is the Commonwealth’s healing in the air.

The Lantern Round. The Luminari dance by night at the Festival of the Flame. Their skin glows gold under strong feeling, and no will can extinguish it. A Luminari woman dancing the Lantern Round glows as the joy builds, and the dance cannot be faked or concealed. It is the one Commonwealth dance in which every watcher can see whether the dancer means it. Weddings among the Luminari are danced in it.
Veyrathi

The men: Ash'kirr, the Claw in the Ash, taught from age eight by senior males. Its pillars are Thar'kesh (the Drop), Veth'ur (the Seize), Kirr'an (the Long Claw), and Ash'vel (the Vanishing). The women: Sael'veth, the Quiet Mask, taught by mothers and elder women. Its pillars are Veth'ael (the Lash), Ilun'kir (the Needle Hand), Sael'ur (the Unseen Read), and Taen'vel (the Mask). Both begin with Sael, the Stillness. The challenge duel, Kirr'thal, remains clan custom among Shaelathi men. In the Oathguard the Veyrathi man carries Ash'kirr.
Rimborn

The Rimborn keep no martial art. Their men are formidable at evasion, endurance, and the defense of chosen ground, with the Still Step and the Warm Threshold. The art they carry is the Road Trial, and Vashrim, the shared speech with beasts. In the Oathguard the Rimborn man carries the Threshold Stance, the stillness and endurance the Guide-Companies use.
IV. Where the Arts Meet
The Pairing Roll: The Hold-Pairs

The Vykril hold that a husband-and-wife fight as two halves of one house: a husband trained in Drek’sol and a wife trained in Vel’kira do not fight the same way, and the covenant joins them. He receives what comes; she makes the ground costly, and when he sings the Hymn, her yielding raises his Clarity. A pair is worth more than a lone Reaver and costs less than one: the wife draws no pay. The Commonwealth saw that and fenced it.

rows.t: The Warrant of the Pair, issued by the Warden of the Oath on the husband’s petition and countersigned by the Commander of the Bloodwind Brotherhood. It enrols the pair on the Pairing Roll, which stands beside the Contract Roll outside the order of battle

A Reaver in good standing with eight years’ service and his wife, wed under full rite. Or a Reaver and his sworn oath-man, in which case no wife is in the field and the Brotherhood posts them together without a Warrant

The pair is tried, not assumed. The pair must have come through one engagement together, certified by their commander, and must dance the Vera’sheth before two Keth’ra of the clans, who declare the pair fit for the Roll

Whole with the husband. Nothing is transferred, leased, or contracted. She is not enrolled and bears no Crown rank. He carries her into the field as he carries his blade, and a wife stands under his Darlorath as a fully subordinate dependent, and he answers for her as he answers for his hearth and his blade

Orders go to the husband, who is the Pair’s only commander of record. She acts on the standing sanction he gives once, in the Warrant, and speaks in the Lowered Tongue to every man but him. No man other than her husband may correct her
None to her. The Crown pays the husband a Reaver’s pay and a stipend of two zarims a month for the keeping of his blade, which is the Thornmaiden rate

Hold and ward only: the chokepoint (Kaen’vel beside Drek’sol: she makes the ground costly and he receives what comes), the rear of a forward aid-post, caravan escort on the Shimmerwind track, and the defense of a post’s household quarter. Never in an assault, never on a sortie, never beyond hearing of the Hymn

A Half-Oath of the Maidenward is attached to every four pairs and holds her extraction under the Order of Response. If the husband falls, the Warrant lapses on the field and she is carried out before the line breaks
About six hundred pairs, drawn from the Reavers and the Shimmerwind clans
Varek, patron of the standing watch, and Zyri, the Yielding Lady, whose yielding to him is the pattern of the house. Each post keeps a small shrine

blocks.text: The Hold-Pairs are the only place in the Warhost where the law of Darlorath, the doctrine of the Vykril, and the interest of the Crown want the same thing.
The Handmaiden’s Hour

Every Thornmaiden posting keeps an hour a day under the Handmaiden of House Elaran and the Matron of the Rose. The Rosewarden’s ledger records it as deportment, and it is that. The Handmaiden teaches the Seraphian Dance as the schooling of bearing: the walk, the stillness, the lowered eyes, the unhurried carriage of Article IX learned as a dance before it is worn as a habit. Behind the bearing the Hour holds the capture-denial of the hearth.

The Capture Rule gives the reason. Aidion, Kaeyria, and the Ritebound Throne enslave captured women, and the Maidenward carries a maiden from the field before she can be taken. The Hour is what she has if the Oath is broken, the Sentinel is down, and the Carry cannot be made. The Maenari maiden gives the cohort the Eight Winds (the pushing palm, the rising strike, the turn that breaks a grip), and every Thornmaiden learns the few joint-breaks and disengagements of Nesh’vel whose only purpose is a half-second of separation, enough to break a hold and reach the gate. It is not war. It is the hearth’s last door.
No man observes the Hour. The Matron grades it, and the Commander’s report says only that deportment is satisfactory.
The Wing and the Gate

The Maidenward holds the wing gate from outside. The Matron of the Rose holds the wing from inside. The Commander’s wife, or a widow serving with her guardian’s consent, takes the post. A Commander whose wife keeps Vel’shara, the wind-dance, or the Long Hearth has the wing held from within, and says nothing of why.
Wives and Widows: Household Defense
A woman who has married has left the Roll and cannot return to it. Her art is her household’s, and the household’s defense is not service.

rows.t: Thryss-Kaer Dryn, near-universal; Velyrthryss Kaela with her husband’s leave; Shaekaer Vesyr rarely and quietly
The household when the men are summoned to the levies; the bastion, under the lord’s direction
Vel’shara with Vel’ura, the ward. A Reaver’s wife of the Pairing Roll is the one who goes to the post
The clan hold; the post household quarter
The false hand; for the Zerii wife, Vethrai Kael
No fighting art. Her defense is her husband’s interposition and her own Lumen Sanandi, with Miracle Healing where she is gifted and trained
The Long Hearth: the Hold at the door, and the Count in the cellar
The guild-hall, the pass; the citadel’s stores
The art of her mother’s people
As above. A Luminari mother defending her children defers to no one

blocks.text: The Ninefold File

The Oathguard (1,800) are drawn in equal measure from all nine peoples. Their unit is the Ninefold File: nine men, one of each people, about 257 files with the remainder on the Captain’s staff. A file is posted as a file and trained as a file, and no file holds two men of one people. The Maenari carries the Song, the Satyrim the Judge’s Stance, the Vykril the bone guard, the Avesari the stoop or the Rootform, the Duraken the Receive, and the Maestrai and Luminari cross between. The Oathguard is the one body in the Warhost where every art stands within arm’s reach of every other.
The Five Watches

The Vigil of the Standard keeps the night at the Ashward palisade, where, as the liturgy retells a night that in fact belonged to a single Satyrim garrison, five soldiers of the five peoples held a collapsing wall until dawn. The Flameward and the Standing Wall keep it in five watches. Each watch belongs to one of the five peoples, whose men stand the wall in the stillness of their art: the Maenari in the Post Stance of Kyrdryn Aethos, the Satyrim in the Judge’s Stance, the Duraken in the Receive, the Vykril in the Drek’sol guard, the Avesari in the Rootform. There is no dance, no music, and no word. The dawn watch belongs to the Maestrai and the Luminari, whom the five peoples made.
V. The Calendar of the Arts

rows.t: The year-class drills the Foundation’s Song before the parish; the discharged class stands as instructors. Fathers who kept faith pass the retired Oath Dagger to their sons
The Oath-Song at the oaths. At evening the Seraphian Dance (Kelena) opens the feast, and the Circle follows. Reaver regiments hold Keth’sol at their discharge feasts
None. The day belongs to Zeylara and is kept identically by all nine peoples
Skyguard stoop-formations; the Wind Trial flown for the crowd; Sunlancer light-work
Recognition of the Thornmaidens; the Farwings’ escorted pair-flights over the display ground
Licensed Lyraeth-Weaving by Emberborn dancers; Tharun-sa by married pairs with the husband as escort; the Lantern Round by night
Pit contests: Kael Serathun, with the Thornlock horn-lock as a trial of will; Kyrdryn Aethos breaking practice, wood to clay to stone; Siralkaer Thyrn displays under the blade-whistle
The mass harvest Circle; Ser-Kael, the Stone Round
The Blessing of the Hammers; each Siegewright names his door; Siegewright and guild trials
The Anvil Round; the women’s Banking
The Five Watches. Kept solemnly by the Flameward and the Standing Wall. No display
Vardeth demonstrated as the three paths in their old argument: the Single Hand, the Twin Hands, the Integrated Weapons, each answering the other’s challenge
The Seraphian Dance by Satyrim girls

blocks.text: The Linhaven dark-halls hold the Nai-Vraha and the Ten Refrains privately, in the Avesari’s season, for the Avesari and their invited kin.
VI. Summary of Standing Institutions

rows.t: Maenari recruits and Fang NCOs, under year-class corporals
Their guild-masters and the Siege Command
Kaelii conscripts in Shield Troops, Marine Hearths, Harbor Guard
The guardian, who signs it, and the Wayfinder commander
Keth’draul and Vel’shara; the fueled Hymn; the Vera’sheth
The Warden of the Oath; the Commander of the Brotherhood. The husband is commander of record
The Handmaiden of House Elaran, with the Matron of the Rose
The Matron; the Rosewarden’s ledger records deportment only
The Ritual Conclaves; the Lifekeepers’ hospital-works
The Legion’s command; the Sisters of Light
The stillness of the five founding arts
The Flameward and the Standing Wall
The Sisters of the Seraphian House
The wife and her husband, no institution
The Covenant alone; the Magistracy answers a breach of its privacy

blocks.text: XIV. INTERNAL CONFLICTS
Political Tensions

The Crown commands the Crown Regulars outright. It commands the Oathguard openly, but does not own it: the men swear to the Commonwealth, the Assembly pays them, Parliament holds the charter, and the corps cannot be dissolved except by the Assembly, then Parliament, then the Crown. The three orders of the Sworn Flame swear their perpetual muster to the Archsworn and the Warden of the Flame instead, a deliberate architectural separation rather than a rivalry: the same design logic that bars a professed brother from holding independent land, so that no arm of the Church becomes a rival center of loyalty to either the Crown or the Patriarchate itself. The sitting Archsworn, Patriarch Ordwin Kaelveth, is on record as colder toward the military orders than his immediate predecessors, on the settled doctrinal ground that a Church built on the worth of a man’s word cannot be seen to favor its sword-arm over its altar.

The King’s Reckoning is the sharpest live contest of the reign. King Theron’s decree suspending title-based precedence and abolishing the sale of commissions stands by executive authority alone; Parliament has been openly challenged to make it permanent law and has not yet done so. Its claimed reach into the rank structure of the three Church military orders is contested outright — the Warden of the Flame and the Archsworn have not conceded that a royal decree binds an internal precedence the Church has always governed for itself, and compliance among the orders is uneven rather than settled. Nothing about this dispute touches the Commonwealth’s underlying unity; it is a fight over where authority over the military sits, conducted entirely within a shared framework neither side disputes, not a fight over whether the Commonwealth itself holds together.

The Ward-Yards. The Crown holds sealed, Crown-only precincts inside citadels that the Order of the Standing Wall garrisons, and the Castellan holds the gate but not the key. The Chapter of the Watch has noticed, has not been told why, and has not yet made an issue of it. The grievance sits beside the King’s Reckoning and will inflame it if the Reckoning’s reach into the three orders is ever forced.

Parliament’s absolute veto over Assembly legislation is a structural check on the elected chamber’s control of taxation, by design rather than by accident — the peerage’s price for accepting a lower house elected on universal male suffrage in the first place.

The Rimborn Exception. The Bureau of Weavefire regulates every working a woman can make except the one a Rimborn woman can call down, and the Bureau has said so plainly to the Assembly. The Church is uneasy that Caedron’s gifts reach a woman’s household without a Circuit to close, and Praesuls of the Threnwood have raised it. The Exception has held because the Rimborn are few, because their gifts do not come before adulthood, and because the Commonwealth has relied on surety and on the Silence instead of pretending to a device. If the Rimborn grow, it is the first clause Parliament will be asked to revisit.
Social Pressures

None of the nine peoples’ inherited customs sit in real tension with Commonwealth civil law on the question of women and property. Where a people’s own tradition differs in emphasis — the Maenari’s daughter-led eldercare duty, the Duraken woman’s proof through sustained endurance rather than a man’s through decisive action, the Avesari’s engineered predisposition toward chosen alignment, the Luminari’s inheritance of both, the Rimborn's hold-tended childrearing, in which the whole hold tends every child under the father's authority— the difference is one of local expression, not of underlying submission to Darlorath, which every one of the nine peoples holds as biologically or doctrinally settled rather than merely imposed. The Commonwealth’s genuine social pressures lie elsewhere — chiefly demographic and economic strain along the frontier marches, not in any contest over the household order.

Indenture. The indenture of daughters is the oldest bound labor law the Commonwealth keeps. It stays because abolition would leave catastrophic debts with no remedy short of ruin. The Court’s order, the father’s recorded shame, the dated collar, and the Indenture Fee are how the Commonwealth is making it unprofitable and shameful before it makes it unlawful. Raising the fee is a standing item before the Assembly’s Treasury Office.
XV. THE COMING STORM

Everything below is projected forward from the present day. Theron Karaya is the sitting King; none of this has happened yet, save the King’s citadel order, which has already been issued. Kept here as projection, not settled history.

The succession. King Theron completes as much of his military consolidation (the King’s Reckoning) as his reign allows; within a year he leaves a banquet saying only that he does not feel well, and is dead by morning, the work unfinished — the “one Crown, one Marshal, one command” ambition still incomplete. Asyre Karaya, his son, who wed a daughter of the Maenari peerage house of Loravae, ascends the throne young, at age 25. The Commonwealth suspects poison and accuses the Aidionic Empire; the accusation opens the coming conflict.

The Ritebound invasion. Within two years of Asyre’s accession, the Ritebound Throne — having recently suffered a hardening internal ideological coup, and now led by a human war-leader of about forty who has bound its quarreling holds into a single host — invades across the Ashward March, explicitly to test the “half-breed king.” The Commonwealth has watched the old passes for centuries and expects raids and probes; it does not expect an army. Over years of winters, the Throne’s enslaved labor gangs have cut two roads through the Thaldrin Ranges, each worked from the Ritebound side and each left closed behind a standing ridge until the last season. One road is built to be seen and the other is built not to be. The first, a scar a kilometer wide, comes out high above Linhaven, and its plug is blown open in full view of the coast. The second, wide enough for artillery trains and heavy horse, comes out in the foothills above Duskhearth, beside and behind the wall-forts rather than in front of them. Some 100,000 fanatics are committed in all — infantry, siege artillery, heavy cavalry, and war-priests working the miracles of Varek — and the greater part of them wait on the second road.

The feint at Linhaven. The war-leader reads the Commonwealth correctly. Linhaven is a city of 380,000 at the mouth of the Ashvael, where the freight of the plain and the ore of the Thaldrin reach open water, and the Royal Shipyards at Keelhold lie 90 km up the same coast. The Throne enslaves captured women, and no Commonwealth government can leave a city of that size, and every woman in it, to that fate. The column on the first road is real, strong enough to take the port if it is not answered, and the Warden of the Oath answers it. The capital’s reserve goes east at once on the Linhaven Line, some fourteen hours by loaded military train. The Oath Line to Duskhearth is five hours from Suraela by express, and the army that might have held it is on the other spoke when the second road opens.

The wall-forts were built to turn raids and delay probes, and the March’s garrisons have held the line like a dam for centuries. Neither was ever planned against a force of this size, and the first weeks go badly. With the capital’s reserve committed to Linhaven, the forts are bypassed or taken from behind, and Ashward falls. The thrust above Duskhearth puts Ironweave Works, its proving ground, the forges of the guild-hold, the head of the Ashvael Cargo-way, and the northern end of the Oath Line within the invaders’ reach. The Cargo-way is cut at its head, and the army at Linhaven is severed from the north except through Suraela. The Ironweave engines stay silent, because the Commonwealth will not spend its one hidden advantage to save a district. Some 20,000 civilians of the March are carried off into the Throne before Ashward is retaken, and their fate shapes the end of the war. The Throne’s zealots threaten to burn the women and children alive, and the threat poisons every attempt at terms; it takes the Royal Army to convince them, in the old way, by brute force. The Royal Rangers carry out the war’s great rescue, striking deep and freeing a massive labor camp. Many of the women, however, were already distributed across the Throne’s holds and are the hardest to reach. King Asyre refuses any terms that do not return the women and children, and that demand becomes the political crux of the peace.

Ashward is retaken only after a hard campaign that decimates the Throne, and its surrender is what finally frees the main army to turn on the Empire. This is the moment Theron’s unfinished reforms are proven or broken in the field, under his son.

The Aidionic push into Zelesti. In the same window, the Aidionic Empire drives first into the Great Zelesti Dark itself, and then out of it into the Forest Realm of Zelesti — three full legions, unconcerned with burning the forest to ash to take it. Zelesti’s rangers, archers, and mages are without peer, but cannot stand alone against legion numbers and Aidionic disregard for the ground itself. The citadel-city ceded at Alexi’s marriage finally earns its keep, and the Commonwealth’s fortification of Zelesti, begun by the King’s order below, is tested in earnest.

The citadel order (already issued). A Maenari field agent, a woman serving the Crown under a ten-year lease authorized by her father, the Admiral of the Navy, a stubborn Maenari lord, who answers for her as her guardian, has spent six months inside the Aidionic Empire and believes, strongly, that the Empire will invade through the Great Zelesti Dark. Her commander disagrees. King Theron splits the difference: he orders the Zelesti citadel fully provisioned and fully staffed, with every repair completed, to stand “at full posture within the year.” He acts unilaterally, as supreme commander of the armed forces, and cleanly: the garrison is already appropriated (voted by the Assembly and assented by Parliament), so he is spending no new money and seeking no new law. His words are matter-of-fact: the money has already been appropriated; do it quicker.

The agent returns to the Empire. The King then asks her to go back and confirm her theory. He gives her a paired resonance crystal, invented by Ironweave Works, which built the cannons, to be set in the collar her cover requires. It speaks with its single twin from 800 km away, and wakes only to her own whispered voice, in a few phrases of Saelkyr, a language the Empire outlawed centuries ago, which she is trained to use only in isolation. The operation is high-risk, and she knows it: the Commonwealth is banking on timing. Only a dozen such crystals exist in the world, and ten of them are still in Ironweave’s vault. Her handler is stationed at the Zelesti citadel with orders to carry any report straight to the King, bypassing the ordinary chain of command, including the commander who disagreed with her.

The Arcano Cannons. Twelve years mounted, twenty deployed, none ever fired in war. When the Aidionic legions reach the Zelesti citadel, its cannon speaks in war for the first time, and the secret ends. Every Aidionic survivor, and every Kaeyrian watcher, learns what the Commonwealth built. Whether the surprise wins the first battle or only costs the Commonwealth its one hidden advantage is left open.

Kaeyria’s betrayal. Kaeyria has secretly allied with Aidion, promised the Zeythari crown once Aidion prevails — a promise the Emperor has no intention of honoring. Asyre’s spymaster reads Kaeyria’s fortification of its own passes as defensive posture against Aidion; a single field agent, a woman, disagrees, and believes Kaeyria intends to march into the Borderlands rather than merely hold them. She is right. The Ritebound invasion lands before the disagreement is resolved.

Asyre and the King of Kaeyria. The two knew each other at Harborlight University. Asyre repeatedly bested him in open debate over Kaeyria’s chattel slavery, a practice the Commonwealth despises and Kaeyria defends. The rivalry is personal on the Kaeyrian king’s side, not merely dynastic.

The shape of the war. Asyre inherits a three-front continental war — Ritebound Throne from the north, Aidion into Zelesti from the west, and a Kaeyrian betrayal still unproven when it lands — fought with the professionalized, increasingly unified military his father spent a reign building. The war becomes the proof of that reform, not evidence that the reform was already finished generations before.
XVI. WHAT MAKES ZEYTHARI DISTINCTIVE
A Commonwealth Forged in Fire and Oath
Constitutional Commonwealth Under Oath
The Crown governs but does not rule unchecked.
Parliament restrains, the Assembly funds, and the Church binds.
The Magistracy judges independently, and any male citizen may bring suit against any office, including the Crown.
Authority is divided so that no single institution may stand alone.
Unity Through Oath Rather Than Blood
Nine peoples share one Commonwealth without abandoning their ancestral identities.
Citizenship is earned through service, not inherited through lineage.
Parish schools, the Oath of the Standard, and mixed-cohort military service deliberately forge a common civic identity.
A citizen is not defined by what people bore him, but by the oath he keeps.
Service as the Price of Citizenship
Political participation, property ownership, and public office follow service to the Commonwealth.
Every male citizen owes labor, discipline, and sacrifice before receiving civic privileges.
Rights and obligations are understood as inseparable.
Citizenship is not granted; it is earned.
A Civilization Built for Endurance
Nineteen centuries of frontier pressure shaped every institution of the realm.
Defensive warfare, professional soldiery, reserve service, fortified borders, and civic cohesion are treated as necessities rather than virtues.
The Commonwealth seeks not conquest but survival.
Its greatest achievement is not victory in a single war, but continuity across generations.
Integration Without Assimilation
The ancestral languages, customs, and traditions of the nine peoples remain alive.
Zeylara provides a common civic tongue without erasing older identities.
The Commonwealth does not demand sameness; it demands loyalty.
Diversity is preserved at the hearth while unity is forged in law, service, and oath.
Pragmatism Without Cynicism
Zeythari prefers principle, but it was built on a hostile frontier and does not confuse principle with self-destruction.
The Crown, Parliament, and Church regularly compromise in order to preserve the realm.
Survival is treated as a moral responsibility rather than an excuse.
Idealism is respected; endurance is required.
The Oath Endures

For two thousand years the peoples of the realm — one at the founding, five by the fifth century, seven since 1780 — have shared one banner and one law, and for the last two centuries one Commonwealth. They have survived invasion, schism, political struggle, and the pressures of a dangerous frontier. They have done so not because they became one people by blood, nor because they eliminated every difference among themselves, but because they built institutions strong enough to bind those differences into a common purpose.
In the Commonwealth’s own understanding, this is its great achievement: not perfect justice, not perfect unity, and not perfect peace, but permanence.
What a man swears at sixteen, he owes at sixty.
By Truth We Stand. By Oath We Endure.

This is Zeythari: a realm where nine peoples remain themselves, yet stand together; where citizenship is earned through service; where authority is balanced by obligation; and where the survival of the Commonwealth is entrusted, generation after generation, to the keeping of the oath.
